Catholic School Parents
AUSTRALIA

CATHOLIC SCHOOL PARENTS AUSTRALIA

SUBMISSION

INQUIRY INTO SCHOOL REFUSAL
The Senate Education and Employment References Committee

8 December 2022

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 30































 Catholic School Parents Australia (CSPA)

Submission to Inquiry into school refusal.

INTRODUCTION
Catholic School Parents Australia is recognised as the national body representing and
advocating for the parents and carers of 785,585 children and young people who attend the
1,755 Catholic schools across Australia.  CSPA works in collaboration and consultation with the
National Catholic Education Commission (NCEC), the Australian Catholic Primary Principals’
Association and Catholic Secondary Principals Australia, and is recognised in our national role
by the Australian Catholic Bishops Conference through the Bishops Commission for Catholic
Education.

Catholic School Parents Australia (CSPA) welcomes the opportunity to make a submission to
the inquiry into school refusal, particularly given the perceived extent of ’school refusal’ across
all school sectors including our own.

CSPA COMMENT
This submission is greatly informed through stories from Catholic schools, as shared by our
CSPA chair from her work in visiting schools and talking with parents.  Evidence is also shared
from CSPA’s 2022 national, Catholic school parent/carer views survey and follow-up forums on
student wellbeing and learning.

The following comments fall largely under a) the increasing number since the COVID-19
pandemic, of young people and their families who are experiencing school refusal and e) any
other related matters from the terms of reference.

i.

ii.

iii.

School refusal is happening as early as year three, but is a greater problem in high
schools. The CSPA chair has talked to parents in most states who have a child who is
refusing to attend school. In all those cases, parents are concerned, but also at a loss to
explain ‘why’ their child is refusing. Hopefully this inquiry offers the opportunity to find
those answers, allowing parents and schools to work together to address the problem.

School leaders have seen an increase in ’school refusal’ since the pandemic. Students,
who undertook remote learning, refused to attend school, when it resumed outside
home. But the problem was also climbing before the pandemic hit and that is an
important point not covered in the terms of reference, as explained below.

CSPA welcomes the terms of reference, however hopes they could be extended under
‘e’ which stipulates the committee will look at “any other related matters’’, two of
which include:

  Any other impetus, apart from the pandemic, behind this trend.
  And secondly, other research has found that up to 100,000 children are not in

the school system - they are not even enrolled in education. An article outlining

2 | P a g e

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 30













 Catholic School Parents Australia (CSPA)

Submission to Inquiry into school refusal.

this can be found at: https://www.themandarin.com.au/205778-australia-is-failing-
the-tens-of-thousands-of-children-who-arent-enrolled-in-school/

The committee’s terms of reference appear to point to those enrolled, but not
turning up. What an opportunity for the committee to also look at those huge
numbers of children who are not enrolled. Is that a permanent state of ’school
refusal’ or what are the factors there? This, in particular, appears to be a
significant opportunity to explore, and address, those children who are lost to
the education system.

iv.

The mental health and wellbeing of school age children is of major concern and this
has been exacerbated by the pandemic and availability of professional support.  This
no doubt impacts a child’s want to attend school.  Some preliminary analysis of a
federal government funded, 2022 CSPA national survey of Catholic school parent/carer
views on their children’s wellbeing and learning found:

  71.8% (4513) of parents/carers described their child’s wellbeing as excellent or
good; however 28.2% (1773) described their child’s wellbeing as fair/average
(21.7%), poor (5.3%) or very poor (1.2%).

  61.7% (3879) of parents/carers noted their child enjoyed attending school

all/most of the time, however 38.3% felt their child enjoyed attending school –
some of the time (30%), hardly ever (6.7%) or never (1.5%).

  A little under 25% of parents/carers felt their child never (2.9%) or hardly ever
(21.9%) got worried or anxious about things, however 60.1% felt this was the
case for their child some of the time and a little under 15% felt their child got
anxious or worried about things all or most of the time.

  34.3% of parents/carers of a child with disability felt their child got anxious or
worried about things all or most of the time.  Notably, this was up to 40% of
parents/carers who had a secondary student with disability, while this was less
than half that (17%) for parents/carers of all secondary students.

  23 % of parents/carers of an indigenous child felt their child got anxious or

worried about things all or most of the time.

  When commenting on the availability of access to health services (e.g. doctor,
counsellor, occupational therapist, psychologist, mental health specialist,
learning support provider) a little under 50% of parents/carers indicated there
was availability all/most of the time, however this drops back to a little under
40% for rural areas.  Generally, 7.4% (465) indicated their child was hardly ever
able to access health services, while 2.5% (157) indicated this was never.

3 | P a g e

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 30












 Catholic School Parents Australia (CSPA)

Submission to Inquiry into school refusal.

A full report from this survey will be available to the government in December this
year.  At a glance, it is of deep concern that, for example, through the eyes of their
parents/carers, over 1 in 3 students with disability are anxious or worried about things
all or most of the time and this is the case for every 1 in 4 indigenous students.  And
that a little under 10% of students hardly ever or never enjoy attending school. While
the most negative responses to the above survey items might appear to be the
response from low percentages of parents/carers, it is significant that, for example,
2.5% felt their child never has access to health services – when this sample is
extrapolated, numbers become worryingly very high.

Also, parent/carer forums, which were conducted with some volunteer parents/carers
as a follow up to their completion of the 2022 CSPA parent views survey, provided
some harrowing evidence of mental challenges faced by some school age children, and
the extraordinary wait times (up to 8.5 months in one instance) to gain access to
professional support through the public health system.  In this particular case, the
parent reported great concern as the child was talking of suicide.

Another parent spoke of the impact of COVID lockdown on their senior secondary
school-age child.  Among the parent’s major concerns was the lack of access to
specialists, including psychologists, and the reality that their child now suffered from
anxiety, depression and had developed an eating disorder.  This parent was finding it
very difficult to get this child to go to school.  Other parents spoke of not knowing how
to get their children back on track after COVID lockdowns and the need of much more
investment into resourcing for wellbeing.

It was gratifying that many parents spoke positively about the support of their
children’s schools while noting the lack of resources in some Catholic schools in some
states when compared with other sector schools.

In yet another case, a parent shared the story of their primary-age child with disability
who refused to go to school.  While the child’s siblings happily attended school, the
child’s anxiety and mental health prevented them from doing so.  This parent was at
their wits end with trying to obtain referrals and accessing a paediatrician diagnosis
and felt there was a lack of understanding of school refusal versus school truancy.  The
parent was unable to work when needing to attend to this child at home and this was
further exacerbated as this was a single parent family.

In the article, 'School refusal': How post-pandemic scourge is making our children too
frightened for classes, it is noted that,

Statistics show that almost one in every seven children
aged between four and 17 suffer a mental health

4 | P a g e

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 30











 Catholic School Parents Australia (CSPA)

Submission to Inquiry into school refusal.

disorder. That adds up to almost 600,000 Australian
children.

One might conclude that many of these 600,000 students comprise a reasonable
portion of those students refusing to attend school, or more accurately described, find
themselves incapable of being able to attend school.

v.

In instances where children are refusing to come to school, and schools are working in
with parents/carers to endeavour to continue a child’s education by some hybrid
model of ‘at-home’ and ‘at-school’ learning, surely an additional workload on teachers
and parents, it seems disappointing if school funding in such contexts could be in
jeopardy where a school is not accredited to deliver learning via such a mode.  It would
be useful if ways could be found to support such initiatives as a workable way forward.

This inquiry is timely and hopefully will go some way to better understanding school refusal
through the eyes of school staff, school counsellors, psychologists, parents/carers and of
course students.  The better the challenge is understood, the more likely that effective,
multifaceted solutions could be introduced.  Whatever costs are required now to address
this challenge would seem a preferred option to the potential life time of welfare
dependence and poor wellbeing that could result for these children and young people, if this
is not addressed.

CSPA stands ready to assist the committee in this work, which we consider vital for schools,
parents, and those at the centre of both - our children.  Whatever the solutions, it would
seem that the best way forward will involve schools and families working in partnership for
the benefit of the children in their care.

An analysis of 202 1 government school referrals showed that t he attendance rate of students
from year s 7- 12 rose by 4 1.3% at  12 weeks post conference. So, we know that one on one

discussions t o r esolve blockages in students attending school  is affective.

Statistics  relating to contr ibuting factors for non-attendance

As part of the referral process t he OER collects information from schools,  parents and w here
relevant children and young people about why the child is not attending school. A n analysis of

conferences up until March  202 1 found t hat the predominant primary reason for referral was
mental health of t he child - a t otal of 29% of referrals cit ed mental health issues for the child as
the main reason for non-attendance.

The second most common contribut or at 28% was low-capacity parenting.  This includes

instances of school r efusal by t he child where the parent  lacks the skills t o manage t hat  r efusal
and to encourage t he child to attend school.

School refusal as a category in its own right and has increased since 20 19.  In 2019 around  13%
of referrals cited school refusal as a cont ri but ing factor in non-attendance.  In 2020 t hat figure
was 24% and in 202 1 it was 23%.  In  2022 it was 23% up to the end of November.

An interesting factor is t hat  even when t he number of conferences being conducted jumped
significantly in 202 1 from  144 in 2020 to 234 in 2021, t he percent age  relating t o school refusal
remained fairly constant.

School refusal is most commonly a factor in secondary school or the last year of primary school
(refusal linked to t he transit ion to high  school most commonly). It  is very often  linked with
anxiety and mental healt h or w ith gaming (or bot h).  Where it appears  in primary school it  is
closely linked wit h low-capacity parenting and often more easily resolved t hrough parental
support programs.

Understanding the reasons for school refusal

The OER has collected anecdotal  informat ion t hrough t he conferencing process around why
students are school refusing.  The most common cont ributors t hat are found alongside school
refusal are:

•  Lack of engagement in school (not engaged w ith the curriculum or no friends and

support network)

•  Lack of parenting skills (reinforcing the need to attend and valuing education and seeing

attending school every day as important)

•  Anxiety ( child or pa,·ent)

•  Gaming ( often also linked to lack of parent ing skills and  no rule setting and leading t o

poor sleep hygiene)

Lack of engagement with the years 7-1 0 curriculum and t he key learning areas is a very common
issue.  For many students who are in t his category of chronic non-attendance, lack of attendance
in the early years has led to a lack of foundational understanding which enables them to interact
w ith the curriculum at the level required in secondary school.  Therefore, they disengage.  The
more they ref use to attend t he worse t he issue  becomes because the lack of understanding, and
competency is compounded for every component  of t he curriculum t hey miss.

3 I Page

Educa,ion

There appears to be a lack of capacity in schools t o cater for this cohort of students in
mainstream classrooms.  The need to adapt t he curr iculum to such a great  extent is just too
resource intensive for t eachers already dealing w ith a wide spectrum of needs in the classroom.

The levels of anxiety in young people in high schools particularly are reported as having become
more extreme post Covid.  Many experience anxiety to a level that  physically restricts t heir
ability to leave the house and go to school.  For many they report that  access t o counsellors or
other support services is simply not available as the health system is struggling to have enough
available people to respond to t he need.  As early symptoms of anxiety are not treated, they
compound to a point that is reported to be quit e disabl ing leading t o school refusal.

Parents who feel ill equipped to manage a teenager who is refusing to attend school is a major
contributing factor.  Many parents report having their own mental health battles and simply not
being able to cope wit h also managing t heir teenage children's mental health issues and  school
refusal.

Coupled w ith a feeling of being ill equipped to manage this behaviour is a level of apathy from
parent s who do not value education and do not see the worth in the battle required to get t heir
child to school.  The road of least resistance is often to acquiesce and let them stay home.  This
is compounded when the child is a 'gamer' and  is often up all-night gaming and simply won't
wake up to go to school.

Where the parent does not have the skills  or the confidence or the inclination to set  and
enforce rules around gaming and sleep, they are also unlikely to be t he encouragement and
support a school refuser needs to get to school.

Conclusion

This is a highly complex area with no one cause or solut ion.  However, there are a number of
areas where increased focus and support are more likely t han not to have a posit ive impact.

I .  Consideration  of clear alternatives to standard classroom delivery of the key learning

areas  in t he Australian Curriculum and capacity for student s to opt out of some areas in
order t o focus on re-engaging wit h school.

2.  Funding for school ref users to enable schools to undertake the one-on-one work
required to re-engage them - it is highly resource intensive and very personal.

3.  Funding for programs to lift parent ing skills and equip parents with t he skills to ident ify

school refusing behaviour early and respond to it.

4.  A community focus on the importance of education and  attending school in a child's life.

submissions.text:
0 n Centre for Excellence in

'l Child and Family Welfare

Submission:

Inquiry into the national trend of school refusal and related matters

The Centre for Excellence in Child and Family Welfare (the Centre) welcomes the opportunity to  provide a
submission to the Inquiry into school refusal for consideration by the Education and Employment References
Committee.

The Centre is the peak body for child and family services in Victoria, representing more than 150 community
service organisations, students, and individuals. The Centre advocates for the rights of children and young
people  to  be  heard,  to  be  safe,  to  access  education  and  to  remain  connected  to  family,  community,  and
culture. Our vision is to see a community that is fair, equitable and creates opportunities for children and their
families to live happy and healthy lives. We work closely with community service organisations, government,
other peaks, philanthropy and business to make sure vulnerable children are seen and heard and supported
to thrive.

Introduction

As defined by the Committee, school refusal refers to difficulty attending school associated with emotional
distress and can mean that children have trouble going to school or trouble leaving home.

Based on consultation with our members, it appears that school refusal is having a significant impact on young
people, their families, and the services that support them. This submission describes some of the main impacts
reported by our members.

Effects of the COVID-19 Pandemic on school refusal

The COVID-19 pandemic and extended periods of lockdown in Victoria during 2020 and 2021 have contributed
to a noticeable increase in school refusal according to our members. In Victoria, lockdowns resulted in several
months of children and young people participating in online learning rather than face-to-face. While school
refusal is not new, it has been exacerbated by the global pandemic. Post pandemic, services have also seen
an increase in primary school aged students experiencing school refusal.

The pandemic has had an impact on young people’s ‘screen time’, including their use of social media, online
gaming, and streaming TV shows and movies with many young people relying on social media as a form of
connection  and  escape  during  the  pandemic.  Bullying  via  social  media  was  highlighted  as  a  common
contributor to school refusal, affecting children and young people’s ability to cope with workload demands and
academic progress. One practitioner from a member agency reported that:

Isolating from schools and peers resulting from COVID lockdowns have increased the school refusal
significantly. Also, during COVID families were required to push children to increased screen time,
which is also believed to have significantly negatively impacted on their mental health, which only
increases the likelihood of school refusal. The ripple effects of a child at home with poor mental
health moved beyond the child to the immediate family causing other negative impacts for the family
and child alike.

Research into the mental  health of  children and parents in Victoria during the  COVID-19 pandemic by the
Royal  Children’s  Hospital  in  Melbourne  found  that  remote  learning  had  a  significantly  negative  effect  on

December 2022

1

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 32


 0 n Centre for Excellence in

'l Child and FamilyWelfare

children  in  Victoria,  who  experienced  loneliness  and  social  isolation  during  lockdowns.1  Remote  learning
affected friendships and connectedness for more than half of children they surveyed, and one in four children
were somewhat, very, or extremely anxious about attending onsite school over a two-week period in December
2021.2  The  research  highlighted  that  in  December  2021,  ’50  per  cent  of  children  were  still  experiencing
negative effects of remote learning on their mental health, 53 per cent had negative impacts on friendships
and connectedness and 52 per cent required extra help with their learning because of a lack of face-to-face
learning in throughout the pandemic’.3

Impacts of school refusal on children and young people

Service  providers  reported  being  particularly  concerned  about  a  decline  in  children’s  mental  health  and  an
increase  in  their  social  isolation  resulting  from  school  refusal.  This  in  turn  affects  young  people’s  ability  to
maintain  support  networks  amongst  friends,  plan  for  their  future,  continue  their  education  after  finishing
school and gain employment. In some cases, service providers said that social isolation is resulting in criminal
offending, self-harm or using violence in the home.

It is difficult to break the cycle of school refusal once children or young people are engaged in it, and service
providers highlighted the complexities faced by parents or carers when school refusal becomes an ongoing
issue. When a young person misses a significant amount of school, they usually fall behind academically, and
over time it can become overwhelming to catch-up on the content they have missed. When students miss a
significant amount of school, they miss vital learning opportunities beyond only academic work. Our members
highlighted the detrimental impacts on a student’s ability to enter future study or paid employment with one
professional describing the negative impact in this way:

It (school refusal) is affecting their mental health as well as affecting their capacity to set long term
goals and effectively transition to adulthood given, they have lost the opportunity to explore
employment opportunities and appropriately interact socially with peers. Some students who school
refuse engage in anti-social behaviours, and this has been something that has also been reported a
lot recently in my role. Further, given the lack of education due to missing school, students and
young people are missing key information such as safe sex education, healthy relationships, AOD
education which can have detrimental impacts on their life trajectory.

If left  unaddressed, school refusal  can result in dropping out from school altogether.4 When young people
drop out of school early, they are at far greater risk of  social exclusion, unemployment, engaging in crime,
low income, and health risk behaviours, highlighting the critical importance of identifying issues and seeking
solutions  early.5  Service  providers  emphasised  how  important  early  intervention  and  prevention  are  when
treating school refusal, and the increased need for services that specialise in treating the early warning signs
of school refusal.

Impacts of school refusal on parents and carers

It is difficult for parents and carers to support children and young people experiencing school refusal. Our
members  report  that  school  refusal  has  led  to  an  increase  in  young  people  using  violence  in  the  home.

1 Royal Children’s Hospital National Child Health Poll (May 2022). Mental health of children and parents in Victoria during
the COVID-19 pandemic, The Royal Children’s Hospital Melbourne, Parkville, Victoria.
2 Ibid, p.4.
3 Ibid.
4 Hancock, K., Zubrick, R. (2015). Children and young people at risk of disengagement from school, Commissioner for
Children and Young People Western Australia, Western Australia.
5 Ibid.

December 2022

2

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 32



 Currently, there is a lack of data surrounding adolescent violence in the home in Australia, and the correlation
between school refusal and increased use of violence requires further investigation.

Service providers identified that school refusal has an impact on parents’ and caregivers’ ability to maintain
employment, as well as a financial impact on families who are supporting children experiencing school refusal,
and on mental health presentations amongst families. Member organisations noted that where families were
unable  to  encourage  children  to  participate  in  school,  this  has  often  been  viewed  by  schools  as  neglect.
Services  highlighted  that  often  schools  may  put  pressure  on  child  protection  to  get  involved  with  a  school
refusal issue when this is  not their specific area of expertise, and they are not  best placed to be assisting
students and families in this manner.  There is a dire need for services to help and  support parents  whose
children  are  school  refusing,  and  currently  the  lack  of  knowledge  and  service  availability  is  impacting  on
families.

Impact of school refusal on service providers

Service  providers  have  seen  an  increase  in  demand  for  programs  relating  to  school  refusal  following  the
COVID-19 lockdowns in Victoria and described how cases are becoming more complex and school avoidance
behaviours  more  intense.  Some  organisations  have  developed  additional  groups  or  programs  to  support
families,  but  they  lack  resources,  including  staff  and  funding,  to  meet  the  demand  these  programs  are
experiencing. There has reportedly been increased demand from schools themselves, who urgently require
assistance with school refusal. Service providers have also experienced an increase in demand for services
relating to adolescents using violence in the home, both directly from families and from other services who
cannot meet the demand.

At present, there is a lack of child psychiatrists and psychologists, particularly in regional and rural areas. This
has resulted in an increased workload for the child and family services sector, who are trying to assist students
to re-engage with school after the COVID-19 pandemic, but lack access to specialists, or must refer families
and young people to specialists with long wait lists. School refusal has affected funding for the sector, in some
cases, services have experienced increased requests for brokerage and funding for tutoring, and the increased
demand from schools to re-engage students has impacted the capacity of budgets.

Victorian Government programs for school refusal

At present, there are few programs that support children, young people, and families with school refusal. In
Victoria, the Navigator program works with disengaged young people aged 12 and over to support them to
return to education and learning.6 However, Navigator is a limited program, which requires additional funding
and expansion, as well as an earlier intervention focus post- pandemic. There is a clear service gap for primary
school aged children younger than 12 who are experiencing school refusal, and services are concerned about
the lack of early intervention and prevention  programs for these  children, as  well as the high threshold  of
disengagement required to participate in Navigator. Once younger students are  starting to disengage from
school, it may already be too late to meaningfully re-engage them in education and learning.

In addition, the Transforming Educational Achievement of Children at Risk (TEACHaR program) is in place in
Victoria to assist children aged 4-18 who need additional help in the classroom.7 TEACHaR has been shown to
be an effective program that collaboratively supports children and young people, their carers/parents, school
staff and other professionals who may be working with them to ‘transform their feelings and attitudes toward

6 State Government of Victoria, Navigator Program, viewed 5 December 2022,
https://www2.education.vic.gov.au/pal/navigator-program/policy
7 Anglicare Victoria, TEACHaR, Specialist Education Support, viewed 5 December 2022,
https://www.anglicarevic.org.au/our-services/education/teachar-tutoring-for-children-and-young-people/

December 2022

3

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 32



 learning’.8 TEACHaR lays the foundation for a successful school refusal program, and could be expanded and
tailored to support the demands schools and services are experiencing following the pandemic.

Recommendations

1.  Increase the number of publicly funded paediatricians and child psychologists in Victoria and locate

the new positions in community health services, with priority given to regional and rural areas.

2.  Expand  the  scope  of  the  Victorian  Navigator  program  to  include  primary  school  aged  children  to

address early signs of school refusal.

3.  Increase funding for and the availability of the ‘TEACHaR’ program, with a stream focusing specifically

on school refusal.

4.  Develop further targeted, early intervention and prevention programs for children experiencing school

refusal, run though schools or community service organisations. Programs must have long-term and

sustainable funding.

5.  Create  a  training  package  for  teachers  focused  on  school  refusal,  including  recognising  the  early

warning  signs,  identifying  available  supports  and  working  in  collaboration  with  students  and  their

parents, created in consultation with all groups involved.

6.  Invest in the expansion of targeted tutoring programs to make sure that all children and young people

experiencing  school  refusal  have  assistance  from  a  qualified  teacher  to  support  their  learning  and

engagement in school.

7.  Fund further research into school refusal to inform programs and build a knowledge base of the drivers

and appropriate responses to school refusal.

8 ibid

submissions.name: Autism Aspergers Advocacy Australia (A4)
submissions.text:
A submission on
the national trend of school refusal and
related matters

Autism Aspergers Advocacy Australia (A4) appreciates this opportunity to respond to your inquiry
into the national trend of school refusal and related matters. School refusal is a serious challenge for
too many autistic and neurodiverse students, and school-age children who are not students. A4
appreciates your recognising that school refusal or 'School Can't' is distinct from truancy.

In Australia, school education is mostly a state/territory issue. Unfortunately, state education
systems have very poor information about autistic students.

•  A4 is not aware of any systematic recording or reporting of autistic students' school refusal.
•  The NDDA education test case1 highlights the failure of schools and the failure of NMDS data

to report on autistic students.

This means there is insufficient information about why autistic students have very the poor
education outcomes, as reported repeatedly by the ABS SDAC reporting on autism. The difference
between NMDS data and other indicators of autism prevalence in the student population suggest
that disability supports for 4 in 5 autistic students are not provided because state education systems
fail/refuse to recognise the students’ disability. School refusal may be a natural and reasonable
student response to school environments that are unsupportive and constantly negative for many
autistic students.

At the same time, the NDIS cuts disability supports for school age autistic student. The NDIS expects
schools to provide 24/7 disability support for autistic students even when the school does not
recognise the student’s disability. Or maybe the NDIS expects students are only autistic for the 30
hours per week that they are in school.

A4 expects that that school refusal contributes to the very poor education outcomes for autistic
students ... and neurodivergent students more generally.

For autistic students, school refusal is often associated with or results from anxiety, trauma and/or
depression. There is a lot of “Accumulating evidence indicates children on the autism spectrum are
more likely to be bullied”2.

Bullying exposure can lead to not only longtime psychological symptoms such as depression
and anxiety, but also physiological symptoms.

1 DSS’s Nation Disability Data Asset’s (NDDA) Education to Employment test case document reported that
there were 2,107 (Table 3) or 1,704 (Table 4) autistic students in South Australia. NDIS data for 2022-23 Q1
shows 10,034 autistic NDIS participants aged 7 to 14 years. There are more autistic children who are not NDIS
participants and whose needs are not met in education settings. The NDDA results are based on NMDS data
that are simply not credible for the number of autistic or neurodivergent school students.
2 https://a4.org.au/node/2450

Page 1 of 2

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 33


 Data from the Longitudinal Study of Australian Children indicate the experience of being
bullied can be associated with a four-fold increased risk of self-harm or suicidal thoughts
among adolescents aged 14-15 years.

Bullying of autistic students is typically mismanaged in schools: frequently, schools ignore autistic
victims of bullying or treat them as perpetrators.

Recommendations: A4 suggests that

1.  to properly address the problem, we must first clearly understand the problem. The first step is
to listen to students with school refusal. We need them to tell us why they are refusing school –
rather than relying on assumptions. We should expect there are multiple reasons for school
refusal and accept that tackling the issue needs multiple evidence-based approaches.

2.  addressing school refusal for autistic students must be part of the Commonwealth

Government's National Autism Strategy. Australia needs a much more proactive approach to
reducing anxiety, trauma, and depression in its neurodivergent school students.

3.  schools must ensure all students, including neurodivergent students and students with a
disability, enjoy learning. This means the curriculum should come second to ensuring all
students like being at school.

4.  the whole mental health sector needs re-education in relation to neurodiversity and disability, a
subsection of the population the mental health sector is recognised to be failing. The National
Autism Strategy is already highlighting the need for radical improvement to mental health
services for neurodivergent Australians. There is need for a particular focus on school students.

If you would like further information on any aspect of this submission, please contact Autism
Aspergers Advocacy Australia via convenor@a4.org.au

submissions.name: Associate Professor Glenn Melvin
submissions.text:
Inquiry into the National Trend of School Refusal and Related Matters

Author: A/Prof Glenn Melvin, Deakin University.

09.12.2022

Background
I am a clinical psychologist and Associate Professor in the Centre for Social and Early Emotional
Development in the School of Psychology at Deakin University. I also hold an honorary Associate
Professor position at the Centre for Educational Development, Appraisal and Research at the
University of Warwick (UK).

My research in the area focuses on understanding the range of interacting child, family, school, and
community factors that underlie school attendance problems and developing interventions and
supports for students who refuse school, their families, and schools. Most recently, together with
colleagues at Monash University, I have developed parenting guidelines for school refusal based on a
Delphi expert consensus study that involved parent advocates, health and education professionals
and academics from around the world. Following this we have adapted a parenting program for
parents of anxious and depressed teens to also address school refusal. Currently ‘coach assisted’ and
‘self-directed’ versions of this parenting program are under evaluation.

Over the last fifteen years I have worked clinically with adolescents who refuse school, their parents,
and schools in my private psychology practice. I have also provided numerous workshops, trainings
and consultancy to many schools and mental health organisations on school refusal and school
attendance around Australia. I am a founder of the International Network for School Attendance
(INSA) and in 2023, I will serve as the President of its Executive Committee.

Submission

I believe that there are sizeable gaps in the provision of information and services for school refusal in
Australia. In addition, we know little of the true scope of the problem. I offer the following
reflections based on my collective experiences and knowledge of the scientific literature in this field.

1.

Lack of School Refusal Data

To the best of my knowledge, we lack data on the prevalence of school refusal in Australia. While I
have also noted considerable concern about increasing rates of school refusal since the Covid-19
pandemic, the issue appeared to be substantial prior to the pandemic. The percentage of school
attendance for each school is collected by ACARA, however these data do not include the reasons
for absence from school. School refusal can be a difficult construct to measure. Lack of knowledge
about school refusal combined with feelings of shame and embarrassment by parents who report
feeling judged about their child’s behaviours are barriers to the reporting school refusal. When does
school refusal become a problem? While a threshold of 10% absence has been adopted in multiple
studies (e.g., Allison, Attisha, AAP COUNCIL ON SCHOOL HEALTH, 2018 ) to the best of my knowledge
it is not based on empirical data, and leaders in the field have recently suggested that we should
look at impairment in functioning to determine when school non-attendance becomes problematic
e.g., interference with academic competence, impact on family functioning e.g., parents reducing
work hours due to their child refusing to attend (Kearney, 2022).

2. Consistent Definition.

School attendance problems including school refusal suffer from the use of inconsistent
terminology. We lack a universally accepted term for and definition of school refusal (Heyne, Gren
Landell, Melvin & Gentle-Genitty, 2019). In this paper we identified 20 terms that have been used in

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 34
 the scientific literature since 1932 to describe the phenomenon of school refusal. I consider the
definition offered by (Berg, 2002) to be most helpful as it is inclusive of the child’s avoidance,
considers parental effort to get the child to school, and is differentiated from other school
attendance problems such as truancy and school withdrawal. Berg’s definition is as follows:

1. Severe difficulty attending school
2. Severe emotional upset (e.g., fear, depression, anxiety) at the prospect of having to go to

school

3. Child stays at home with the knowledge of the parents (in contrast to truancy)
4. Parents make reasonable attempts to secure their child’s attendance at school (in contrast

to school withdrawal)

5. Absence of severe antisocial behaviour (in contrast to truancy)

Addressing these first two issues by adopting and implementing a consistent definition of school
refusal and collecting meaningful and representative Australian prevalence data is critical to
understanding the actual size of the problem in Australia. Establishing a baseline rate of school
refusal will also be critical to determine if our increasing efforts to address this problem are indeed
effective and limited funding is being spent on strategies that work. Currently, we are very much in
the dark about how big this issue was before the pandemic and how much it has grown.

3.

Impact of School Refusal

School attendance problems including school refusal can be thought of as an outcome of a range of
interacting underling symptoms (e.g., elevated anxiety, depression) and struggles (e.g., difficulty
with school work, social isolation) experienced by the child combined with exposure to negative or
harmful circumstances, experiences, or environments (e.g., bullying, poor student-teacher
relationships, unhealthy school climate, parental experience of mental illness; Melvin, Heyne, Gray,
Hastings, Totsika, Tonge, & Freeman, 2019). School refusal can result in chronic school absenteeism.
Chronic absenteeism is associated with a wide range of negative outcomes including poorer health
and mental health, low academic attainment, early school leaving, social difficulties, loss of income
and greater rates of unemployment (for review see policy statement, American Academy of
Pediatrics – Allison, Attisha, AAP COUNCIL ON SCHOOL HEALTH, 2018). As well as impacting the
child, school refusal has been associated with challenges for parents. For example, our study on this
topic demonstrated that parents of teens with school refusal experienced higher levels of anxiety,
depression and reported lower levels of parental self-efficacy and higher levels of family dysfunction
compared with parents who did not have a child who was refusing school (Carless, Melvin, Tonge &
Newman, 2015). Little is known about the longitudinal course of school refusal, however it can have
its onset across the school aged years and can manifest as a chronic relapsing remitting problem
over multiple years. Within mental health services school refusal is widely considered as a
psychiatric emergency (Prabhuswamy, 2018) requiring prompt and comprehensive support and
intervention.

4. A coordinated approach to school refusal

A coordinated approach is required to address and alleviate the current demands on schools and
service providers who are supporting students with school refusal. Such an approach to school
refusal (and school attendance problems, more broadly) must caters to the needs of multiple
stakeholders (students, families, education, primary health, mental health professionals as well as
the wider community) across multiple tiers (prevention, targeted for those at risk, indicated for
those who are refusing school) and across government departments (education, health, justice at
local, state, and federal government levels). The following are considered to be key components.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 34
 Accessible Information: Widely available information and resources on school refusal are required.
We currently have some good information about school refusal  available on Australian websites for
parents (e.g., Raising Children Network and Headspace), but we lack a central online site and
repository for all stakeholders including parents, students, and health and education professionals to
access coordinated information about addressing school refusal and other attendance issues that is
informed by best practice and experts in the field including those with lived experience (parents,
young people), health, mental health and education professionals, and researchers. Providing
accessible information, such as our parenting guidelines would likely play a role in reducing the
stigma associated with school refusal and lead to quicker access to supports which is key, as the
longer non-attendance from school persists the harder it tends to be to address. Such a site could
include moderated forums that allow parents to gain peer support, access to preventive and early
intervention strategies, methods of empowering school students to develop solutions that improve
attendance within their schools and create welcoming environments, guidance for education and
health professionals about how to proactively address the issues underlying non-attendance. Taking
a multicultural and diversity lens to such a resource is critical to reach all Australian families and
schools.

School-based support: School-wide approaches to addressing attendance problems including school
refusal have been developed, but in my anecdotal experience are rarely implemented in schools. For
example, the Multi-tiered system of support model to promote school attendance and address
school absenteeism developed by Kearney and Graczyk (2020) can be applied within schools to
develop nuanced approaches to prevention, early intervention for school refusal and coordinated
responses to students where an attendance problem exists. Such approaches are being scaled up
and evaluated in other countries such as the Netherlands where A/Prof Graczyk has been
collaborating with a local school districts (Graczyk, 2022). It is anticipated that greater capacity
within schools to detect and respond earlier to school refusal will result in a reduction the number of
students who refuse school and a reduction in the amount of school missed by students who do
refuse.

A trained workforce: A coordinated approach would rely upon a trained workforce. Incorporation of
curriculum on school refusal and school attendance problems into teacher training programs would
provide the skills and knowledge required to intervene early and work collaboratively with families
and external providers of health and mental health services.
Equally, mental, and allied health (e.g., psychology, psychiatry, social work, occupational therapy,
mental health support workers) and health professionals (e.g., general practitioners) who work with
children and their families need access to training in assessing and managing the factors underlying
school refusal and skills in working within and between school and family systems, as well as
evidence-based interventions.
Establishing school attendance as a specialist discipline that cuts across health and education with
graduate training courses for professionals working in these fields would provide a level of expertise
and leadership within schools and services that are very much needed. Such courses would equip
schools and services, such as the recently expanded Navigator program in Victoria, with new staff
equipped to meet the challenges of refusal. At present, such courses are missing from the training
programs available to health and education professionals.
In addition, to these professional groups, we should be harnessing the expertise and advocacy of
parents and young people with lived experience. These stakeholders provide an essential and unique
perspective on solutions to school refusal and guide and support others who are struggling with the
issue.

Evidence-based approaches to school refusal: A modest body of research exists to guide
practitioners about how to best support young people, their families and schools when school

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 34

 refusal occurs (see Elliott & Place, 2019). In Australia, our group has evaluated cognitive behavioural
therapy adapted for school refusal (Melvin et al., 2018), which is currently the most evidence-based
treatment approach, however novel and accessible approaches are needed, as after treatment less
than half of students we treated were able to attend school 80% of the time.
It is clear that we need a range of educational options for students whose needs may not be catered
for in mainstream schools. However, evidence is urgently needed into the efficacy and outcomes of
the various education environments that are currently available for students who have refused
school (e.g., flexible learning settings, mainstream face to face school, virtual/distance learning) in
an environment where it appears that distance/virtual learning is becoming an increasingly popular
option. We need to know what works for whom, to guide families and educators as to their best
option given the well-established and broad ranging positive impacts of education. Evaluation of
these education environments would also provide insights into how best to improve current
offerings as well as informing the development of new and innovate models of education.

Targeting Supports: Some child and family factors associated with school refusal have been
identified. For example, we are aware that autistic children experience high levels of school refusal
(Adams, 2021; Totsika, Hastings, Dutton, Worsley, Melvin, Gray, Tonge & Heyne, 2020). These
findings mean we have the capacity to co-design and evaluate targeted preventative interventions
for school refusal.

5. Attendance issues other than School Refusal.

School refusal is often thought of as one of a number of school attendance problems. Different types
of school attendance problems have different underpinnings and require different solutions. I would
like to draw the Committee’s attention to the existence of other school attendance problems
including truancy, school withdrawal and school exclusion.







Truancy is unauthorised absence from school typically without the knowledge or permission of
parent. Students typically attempt to conceal the absence.
School withdrawal occurs when a student is absent from school due to their parent’s choice or
with a level of parent acceptance or cooperation. The circumstances behind school withdrawal
can vary enormously from parents withdrawing their children from school to take additional
holidays during school term through to parents neglecting their child’s education. School
withdrawal may occur when parents elect not to send their child(ren) to school in fear that
harm will fall on their children while at school, for example bullying or Covid-19 infection.
School exclusion refers to absenteeism that is attributable to the school for example,
inappropriate disciplinary exclusion or through the inability of a school to provide adequate
supports that are required for a child’s education. School exclusion may be overt or covert and
was noted as a key concern in a report titled “Held Back: The experiences of students with
disabilities in Victorian schools – Sept 2012” by the Victorian Equal Opportunity & Human Rights
Commission.

While school refusal is certainly a key concern in Australia, I believe it is important to examine all
school attendance problems, determine the school, family and community wide factors that
contribute to their development and maintenance in order to inform the necessary and appropriate
supports that are required.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 34

Submission to: Inquiry into the national trend of school refusal and related matters

Thank you for the opportunity to contribute to  the  Inquiry into the national  trend of school refusal and
related matters. Below we address some of the terms of reference to this inquiry: a) the increasing numbers
of  young  people  and  their  families  experiencing  school  refusal,  and  c)  the  impacts  and  demands  of  the
increasing case load on service providers and schools to support these students and families. We also outline
how issues of systemic racism and other forms of discrimination, school competition, and curriculum design,
can impact on and feed into school refusal.

While school refusal and school exclusion may not immediately register as connected, we urge the Inquiry
to consider school refusal in the context of a well-established ‘school-to-prison pipeline’, issues of truancy
and school exclusion that disproportionately impact First Nations and other racialised communities.1

We include references in footnotes for further exploration by committee members and interested parties.

Increasing numbers experiencing school refusal
COVID-19 has exacerbated already brewing or existing social inequalities.2 This means that any issue that
has emerged out of the global pandemic should be understood in the context of histories of inequality. We
urge the Inquiry to consider issues of school structure and expectation, rather than an individual deficit or
failure located in the student, their family or community. School should be understood as a social experience,
just as much as an academic experience. This means that addressing issues such as school refusal are about
connection to a school community as well as connection to curriculum and a social environment that enables
a sense of choice and agency. It is well known that issues such as racism, homophobia, ableism and sexism
(that  are  sometimes  hidden)  impact  student  wellbeing,  strength  of  relationships  and  trust  at  school  and
capacity to advocate for oneself and one’s needs.3 These structural injustices must be addressed to ensure
schooling environments are safe places for all students.

Impacts and demands on service providers and schools
It  is  well  known  that  schools  are  already  chronically  underfunded,  particularly  government  schools  in
disadvantaged areas.4 Teachers and unions have been calling for smaller class sizes, more planning time and

1

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 35








 greater wellbeing support staff in schools for many years to address issues of inequality and disadvantage.5
The Inquiry should consider the level of resourcing that teachers indicate is needed to ensure schools can
cater to the diverse needs and aspirations of every single student.  Good learning happens when students
have strong relationships with teachers, other adults in the school and their peers – this takes time and care
– resources should be directed to schools to enable them to maximise the time and care required to build
these relationships. As indicated above, addressing structural inequalities and embedded prejudices, such as
racism, ableism, homophobia and sexism, should also be a priority. This is ongoing, relational work, that
involves  schools  developing  culturally  safe and  relationally  secure  environments  for  learning.6 This  is  a
collective project and requires resourcing.

School refusal, exclusion and incarceration
The newer emergence of school refusal of the kind being addressed by this inquiry sits within a history of
school exclusion that is important to consider. The broader impacts of school exclusion, such as an increased
likelihood of contact with the criminal justice system and incarceration, are issues that should be understood
as  connected  to  the  problems  of  school  exclusion.7 The  Inquiry  would  benefit  from  reviewing  previous
national inquiries and research reports into school exclusion and refusal, particularly the 1984  Research
report on skipping school: An examination of truancy in Victorian secondary schools and the 1996 Inquiry
into truancy and exclusion of children and young people from school.
It should also be noted that high competition environments undermine  relationships and solidarities that
help to build student connection to school – we believe it would be beneficial to rethink things like NAPLAN
and MySchool and the impact that these practices have on the capacity for schools to realise their purpose
of  supporting  every  young  person. 8 Curriculum  exclusion  can  also  contribute  to  students  feeling  less
connected to school  (see experiences of First Nations young people as an example of this).9 Curriculum
reform should be considered as part of the solution to making schools relationally safer and stronger places.
While the Inquiry is focussed on students who refuse to come to school, it would also be beneficial to think
alongside this issue, about students who are more often excluded from school, such as First Nations, disabled
and queer students. If schools were to work with these students and their communities to enable them to
have an active role in developing solutions to this problem, schools would become places that are  more
welcoming  and  safer  for  all  students.  Communities  who  experience  the  issues  of  school  refusal  and
exclusion have core insights on what schools need to do to address the issues.

Thank you again for the opportunity to contribute to the Inquiry into the national trend of school refusal
and related matters.

submissions.name: Dr JUDITH LOCKE
submissions.text:
Submission for The Senate Education and Employment References Committee on the
National Trend of School Refusal and Related Matters.

by Dr Judith Locke and Dr Danielle Einstein, Clinical Psychologists

As clinical psychologists, we see a lot of school refusal, where children won’t attend school.
The issue has been increasing for some time, but particularly recently.

Many times, a child might indicate fears of school, separation anxiety, or sadness or
overwhelm. Alternatively, they might have symptoms of panic, such as ‘funny tummy’ or
feeling lightheaded - normal responses to temporary discomfort. These physical symptoms
may be catastrophised by the child as an indicator of illness.

There’s a typical trajectory to long-term school refusal. Children or teens may request a
‘mental health day’, to overcome school stress, such as assignment or friendship challenges,
anticipation of missing their parent, panic symptoms, boredom, or difficulty focussing in
class. The child might believe they can’t cope with the upcoming school day. Parents,
concerned about their child’s wellbeing, might agree.

Later, the child may present a carbon copy of the request that got results the first time. The
parent now has difficulty in responding differently to insist their child attend.

Children may use aggression, extreme tantrums, or highly emotional statements or threats
about what they will do, such as self-harm. Parents have difficulty refusing, particularly if
they lack skill to manage such situations. Also, children may have more dominance than
parents in the home, due to extreme child-centred parenting approaches.

Unfortunately, once a pattern is established, it’s difficult to change.

Why is school refusal such an issue, now? Many cite the pandemic impacting students’
coping skills. Also, having had ‘school at home’, children might see this as a viable
alternative.

While many children had their schooling disrupted and may be understandably impacted,
we see current practices that must be addressed to reverse the current school refusal trend.

1.  Currently there’s some hypervigilance around anxiety and mental health. When
children face momentary challenge, many parents and schools over examine
temporary feelings with children and/or allow them to avoid facing difficulty. This
suggests that anxiety isn’t normal, and requires special assistance or allowances.

2.  There’s a popular narrative suggesting an inevitable and somewhat permanent
mental health impact from the pandemic. This unnecessarily discounts many
children’s fundamental resilience and their future potential.

3.  The oft-cited concept of ‘mental health days’, suggest school is overwhelming and
students need days away. This belief implies that the daily challenges of school are
insurmountable – which is not the case for the majority.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 36









 4.  The overwhelm of school might be more to do with inadvertent pressure by society
for the child to be successful in every endeavour. Also, some students have reduced
coping skills due to previous over-protection from minor challenges.

5.  Technology is a major contributor to school refusal.  Children with access to a

personal device prevents them from fully experiencing the full gamut of school
experience, and learning to manage occasional anxiety or boredom.

6.  Days off can be valid, such as for illness. But parents must ensure days away are
time-limited, and not excessively rewarding for children. Gaming and screen
distraction shouldn’t be used as a diversionary activity during the day. Being home
with their screens may become the child’s preferred activity.

7.  Children being picked up midway through a school day, via emotive texts to parents,
must also be restricted. They should not be in contact with their parents during their
school days.

8.  Should bullying be an issue, it needs to be effectively addressed rather than

temporarily avoided.

9.  If children’s coping skills are lacking, there are proven ways to teach parents to coach

their child to improve these. But, this will always involve the child slowly facing
increasing difficulty, and learning they can manage. Intermittent avoidance of
challenge will always set progress back.

10. Medicare rebates prioritise the child as the client to receive treatment, rather than

parents. Children lack cognitive capacity and motivation to overcome something that
essentially results in a short-term reward for them – such as a day watching screens
rather than school. Thus, parents are much better to receive treatment assistance
for school refusal – but Medicare rules would need to change to not disadvantage
parents.

SUBMISSION
SCHOOL REFUSAL INQUIRY
JANUARY 2023

Thank you for including Aspergers Victoria in your invitations to submit to this forum.

Key Assertions

1.  We have had a lack of School connected ness and with that Schools Can’t in our Autistic
community since AV was formed in 1991, before Aspergers was a diagnosis in the DSM
diagnostic manual. Our Australian COVID-19 lockdowns have created anxiety and social
dislocation for many school-age children and the prevalence of school refusal following this
continues and is often unrelated to that traumatic period. Rather, lockdown home-schooling
opportunities created a generation of young people that realise or regard school attendance
in an unsafe environment is simply an alternative way to learn. They choose to stay home
where they feel safer and can choose to learn what they want and what they are more
interested in online.

2.  School exclusion leads to autistic economic and social exclusion and mental health pathways
which impacts their entire lives as well as their whole family. Autistic unemployment is the
highest of all disabilities and 6 times the rate for the general population.

3.  School can’t is more due to the school culture and system which fails to build autistic

connectedness nor meet the learning and support needs of capable autistics and other
neurodivergent with hidden learning differences and different social approaches.
4.  Autistics are all too often traumatised by their school experiences and resulting societal

exclusion as mentioned above leading to mental health pathways if they don't receive the
right supports.

5.  School can’t has a ripple effect across the entire family especially parents/carers and siblings

as outlined below.

6.  The reasons why children feel unsafe to attend school are varied and are often a complex
mix. One important reason is that students who are categorised as different learners can
feel invisible, unsupported, unsafe, unwelcome and lack belonging. Some of this is due to :
1.  the harsh curriculum and lack of adjustments due to the VCAA approaches to

learning differences. Current adjustments available once you reach high school are
minimal and difficult to access – needing evidence to prove need from deficit-based
specialist examinations.

2.  Lack of flexibility and respect in reasonable adjustments and assessment: our

students are often not listened to when they attempt to explain their learning and
processing needs. This is a lack of respect of the student and their opinion. They are
instead forced into the method of that school or teacher. This extends to University
and TAFE as well.

3.  Schools cultures lack acceptance of different learning styles: Lack of teacher and

Principal training and acceptance is part of this as well as acceptance of differences
by parents of other students. The reality is Schools still refuse to accept autistic
students due to this perception.

4.  Lack of strengths based educational approaches as well as a lack of funding for non-
deficit based supports. Our students want to feel welcomed and appreciated, not
singed out as being less in some way.

5.  COVID has added to the anxiety that school creates for our autistics and is one more

reason for overwhelm and traumatic wounds caused by their school journey.

6.  Students are unable to voice their needs or be heard in School.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 37

 7.  Students feel disempowered from the pathway to life and independence towards

work of their peers due to deficit based approaches to their needs.

7.  Often our niche autistic students are highly capable, camouflage their needs with the

concurrent lack of teacher training means they are not diagnosed until later in the system
when they are in crisis with anxiety high and some traumatic experiences such as bullying by
students, parents or teachers, leaving residual safe and lack of safety.

8.  Lack of Autistic Work Readiness during School: Research shows and we see in our teen

autistics that many do not understand the importance of school in their future career. AV
has discovered directly from our autistic student that the current work experience and
career subjects in Schools fail to meet autistic learning needs with the result that autistic
students often miss out on the benefits and insight that career understanding and especially
work experience builds and with that the motivation to complete school to gain a job. Due
to this we developed a codesigned AV Teens Work KnowHow Program which specifically
aims to  build career readiness and understanding in School students. It also provides
support at a stage when School Cant can disempower our students and instead provides
customised and understanding support.  Increased student engagement in School after
completing our Program is so insightful for all.

WHAT IS ASPERGERS AUTISM?
Aspergers is now known as Autism Spectrum Condition Level 1 or 2 or ASD-1 or some individuals now
diagnosed more with ‘Social Communication Disorder’ under the DSM5. Aspergers autistics fall under
the umbrella term of neurodiversity of cognitive function and is considered to be in three percent of
the population in Australia (Amaze 2021).

Aspergers autistics essentially have a hidden differences in how we learn, communicate, socialise and
process  our  world.  We  mainly  have  an  average  or  above  IQ,  specialised  knowledge,  and  often
extraordinary  creative  talent,  focus  and  productivity.  Research  shows  that  at  least  90  percent  of
Autistics  are  highly  sensitive  to  either  sound,  sight,  taste,  smell,  or  touch.   We  do  not  have  an
intellectual disability and have high cognitively capability, often with different processing approaches
to information. Our minds create a mainly hidden or unexpected differences so people and especially
schools, teachers, assessors and parents often misunderstand and misjudge us and our behaviours.
At AV we see our behaviours as part of our communication.

School’s Trauma Impact : Living in schools and a world that isn't designed to support or respect
these sensitivities can be traumatic, especially if you are more sensitive, feeling unsafe, and lack
support and understanding at school for 6 hours each day. Research also has shown that Autistics
also have a higher sensitivity that causes trauma and distress more readily such that specific stress
experiences can give them similar symptoms to PTSD without that level of serious trauma more from
repetitive incidences where they feel unsafe. This article in Psychology Today postulates that School
is giving our Student PTSD: Are We Giving Autistic Children PTSD From School?(2021). This traumatic
start to their lives set in motion a life of isolation and barriers without the right understanding and
supports.

Our  community’s  parents  and  carers  have  been  found  in  research  to  have  a  level  of  fatigue  and
overwhelm similar to that in military campaign soldiers. Many of our parents have some of autistic
characteristics themselves, or find they are caring for an isolated autistic student with mental health
trauma. This then impacts their employment ability as they step more into a carer role – and their
own mental health challenges. Our peer groups and help team being a key support that understands
and  validates  their  lived  experience,  where  they  can  share  their  story  and  feel  understood  and
welcome.

 Also when a family have a student who is refusing to attend school it has a ripple effect  across the
siblings and other family members as well with a judgemental stigma of exclusion and inability.

Our  autistic  cohort  are  intelligent  and  capable  students  and  if  given  the  right  supports  including
sensory supports, the right environment and an appreciative teaching and school approach that suits
our individual needs we can manage school and employment and thrive. We are highly productive,
loyal,  creative,  innovative,  analytical-driven,  and  specialist  thinkers  with  phenomenal  attention  to
detail.

School Can’t (Refusal) in our community

AV has direct experience of School challenges for our community through:

-
-

our Teen Work KnowHow Program which provides a full support work experience for eligible
autistic teens and we include Teens who have had school refusal or at risk.
our Teen peer group which meets monthly for over 15 years
our parent peer groups which meet online and in person for over 32 years

All of our activities are codesigned to support our autistics managing school refusal challenges and
their  families.  We  provide  trauma-informed  supports  to  assist  and  guide  our  members  with  this
challenge.

We  assisted  with  establishing  a  ‘School  Can’t’  parent  peer  group  6  years  ago  which  then  became
independent. We did not have enough resources to support the running of this group and continue to
have limited resource support with no ongoing government funding. This peer group was established
due to the already existing need across our community prior to COVID. We find that more than 50%
of  the  teens  who  attend  our  monthly  teen  peer  group  are  dealing  with  or  have  had  School  Can’t
challenges.    The  challenge  with  such  a  parent  peer  groups  is  ensuring  a  positive  and  empowering
approach is taken to ensure the peer group does not become about everything that is wrong with that
child or that situation. It must be empowering. Often the parents are in as much of a traumatised state
as their child once the child is out of school.

The  School  Can’t  is  noticeable  higher  as  our  students  reach  the  higher  levels  of  secondary  school
where assessment and the curriculum narrows with less options to suit their needs.

We call it ‘school can’t’ as it not that our autistic neurodivergent children are refusing to go to
school. They are unable to go to school for a variety of reasons. These signs include

Knowing they are not safe and don't feel welcome

-
-  Nausea and vomiting at the thought of school
-  High anxiety to the point they can’t leave their home if school is their destination
-

parents and other students

A recent Autism CRC report The Australian Autism Educational Needs Analysis – What are
the needs of schools, parents and students on the autism spectrum? Reports:

 “Over the past decade, educational and public health researchers have recognised the
importance of social and psychological connectedness to school as a protective and
promotive factor for all youth (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), 2009;
Griffiths, Sharkey, & Furlong, 2009; McNeely, Nonnemaker, & Blum, 2002; Resnick et al.,
1997). In addition, school connectedness is influenced by educators’ and parents’

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 37




 perceptions of school connectedness to the school environment. School connectedness
has been defined by Goodenow (1993) as “the extent to which students feel personally
accepted, respected, included, and supported by others in the school social environment” (p.
80).  Overall, educators and specialists felt some connection to the organisations they
worked with, with specialists rating their connection lower than that of educators. In
comparison, parents of students on the spectrum rated their child’s connection with
the school as low. Overall, ratings from the students themselves were the lowest, indicating
low levels of school connectedness amongst students on the spectrum. “ This report has
extensive details about how Schools need to accommodate autistic students.

As the school model is changing and becoming less flexible and more streamlined especially from
year 9 and in VCE years, with mainstream approaches to social and team activities a key
requirement, many autistics are facing barriers to inclusion and traumatic experiences in their school
and work lives. Due to misunderstanding of our communication and social differences, many people
assume disability and total incompetence.

Work Readiness from School: Many autistics do not understand the importance of school in their
future life and career. This is partly due to our difficulty with generalising new experiences and their
impact on our future without additional and autistic-suited explanation.
AV has discovered that autistic students often miss out on the benefits and insight that autistic co-
designed career development in School provides and with that the motivation to complete school
towards gaining a job.

Due to this we developed a codesigned AV Teens Work KnowHow Program to build career readiness
and understanding in School students. One of the interesting program outcomes is students’
increased engagement in School after completing our Program. As awareness of our program grows
we find more and more neurodivergent but also non-neurodivergent students want that career
insight and to understand more about how school is relevant to that future pathway into work.

“”For school leavers on the autism spectrum, regardless of academic ability, the rates of successful
participation in post-secondary education or further training are only half that of students without
disability, and only one-quarter that of all other students “ source

TRANSITION TO POST SCHOOLING FOR AUTISTIC YOUNG PEOPLE” prioritises for our autistic students
a Recommendation 6: More Resources and Access to Work Experience is Needed in Schools to
Support Autistic Young People to Prepare for Transition .

The Evidence of a lack of student engagement in career understanding is glaring and needs
improvement. AV already has extensive learning about this from our AV Teen Work KnowHow
program which needs more funding from government and commitment to building work experience
as a student school engagement strategy.

Anxiety support: The key theme is autistics develop high anxiety due to differences in our
communication, lack of others’ understanding, trauma in our lives and lack of suitable simple
adjustments and supports. Many of our adults are discovering their own Autism following their
child’s diagnosis and struggles with their own anxiety.  Autism is genetic and often at least one
parents share characteristics of their autistic child.

Many Members who have key strengths and capabilities, also have a wide and differing range of
individual hidden differences and challenges with social communication, executive function and
sensory challenges that are misunderstood - or seen as non-compliance - and that misunderstanding

 limits our successful study, completion of school and employment. Without understanding with
system adaptations, acceptance and accommodations, we often experience anxiety, isolation,
bullying and trauma at school and then in the employment system, ending up with chronic
unemployment, anxiety and other mental health issues and social and economic isolation.

This resulting economic and social exclusion impacts their entire lives as well as their whole family.

Victorian Department of Education

We believe that this is a public health, education, and disability crisis that requires system levels
change and quickly to change this trajectory. The education engagement level of our community is
dropping and fast.

We are part of the Autism Advisory Group supporting the hard work of the Inclusive Education team
at the DET Victoria who have various plans to improve a limited number of schools approach to be
more autistic-led. However, they face the difficult reality that the current mainstream education
system and its culture is unable to meet the cognitive, social and emotional needs of many of our
neurodivergent learners. They also lack the funding to deliver real change. Their lack of funding
means their new inclusive programs only reach a small number of state schools, not independent or
Catholic.

The key failure here starts with government and then leadership in DET and VCAA who fail to regard
school change, changes in curriculum plus assessment approaches and School Can’t as a priority to
invest in major changes. This flows onto a lack of accountability in Schools around this with what
seems to be a lack of transparent external reporting and measuring of this by independent
processes.

We believe that most schools do not have an inclusive education culture, environment, that most
teachers are not trained or equipped with the skills or flexibility in curriculum to teach diverse
students with neurodevelopmental conditions or children with mental health conditions.

Our school system needs major consistent overhaul across Australia to:

Ensure Education leaders make this a priority before it becomes a tsunami

trauma informed based approaches with wellbeing a key KPI

measures and transparent reporting for families/community
