Benjamin Cronshaw

1

December 1st 2022

Submission to the Inquiry into School Refusal

Education is a human right, which all children have a right to access and benefit from. Education

is  important  to  give  children  skills  and  knowledge  that  they  can  take  into  their  adult  life,  for

whatever paths they end up taking. All children should not only have access to education, but be

supported with their specific needs and learning styles to benefit and reach their potential from

education in a way that works for them. It should be recognised that not all children are the same.

They have different needs to help them with their learning. Not all children need to learn the same

way, or about the exact same things. Some children will need additional support for adjusting into

school  and  their  learning,  such  as  for  learning  or  physical  disabilities,  low  literacy,  a  different

cultural background, mental health challenges, or behavioural challenges. However, this does not

mean that schools - or we, as a society - should let these children down because it is too hard.

I  note  that  school  refusal  refers  to  school  non-attendance  or  staying  home  from  school.  It  is

generally when the child feels unable to attend, including because of anxiety issues. One article

describes  it  as  not  “wilful  truancy”  but  “the  emotional  distress  that  students  (of  any  age)  can

associate  with  attending  school.”  While  they  may  even  want  to  attend  school  and  learn,  they

“simply … can’t.”1

One option could be home-schooling or tutoring. This would give the child the opportunity to learn

within the home, hence not needing to attend school if that distresses them. However, that is clearly

not always possible for families, whether from the lack of time, money to hire a tutor, or not having

the knowledge for home-schooling.

Partnering with charity groups, such as the Smith Family mentoring program, can be another way

of supporting students to stay engaged with their schooling.

It is important to recognise that school refusal is a mental health problem, rather than a behavioural

1 Black 2022.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 38 Benjamin Cronshaw

2

problem.  Children  experiencing  distress  should  be  supported  with  mental  health  support  &

counselling (as needed), and being empathetic rather than judgemental. Ultimately, we need to do

what is for their benefit, rather than imposing expectations on them.

While  problems  with  disengagement  (students  struggling,  or  finding  it  hard  to  pay  attention  at

school) and detachment (withdrawing from school altogether) have existed for a while, these seem

to have been exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic. The sudden and disruptive impact from the

COVID-19 pandemic and switching to online learning, along with lockdowns in some areas, would

have  been  traumatising  and  disruptive  for  many  kids.  Even  as  a  young  adult  going  through

university  in  Melbourne,  there  were  challenging  periods  for  my  mental  health  and  study.  The

impact on younger people, especially as school is a big part of their routine and social lives, would

have been immense.

This underlines the importance of studying this issue, listening to the students themselves about

how they are feeling and what they want to do for their education, and providing mental health

support and any other educational supports they need to learn or adjust back into school.

I  appreciate  the  work  of  this  Inquiry  to  support  the  education  of  young  people.  Thank  you  for

considering my submission.

Benjamin Cronshaw.

Please accept this letter and response to the terms of reference (refer Appendix A) as Children
and  Young  People  with  Disability  Australia's  (CYDA)  submission  to  the  Education  and
Employment  References  Committee's  Inquiry  into  The  national trend of school refusal  and
related matters (Inquiry).

Students with disability face  multiple barriers and difficulties in accessing education , support
for  reasonable  adjustments  and  the  same  curriculum  as  their  non-disabled  peers,  placing
enormous  pressure  on  them .  Significantly,  the  lives  of  children  and  young  people  with
disability  have  been  thrown  into  turmoil  throughout  the  global  COVID-19  pandemic  period ,
further exacerbating and increasing the experience of school refusal.

The experience of school refusal  is a significant challenge for students, families and schools
but there are many areas of the experience that need more research, resources and evidence
based data to support all parties.

CYDA welcomes this Inquiry as an opportunity to examine:

1.  how  students with  disability are supported to  ensure attendance  and  engagement at

and with school across the curriculum and social and extra-curricular activities

2.  how school refusal exacerbates and/or is driven by existing system inequity
3.  how families and schools respond to the experience of school refusal and the impact

of ableism and societal beliefs

4.  how can existing  and  future  school-based  measures of wellbeing  and  inclusion  help

address experiences of school refusal

Without  targeted  and  adequate  research,  data,  policy  responses,  action  and  intervention,
children and young people will  continue to feel the social and economic impacts for a lifetime.

Please  refer  to  the  attached  Appendix  A  for  more  detailed  responses  to  select  terms  of
reference and Appendix B for further information on CYDA's relevant policy work. If you would
like to know more about our submission or CYDA's work,  please feel free to contact CYDA's
Policy and  Research Manager, Dr Liz Hudson on (03) 9417 1025 or lizhudson@cyda.org.au.

Kind regards,

Skye Kakoschke-Moore

Submission for the 2022 inquiry into the national trend of school refusal.

The Australian Parents Counci l thanks the Senate Educat ion and Employment Committee for the opportunity to
participate in th is inquiry and puts forth the following perspectives.

Social and emotional support services, wrap-around care and therapies need to be co-located in educational
settings.

Stigma still exists for students with mental health issues and their families. This needs to be addressed by school
communities.

Authentic methods of parent engagement including home visits have a tremendous impact on the success of
reintegrating students back into school

Trauma-informed practice needs to be embedded in schools alongside increased knowledge, awareness and
understanding of school-induced emotional distress.

The Australian Parents Counci l is a representative body that bridges the gap between parents and government
policymakers. We are on a mission to help all children thrive in non-government schools. To be successful in this goal
we need both sound government policy and empowered parents to ensure academic, social and emotional success
in all students.

The  Austra lian  Parents  Council  has  provided  this  service  and  prov ided  parents  w ith  an  avenue  to  participate  by
delivering a trustworthy voice on education policy for over 60 years. We are a non-denominational, non-party political
organisation that advocates for parents with children in non-government schools (Catholic and Independent) and for
Austra lian  parents more generally. We are an  independent,  diverse,  and  inclusive  organisation of parents from  all
states and territories of Australia.

The  work  of the  Australian  Parents  Council  over  many  years  has  contributed  to  the  improvement  of children' s
educational  experiences  and  outcomes,  progressive  reforms  in  schooling,  and  investments  in  the social  capital  of
school communit ies throughout Australia.

We welcome this opportunity to contribute our views on the 2022 inquiry into school refusa l and related matters from
the parent perspective.

Kind regards,

Jenny Branch-Allen
President
Austra lian Parents Council

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 40 It is increasingly becoming apparent that there are long-lasting impacts on students' social and emotional health
from not only the switching back and forth to remote learning but also the pandemic itself. To prepare for this
submission the Australian Parents Council spoke to parents, support services and overseas experts to address the
specific terms of reference for this inquiry.

TERMS OF REFERENCE

1.      The increasing number since the COVID-19 pandemic, of young people and their families who are
experiencing school refusal;

 The Australian Parents Council has been having conversations with parents about School Anxiety as early as 2019.
We can confirm that Covid-19 and the actions taken to mitigate the spread of the disease have not only impacted
the students already experiencing school anxiety but it has exacerbated the situation. Our 2022 parent sentiment
survey supported this statement with some parents reporting the pandemic being the catalyst for change or school
choices.

“My youngest child decided they hated being at school because she had separation anxiety and didn't feel safe.
She was home-schooled with my other child for the first 2 months of this year. I decided to send them to a Steiner
education instead and it's been much better since.”

-        Parent from South Australia

 The research supports the idea that school anxiety and refusal in based in emotional distress. The support services
that we consulted in this process support this statement citing that their clients are experiencing stress and anxiety
around the school environment particularly due to the unpredictability and overwhelm of a changing school
environment. Many parents report that the practicalities of the changes exacerbated the distress of children that
were already experiencing school anxiety. Many of these could have been mitigated with small changes but these
were not forthcoming in such a chaotic transition. They also report that decisions made by education directorates,
not schools themselves contributed to the problem.

“The Education Directorate changed the settings available on Chromebooks, so he could no longer have a dark
screen or a different cursor character. These may seem minor, however they had a big impact on his ability to
cope with the changes brought about by the lockdown.”

-        Parent from the Australian Capital Territory

 2.     How school refusal is affecting young people and their families and the impacts it is having on the
employment and financial security of parents and carers;

 The impact on young people suffering from school anxiety has also reached beyond the school gate. Parents report
some have been lucky to access the luxury of flexible working arrangements or the ability to take long periods of
time off work. However, this is the exception, not the rule. All speak of the hardship of juggling their work with the
needs of their child. Additionally, those who seek alternatives for their children to enable them to get access to
education speak of the expense.

“My daughter reached school refusal, so we now home-school and it works for her but I had to give up my
job and it costs a lot of money (we get tutors to help) but no funding from the government.”

-        Parent from New South Wales

“My son qualifies for additional funding because he has ASD. However, on the days when I can get him to school,
he doesn’t have the additional support his funding should afford him because the school has obviously spent it on

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 40



 other high-needs students. However, that money should be able to be used to assist in mitigating his issues. He is
selectively mute so it's not like he can speak up for himself either.”

-        Parent from the Australian Capital Territory

Further to that, the difficulty in gaining access to support services needs to be addressed. Parents with children in
the non-government sector may have some ability to access additional therapies and services.  This is supported in
the research with Devenney & O’Toole stating that parents from higher socio-economic backgrounds have more
choice in accessing private services for assessment and therapeutic support. (2021, 35)  Increasingly non-
government schools are employing occupational therapists or speech therapists as a method of trying to meet the
needs of their community. However, these roles do not necessarily directly address the need of students with school
anxiety however they may be able to play a preventative role in the future. The public school system needs to have
the funding to be able to do the same. Predominately, however, these services are all procured outside of the
educational system and very hard to access. Finally, the research shows that getting children to therapist
appointments to address their needs is a contributing factor to school absences. (Adams 2021) This suggests that a
cohesive approach that co-locates support services within school settings would benefit children experiencing school
refusal.

3.      The impacts and demands of the increasing caseload on service providers and schools to support these
students and their families;

 It is very clear from a parent’s perspective that schools are not coping with the increasing demands of meeting the
academic, social and emotional well-being of their students. Schools, teachers and principals are stretched,
exhausted and disenfranchised. As are the parents of children with school anxiety/refusal. Added to this, health
services are also stretched and exhausted. Collaboration and co-location of services within school communities is
imperative. Additionally, an array of support is required to form a cohesive support structure including social
workers, psychologists, school chaplains, learning support officers and Family and Community Engagement officers.
(Heyne and Brouwer-Borghuis 2022, 35) More capacity must be built into the system as well as collaboration across
sectors. Information sharing is imperative and education services to inform parents of the importance of this need to
be undertaken.

 Finally, it has to be noted that not all families have the ability or the means, both financially and physically to access
services to support their children to meet their social and emotional needs.

4.     How relevant state, territory and federal departments are working to monitor and address this growing
school refusal challenge;

 No parent or support service we spoke to were aware of any programs or funding conducted by their state or
territory to support them in this issue. Many actually felt they had exhausted all of their options and were left alone
in working towards a solution.

The Australian Parents Council advocates that the following solutions be considered in addressing this issue.

Social and emotional support services, wrap-around care and therapies need to be co-located in educational
settings.

Speaking to parents who are responsible for children who are refusing to go to school has been daunting. One thing
is very clear parents are beside themselves and have exhausted themselves trying to find solutions for their child.
The parents we spoke to have thrown every available resource to support their child. They are feeling abandoned by
their child’s school. Parents and the services they employ to support them expressed that the interventions and
school support they were requesting from school or government departments were not onerous. However, they
directly experience the pressure the education system is under.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 40



 “As my son withdrew, and as the general functioning of school got more difficult, it seemed his supports
around the school disappeared. This exacerbated the situation to the point where the last half of this year he
has been unable to attend more than a few times. Several attempts to have meetings with the school
executive to work out a plan to get him back to school were ignored or missed and after many years of
fighting for him, I simply gave up. There were other areas of his life that needed attention now, and I no
longer had the emotional capability to try to engage a school that seemed to have abandoned both of us. No
one from the school checked in to see how we were or offer help, and this highlighted to me how kids get lost
from the school system. Students generally do not disengage from the system unless there are a number of
factors involved, and schools need to realise they play a critical role in minimising this, especially when
parents are reaching out for help.”

-

Parent from the Australian Capital Territory

The research in this area also supports the lack of understanding of the complexity of an issue like school avoidance,
anxiety or refusal.

Stigma still exists for students with mental health issues and their families. This needs to be addressed by school
communities.

The research strongly suggests that for parents there is a stigma attached to school refusal with this perception from
school staff creating a disconnect and barriers to crucial information about the situation being shared between the
home and school. (Eccelston 2021, 13) Deveney and O’Toole discuss the criticism that families can face and the
assumption that this is a family problem and not a school issue. (2021, 34) All of the parents and support staff we
spoke to acknowledged this issue and spoke of the difficulties they faced in addressing this bias.

“Parents feel blamed and judged so try to solve the issue by themselves rather than ask for additional assistance
from the school. We find often parents will make an approach to the school asking if they have noticed anxious
behaviours or for help identifying anxious behaviours but because teachers aren’t trained to recognise initial
signs and symptoms a critical intervention point gets missed.”

-        Social support worker from the Australian Capital Territory.

There is also a very strong correlation between school anxiety/refusal and autism spectrum disorder. (Adams, 2021,
3355) Compounding this, parents of children with ASD have a higher prevalence of mental health issues, contributing
to the trauma that impacts school anxiety/refusal. (Adams 2021, 3355) Additionally, family trauma or other adverse
childhood experiences are also contributing factors to school refusal. These factors create a very complex situation
whereby only professional specialist services like school psychologists and social workers have the skills to assist.

The families we spoke with felt that the school was hesitant, unwilling or unable to address their issue as it was
beyond the usual scope of academic conversation expected from the teaching profession, understandable when you
consider that teachers have only been trained to address the academic needs of their students. The research also
supports the position of these parents with a US research project showing that 88% of parent participants viewed
communications with teachers as being centred on academic performance concerns.  Parents reported there were
few positive opportunities to discuss and support interpersonal relationships between parents and teachers.
(Eccelston 2021, 48)

Teachers are increasingly being called upon to be knowledgeable and responsive to the mental health of the young
people that they work with. Teachers want to be responsive to the social and emotional needs of the children under
their care but they need to be supported to achieve this. To be successful they need to have access to mental health
education from their initial training, with refresher training along their career journey. Or alternatively, they need to
have access to professionals that can support students complex needs at their fingertips.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 40



 •           Authentic methods of parent engagement including home visits have a tremendous impact on the success
of reintegrating students back into school

Never before has the importance of the home-school partnership been so apparent. The Australian Parents Council
represents parents with children in the non-government sector therefore the parents we spoke to have a greater
capacity to have access to support and services to assist them in aiding their child. However, the restrictions of the
pandemic not only disrupted the child’s school environment but their therapies as well.

“When school resumed, most of the non-academic activities that helped him manage his schoolwork had
ceased, so he no longer had the outlets that eased his anxieties. After the second lockdown in 2021, the rest
of the non-academic activities stopped, the school timetable completely changed and students were no
longer able to be inside during break times. All this meant school was now seen as more unpredictable and a
less safe place to be.”

-            Parent from the Australian Capital Territory

In our consultation with Dr Kristen Eccelston, she outlined her very successful program at MacGruder High School
where an Enhanced Social Emotional Education Service was designed for students who couldn’t attend mainstream
education. The program was heavily supported by social workers, psychologists and teacher support assistance. All
students had an Individual Education Plan and the educational philosophy was heavily embedded in project learning.
A key part of the program’s success was home visits by the support staff. Debbie Pushor is a leading academic in
family engagement whose work has centred on the impact teachers and school staff visiting the family home can
have on student engagement and outcomes, especially in low socio-economic communities. (Pushor and Ted 2018,
211)

The Australian Parents Council strongly supports the embedding of an authentic parent engagement policy to
support families facing the difficult task of re-engaging their children in school while working in partnership with
teachers and principals. We also advocate for school leaders to value the knowledge that families bring to the table
in terms of adjustments, strategies and understanding of their child.

 •           Trauma-informed practice needs to be embedded in schools alongside increased knowledge, awareness

and understanding of school-induced emotional distress.

Balancing the needs of teachers to meet the demands of the curriculum as well the needs of their students is well
documented to be a difficulty of the education system. (Deveney 2021, 37) Added to this the focus of teacher
training to become increasingly academic rather than relationally focused leaves needs unmet in the classroom.
(Eccelston 2021, 27) Despite our best efforts schools are not safe spaces for all students and a greater effort must be
made to understand the requirements of diverse students to ensure a safe environment for all students. This can be
achieved via a variety of environments. One aspect we heard loud and clear from the parents who engaged with us
was that they felt they only needed little adjustments from the school to achieve this but the school was unwilling to
meet these requests. Because whilst only small they fell outside of normal policy areas and school leadership were
unwilling to bend the rules.

“My child flourished in Agriculture class; it was the only class he was somewhat enthusiastic about attending. We are
realistic about our child’s ability and we see him having a happy future being a farmhand. We would have happily
had him attend Ag class as often as possible as the method to reintegrate him back to school. But this wasn’t allowed
by the school. There was the expectation that if he could attend Ag he could attend all classes.”

-

 Parent from Victoria

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 40

children on the Austism Spectrum.” Journal of Austism and Developmental Disprders, 3353-3365.

Professionals on School Refusal.” International Journal of Educational Psychology, 21-47.
doi:https://doi.org/10.17583/ijep.2021.7304.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 41


 Executive Summary of Recommendations

Terms of Reference a

- the increasing number since the COVID-19 pandemic, of young people and their families who are
experiencing school refusal

Recommendation 1

Covid has exacerbated the experience of school refusal but in the main is not the cause. The Inquiry
needs to identify the causes of school refusal, focus on solutions and how the education system in
Australia can address these with preventative, early intervention, and re-engagement strategies.

Terms of Reference b

- how school refusal is affecting young people and their families and the impacts it is having on the
employment and financial security of parents and carers

Recommendation 2

Data identifies the need for wrap-around support services that go beyond the individual student and
must  provide  assistance  to  families/carers.  Home  life  and  families/carers  can  unintentionally
become hinderers of otherwise successful supports to the student.

Terms of Reference c

- the impacts and demands of the increasing case load on service providers and schools to support
these students and their families

Recommendation 3

The complexity of reasons leading to school refusal must be met with a complexity of strategies to
address  these;  there  is  no  quick,  one-size-fits-all  solution  and  therefore  a  highly  personalised,
targeted approach is required.

Prevention:

•  Schools to upskills staff in trauma informed teaching and support practices.

•  Schools  to  be  provided  with  tools  to  identify  students  at  risk  of  school  refusal;  early
attendance  data  alone  is  insufficient  and  narrow.  Identifier  must  include  social-connection
and wellbeing indicators.

Early-intervention:

•  As soon as a student is identified as at risk of school refusal, a dedicated, fully funded and
reportable process needs to be initiated within a given short period (e.g., four weeks). This
process must include trained wellbeing staff, school leadership, student, families/carers.

•  Schools must be mandated to report on numbers of  students identified as at risk of school
refusal (disengaged) and/or as school refuser (detached), including action taken to support
re-engagement and outcomes.

•

Intervention  services  identified  must  be  fully  funded,  including  psychological  diagnostic
testing and treatment for the student, family intervention services based on need (financial
counselling  and  aid;  mental  health  support  to  families/carers;  housing;  education  and
employment support e.g. via Skills First Reconnect; family violence  interventions;  outreach
services; …)

•  Schools must follow a mandatory process of providing student and their families/carers with
information and/or referral about flexible learning options, special assistance and specialist
secondary schools in their area.

3

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 41
 Specialist intervention (re-engagement)

•  Expand flexible learning programs at all secondary schools with a view to enable students to
return  to  their  mainstream  classrooms.  This  must  be  overseen  by  members  of  the  school
leadership team, transition to re-engagement needs to be leadership responsibility.

•  Expanding funding to special assistance and specialist secondary schools to ensure all young

people can have access to a specialist provider within their local government area.

Terms of Reference d

- how relevant state, territory and federal departments are working to monitor and address this
growing school refusal challenge

Recommendation 4

•  Recognise  school  refusal  as  mental  health  issue  to  be  included,  for  example  in  NCCD

(National Consistent Collection of Data on school students with disability) funding.

•

•

In  line  with  the  recommendation  Terms  of  Reference  c,  early-intervention,  States  need  to
fund  school  processes  and  timelines  that  schools  need  to  report  on  illustrating  their
responses to school refusal. States need to publicly report on the findings.

In  Victoria,  expand  the  Navigator  program’s  terms  of  reference  to  avoid  students  being
exited when not reengaged (rigid timeframes are ineffective and not student centred).

•  Explore expanding the Navigator program’s terms of reference to include support (practical,
financial, mental health) to families/carers of students in the program to ensure that wrap-
around services are addressing all factors contributing to school refusal.

•  Ensure  young  person-centred  transitioning  between  existing  programs,  e.g.  in  Victoria

between Navigator and Skills First Reconnect.

Terms of Reference e

– any other related matters

Recommendation 5

•

Include  school  refusal  indicators,  impact,  risks  and  support  strategies  into  Youth  Mental
Health First Aid Certificate.

•  Advocate  for  the  inclusion  of  trauma-informed  teaching  practice  in  all  Master  of  Teaching

programs.

•  Advocate  for  the  inclusion  of  wellbeing  and  trauma-informed  practice  in  all  Education

Support Certificate programs.

•  Re-evaluate and improve (including funding) existing processes around Individual Education
Plans/Individual  Learning  Plans  in  secondary  education,  making  them  meaningful  and
student based with the involvement of parents/carers.

•  Provide  additional  funding  for education  support staff  (teacher  aides)  to  assist  students  in
building  their  capacity  and  re-engaging  within  the  classroom  space.  Ideally,  every
mainstream  classroom  should  have  an  accompanying  education  support  worker  given  the
increase in students’ needs and the overwhelming number of undiagnosed students.

•  Key  support  programs  need  to  receive  specific,  funded  training  on  school  refusal  and

intervention approaches, e.g. in Victoria Navigator, Skills First Reconnect.

4

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 41
 Introduction

Mainstream education systems have increasingly been unable to address the complexity that leads
to school refusal. Research documenting the causes leading to school refusal, the negative long-term
impact of school refusal on the individual and society, and policy solutions to circumvent the issue
has been manifold spanning the past twenty years. Below is a selection of this research highlighting
key points.

Causes

A US report from 20121 describes 3 broad categories of causes:

(1) students who cannot attend school due to illness, family responsibilities, housing instability,
the need to work or involvement with the juvenile justice system;

(2)  students  who  will  not  attend  school  to  avoid  bullying,  unsafe  conditions,  harassment  and
embarrassment; and

(3)  students  who  do  not  attend  school  because  they,  or  their  parents,  do  not  see  the  value  in
attending  school,  they  have  something  else  they  would  rather  do,  or  nothing  stops  them  from
skipping school.

A recent Australian report notes that factors affecting disengagement leading to detachment include
identity  issues,  learning  difficulties,  lack  of  financial  resources,  family  dysfunction,  mental  illness,
extra-curricular  activities,  school  connectedness,  academic  motivation,  relationships  with  teachers
and peers, and bullying2.

Below are numerous additional studies support the above findings.

•  Housing  and  living  arrangements,  employment  hours,  medical  reasons,  custody  issues,  or

disruptive living situations all contribute to why students miss school frequently3.

•  Students  living in poverty are more  likely than students  from higher-income  families to be

chronically absent from school4.

•

Individual  factors  (such  as  hyperactivity,  conduct  problems,  and  poor  perceived  health),
family  factors  (such  as  low  maternal  education  and  high  levels  of  unemployment),  and
school  factors  (such  as  not  feeling  safe  or  not  feeling  treated  with  respect  at  school)  all
contributed  to  students’  poor  attendance.  They  include  bullying,  gender  identity  and
sexuality, and adverse childhood experiences. (Ibid)

•  Wood et al. (2012) found that students who exhibit mental health issues one school year are
more likely to be chronically absent the following year. Another psychological influence on
absenteeism is social anxiety disorder or social phobia.

•  Students with high anxiety are likely to have phobic reactions to school as a result of inflated
perceptions  of  threat,  such  as  separation  from  parents,  social  evaluation,  or  academic
difficulty5.

•  Children  with  a  history  of  maltreatment  or  exposure  to  major  trauma,  such  as  witnessing
domestic  violence  or  experiencing  a  natural  disaster,  are  more  likely  than  those  without
these  exposures  to  experience  absenteeism,  truancy,  school  suspension,  and  school
dropout6.

Longitudinal cohort studies have  revealed that conduct  disorder and depressive  symptoms

Impact

•  Researchers  have  shown  the  negative  impact  of  low  school  attendance  on  negative

academic achievement and educational opportunities7.

•  Refusing to attend school can have long term adverse implications on students’ physical and

mental health8.

•  A  US  study  2003-2008  found  that  educational  factors  such  as  chronic  absenteeism  were

stronger predictors of justice system involvement than allegations of maltreatment9.

•

In Australia, the social cost of disengagement and young people dropping out of school has
been  calculated  by  Stephan  Lamb  and  Shuyan  Huo.  It  includes  loss  of  earnings,  reduced
quality  of  life,  private  health  and  taxation  costs  among  others.  The  conservative  estimate
that each early school leaver has a fiscal cost of $334 600 over their lifetime and a social cost
of $616 200 over their lifetime.10

Policy solutions

School attendance problems are complex and often very challenging to address. And for responses
to be effective in getting students to school more often, they need to reflect this11.

School  disengagement  and  refusal  requires  a  conceptual  framework  that  helps  to  organise  policy
responses within all levels of the educational system, as well as extending into other areas of social
public policy.  That responses  need to  recognise  the importance of school attendance  on students’
well-being.  Solutions  need  to  include  dismantling  systems  that  hinder  students  from  attending
school regularly or reproducing deficit narratives about students who have to miss school. 12

An  Australian  longitudinal  study13  points  to  the  importance  of  professional  development  for
educators, teachers and school leaders in relation to:

(i)  creating environments that are high in emotional support,

(ii)  fostering children’s ability to develop, practice and enhance self-regulation skills, and

(iii) promoting children’s oral language development in the early years.

The role of federal policy

Australia  is  a  signatory  to  the  International  Covenant  on  Economic,  Social  and  Cultural  Rights
(ICESCR).  The  right  to  education  is  contained  in  article  13  of  the ICESCR  and  considered  a  human
right18.

The  Australian  Government  has  a  role  in  education  funding  and  national  policy.  While  the
Commonwealth  does  not  operate  any  schools  or  employ  any  teachers,  funding  responsibility  is
shared  between  the  Australian  Government  and  state  and  territory  governments,  and  national
education policy is decided by all governments working together through the National Cabinet19.

All  Australian  governments  have  committed  to  young  people  finishing  school.  In  1990,  Australia
ratified  the  United  Nations  Convention  on  the  Rights  of  the  Child,  which  requires  Australia  to
recognise the right to education for everyone under the age of 18 years.

In  2009,  the Council  of  Australian  Governments  agreed  on  the  National  Partnership  on  Youth
Attainment  and  Transitions setting  the  goal  that,  by  2015,  90  percent  of  young  people  would
complete  Year  12  or  its  equivalent,  up  from  83.5 per  cent  in  2009.  To  support  this,  governments
agreed  to  a  range  of  initiatives  like  the  national  program  Youth  Connections,  explicitly  focused on
linking  young  people  who  were  disengaged  from  education  back  into  school  or  an  alternative
setting.  Around  4000  young  people  per  annum  were  re-engaged  with  education,  with  survey  data
showing the majority who were engaged to education stayed after exiting the program. The program
was cut after a change of federal government making states responsible for education.

Background - Djerriwarrh Community College

Djerriwarrh Community  &  Education  Services  (DCES)  is  a not-for-profit organisation delivering  a
range of community services in the western suburbs of Melbourne since 1989. Numerous of these
programs  have  been  targeting  disadvantaged  young  people.  DCES  became  a Registered  Training
Organisation in 1996 and started offering VCAL courses as a non-school provider over a number of
years recommencing in 2015.

Close  relationships  were  developed  with  local  schools  and  referrals  to  the  VCAL  program  were
consistent. Given its non-school provider status, the VCAL program had significantly fewer financial
resources  than  schools  while  supporting  high  needs  students  whose  needs  weren’t  met  at
mainstream schools. Student cohort key issues were on the one hand relating to unmet emotional
and mental health needs, including bullying experiences, and on the other hand behavioural issues
resulting to suspension/expulsion. This complexity created several challenges including the inability
to attract experienced teachers and limited options to employ support staff such as youth workers.

After running at an increasingly financial loss of the VCAL program in 2018/19, in 2020 DCES applied

Anecdotally, DCC staff have noted that since Covid, staff turnaround and absences are significantly

Two (18%) of the students completing the survey still identified as school refusers.

Covid has exacerbated the experience of school refusal but in the main is not the cause. The Inquiry
needs to identify the causes of school refusal, focus on solutions and how the education system in
Australia can address these with preventative, early intervention, and re-engagement strategies.

early  diagnosis  of  dyslexia,  his  child  had  to  sit  weekly  spelling  tests  at  primary  school  fostering  a
sense of worthlessness in his child who felt like “the dumbest kid in class”.

This parent noted:

“It took two suicide attempts for my child to be referred to Djerriwarrh Community College
via the hospital.”

Another carer noted that mainstream schools push a narrow path with an inability to listen to what
students need or want. This was supported by another parent who noted that every time they called
the mainstream secondary school they had to reexplain their situation as if nobody knew their child.

 Recommendation 3

The complexity of reasons leading to school refusal must be met with a complexity of strategies to
address  these;  there  is  no  quick,  one-size-fits-all  solution  and  therefore  a  highly  personalised,
targeted approach is required.

Prevention:

•  Schools to upskills staff in trauma informed teaching and support practices.

•  Schools  to  be  provided  with  tools  to  identify  students  at  risk  of  school  refusal  early
attendance  data  alone  is  insufficient  and  narrow.  Identifier must  include  social-connection
and wellbeing indicators.

Early-intervention:

•  As soon as a student is identified as at risk of school refusal, a dedicated, fully funded and
reportable process needs to be initiated within a given short period (e.g. four weeks). This
process must include trained wellbeing staff, school leadership, student, families/carers.

•  Schools must be mandated to report on numbers of  students identified as at risk of school
refusal (disengaged) and/or as school refuser (detached), including action taken to support
re-engagement and outcomes.

•

Intervention  services  identified  must  be  fully  funded,  including  psychological  diagnostic
testing and treatment for the student, family intervention services based on need (financial
counselling  and  aid;  mental  health  support  to  families/carers;  housing;  education  and
employment support e.g. via Skills First Reconnect; family  violence  interventions;  outreach
services; …)

•  Schools must follow a mandatory process of providing student and their families/carers with
information and/or referral about flexible learning options, special assistance and specialist
secondary schools in their area.

Specialist intervention (re-engagement)

•  Expand flexible learning programs at all secondary schools with a view to enable students to
return  to  their  mainstream  classrooms.  This  must  be  overseen  by  members  of  the  school
leadership team, transition to re-engagement needs to be leadership responsibility.

•  Expanding funding to special assistance and specialist secondary schools to ensure all young

people can have access to a specialist provider within their local government area.

As a special assistance senior secondary school, Djerriwarrh Community College knows first-hand
how resource intensive re-engagement support is. Some of our experiences are listed below.

Schools – Extra workload outside of class time

•  Phone calls to students and their guardians checking in on the student and encouraging

engagement.

•  Meetings with the student or guardian often cancelled at last minute, rescheduling.
•  Creation/collation/photocopying of work for students to complete at home, staff member to
clarify instructions and task demands to student over the phone or in person. Distribution of
completed work to appropriate teachers.

•  Extra space required for students to work in when anxiety prevents them from being in the

classroom.

17

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 41



 Service providers

•  Waitlists (listing services who have waitlists that support e.g. Headspace, Orygen, Navigator

etc.)

•  Mental health providers - costs, inaccessible, waitlists, barriers (e.g. stigma, cultural

security), eligibility

•  Staff turnovers in community and health sectors
•  Changing of workers- e.g. Headspace having non-set therapist/ workers/ interventions
•
Lack of referral options specifying in certain areas e.g. Cognitive disabilities, MH etc.

Recommendation 4

•  Recognise  school  refusal  as  mental  health  issue  to  be  included,  for  example  in  NCCD

(National Consistent Collection of Data on school students with disability) funding.

•

•

In  line  with  the  recommendation  Terms  of  Reference  c,  early-intervention,  States  need  to
fund  school  processes  and  timelines  that  schools  need  to  report  on  illustrating  their
responses to school refusal. States need to publicly report on the findings.

In  Victoria,  expand  the  Navigator  program’s  terms  of  reference  to  avoid  students  being
exited when not reengaged (rigid timeframes are ineffective and not student centred).

•  Explore expanding the Navigator program’s terms of reference to include support (practical,
financial, mental health) to families/carers of students in the program to ensure that wrap-
around services are addressing all factors contributing to school refusal.

•  Ensure  young  person-centred  transitioning  between  existing  programs,  e.g.  in  Victoria

between Navigator and Skills First Reconnect.

Recommendation 5

•

Include  school  refusal  indicators,  impact,  risks  and  support  strategies  into  Youth  Mental
Health First Aid Certificate.

•  Advocate  for  the  inclusion  of  trauma-informed  teaching  practice  in  all  Master  of  Teaching

programs.

•  Advocate  for  the  inclusion  of  wellbeing  and  trauma-informed  practice  in  all  Education

Support Certificate programs.

•  Re-evaluate and improve (including funding) existing processes around Individual Education
Plans/Individual  Learning  Plans  in  secondary  education,  making  them  meaningful  and
student based with the involvement of parents/carers.

•  Provide  additional  funding  for education  support staff  (teacher  aides)  to  assist  students  in
building  their  capacity  and  re-engaging  within  the  classroom  space.  Ideally,  every
mainstream  classroom  should  have  an  accompanying  education  support  worker  given  the
increase in students’ needs and the overwhelming number of undiagnosed students.

•  Key  support  programs  need  to  receive  specific,  funded  training  on  school  refusal  and

intervention approaches, e.g. in Victoria Navigator, Skills First Reconnect.

Submission

The national trend of school refusal and related matters

Education and Employment References Committee

9 December 2022

BRIEF SUMMARY:

Although  there  has  been  no  research  into  school  refusal  and  gifted  students  in  Australia,  our
members indicate that school refusal most commonly occurs when the special needs of their gifted
children  are  not  being  adequately  met  by  schools.  Early  school  leaving  has  been  described  as  the
‘end-point’ of disengagement, and research shows that disengagement for gifted students becomes
exponential  without  appropriate  provisions.  In  Australia,  it  is  estimated  that  up  to  40%  of  gifted
students  dropout  before the  end of  Year 12. Research also  shows most families of  gifted  students
who  homeschool  are  driven  to  do  so  after  numerous  unsatisfactory  attempts  to  stay  within  the
school  system,  and  that  some  2E  students  describe  homeschooling  as  a  way  to  address  their
emotional  distress  of  not  coping  with  regular  school.  We  found  gifted  students  in  Tasmania  were
adversely  affected  by  the  Covid-19  pandemic  due  to  impacts  to  their  support,  including  delays  in
psychological assessment, Professional Learning for teachers, and redeployment of teachers behind
online gifted programs. We note the majority of gifted students in the population are unidentified,
and  likely  to  be  at  extreme  risk  of  school  refusal  due  to  their  special  learning  needs  not  being
identified or addressed.

Tasmanian Association for the Gifted Inc.
GPO Box 1942, HOBART TAS 7001
Phone: 0467 528 048
Email: tasgifted@gmail.com

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 42









 Tasmanian  Association  for  the  Gifted  Inc.  submission  to  the  Education  and  Employment
References Committee regarding the national trend of school refusal and related matters

9 December 2022

INTRODUCTION

The  Tasmanian  Association  for  the  Gifted  Inc  (TAG)  is  a  non-profit  organisation  whose  primary
objective  is  to  provide  support  to  gifted  children,  their  families  and  teachers.  Our  committee
comprises  educators,  researchers,  and  parents  of  gifted  children,  and  we  represent  107  members
including families of gifted children and schools. Our focus is on supporting gifted children and their
families, and providing education to both members and non-members through monthly seminars on
gifted  issues  given  by  national  and  international  experts.  TAG  is  also  affiliated  with  the  Australian
Association for the Education of Gifted and Talented and is represented on its committee.

Who are gifted children?

Most  Australian  educational  policies1  use  Gagné’s  (2010)2  Differentiated  Model  of  Giftedness  and
Talent  with  respect  to  conceptions  of  giftedness.  This  theorises  that  a  gifted  child  has  ability  or
aptitude that places them in the top 10% of their age peers. Generally in Australia this is identified
through IQ tests administered by psychologists. It is important to note however that gifted children
are  not  necessarily  ‘top  of  the  class’.  Accurate  identification,  along  with  educational  support,
influences their talent development trajectory and underachievement remains until talent evolves. 3

The  learning  needs  of  gifted  students  are  as  different  from  the  norm  as  children  with  learning
disabilities  at  the  other  end  of  the  spectrum4.  Gifted  students  also  experience  and  respond  to
external influences quite differently to many of their same-age peers of average ability due to their
intellectual  development  and  their  social  and  emotional
asynchronous  chronological  and
complexities.5 Research reiterates that the unique characteristics of gifted children require accurate
identification  and  supportive  educational  provisions  to  enable  the  holistic  development  of  their
intellectual, social, and emotional growth. 6

Students. In: Frydenberg, E., Martin, A., Collie, R. (eds) Social and Emotional Learning in Australia and the Asia-
Pacific. Springer, Singapore.
2 Gagné, F. (2010). Motivation within the DMGT 2.0 framework. High Ability Studies, 1(2), 81–99.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 42



 Why is TAG’s work necessary?

Despite  two  Senate  inquiries7  8,  a  Victorian  Parliamentary  inquiry9,  and  numerous  policies  and
empirical  studies,  attitudes  persist  that  are  unsupportive  of  gifted  education  in  Australia10.
Generally,  Australian  gifted  education  “remains  fragmented  and  inconsistent,  reliant  more  on  the
goodwill of principals, and the efforts of a few dedicated teachers and parent advocates, rather than
on a well-designed systematic approach” 11.

Nationally,  research  continues  to  indicate  that  teachers  and  school  psychologists  lack  essential
knowledge,  skills  and  confidence  to  identify  and  meet  the  needs  of  gifted  children12  13  14  15.  In
addition,  research  shows  that  belief  in  myths  and  misconceptions  regarding  the  needs  of  gifted
children are pervasive amongst Australian educators16 17  18. Our members’ experiences support this
e.g.  a  school  psychologist  told  a  member  they  didn’t  believe  gifted  students  existed;  a  school
Principal  attempted  to  dissuade  a  member’s  early  school  entry  for  social  reasons,  despite  no
research supporting this stance and early entry being supported by Department of Education policy.

Without  accurate  identification  and  appropriate  educational  provisions,  gifted  children  suffer.  In
Australia, it has been reported that up to 75% of gifted students underachieve19 and up to 40% of
gifted kids leave school without completing Year 12. It is further estimated that 20%-25% of gifted
kids  have  social  and  emotional  difficulties,  about  twice  as  many  as  in  the  general  student
population20.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 42


 TERM  OF  REFERENCE:  How  school  refusal  is  affecting  young  people  and  their  families  and  the
impacts it is having on the employment and financial security of parents and carers.

School  refusal  has  resulted  in  emotional  distress  and  anxiety  around  schooling  for  our  members’
gifted  children,  stress  for  their  families,  financial  impacts  such  as  taking  time  off  work,  and  the
additional burden for parents of becoming advocates for their gifted children’s needs along with, for
those  who  have  the  means,  financial  costs  in  pursuing  this  e.g.  private  psychological  assessment,
private schools, homeschooling.

School refusal has been reported by our members specifically when a child’s special needs as a gifted
student are not being adequately met by schools. For example:

“My  son  was reading  lengthy  books  prior  to  entering  Kindergarten21.  By  grade  2  -  my  son  was
extremely anxious and unhappy at school, due to several (grade 1+2) disengaged teachers.  One
teacher indicated while she knew he "could read chapter books by prep", but that he would just
have to read the same books as the others in the class.  She didn’t have to time to differentiate.

She said the only way we could get him extended was to pay for a gifted assessment through a
psychologist ourselves or wait 3 years to go through the school system.  We opted to pay for a
private assessment.  He received an assessment of 97th percentile, her ‘extension’ of him in class
was to allow him to do Minecraft when he had finished his work.  This could happen 7-10 times a
day.

My son ended up hating going to school, with major meltdowns and crying and clinging to us at
the gate of school every day.”22

In the above case, the parents claimed sick leave when they could not get their child to school.

Parents also express fear for the future:

“We have been affected by school refusal. We are lucky that she is only young so we can get her
there, but I hate leaving her crying and upset. We are also dealing with it after school as she is so
unregulated. I am dreading what will happen as she gets bigger and older. I feel that it will be
very hard to get her there. There has been no increase in support. If anything, there is less. They
(the school) admitted that they let students down who needed extension work and would try to
do better, but their concern was to catch the ones up that were behind.” 23

Some  of  our  members  are  able  to  intervene  with  solutions  before  their  child’s  disengagement  or
school refusal becomes significant, such as finding another school to address their child’s needs:

“The  teacher  basically  refused  to  deal  with  his  advanced  needs.  He'd  come  home  with
comments like "the work is a waste of the lead in my pencil" and telling about daydreaming.
Afraid  of  complete  disengagement  and  refusal,  I  contemplated  homeschooling  but  did  not

21 In Tasmania, Kindergarten is the equivalent of Preschool
22 TAG Member correspondence received 5/12/22
23 TAG Member correspondence received 1/12/22

3

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 42








 feel  competent  to  teach  him  the  literacy  side  of  the  curriculum  and  it  would  have  meant
giving  up  work  -  which  would  have  had  huge  economic  impacts.    We  looked  at  a range  of
schools, including private (which would also have had huge economic impact) and eventually
settled  on  a  different  government  school  with  a  classroom  teacher  who  took  the  simple
approach  that  if  he  was  capable  of  working  above  grade  level,  that  is  the  sort  of  work  he
should be given.”24

But  some  parents  have  limited  options  for  their  child’s  education,  and  may  not  find  solutions
through traditional schools. One member’s child recounted her troubled experience of Year 4:

“I would have to repeat and repeat and repeat and repeat the same work.”25

Her mother clarified:

“So basically, she was given the same work (as everyone else) and when she’d finished the
work she would be told to redo it because everyone else was still doing it. And it got the point
that  she  came  home  one  day  and  said  “That’s  it.  I’m  not  going  back”.  And  that’s  why  she
now homeschools.” 26

In Australia, motivations to homeschool gifted students vary from those of the general homeschool
population:  research  shows  most  families  of  gifted  children  are  driven  to  homeschool  after
numerous  unsatisfactory  attempts  to  stay  within  the  school  system,  rather  than  choosing
homeschooling due to lifestyle or moral choices 27 28 29 30; and in a narrative-based Australian study,
2E students (gifted students with identified disabilities) describe homeschooling as a way to address
their emotional distress of not coping with regular school31.

Although  Tasmania’s  Department  of  Education  (“DoE”)  acknowledges  “that  without  intervention,
gifted  students  are  at  high  risk  of  under-achieving,  disengaging  from  learning  and/or  developing
emotional  and  behavioural  problems32”,  our  members  indicate  this  often  does  not  translate  into
school  action.  Effective  interventions  such  as  Acceleration,  which  is  both  supported  by  a  strong
empirical research base33  34  35 and outlined in DoE Procedure36, are uncommonly presented to our

 members. Research has shown that educator opposition to such interventions are common, due to
belief in pervasive myths e.g. that such interventions are harmful to social adjustment, or that gifted
students will achieve even without intervention37 38 39. And so, gifted students suffer:

“I’ve probably learnt about 2 or 3 things this year. I don’t learn, I just repeat the same thing
over  and  over  and  over..  Maths  -  I  just  couldn’t  concentrate.  I  was  that  bored  I  got  a  few
wrong and the teacher didn’t know I was actually good at it. I was just so bored.”40

Without appropriate provision, disengagement for gifted students becomes exponential41, with early
school  leaving  described  as  being  the  ‘end-point’  of  disengagement42.  In  Australia,  it  is  estimated
that up to 40% of gifted students dropout before the end of Year 1243.

To minimise school withdrawal as a consequence of ‘indirect school push out’, Jolly and Matthews
(2018)44 affirm that more attention and resources are needed at the school level to meet the needs
of gifted students. Conejeros-Solar & Smith (2019)45 note this is:

“a red light for the school system, a warning that questions the schooling model that in most
cases expels gifted students without even noticing. All students should be valued regardless
of their capacities and none should leave school because they did not fit in or because their
learning needs were not respected as evidenced by irrelevant programming or provisions.”

School refusal for gifted children is not limited to Tasmanian students – it is an Australian issue. A
search  of  the  Facebook  page  ‘Parents  of  gifted  children  Australia’46  reveals  over  a  hundred  posts
regarding school refusal. Due to confidentiality of the group, these cannot be shared here.

 Finally, we stress that the examples of school refusal from our members and the research outlined
above,  all  refer  to  identified  gifted  children.  We  predict  that  approximately  5,000  Tasmanian
students in public schools alone have not been identified47, and loose extrapolation to an Australian
estimate  of  unidentified  gifted  students  results  in  around  half  a  million  unidentified  gifted
students48. Unidentified  gifted  children  are  likely to  be  at  extreme  risk of  school  refusal and  other
detrimental issues due to their special learning needs not being identified or addressed.

TERM OF REFERENCE: The increasing number since the COVID-19 pandemic, of young people and
their families who are experiencing school refusal

We have outlined above how school refusal has been reported by our members specifically when a
gifted  student’s  special  needs  are  not  being  adequately  met  by  schools.  Members  have  reported
impacts to support for gifted children’s needs due to the COVID-19 pandemic:

“Covid has impacted education greatly as for the past 2 years a lot of (gifted) children have
not  had  the  support  they  need  or  the  intervention  and  there  are  not  enough  services
available in most cases a 2 year wait to even see anyone.”49

Earlier this year TAG was left to petition Government Ministers when the Department of Education’s
Gifted  Online  programs  were  cut  due  to  teachers  of  this  program  being  redeployed  to  deliver
general online learning to students quarantining at home. Many of our members reported the Gifted
Online program was a key reason for their students to maintain some enthusiasm for returning to
school. Although Covid provisions must be made for all students, they were made at the expense of
the needs of gifted students.

A  6  hour  Professional  Development  course  available  (at  the  discretion  of  school  Principals)  to
teachers working with gifted children was also delayed a term due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

CONCLUSION

Two  previous  Senate  inquiries  into  the  education  of  gifted  children  in  Australia  revealed  that  our
education  systems  regularly  fail  gifted  students,  and  that  gifted  students  regularly  suffer
psychological  distress,  boredom,  frustration,  and  underachievement.  There  has  been  very  little
implementation  of  the  many  recommendations  of  the  previous  inquiries,  to  the  detriment  of
hundreds  of  thousands  of  gifted  children  around  Australia.  Unfortunately,  school  refusal  in  gifted
students appears to be yet another symptom of this inaction.

47 Based on: 2019 Tasmanian government schools headcount of 62,297 students (https://publicdoc
umentcentre.education.tas.gov.au/library/Shared%20Documents/DoE-Annual-Report-2018-19.pdf). Australian
educational policies use Gagné’s Differentiated Model of Giftedness & Talent which predicts gifted children
comprise the top 10% of the student population (https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-981-10-
3394-0 8). Therefore, we would expect ~6230 gifted students in Tasmanian government schools. Gifted Online
courses are available for gifted & highly able Tasmanian students, and in 2019 were provided to 1279 students.
48 With the Tasmanian population being 2.2% of the Australian population, we extrapolate from our above
estimate of unidentified gifted students in Tasmanian government schools
(https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/people/population/national-state-and-territory-population/latest-release)
49 TAG Member correspondence received 1/12/22

6

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 42





 In a 2019 speech to Federal Parliament, Andrew Wilkie MP said:

“In every Tasmanian classroom, there are on average two or three gifted children but we are
letting them down. The result being that thousands of gifted kids are not being identified, not
being  given  the  opportunities  they  need,  and  not  being  allowed  to  reach  their  potential.
Deputy  Speaker,  this  country  can  afford to  support  all  students  with special  needs  not  just
those with learning difficulties. So, it is deeply troubling that achieving potential is too often
the  preserve  of  the  rich  and  vocal, or  that so  many gifted kids go unrecognised,  or that so
many parents have to fight to have their child assessed only to then wait a year50 to see  a
school psychologist.

Frankly,  we  need  a  system  redesigned  because  teachers  51must  be  trained  to  identify  and
cater for gifted children, schools need to be better resourced, and there needs to be a shift in
mindset. This is not about benefiting an elite group of students but rather understanding that
gifted  children  have  special  learning  needs  and  failing  to meet  them  can  lead to  boredom,
disengagement,  and  underachievement.  Remember  bright  kids  don’t  do  well  not  matter
what. In other words Deputy Speaker, we are letting some of our most brilliant minds go to
waste and that is unfair, counterproductive, and sometimes downright cruel.”52.

We concur.

 IMPACT ON ABORIGINAL AND TORRES STRAIT ISLANDER
YOUNG PEOPLE IN THE MALLEE

Introduction

As an Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Organisation (ACCHO), Mallee District Aboriginal Services

(MDAS) is making a submission to this Inquiry through the lens of impact on Aboriginal and Torres Strait

Islander children and young people.

MDAS has over 260 staff based in offices in Mildura, Swan Hill and Kerang, providing services for a client

population of 5000 people, located in a catchment of 32,618 km2. Priding itself on offering culturally safe,

evidenced-based support, MDAS delivers community services, which provide support for families, children,

youth, and adults, and include disability, social and emotional and wellbeing, housing, chronic disease

management and health and fitness, with a focus on early intervention, prevention, and empowerment.

MDAS consults widely to ensure local knowledge and voices inform our decision making and service delivery,

and that our programs meet the current and emerging needs of our communities.

There are a range of challenges faced by Aboriginal communities in the Mallee, many of which are consistent

with the lived experience of First Nations people across the country, within the paradigm of intergenerational

trauma, displacement, and inequity. The circumstances and life outcomes for Aboriginal people living in the

Mallee are exasperated by poorer access to services and supports, geographic isolation and an enduring bias

that sees the needs of regional, rural, and remote areas largely overlooked in the development of policy and

funding models.

These challenges and their impact on our Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children and young people are

articulated in Table A (page 5) below comparing key domains of Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal people at a local

(Mildura LGA), state (Victoria) and national level. Prior to the pandemic, we had already failed to meet the

Close the Gap target that aimed to reduce, by half, the chasm between Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal school

attendance by 2018. The 2020 Close the Gap Report identified that school attendance for Indigenous children

had not improved in the five years preceding 2019, indeed statistics showed that attendance rates had

Page 3 of 11

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 43





 declined. With Aboriginal children on average, attending one less day of school per week than their non-

Aboriginal peers, the gap is an obvious precursor to further disparities in the life journey.

One of the frustrations in developing a clear picture of the status of progress or lack thereof, is inconsistent

reporting, across jurisdictions. Gaining access to current data that is reported upon, year on year, using the

same measures, is exceedingly difficult, as is the ability to find statistics that are mirrored across agencies and

departments. Compounding that, there are also discrepancies between the measures and definitions applied to

reporting and analysis of Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal cohorts. Providing comparative data that could support

investment in the programs and services is hampered by these factors.

COVID-19 and School Refusal

Our experience during the pandemic has elevated our concerns around school engagement and educational

attainment, with many of our community’s school age children, unable to recommence education due to

anxiety and other mental health and wellbeing issues. We know that prior to COVID-19, Aboriginal and Torres

Strait Islander children in our region were already falling behind the Close the Gap targets. While overall

datasets that appear in Close the Gap annual reports show positive progress, a cursory drill down tells a very

different story. By way of example, the 2020 Report identifies that year 12 attainment decreases with

remoteness. In fact, year 12 attainment for young Aboriginal people living in the outer regional areas of

Victoria has gone backwards. There is a ten-percentage point decline from 2012 to 2019. Arguably, this

indicates that there needs to be further work and investment done in addressing school engagement,

attendance, and attainment in communities outside metropolitan areas.

In understanding the impact COVID had on school attendance in our region, it is necessary to first consider the

pre-existing complexities that we know influence a child’s education. Table A illustrates the challenges faced

locally. Mildura has some of the highest rates of family violence, unemployment, housing stress and single-

parent families in the state, and some of the lowest rates of income and educational outcomes. These

pressures are even more dominant in our Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander community.

When challenges such as those depicted in Table A were coupled with the pandemic and associated lockdowns

and school closures, the consequences for many people were dire.

“The commonality was that prior to COVID, some children already had issues with school attendance and

the COVID environment exacerbated it. On the one hand it allowed the child to be home where they felt

comfortable and safe and it’s where they wanted to be. But on the other hand, it didn’t allow for the

natural exposure to the things that they were less comfortable with. In essence, it restricted their ability to

develop resilience.” – Pauline Ugle Director Family and Community Services MDAS

The Terms of Reference for this inquiry primarily seek input evidencing the impact of school refusal on the

employment and financial security of parents and carers. However, our submission highlights the

corresponding risk to employment and financial security for Aboriginal students who disengage from

education.

The importance of education as a means of breaking the cycle of intergenerational disadvantage, and thus

creating better outcomes, is broadly acknowledged.

“Education is an important foundation for realising improved outcomes in many aspects of life. Year
12 or an equivalent attainment is particularly critical to supporting entrance into further education
pathways and improved employment outcomes.” Closing the Gap Commonwealth Implementation
Plan.

The Kids Helpline & Australian Human Rights Commission report, ‘The Impacts of COVID-19 on children and

young people who contact Kids Helpline September 2020’, found the leading concerns raised by Aboriginal and

Torres Strait Islander children and young people were changes to essential services and supports, mental

health concerns, social isolation, and educational impacts.

The Mission Australia/Orygen ‘Clusters of COVID-19 impact: Identifying the impact of COVID-19 on young

Australians in 2021 Report’ identified the young people most impacted were those living in Victoria and NSW

and those who identified as Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander.

Page 6 of 11

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 43




 Victorian students undertook 174 remote learning days during the COVID-19 lockdowns.  This caused

significant issues for students who had limited access to technology or devices due to financial disadvantage

and academic achievement was further impacted in circumstances where carers or parents were unable to

support their children by taking on the role of educator.  Conversely some children preferred online to face-to-

face learning as it cocooned them from issues, such as anxiety, that they were experiencing.

Children who were already struggling with school, found themselves increasingly isolated and overwhelmed.

Anxiety and other social and emotional wellbeing issues escalated. When students were finally able to return

to the classroom, many were incapable of making the transition and poor engagement became school refusal.

Essentially two years of lockdowns provided a buffer between the child and the challenges of everyday school

life. As a result, they lost the confidence and the skills to confront and overcome difficulties. COVID taught

them how to retreat but as a society we have failed to teach them how to reconnect. This is particularly

troubling in regional areas where lack of services means children often go without the support they need to

recover and rebuild.

Without an immediate response to this upsurge in school refusal, we risk a significant cohort of Aboriginal

youth falling further behind, diminishing educational and employment opportunities.

Education and Support

“Where I lived previously, with my own daughter, we had quite significant school refusal. She was
the only dark-skinned Koori student and she seemed to get injured a lot and I don't think the
teachers were deliberately biased, but my daughter’s reports always said she was below average
except for things they couldn’t disregard, such as her being able to read at the highest level.  At her
current school there are lots of other cultures, it’s normal to be darker skinned and they really
understand the background of the students. She is now above average and enjoys going to school.
One of the reasons, I think, is because the teachers have tailored their teaching to a more visual
learner.” - Parent

Whilst Victoria is leading the charge in addressing wellbeing needs within the school environment, more work

is required in developing a whole of system approach to ensure the drivers of potential school refusal are

identified as early as possible.

Page 7 of 11

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 43




 As is highlighted in the family experience in this section, school refusal is borne from many things and therefore

the response required to address it must be multi-faceted. Resources and funding must be dedicated to

developing the scaffolding that will provide both the uplift and support required for our young people to learn

and thrive. This includes creating teaching models that accommodate a range of learning styles – visual, oral,

and traditional – and supporting capacity for schools to offer mental health and wellbeing for students and by

extension, their families. Particularly in regional and remote areas, access to health and wellbeing services are

dangerously lacking and sadly, this means that for many young people, their schools become their refuge and

only hope for intervention, prevention, and support. This has complicated the issues around school refusal,

with children not getting the help they need. Some of these children are seen through the lens of truancy and

this misunderstanding of their mental health has created further barriers to their treatment and recovery. It is

also worth emphasising that even where supports are available, it often requires the capacity of parents to

identify the need for help and ability to pursue it. Trained staff within a school are at times better placed to

observe the need and respond to it but this relies on regular school attendance.

“To access any mental health services that are youth focused, regionally based families often need
to go out of town and it’s just not possible for some families to do that. This was especially the case
when lockdowns were in place.

“The schools are doing the best that they can, but they’re carrying a big load. Some teachers are
expected to be wellbeing officers whilst also teaching so they are really stretched, and they often
don’t have the capacity they need to truly cater for the wellbeing needs of troubled children.” –
Parent

Results of the recent Australian Psychological Society Survey has identified an alarming increase in depression,

anxiety, and suicidal ideation amongst 13 to 18-year-olds and increases in social anxiety disorders amongst 6 to

12-year-olds.

Whilst MDAS does receive funding to deliver mental health and wellbeing support, it is restricted to adult

cohorts. Culturally safe mental health services for our youth in the Mallee region are woefully inadequate and

funding is urgently required to address this oversight in service provision.

Page 8 of 11

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 43






 Parents under pressure

There are several reports that have exposed the impact of COVID-19 on families, parents, and young people.

The recently released Household Income and Labour Dynamics In Australia Survey showed some worrying

trends in education as the pandemic wore on, particularly in Victoria, which lived through the longest lockdown

in the country. Over 50% of parents described the online learning experience as ‘worse than physical learning’.

Parents who may have been adapting to reduced work hours, or working from home, were also suddenly in the

position of managing their child’s day to day education. We have heard many stories of parents who had to

cease working as they were unable to manage the roles of employee, carer, and teacher. There was an obvious

financial impost related to this and when schools reopened and their child refused to recommence in the

classroom, some parents have continued to struggle with financial and emotional pressures – they cannot

leave their child at home unsupervised – and because school refusal doesn't meet the criteria as a mental

health issue, they are not eligible for support.

“I know of women who had to stop working. They stayed home to be with their child. So now
they’re a one income family. It’s hard and it’s difficult for them to find a pathway out.” –Parent

Whilst this is a picture that would be familiar to many families around Victoria, there is a darker truth that

resides just underneath, and this truth relates to the families impacted by intergenerational unemployment

and low education. Often these families live without reliable internet connectivity and very little in the way of

capacity to assist their child to learn from home. Nor do they have the support and solutions to help their child

re-engage with school. It is their children who have truly fallen in the gaps, and it is these children we must

fight hardest to re-engage with education.

Page 9 of 11

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 43













 Recommendations

1.  MDAS calls for a review of the parameters used to define mental health issues in children and young

people to allow more families to benefit from NDIS funded mental health support services

2.  Aboriginal Community Controlled Health Organisations are fully funded to deliver culturally safe mental

health services for our youth in their communities.

3.

Immediate improvements to collection and collation of demographic and socio-economic data to ensure
standardised national measures and reporting.

4.  Schools are fully funded to embed culturally safe models of teaching and wellbeing support into their

programs

5.  Schools are fully funded to provide wellbeing (including outreach) services to both students and where

appropriate, their families.

6.  Schools are fully funded to provide teaching and administration staff with Mental Health First Aid Training.

7.  Schools are fully funded to provide teaching and administration staff with professional development in

neurodivergence and trauma-informed mental health approaches.
