Catholic Education Diocese of Bathurst
Response to national trend of school refusal - 9 December 2022

Committee Secretary
Senate Education and Employment Committees
PO Box 6100
Parliament House
Canberra ACT 2600
Phone: +61 2 6277 3521
eec.sen@aph.gov.au

Summary

● The key issues contributing to school refusal as reported by school principals in the

Catholic Education Diocese of Bathurst include:

○ increased time away from school when students are unwell, and in particular

when they display cold and flu like symptoms

○ increase in students presenting with symptoms of anxiety post COVID-19
○ parents enabling their children to stay home from school when school refusal

becomes too challenging to manage at home

● School refusal is negatively impacting families financially, socially and emotionally
● For families who are willing to engage with services, there is often a significant delay in

accessing due to availability.

● External services are often reluctant or unwilling to share information
● School attendance is not seen as a priority to relevant government departments. It is

seen as the sole responsibility of educators, yet educators have limited resources and
little capacity to work with children and families  who are “unavailable” to the school.
● Relevant government departments do not recognise educational neglect in connection

with other vulnerabilities the family may be facing

● There is a lack of early interventions, proactive strategies and resources to support

families and schools

Overview
Catholic Education Diocese of Bathurst (CEDB) responds to the Australian Parliamentary
inquiry into “School Refusal” (the Inquiry) on behalf of 33 Catholic schools in the Diocese of
Bathurst in New South Wales.

CEDB has day-to-day operational responsibility for the Catholic systemic schools within the
Diocese. The CEDB is committed to creating child-safe environments where the safety,
wellbeing and dignity of all children is paramount.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 60





 CEDB acknowledges the important legal, moral and spiritual responsibility to create a safe and
nurturing environment for students and comply with all laws that apply in the  Education sector.

This submission is informed by feedback from schools within this diocese and provides a
response to the Review’s discussion questions and Terms of Reference.

About Catholic Schools in the Diocese of Bathurst

Catholic schools in the Diocese of Bathurst have been an integral part of the education
landscape for more than 150 years and see themselves as partners with families, government,
and the broader community in delivering high-quality education across the Diocese.

The Diocese of Bathurst comprises 33 schools, educating over 9462 students and employing
over 1400 staff. Schools within the Diocese of Bathurst are geographically and
socio-economically diverse.

Introduction

Since the COVID-19 pandemic began, the Catholic Education Diocese of Bathurst (CEDB) has
recorded a 25% increase in students who are not meeting the expected attendance
requirements in our schools.

1.The increasing number since the COVID-19 pandemic, of young people and their
families who are experiencing school refusal;

The key issues impacting school refusal, as noted within the CEDB are:

a. concerns related to children who are presenting with cold and flu symptoms
b. prevalence of mental health issues affecting students
c. a shift in attitudes about face to face schooling

Principals within the CEDB have noted parents are keeping their children home for longer
periods of time when they are unwell, particularly when the illness involves cold and flu-like
symptoms. They have also noted parents are more rigid around not sending their child to school
when they are displaying these symptoms, even if they are not ‘unwell’. Prior to COVID-19,
parents were much more likely to send their children to school in these circumstances.

Anecdotal evidence from principals indicates a large number of students are struggling to return
to school, especially the playground, where unstructured play time can highlight difficulties in
many children's social skills.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 60





 There are a significant number of students within the CEDB schools who do not attend school
regularly due to anxiety or other mental health issues. For many of our students, school refusal
goes hand in hand with social anxiety or depressive disorders that impede their ability to engage
successfully in mainstream schooling on a full time basis. Whilst many of these students do
have formal diagnoses of anxiety and or depression, often the more problematic situation arises
when they do not.

“…families are often overwhelmed by the anxiety or school refusal of their
children. They express a deep sense of shame and find it difficult as they are
unable to get their children to school. Many have spoken of the judgement they
feel from others, including their own family support network, and the pressure
from the school system.”

In many cases parents want to work with the school to improve their child’s attendance,
however, they are often not able to make any positive impact to change school refusal at home.
This is often seen to spill over into a refusal to engage with any kind of therapeutic intervention,
which exacerbates the situation as schools request medical documentation to support absences
related to health and mental illnesses.

A closely linked factor is the perception some parents hold that face to face schooling is no
longer as important as it once was. There is a continued belief, or expectation in some cases,
that it is a school’s responsibility to provide work to their child if they do not attend face to face
schooling, as was the case in the COVID-19 ‘lockdown’ periods.

“There is also a need to re-establish in parents the attitude that attending school
is a significant priority”

Parents often believe they are protecting and supporting their children by not ‘making’ them go
to school. They do not recognise the detrimental effect this can have on all aspects of their
child’s wellbeing.

Within the CEDB, there are an increasing number of families taking leave during the school
term. Whilst some families follow the process of applying for leave, others do not. If a principal
does not approve the leave, this does not stop families taking the student out of school for a
family holiday, and schools are powerless to stop this. In our experience, this can have a flow on
effect in relation to school refusal. As explained by one of our principals:

“Children are very intuitive and clever beings and they learn very quickly how to
get out of going to school.  In a time where it's very easy for parents to justify
keeping their children home, this has become a vicious cycle for many.”

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 60





 2. How school refusal is affecting young people and their families and the impacts it is
having on the employment and ﬁnancial security of parents and carers;

Connection to peers through seeing them at school is no longer an issue thanks to technology.
Students are more connected to a cyber world and often the way they relate to peers is through
technology. Whilst there are benefits to technology, parents often also struggle to manage the
amount of screentime their child engages in.

Often children who are disconnected from school are challenged socially and emotionally. The
lack of understanding of social cues leads to children feeling left out or victimised which then
becomes a major barrier to attending.

“This reliance on digital technology has fuelled concerns from parents, teachers,
governments and young people themselves that digital technologies and social
media are exacerbating feelings of anxiety and depression, disturbing sleep
patterns, leading to cyber-bullying and distorting body image1”

For many other students, school lacks relevance to their lives and post COVID-19 they know
there is a different way educational outcomes can be achieved. All of this coupled with
developing mental health issues, results in a complete disconnection to school.

Many students find it difficult to articulate why they cannot participate in school, coupled with a
lack of information from any other source (medical, allied health and parental insights) results in
it being difficult to determine how to best support the child.

With many students being absent for long periods they are disconnected from learning and
develop gaps in their knowledge making it more difficult to assimilate into the class. One family
has described their experience of their child’s school refusal and the impact it continues to have
on their family. A de-identified copy of their letter can be seen at Appendix A.

It could be hypothesised that families need to make adjustments to their work and home lives to
accommodate students who are not attending school regularly. There are a significant number
of meetings between parents, students and school to address attendance issues, which may
mean parents need to request adjustments to their working times to attend. Additionally some of
impacts a parents work
the adjustments made to accommodate a child’s return to school
schedule, such as late starts or early pickups. Oftentimes when a child does get to school
parents are called to pick the child up if the strategies in place are not working to keep them and
others safe in school. This dynamic can place additional stress on parents' employment and
financial security.

Whilst COVID-19 has seen an increase in flexible work arrangements such as working from
home,
this is not an option for many who cannot work without physically being in their
workplace. One principal commented:

“As we are a secondary school, many parents are happy to have their secondary aged
child home alone whilst they work”

1 Organisation for Economic and Cooperation Development, 2018,
Children-and-Young-People-Mental-Health-in-the-Digital-Age Shaping the Future

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 60





 In some situations if employment becomes tenuous as a result of this, families will certainly
choose financial security over daily battles to get their child to school and in many cases
children are left to get themselves to school.

Some parents will gain assistance from grandparents which then impacts further on the
relationships and connections within the family. It can cause conflict between generations,
negates the responsibility of the parent, or creates an alliance between child and grandparent
which makes the situation more difficult for the parent to manage.

The evidence necessary to demonstrate why a child is not present impacts family time and
financial resources when required to seek medical review, if they are able to engage with
services due to a shortage of services in local areas. It is not uncommon for services to have no
availability for appointments, with some services having closed their books to new patients..

Finally many children and parents have had their sense of safety and confidence in the world
eroded. Resulting in refusing to send children back to school and moving their child to distance
education or home schooling.

3. The impacts and demands of the increasing caseload on service providers and
schools to support these students and their families;

Access to some allied health services in rural and remote areas was a challenge prior to
COVID-192 with a “strong unmet need for more allied health services in rural and remote
Australia.” The location of many of the schools within the CEDB are classified as rural. This
also can be said for some specialist health services. Even in our regional centres, such as
Dubbo, the wait list to access a paediatrician can be up to 12 months3.

Access to health and allied health services is often required to support diagnoses and inform
school intervention and adjustments, as well as explain absences related to school refusal. It
can take many months before appointments become available with these professionals. Whilst
telehealth can be an option for some children it is also difficult for some children to engage via
this method.

Additionally,
inconsistent care, delays, and at times, early discharge due to competing priorities.

in these services frequently change roles leading to

in our experience, staff

COVID-19 also impacted the NDIS scheme which many children also relied on to support their
needs. Whilst NDIS service providers made adjustments as best
they could during the
pandemic, children and families were still impacted as a result of the inability to deliver services
face to face4. Anecdotal evidence indicates children and families requiring some NDIS services
are still experiencing delays in some areas, particularly allied health services.

2 New South Wales Health, March 2020, Improvement of Access, Quality and Distribution of Allied Health
Services in Regional, Rural and Remote Australia
3 Western New South Wales Primary Health Network, February 2020, Dubbo HS Paediatric Outpatient
Clinic Referral Framework
4 National Disability Insurance Scheme, 6 October 2022, The impact of COVID-19 on NDIS, allied
healthcare services and consumer experiences transitioning to telehealth

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 60





 School staff are overwhelmed due to the number of students they are trying to manage who do
not have adequate attendance levels and as a result, many slip through the cracks. Teachers
are challenged by a crowded curriculum and increased work loads. School refusal may develop
gradually and oftentimes, schools and families are not seeing the pattern of behaviour until it is
a well established problem. Teaching staff may also lack the experience to identify the early
signs.

School refusal results in the need for attendance planning with students, families and other
stakeholders. It is time consuming and oftentimes has little impact on attendance patterns over
extended periods of time. Whilst some initial improvement may be seen, when the attention is
diverted to another student, attendance will often lapse again.

In other cases, when the school starts to apply some pressure to students and families around
improving attendance, relationships may deteriorate, families stop engaging and/or they may
withdraw the student from the school.

All of these factors mean that there is often a delay in appropriate supports being accessed and
children remain at risk as a result.

4. How relevant state, territory and federal departments are working to monitor and
address this growing school refusal challenge

In an increasing number of instances, CEDB school support teams need to request information
from other agencies under Chapter 16a. Often, government departments, including health and
allied health, and other medical professionals demonstrate a lack of willingness to share
information. This in turn makes it difficult to gain insight into the needs of the child and to
implement appropriate adjustments.

As mandatory reporters, principals have an obligation to make risk of significant harm reports.
However, there appears to be little engagement from agencies, such as the Department of
Communities and Justice (DCJ), when it comes to educational neglect. Principals have reported
the following:

“We don't see any action here. DCJ reports are rarely followed up and from my
perspective have very little, if any, impact.”

“When reporting educational neglect matters to DCJ over the last 4 years, I have had
one instance of them opening a case. However, when we worked through the steps the
school had taken, the matter was closed. It has since been re-reported however no
further action or involvement from the statutory body has occurred.”

“The reality is that a child not coming to school is never going to be seen as a priority in
the context of child protection services even though absenteeism is often a symptom of
many other related issues.”

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 60





 this was also the case prior

Whilst
the increased number of reports for
to COVID-19,
educational neglect would undoubtedly impact upon DCJ’s capacity to effectively process and
allocate the volume of reports.

When the level of attendance leads to discussion of Compulsory School Conferences or
Compulsory Schooling Orders, parents often choose to end the child’s enrollment and enrol
them in a different school, without addressing the problem. There have also been numerous
examples of children with a history of school refusal presenting to enrol in schools within the
CEDB.

At times, schools hold wellbeing concerns for students who are refusing to attend, particularly
where parent engagement is also poor. In some instances, schools request NSW Police support
to conduct a welfare check on the student however this can be counter productive to
relationships. This is the only method available to systemic Catholic schools who do not have
the home school liaison program5 available to NSW state schools.

School refusal may also negatively impact school funding. When a student is absent for more
than 80% of the available school days prior to the annual August Census date, the system
potentially faces a loss of Commonwealth and State Government funding for the student. This is
problematic considering the labour and resource intensive requirements to improve poor
attendance that results from school refusal. CEDB has experienced loss of funding for some
students in the 2022 school year.

5. Other related matters

Across the Diocese our data mirrors national trends6. The 2021 Mission Australia Youth Survey
found that;

‘One in two respondents to the survey said their mental health had been
negatively impacted by the COVID-19 pandemic. COVID-19 has highlighted
just how precarious young people’s mental health has become”

This increasing presentation puts additional pressure on teachers and school leadership teams
at a time when their own wellbeing and workloads are a cause of concern.

School refusal post COVID-19 has impacted on students' capacity to achieve educational
milestones such Record of School Achievement (ROSA) at the completion of Year 10 and the
Higher School Certificate (HSC) at the end of Year 12. Students' disengagement from school
and inability to complete assessment
tasks and participate in exams has meant that an
increasing number of Non-Completion (or ‘N’ determinations) have been given.

Support for parents in managing their responsibility with regards to their child's attendance
needs a whole of government approach. Schools and systems are working continuously to

5 New South Wales Department of Education, 8 June 2022, Attendance Support Program
6 Mental Health and Stress Top Concerns for Young Australians, December, 2021,
<https://www.orygen.org.au/About/News-And-Events/2021/Mental-health-and-stress-top-concerns-for-you
ng-Au>

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 60





 increase school attendance, however without engagement of parents this becomes a frustrating
process. As one of our Principals indicated:

“There needs to be much more focus and responsibility placed on parents. Imposing
significant penalties is a start, if students do not have legitimate reasons for
absenteeism. Having had the experience of taking one family to court over such a matter
after two and a half years of chasing and being told that the school has to deal with it,
tells me that the authorities are not taking this at all seriously. It appears as though the
penalties (significant fines) are never applied once students reach high school, if at all.”

6. Considerations for the future

We would like to offer the following points for the inquiry to consider:

a) Community focused education about the importance of students attending every day,

such as through media campaigns

b) Targeted campaigns for Aboriginal and or Torres Strait Islander peoples, and those from

culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds

c) A national approach with resources for families and schools which are evidence based
d) Training opportunities for all levels and sectors of education in relation to understanding

and managing school refusal

e) Greater support in the home for families who have a child who refuses school, including
education programs that aim to increase parents skills, provide strategies to successfully
navigate school refusal, understand the impact of non-attendance
Increased education for parents about the importance of pre-school and routine for
children prior to commencing school
Increased options for students who have not completed Year 10 and are disengaged
from school

g)

f)

h) Greater support to students who have mental health concerns or other diagnoses at
significant transition periods such as preschool to primary school, primary school to high
school

i) Consideration of  what successfully completing school means. Is the HSC process still

relevant for students who wish to further their education?

j) Availability of alternative education platforms for children who cannot successfully

engage in face to face schooling

Face to face learning is the best option for most students however, for some students and
families it is no longer viable. Alternative options could lead to learning rather than complete
disengagement from education.

Terms of Reference

On 27 October 2022 the Senate referred the inquiry into the national trend of school refusal and
related matters to the Education and Employment References Committee for inquiry and report by
22 March 2023.

The national trend of school refusal or 'School Can't' – as distinct from truancy – that is affecting
primary and secondary school-aged children, who are unable to attend school regularly or on a
consistent basis, with specific reference to:

a)  the increasing number since the COVID-19 pandemic, of young people and their families

who are experiencing school refusal;

b)  how school refusal is affecting young people and their families and the impacts it is having

on the employment and financial security of parents and carers;

c)  the impacts and demands of the increasing case load on service providers and schools to

support these students and their families;

d)  how relevant state, territory and federal departments are working to monitor and address

this growing school refusal challenge; and

e)  any other related matters.

Our submission

Our submission relates to the terms of reference, particularly:

a)  the increasing number since the COVID-19 pandemic, of young people and their families

who are experiencing school refusal;

b)  how school refusal is affecting young people and their families and the impacts it is having

on the employment and financial security of parents and carers;

and

e)   any other related matters.

About Parents for Change

Parents for Change are parents with lived experience of youth mental health challenges focused on:

  building capacity and community through information and support for parents of children

with mental health issues/needs

  advocating for parent voice and lived experience of caring for children grappling with mental

health emergencies, life issues or crisis events

  South Australian youth mental health system reform, particularly reducing the risk of

suicide for young people under 18.

Parents for Change is not a provider of clinical or professional advocacy services. Our role is to:



support parents dealing with mental health issues in their children, including directing them
to services and information

  help parents advocate for their children, including linking them with specialised help or

access to targeted members of Parliament offices

  offer parent voice and lived experience to government, youth mental health service

providers, NGOs and philanthropic organisations

  proactively advocate for adequate/better state/community services and responses to

families in a mental health crisis.

Parents for Change’s key youth mental health focus areas

  The desperate need for South Australian crisis residential care and step up/down options

(eg a short-stay facility for under 18s) separate from CAMHS

  Reducing barriers, particularly for children with mental healthcare needs who are also on
the NDIS (such as Autistic young people who have high/extreme mental health needs,
especially those refused access by hospitals)

  The ‘missing middle’ (young people with sustained/complex mental health presentations,

often a ‘diagnoses’ but who have nowhere to go for treatment/health care)

  Children who are falling into the system gap of 17-18, or under 12
  The impact of mental health on school refusal/missing out on an education (which is their

right) and will have lifelong effects

  WCH Emergency Department and frontline hospital presentation issues (such as culture,

privacy, respect, referrals) – we support mental health presentations directed away from the
hospital emergency department environment, as per Suicide Prevention Australia’s position

  Transition from youth mental health care to adult mental health care.

Our observations and lived experience

Through the Parents for Change Facebook page, meetings, sessions and conversations, we have
listened and seen firsthand the impact of mental health issues on school attendance and
engagement in mainstream school education.

Many parents who contact us find themselves at the ‘extreme’ end of the spectrum, with a child or
young person who:

refuses to attend school in any form
is disengaged with school education
cannot see a future for themselves
is self-harming or actively planning suicide





  has attempted suicide.

Other parents contact us because they feel confused, angry, desperate or at a loss for what to do
about their child’s state of mental health. Often, they have attended our children’s hospital’s
Emergency Department in a suicidal crisis and after waiting many hours, have been sent home –
usually with no referrals, information or support.

A common issue of concern among parents of a child with a mental health problem is how to get
them to attend school. Sometimes these parents have spoken to or had meetings with their school
about the matter, to varying degrees of success. Problems attending school occur across sectors and
socio-economic groups, locations and family makeup. Increasingly, we hear of younger children
having problems with school attendance from as early as Reception or Year 1. We have included
some screenshots from our Facebook page to illustrate this.

In our collective view, based on our shared but separate lived experience of having one or more
children ‘refuse’ school over many years, the problems can be simply summarised. Solutions are not
so simple to envision or enact, but we propose several alternative models or thematic programs of
work that already have varying degrees of success, or may be part of the answer:

  Flexible learning options – FLO models that attempt to engage young people through a

different method rather than ‘classroom’ and conventional school learning. Unfortunately,
FLO options often set a very low bar and attract young people with behavioural issues, drug
and alcohol issues or low educational attainment. This is completely understandable, given
that some children are not receiving even basic literacy and numeracy education, sometimes
due to learning differences such as dyslexia, or to complex family backgrounds or lack of
support at home for learning. Rather than seeing FLO as a place for ‘no hopers’ and
‘troublemakers’, it should be re-branded as a serious option for self-directed learners as well
as those who don’t thrive in the mainstream. (In our view, that’s most kids.)

While not a FLO program exactly, it’s worth reiterating that at least a third of young people
are not interested in or capable of attending university. Rather than tertiary study, they
should be just as valued for their social and economic contribution as trades people or
service industry staff. Schools need to do better at creating alternative pathways, such as
the Vet in Schools program, so that young people can see a better future for themselves that
does not involve school or study. More than simply offering these alternative pathways, they
must be actively promoted and encouraged in practical ways – linking the young person with
a mentor, making sure they have their application in, supporting them to find work

experience placements, helping their parents and engaging both child and parent in making
those pathways a reality. The payoff is a productive, skilled young person who works hard,
saves and contributes to the economy as well as society. These trades skills are desperately
needed all around the country.

  Alternative school models such as SASY (Specialised Assistance School for Youth) in

Adelaide, also play a part in change. SASY is a new type of school that focuses on core
wellbeing and support first, in flexible learning environments that promote student choice
and control. The downside of this often very successful model is that young people with
behavioural issues who are disengaged from school or education may disrupt learning
opportunities for other students. The cohort also seems heavily made up of young people
with Autism or other developmental disabilities, so it is a further challenge to create calm
and quiet environments (or breakout spaces) for young people who do not thrive in noisy,
chaotic locations. There are many great things about the SASY model though, and I
personally can credit my own son’s now strong mental health and successful trades career
pathway to the flexibility and emotional support he received at SASY.

  Greater flexibility in existing schools – this may involve creating hubs or off-campus/other-

campus spaces for young people who have different learning needs.

Some may prefer to be self-guided, or need closer supervision and assistance, which is often
impossible in a class with 25-30 other young people. Some may need 1:1 supervision from
an SSO/assistant in order to stay on track, or to understand what is asked of them. Some
may respond to a tailored curriculum that meets their interests and tailors the learning to
them. Some young people need quiet environments that do not overstimulate or distract
them, and a focus on engagement in learning rather than rigidly applying a curriculum.

All these options ‘meet the child where they are at’, rather than expecting every child to fit
into a mould based on the past century of schooling. It is clear that those educational
models and modes are no longer working, if indeed they ever did. Young people today have
unique pressures and life experiences that differ from any previous generation.

Schooling that builds mental health and resilience in meaningful, real-life ways will set these
children up for success in a rapidly changing world. A strengths-based curriculum that
centres of a child’s needs is the way forward, and our educational bureaucracies could learn
from experts such as Sir Ken Robinson about the innate value of creativity and personal
inspiration in our school systems.

  A renewed focus on mental health in schools – by this I mean practical instruction in help-
seeking behaviours, life skills, interpersonal relationship dynamics and the necessary
strengths required to succeed in diverse pathways – such as how to prepare for and do well
in a job interview, how to relate to peers or co-workers, how to handle a ‘bad day’ or a low
period in life (coping strategies for anxiety or low mood), the importance of exercise, suicide
awareness and how to respond to a friend expressing these thoughts, or how to manage
these feelings in themselves.

Emotional literacy is a critical skill needed throughout life and voluminous studies show our
prisons are full of (often) young men who have low emotional ‘intelligence’ or who are
scarred by trauma and poor parenting. These young men have rarely received the education
that all children deserve. Schools can’t do it all, but they are the obvious place to see and act
on the early signs of poor coping behaviours, signs of abuse or neglect, signs of learning

difficulties or a need for deeper attention that children and young people so rarely receive.
Resource schools better to manage these emotional/educational needs that are currently a
signpost to poor life choices and the consequences of a prison sentence or life on
unemployment benefits (or worse).

  An education system that has awareness of the impact and signs of Autism (and related
developmental or cognitive issues, inclusive of ADHD) – one that is proactive to help these
children adjust, learn social/emotional skills, and one that ‘meets them where they’re at’
developmentally, or one that is in tune with a child’s personal interests and
skillsets/strengths.

The tsunami of social issues that flow on from the rising numbers of autistic children in the
education system as they hit puberty is already being felt in schools and in society more
generally. In our core Parents for Change group, and also reflected in the families that seek
help from our page or by contacting us directly, there is a huge over representation of
families with an autistic child, or children with multiple disabilities.

Many (or most) of these families are forced to become a one-income family (or one reliant
on benefits, especially as it is mothers who are so often left to cope with a ‘difficult’ child
alone) so that the parent can try to meet the increasingly complex needs of the
child/children. This often involves navigating the state health system combined with the
differently focused NDIS system, which does not see ‘crisis’ or emergency issues as its
responsibility, and psychiatrists are not funded. Though child psychologists are sometimes
approved for children with an NDIS plan, in many regions and in our state, they are rear
impossible to find and access. It can sometimes be a full-time job to navigate the NDIS alone,
particularly in a family with multiple registered children needing supports.

Schools need to take Autism seriously, given the increasing numbers of Autistic children in
our midst. Also, considering the research that 80% of children with ASD have ‘serious mental
health issues’, schools and the health system need to make mental health supports easily
and universally available to families in need. (Source: ‘A Submission on Health Care For
Autistic Australians’ for the Disability Royal Commission cites the Australian Government's
Raising Children website as stating that “nearly three-quarters of children with Autism
Spectrum Disorder (ASD) also have another medical or psychiatric condition”).

Early intervention should not just be a government slogan but fully enacted in every ‘service’
that touches a child’s life – child care, kindy, preschool, school and beyond. Needless to say
early intervention should be swiftly applied in our health and hospital system – and yet it is
not. Early intervention in age as well as in the life of the problem is critical to turn around
the dire statistic that it generally takes 11 years to ‘diagnose’ a child with a mental illness.

Similarly, the ‘no wrong door’ approach should be standard government policy so that cross-
sector agencies connect based on the child’s or family’s needs, and not according to their
own agendas or perceived jurisdictions. ‘Joined up’ services that talk to each other and
cross-refer seems to me to be an essential part of a successful social safety net.

On page 10, I have added a copy of our policy focus areas and highlighted issues related to
school avoidance as complex social problems that have their roots in both the health and
education systems.

from Foundation through to Year 12. W ith 2022 enrolments in excess of 6000, more students enroll w ith
Virtual School Victoria than any other school in Victoria.  Approximately 2700 students are enrolled full
time, w hile around 3300 students, most in years 11 and 12, complete subjects w ith us w hile based in
other schools.  Enrolment levels have been increasing consistently in recent years and this has been
particularly marked since the start of the COVID pandemic.

As they become more protracted, school absences that precede refusal lead to significant gaps in
learning, resulting in a w idening distance between the educational abilit ies of students and their peers.
This in turn reinforces a sense of failure related to school and the desire to avoid school as the source of
this shame. This cycle of struggle and avoidance can result  in diminished capacity for resilience as
exposure to the cha llenging situations inherent in school participation go unmet.

As school attendance diminishes, students often experience a breakdown of peer relationships. The
increasing impact of social anxiety and depression spiral together w ith this to compound social isolation,
leaving many of our students struggling to leave their home, or in some cases,  even their bedroom.
Relationships between students and parents/ carers and siblings deteriorate under the pressure of
living and learning at home, w ith reports of ongoing confl ict escalating to aggressive outbursts from
students, violence w ithin the home and acute mental health concerns including self-harm and suicide
risk.

While access to mental health and social support services for young people and families has been
difficult for many years, the impact of the pandemic has exacerbated the situation. Reluctance to help
seek is already an issue for many young people. Wait  lists of over six months mean that access to health
services for treatment of school refusal and related issues result in emerging condit ions becoming

3

\I

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 62 VIRTUAL
SCHOOL VICTORIA

chronic and entrenched before treatment can be available. When an appointment is available, the
dearth of outreach services acts as further obstacle to access.

For many families the spira lling demands related to the school refusa l experience also bring financial
hardship. While there are no school fees payable to attend VSV,  a parent or carer must commit to acting
as an education supervisor to support their child to engage in on line learning. This can require forfeit ing
paid w ork in order to fulfi l these responsibilities.  For low income or single parent families this can result
in significant financial disadvantage. Once out of pocket expenses for hea lth practitioner services are
added to their regular bills, the affect can be crippling.

For Centreli nk recipients, there is a risk that payments w ill be impacted and over-payment debts
incurred if their child is unable to maintain the required level of participation in schooling. When
coupled w ith the need to also provide age appropriate parental supervision, parents may also face child
safety considerations as they try to maintain some income.

The impacts and demands of the increasing case load on service providers and schools to support
these students and their families;

The comorbidity data above helps VSV  understand the complexity behind the language of 'school
refusal'. It allow s us to differentiate when the engagement challenges are linked to the school
environment itself, e.g. experiences of bullying or sensory difficulties linked to ASD.  It  helps us to
understand the contribution anxiety disorders, depression and other mental health and social
circumstances have on the experience of students and to target engagement, learning and w ellbeing
supports accordingly. Most importantly, it  highlights the sheer scale of the problem. A combination of
school factors/ family factors/individual factors resu lt  in school refusal.

There is little sign in the VSV enrolment demographic that the evidence-based models of practice  are
being implemented in timely and effective ways in mainstream schools. It is also clear that these same
models are not scalable to the numbers w e hold, on the resources w e are assigned.

At VSV this creates significant demands for all staff. Each teacher holds a pastora l care role as Learning
Advisor for a small group of students. The school invests three hours work time each week for each
Learning Advisor to focus on engagement, connection, communication and support for each student. In
practice, for student w ith complex school refusal histories, the t ime required to undo the negative
experiences of the past and successfully build this relationship far exceeds the t ime allocated, but is vita l
work if the student is to become 'learning ready'.

As subject teachers and course writers, VSV staff must also invest in development of reasonable
adjustments and differentiation to curriculum in on line classes and through asynchronous course work
to accommodate w ide and disparate learning needs. Despite our efforts, engagement and participation
levels are low  for many students, reflecting the entrenched disengagement and refusa l histories  of many
students when they come to us. Over the last t w o years, the toll this has taken on staff has become
more and more evident. Levels of frustration, fatigue and signs of vicarious trauma are growing.

VSV investment in student Wellbeing, Inclusion, Engagement and Learning specialist staff underpins the
work of support w ith students and families and the capacity building and professional learning supports,
such as our trauma informed practice, of the w ider staff team. Instead the school calls on Student

4

\I

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 62 VIRTUAL
SCHOOL VICTORIA

Resource Package (SRP)  budgets to employ multi-disciplinary teams to provide case coordination
support, to liaise with referring practit ioners and to develop and deliver Individual Education Plans in
order to bring collaborative systems support to students with complex needs, including school refusal.
Our Engagement team have provided individual case  plans supports to 200 students and provided
guidance to staff on many more.

Although our enrolment criteria requires students in our Medical and Young Adu lt  categories to
demonstrate secure health supports at time of enrolment, the levels of students requiring referra l to
the Wellbeing and Inclusion teams has exceeded 550 this year. Each referral reflects a level of need not
being met by external support services, or the breakdown of the services during the course of the
academic year. As demand for targeted support grows, our efforts to recru it wellbeing and inclusion
coordination staff are frustrated by the short fall of professionals trained and available for work due to
the demand for their skills.

Quite simply, the education and health systems are overwhelmed by the levels of demand linked to
disengagement and refusal experiences and bound by policy and models of practice that are
unresponsive to the needs of young people and their families.

How relevant state, territory and federal departments are working to monitor and address this
growing school refusal challenge;

The Victorian DET have a range of programs and initiatives  in place to address school engagement and
attendance supports for students. However, the majority of DET services (e.g. School Nursing program,
Mental Health Practit ioners, Health and Wellbeing teams) can only be accessed on site at the school the
student may be intent on refusing.

The Navigator program is one of the few init iatives provided by DET that is providing outreach support
to the family home and seeking to understand engagement cha llenges in the context of the home
environment. The levels of demand on this service are so high that six month wait  lists are common,
negating the opportunity for early intervention at the t ime the concerns are first identified. The
recommendations from the recent VAGO review of navigator program may help to address this
challenge.

The range of services offered by DFFH, DET and others are not targeting parents/ carers in an accessible
and t imely way. Despite parents reporting they are feeli ng blamed, overwhelmed and disempowered by
their efforts to keep their children engaged, those seeking help early are met w ith delays due to service
demand . Those unwi lling or unable to seek help early are left w ith responses driven through child
protection systems that are once again, overwhelmed and focussed on more acute abuse priorit ies.

Despite a large enrolment cohort of students previously assessed and approved for funding under State
and Federal disability programs, VSV does not receive dedicated funding for this purpose. DET suggests
that State disability programs are 'not fit for purpose' for VSV,  but the experience of supporting
students with additional needs in remote learning would suggest otherwise.

5

\I

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 62 VIRTUAL
SCHOOL VICTORIA

VSV staff strive to build collaborative partnership w ith referring practitioners and families, but this is
hindered by the limitation of the service delivery models dominant in our health system. The majority of
referring specialists are private practit ioners working under a fee for service  model that does not cover
case  plan coordination or consultation. When it  does, it  is often at the cost of a direct care session for
the young client and their family. The public health services that provide invaluable assistance (CAM HS,
headspace, etc.) are more often w illing to engage in joint practice, but can struggle to make the t ime for
this in the face of their work loads. We continue to be stuck in a silo approach despite all evidence
behind collaborative systems response.

Fundamentally, a key issue of school refusal lies in the school system . Increasing school sizes  result  in
students becoming lost and their operating policies and structures are unresponsive to the needs and
vulnerabilities of students.

I am writing my submission as my family has been significantly affected by school refusal with

with a good understanding of the healthcare system and a

my children. I hope my experience as a single parent with multiple school refusers can inform
this inquiry.

Brief history of school can’t for my child
My  family  moved  from  a  tiny  town  in
  to  a  slightly  less  tiny  town  just  before  the
outbreak of COVID to be nearer family support. All my children were happy, socially well connected
with good school attendance prior to COVID. They played sport, attended church and had some great
friends. At the time of the first lockdowns my children were
 The two youngest
bounced  back  fairly  well  but  my  three  older  children  have  been  significantly  affected.  They  have
become anxious, socially withdrawn, suffered from panic attacks during attempts to bring them to
school,  left  class  in  the  middle  of  the  day,  become  irritable  and  combative  at  times  despite  my

Impact of School Can’t on my child, my family and myself:

Impact of School Can’t experience on my child:

All
of my children have suffered significant setbacks in the social, academic and mental health but
it has been very serious and prolonged for my oldest three. Two years later they don’t attend church,
have few or no friends and are much more fragile and less self confident in all aspects. One of my
teens has not been to school since the start of the pandemic and the other two have attended well
under 50%. They find it very difficult to open up to me or to supportive family in our life, and I am
frightened for their future with such a seriously interrupted education. I am sure they share the same
anxieties.  They cannot engage with mental health care workers, particularly as there have been very
long delays in accessing care and significant staff turnover. I can’t think of any positives about our
experience.

Impact of School Can’t experience on our family and myself as a parent:

I am exhausted. I don’t believe that anyone actually cares about our struggle with school refusal. We
feel  invisible.  I  feel  like  I  am  doing  this  by  myself.  I  am  lucky  to  have  an  excellent  employer  and

 colleagues who make allowances for my parenting needs. However, I can’t work full time and have
missed out on promotion due to my complex parenting responsibilities. We always struggle financially
(as many single parents do) which is compounded by extra sick days, late starts and finishing early in
order to support my children to attend school when they can. I have to drive significant distances and
take time off work to get them where they need to be which impacts my ability to earn a living and

My whole family has suffered a great deal in our social and emotional well-being. The distress of one
child impacts the welfare of the others and having multiple children with school refusal feels almost
impossible. Family and friends pity me and I have felt at times some judgement and shame. I feel like
I am failing as a parent and I worry constantly about my children’s future. Obviously, with the demands
of caring for

to reduce my work, we are often limited in what we do. I earn just over the financial threshold to be

Dealing with the school has been more difficult, perhaps because my expectations of their knowledge
and skills are higher. However, I have felt judged by the school and believe they treat us as though we
created this problem. They seem to think the kids are lazy and disobedient and don’t understand the
severe anxiety underlying their avoidant behaviour. Far too often I feel they have washed their hands
of us, they believe my children are responsible for their disengagement and also for finding their own
way back. I would happily put in enormous efforts if there was some sort of plan and direction, but so
often I have to do my own research as nobody at the school seems to have the expertise or knowledge
to advise me. The school has had issues with staff turnover and sick leave due to COVID making it
difficult for them to provide consistency and often communicate with me. After seeking meetings with
the school, the school ask me what I think they should do. I DON’T KNOW. No one knows. I am left
feeling overwhelmed and helpless. I fight the same battles every single day. I am so tired.

I recognise the school has grossly inadequate resources and the whole state has been overwhelmed
by the scale of this problem, but it does feel like the school’s focus is on children who attend. Outside
of the actual lockdown they have rarely sought my feedback or checked in with me to see how we are

Monitoring and identification of School Attendance Difficulties:

My children have learnt that there are actually no consequences (yet) to not attending school. The
school don’t follow up on absences and most of their teachers are not genuinely concerned with their
wellbeing. We have had some very inappropriate comments from teachers which have embarrassed
my  children  in  front  of  their  peers  and  placed  a  barrier  between  student  and  teacher.  The
communication between school and home is inadequate and mostly initiated by me when something
goes wrong. I wish the school would celebrate the kids effort and encourage them. School reports are
depressing to read as they mostly contain no information or state absences were high etc. Surely there
are positive things to comment on even if it was only that one class or project. The opportunities to
positively influence the kids are seriously underestimated by the teachers. I feel like the school are
always trying to defend themselves and blame my children. I just want us to work together for the
common goal of reengaging the kids in their education. I don’t feel like the school wants to work with
me.

Barriers to attendance.  Things that have worked and things that haven’t:

Thinking about treatment/responding to school can’t:

School bus transport has been an issue for all 3 children. Overcrowding, rowdy kids and
inappropriate behaviour had led to 2 of my children requiring me to drive them. I raised these issues
repeatedly with the school immediately initially until we realised nothing would change and I no
longer sent my children on the school bus.
1 very patient counsellor from

All interventions have left me to gently prod, encourage, support, nag and sometimes strenuously
argue with my teenagers. This takes its toll on our relationship and keeping the lines of
communication open has been an ongoing struggle.

 whose consistent approach reached one of my children

Thinking about proactive strategies to prevent school can’t:

Previously my children have been pleasers who are respectful and would get their work done and
participate in all classes so as not to get in trouble or fall behind. I think that is still in them to a
degree. Incentives and positive reinforcement would help my children. I have raised this with the
schools but unfortunately the school has been inconstant with their approach. I wish there was a

 team of staff who we could regularly communicate with. School refusers are next level when it
comes to needing wellbeing and academic support. Because they are not attending they miss out on
access to these staff. They need their own specialised team.

How has your relationship / conceptualisation of education changed or been challenged as a
result of your parental lived experience of school can’t?

When the kids are getting awards and reports and feedback for projects and assignments completed
(which certainly is my past and present experience with my primary aged kids) school is wonderful。
I am excited and looking firmly toward their futures knowing that they will find their place in the
world。 But with my teens I wonder if they will be able to navigate adulthood with their current
level of education。 Will there be available to them, opportunities in future to catch up。 The
model presently being offered is somehow not meeting their needs。 Is it really the kids or is it a
break in the system which is unable to meet them where they are？ The teachers are tired I think。
The schools are encountering a problem on a scale not ever seen before。 And they can’t handle it
。  I am certain that they don’t know what to do。

Summary and recommendations for the committee:
The impact on my family has been exceedingly severe and long lasting, and I am afraid the damage to
their education and social connectedness may well impact my children for some time to come. There
seems to be very little by way of planning and organised support at the school level, and delays to
access youth mental health and specialist services are so long that my family’s problems have become
much more severe and entrenched than when we initially sought help. I feel we have sacrificed the
mental health and welfare of our children to save the lives of the old during the pandemic, and if not
addressed this will have very serious and long lasting consequences for our society. I do not grudge
this decision but to deal with the impact surely we need to fund services for young people at a much
higher level, as they have born the brunt of the impact.

I believe the following recommendations would have improved the lives of my children and the many
others who have been affected by school avoidance both before and especially after the pandemic:

Recommendations:

1.  Triage for services needs to be improved, based on the number and severity of risk factors. Surely
after my eldest two children had been absent for months it should have been easy and QUICK to
get help for my third. Possible criteria for triaging services could be number of affected children,
combined number of days absent, co-morbid mental health diagnoses, financial stress, housing
insecurity, family separation, recently moving schools/poor support network. I know these criteria

2.  Treat funding for early intervention services in childhood education and youth mental health as

funding. I am very confident that if my children had received early assistance they would have

3.  Formally  fund  peer  support  networks  such  as  School  Can’t  Facebook.  This  has  been  more

informative and useful than any other resource offered to me.

4.

Improve the training and resources available to schools and teachers so they can respond more
usefully than just victim blaming in cases of serious school avoidance.

5.  Fund

 at TAFE for students under the age of 18. Surely if it is suggested as an alternative to
mainstream public school then families should not have to pay for it. Risk factors cluster together
and needing to come up with thousands of dollars for alternative education when my income is
reduced and the needs of my other children are so high has been extremely stressful

6.  Consider access to care and services in rural areas particularly increasing frequency of bus services.
This not only restricts the ability of children to attend social and community activities but trying
to  access  specialist  education  means  my  children  have  attended  several  different  schools  in
different  towns.  Public  transport  options  are  very  limited  and  I  often  feel  despair  at  trying  to
support
 children going to several different sites at the same time. Having to decide which
of my children will receive an education is a choice a parent should not have to face.

Thank you very much for taking the time to read my submission and I profoundly wish you good luck
in combating the current crisis in youth education and mental health.

To: Committee Secretary

Re: The national trend of school refusal and related matters Senate Inquiry

My name is
lived experience of school refusal. I will specifically address point b. of the Inquiry Terms of
Reference:

 and I am writing as one of many thousands of parents who have

b. how school refusal is affecting young people and their families and the impacts it is
having on the employment and financial security of parents and carers.

My son is 16 and has just completed year 10 at
he has made it this far in his schooling is no small feat.

 in

That

Our journey with school refusal began in 2018 when our son was in year 6. He had already
been diagnosed with anxiety and had struggled with separation anxiety in childcare,
kindergarten and the early years of primary school. It was in year 6 that his avoidance
became extreme. He would freeze up in the morning, without moving or speaking, and it
became impossible to make him physically get out of bed. This response completely
shocked and upset us and we spent weeks struggling to understand what was happening.
He wasn't being bullied, and seemed to be managing academically. We were at a complete
loss to explain to his school what the problem was, and the leadership seemed more
concerned with his attendance record than his wellbeing. Our extended family did not
understand, and the general assumption seemed to be that our son was faking it and just
needed to be "more resilient".

Initially we would, to our regret and shame, try to badger and cajole our boy into going.
We shouted, pleaded, bribed and physically attempted to force our son to get up. He
remained completely unresponsive, and we would leave for work defeated, depleted and
depressed, leaving him alone, often curled up in a fetal position, traumatised.

It was extremely upsetting and the relationship with our son, his 2 brothers, our marriage,
work, and extended family were all significantly impacted.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 66
 Mid-way through year 7, with our son having missed the bulk of year 6 and the school
pressing for a firm decision of attendance or withdrawal, the emotional struggle took its
toll. I broke down at work and admitted to my manager that we were struggling, leaving
our 12 year old at home alone every day in a traumatised state, and could no longer
continue. I withdrew from a valuable secondment, took 6 months leave without pay, and
we put our mortgage on hold so we could try alternative, home based arrangements.
During this period, we tried
considered selling our house so that I could quit work entirely and home school our son.
We really did not know what to do.

 with minimal success. At one stage we

We were, however, determined that our son retain some social connectivity, so we
enrolled him in on campus year 8 high school in 2020 with a learning management plan
that acknowledged his anxiety and school refusal, and made allowances for attendance
and assessment. Since 2020 his attendance has been sporadic, averaging 3 days a week,
but we learned not to pressure him in the morning but to just play it by ear. I have
continuously advocated for him with the school, and they have been largely
compassionate and patient. The critical support I have received from the school has come
from 2 or 3 teachers who seem to understand and support students like our son to achieve
their best notwithstanding their personal challenges. Other teachers seem to have little to
no understanding.

Throughout this journey I started a support group of parents and friends who have
struggled with school refusal in their family. Our united challenge is to get ourselves and
our young people through ‘the system’ in one piece. We have all felt pressure to conform
and we worry about the future for our kids. We all know that our kids are smart, capable
young people but their academic record with the education system would reflect
otherwise.

School refusal is a complex problem with interrelated issues, not the least of which is
mental ill health. Families need support and to know they are not alone. Young people
need patience, compassion and flexible options. Professionals including teachers,
principals, GPs, and psychologists need to be educated on ways to best support families
experiencing school refusal. The school system needs to radically change to adapt to the
diverse needs of students including neurodivergence.

Recommendations:

1. Professional development programs for teachers and school leadership on school
refusal. This would include: how to communicate with and support parents and carers;
how to adapt assessments and learning plans for students; how to respond to students
when they are on campus.

2. Peer mentoring programs established with a dedicated focus on school refusal.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 66 3. Parental leave policies that explicitly include care for school refusal students.

4. Information brochures/leaflets widely available through schools, GPs, psychologists etc
that discuss school refusal and outline approaches to manage it.

It is hard to fully capture in words the impact of school refusal. It is difficult to understand,
confronting, challenging and frustrating. It impacts parents, students, siblings, extended
family, and work places. But it can also teach us about our young people, and what their
needs are, and how sadly inflexible and inaccessible the mainstream school structure is for
them and others like them. This has got to change.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 66

I enclose a personal submission to the Senate Standing Committee on Education and Employment
for the inquiry into ‘The national trend of school refusal and related matters’, for inquiry and report
by 22 March 2023.

I write this submission as a parent of two ‘school refusers’ in
opinions in this submission are informed by the experiences of my family.

 public education system. My

My first child stopped attending school in 2020 due to bullying and the subsequent deterioration of
mental health. Alternate schooling options were made available to my child mid-2022.

My second child stopped attending school Term 2 2022, triggered by delayed impacts of COVID-19
related school closures and at-home learning, the cumulative effects of bullying throughout their
schooling life, and witnessing first-hand the struggles of a sibling.

I am experienced in teaching and have working knowledge of current education issues.

It is my hope that through this submission, the Committee may gain insight to some of the struggles
and long-lasting impacts on families who experience school refusal.

I encourage the Committee to consider the proposals outlined, as a starting point to address some of
the many contributing factors to school refusal.

I thank you for the opportunity to contribute to this inquiry.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 67














 Submission: The national trend of school refusal and related matters

PAGE 2 of 4

The national trend of school refusal and related matters

Terms of Reference

a.  The increasing number since the COVID-19 pandemic, of young people and their families who

are experiencing school refusal.

b.  How school refusal is affecting young people and their families and the impacts it is having on

the employment and financial security of parents and carers.

d.  How relevant state, territory and federal departments are working to monitor and address this

growing school refusal challenge.

Key issues and solutions

Framing school refusal in context of the COVID-19 pandemic risks overlooking key causes
and solutions

1.  Trends in school refusal should be considered alongside trends in return to work at an office

-  For some young people, the cause of school refusal may pre-date the pandemic. Time away
from school as a result of school closures may have reinforced negative perceptions about
the extent of the problem that is preventing young people going to school.

-  What percentage of the adult workforce continues to work from home some or all of the

time?

School refusal isolates young people and families, fractures relationships, leads to poor
physical and mental health, and diminishes the capacity of parents/carers to engage in
employment

2.  Governments and schools should reframe the terms they use, informed by perspectives of young

people

-  The term ‘school refusal’ shifts and ties the problem to the young person rather than

acknowledging the problem is separate. This negatively impacts the mindset of the young
person and leads to poor mental health and isolation.

3.  Schools should provide access to continuous learning support when young people are not at

school

-  Schools provide minimal to no instruction in learning (or learning support) when a young

person is not at school because of school refusal.

-  The young person ‘falls behind’ in their learning, which leads to increased anxiety about

going to school, poor mental health, continued school refusal and isolation.

-

In the absence of learning support the young person turns to other activities, such as online
gaming, to keep them occupied, making it harder for families to break the cycle of school
refusal.

4.  Governments should run a national education campaign targeted at parents and the broader
community, noting how friends and family can support those experiencing school refusal

-  Extended family and friends do not understand school refusal. Their lack of understanding is
reflected in ill-informed advice and leads to diminished trust in relationships and increased
stress for the family experiencing school refusal. Families experiencing school refusal
become isolated.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 67 Submission: The national trend of school refusal and related matters

PAGE 3 of 4

5.  Governments should provide holistic support for both the young person and the family of the

young person experiencing school refusal

-

Increased stress leads to poor physical and mental health for everyone in the family unit –
the young person experiencing school refusal, parents/carers and siblings of the young
person.

-  Siblings may resent the school refuser, perceive the situation as unfair and start to refuse to

go to school themselves.

-  Parents/carers and siblings cannot support the young person experiencing school refusal if

they do not know how. Targeted support is needed for the whole family unit.

6.  Governments should make it easier for families to find and access timely support, locally

-  There is an overwhelming amount of information for families to sift through, to find support

services suited to their needs.

-  Families experience extended waiting periods to access services, during which time the

health of the entire family deteriorates.

7.  Governments should support employers to provide ongoing assistance to employees who are

caring for young people experiencing school refusal

-  The varied and unique needs of school refusers leads to an increased level of time and
specialist support needed from parents/carers, schools and health professionals.

-  Parents/carers need to work from home to supervise their young person, often commencing
work late, working reduced hours or working after hours to accommodate their young
person’s needs during working hours. This leads to poor physical and mental health.

8.  Schools should enable young people to return to school at their own pace, and not place

increased pressure on young people and their families

-  Schools and teachers place primary emphasis on school attendance, not student learning.

-  Support plans offered by schools are generic and time limited; they do not reflect an

understanding of school refusal.

-  Blame is shifted to parents/carers and the young person. Schools threaten parents with
litigation and issue warnings of non-completion of mandatory school requirements. This
diminishes already stressed relationships of families and young people and exacerbates the
situation.

State, territory and federal departments place too much emphasis on school attendance
when they should be working to monitor and address school refusal by reviewing school
structures, providing at-home learning support, and approaching school refusal holistically
in partnership with health services

9.  Sectors and schools should review whether it is appropriate to apply legislation on school

attendance to circumstances of school refusal, and whether the legislation was intended to be
applied in this way

-  Commonwealth, State and Territory Education Acts mandate school attendance, being at

odds with the issue of school refusal. Is it assumed that attendance implies a young person is
engaged with, and is making progress in learning, and is it fair to make this assumption in
2022?

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 67 Submission: The national trend of school refusal and related matters

PAGE 4 of 4

-  Support plans developed by schools to assist young people to return to school often focus on

attendance, when they should instead focus on addressing reasons why the student is
refusing school, for example diverse learning needs not being met, bullying and/or health.

10. Schools should accurately record non-attendance and acknowledge a young person’s effort to

attend school

-  Student absences are assigned a category from a list of limiting options in databases that
record school attendance. Free-text fields may not accurately capture reasons for non-
attendance (for example, bullying) or part-day attendance.

-  Young people who attempt to attend school and stand at the school gate for an hour, or
who spend time in the school office but not in a classroom, are likely recorded as absent.
Their efforts are not recognised.

11. Schools should provide access to continuous learning support when young people are not at

school

-  Sectors and schools have established systems to engage with young people when not
physically present at school, for example, the systems set up to deliver online learning
during the COVID-19 pandemic. What responsibility do schools and teachers have to
continue to provide learning support to young people who cannot attend school because of
school refusal?

12. Schools should structure the school day around the needs of young people

-  Schools set timetables. Timetables should reflect the needs of young people. Is there a need
for constant change and disruption to learning during the school day, particularly in high
school? What impact does constant change have on young people who are struggling to
attend? Is it a precursor to school refusal?

13. School systems should provide timely access to alternatives to mainstream school. Home

schooling is not an alternative

-  The NSW Government has alternative schools, including distance education and schools for
specific purposes. However, strict criteria precludes students from enrolling in these schools
until their condition has significantly deteriorated and the circumstances of school refusal
are extreme. Families and young people are made aware of alternative schools very late in
the process of school refusal. Alternative schools should focus on prevention and early
intervention.

14. Schools should prioritise the wellbeing of young people over student achievement and results

15. Governments should provide access to adequate training for teachers

16. School sectors should reconsider the purpose of various school support roles – are they

achieving positive outcomes for young people?

-  For example, the NSW Department of Education has multiple roles in wellbeing and home
school liaison. Is it a requirement of appointment to these roles, to understand school
refusal and have the skillsets needed to work with young people and families? Are these
roles achieving positive outcomes for young people and families?

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 67

9 December, 2022

SUBMISSION TO THE SENATE EDUCATION AND EMPLOYMENT REFERENCES
COMMITTEE INQUIRY INTO SCHOOL REFUSAL

Dear Senators,

Parents Victoria (PV) is a state wide democratic organisation representing parents of
students in Victorian government schools.  PV welcomes the opportunity to make a
submission to the Senate Education and Employment References Committee Inquiry into
school refusal.

PV is also a State Affiliate of the Australian Council of State School
Organisations (ACSSO). ACSSO being the national voice of parents and children in
Australia’s public schools and their school communities, we also support their submission
into this inquiry.

PV would like to take this inquiry opportunity to outline how we view school refusal
through a parent’s lens from a Victorian perspective.

School refusal is relational

The Problem & Solutions

> The child does not wish to enter the trench warfare that is purely relational in the school.
The relationships the children have to form or encounter can just be too much for them.

> The learning side of things is not the real challenge it is the lack of “social security” which
denies them the proclivity to enter the school environment. The relationship matrix that is
the school, frightens them and they feel out of control.

> Families likewise struggle with this trench warfare for they try to set strategies to encourage
their child but find that they in the end; in trying to maintain a care relationship with their
child, are compromised and feel without direction. These families can feel shame and as
parents they “hide” by establishing explanations that deflect away from shame and blame.

> Schools are not equipped with people to deal with these challenging cases and therefore
are unable to really assist the child so behaving, or the family.

> Special training is needed - and much care as the school works with the parents in the first
place - and then with the child. This is quite an investment and is critical.

1

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 68











































 > Sometimes the psychologists are not helpful for they are looking for weaknesses in
upbringing and thus find themselves on the shame/blame path. Parents find this off putting
and unhelpful.

> Each circumstance requires care and different attention. This takes time and patience and
“active and constructive listening” before beginning to, with the parent and the child, set a
process jointly and then erode the refusal. Often steps are made and then lost in this process
so the process has to be resilient and manage the failures constructively without harming any
of the stakeholders.

> There are too many do-gooders who have the answers for schools and parents, but who
have not worked with real circumstances families are facing.

> It is easy to advise at arms-length however actually working with these circumstance-driven
individuals and families requires establishing a quality relationship, trusting all, having faith in
one another, forgiving one another, not harming anyone, injecting hope - as a key
ingredient - for it eventually provides the child with a sense of control (and the family).

> Everyone needs to understand that the overall intention is the care for the child.

> Understanding the five elements of a quality relationship, being forever referred to and
attended to by all parties. Refer to our recent work with Relationship based Education (RbE).
https://www.parentsvictoria.asn.au/issues category/relationship-based-education/

> The overall aim is to help and to give a sense of relational security and relational
confidence which then allows the school-refusing student to be more courageous and to
step more confidently into the relational unknowns they all face when they attend school.

PV acknowledges every school refusal case is unique, it must be treated differently and with
care. The above is an attempt to give an outline to what can work in all cases but
remembering that such does need to be nuanced to each case.

It is not uncommon for schools to enforce part time attendance or suspend primary school
aged students for complex behaviours.   Those families impacted constantly question how
can this be acceptable when schools and the government advocate it’s not OK to be away
and how absenteeism impacts on learning?

PV would like to express our deep concerns that student bullying in schools has a direct
correlation with poor student attendance.  This can often lead to school refusal if the bullying
is not addressed quickly and child feels unsafe.

Finally, PV would like to take this opportunity to suggest a further solution as a form of
prevention measure – Family Engagement Officers.   This added human resource would
enable teachers to know and engage families more effectively.  It would reduce the
demands on teacher workload and potentially address the challenges teachers are raising
with their employer to prevent them leaving the profession.
https://www.parentsvictoria.asn.au/issues/family-engagement-officers-in-schools/

PV looks forward to hearing about the findings from this inquiry and more importantly the
solutions that result from it.

Sincerely, Gail McHardy, Chief Executive Officer

2
