Introduction
I am the mother of children who have struggled with school attendance difficulties. I am a qualified
teacher, having retrained to teach primary school when my children were little. I am now

for the School-Can’t parent peer support group on Facebook.  I have done a lot of

reading and networking and listening and writing to make sense of my children’s experience in
education and my own as their mother. I have found that there are knowledge and practises and
frameworks for understanding that could make a huge difference to a child’s experience of school,
but these are not widely proliferated, such as problem-solving models that seek to identify and
address the barriers and stressors that our children experience in school, to aligning educational
practise with what neuroscience teaches us about the human autonomic nervous system and the
importance of relationship.

“Do the best you can until you know better. Then when you know better, do better.”
- Maya Angelou

We are all learning. It takes time to move from an idea, to an evidence base, to systemic change.  I
believe that current, culturally embedded, ways of thinking, in particular around inclusion and
behaviour, are acting as an impediment to making our education system better.

“There comes a point where we need to stop just pulling people out of the river.
We need to go upstream and find out why they’re falling in.” - Desmond Tutu

Much of this same knowledge can also be applied in re-engaging children in school, but at this point
is will be much harder to do, as relationships are damaged, and children are traumatised. My
recommendations constitute proactive strategies to promote student engagement and wellbeing
with the aim of preventing school attendance difficulties, and strategies that can be used to support
children and families when school attendance difficulties occur.

“People do well when they can.” – Dr Ross Greene

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 70 Recommendations
Universal Inclusive Education
Students with disability who are in more inclusive educational settings experience fewer discipline
incidents and less absenteeism (Anderson, K. P. ,2021, https://doi.org/10.3102/0162373720968558).
As a society Australia must make and implement a plan to desegregate our education system, and to
move from a system of mainstream and specialist settings to one of universal settings that support
all children and young people.

Non-Segregated Education is a Human Right
According to Article 24 of the United Nations Conventions on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities,
to which Australia is a signatory, our children with disabilities have a right to an inclusive (non-
segregated) education. These human rights obligations must be enshrined in Australian law, and
education departments around the country must be held accountable for ensuring these obligations
are met.

End Gatekeeping
We must train our teachers in inclusive educational practise. We must set the expectation that all
children have a right to a non-segregated education in a classroom with non-disabled peers. We
must ensure that schools are not tempted to exclude students that they consider too hard or to
recommend that they be educated elsewhere. We must appropriately resource our schools.

Talk Positively About Students
We must change the system of disability funding so that parents and clinicians do not have to paint
children with disability in the worst possible light in order that schools get the funding to support
them, and so that families are not advised to set their children up to do poorly at IQ tests to meet
eligibility criteria for specialist settings. Words matter, and the way we talk about students, can
impact our interpretation of their difficulties, and their view of themselves.

Be Responsive to Need
Schools must become a lot more flexible about meeting the needs of students with disability. I feel
that words like consistency and routine and fidelity, and building resilience, are often used an excuse
to do more of the same, when what is really required is a different approach. The uncertain and the
unpredictable can be countered with compassion, coregulation, responsiveness to need, a
restoration of agency and respect. We do not make progress by keeping things the same. There is a
saying, that equity is not everyone having the same thing, but everyone getting what they need to
succeed.

Never use resilience as an excuse to forgo support. Scaffolding is vital. We teach children to swim in
the shallow end of the swimming pool and use floatation devices to help them when the water gets
too deep. We don’t simply throw them in the deep end because they need to develop resilience.

Teach our Children where They are At
Learning loss is an artificial concept, as children never stop learning. Each one of us can build on
what we already know. Children can just pick up from where they left off if we are prepared to teach
them where they are at. It’s only of concern when we insist that children of the same age or year
level must be at the same position on a standardised learning timeline.

Page | 3

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 70 Social Model of Disability
The social model of disability says that disability is a caused by environments and contexts that do
not meet the needs of a person. We must recognise that people with disabilities experience barriers
and stressors in daily living and in attendance at school, that those without disability do not. If a
child with disability is not coping at school, you will see stress behaviour. It is a sign that there in an
unmet need. Something, perhaps many things, in the environment, whether physical or social or
embedded in the very expectations we have for that child, is getting in the way of what that child
needs.

Unconditional Positive Regard

“Treating behaviour like misbehaviour means we punish. Treating behaviour as stress behaviour
means we help.” - Stuart Shanker‬

We must send the message to our children that they belong and that they will be supported when
they find things hard. Do not use a child’s relationships as a tool for manipulating their behaviour.
Those relationships are critical to their wellbeing and must never be compromised.

There might be a time when a child is overwhelmed or exhausted and needs a break from school. Let
them have a break, even if it means that they head home with their grownups for the rest of the
day, or take a few days away from school, but set the context that they are not in trouble, set the
context that the teachers care and that there is an unmet need for down time, with the full
expectation that they will be welcome and valued when the child feels rested and ready to return to
the classroom or to school.

Don’t use public traffic light systems, wherein you write children’s names on the board, or move a
child’s peg up and down a chart for demonstrating off task, inattentive or fidgety behaviour. Don’t
shame children publicly when they are having a hard time in the classroom. Shame is not going to
help a child behave more to your liking. It will add to their stress load, make that child feel othered,
and point him out to all the bullies as the most vulnerable child in the room.

Don’t hold special events that rely on students meeting an attendance threshold or having enough
Class Dojo points to prove their worth. These systems are exclusionary, and shaming, and penalise
students for their struggles.

Maintain Boundaries Between Home and School
School staff do not get to dictate what happens inside the home. Home must always be a safe place
for a child, where they can be themselves, rest and restore and find refuge when things are hard. Do
not advise parents to make home boring so that school is more appealing by comparison.
Concentrate instead on making school accessible, welcoming and inclusive; a place where our
children experience belonging, connection, a sense of success and purpose.

Make It Easier to Change Schools
We must also make it easier for students to change schools, when things have gone badly at their
current school, and the relationship between a student and their school has fractured. We cannot
expect all students to return to environments in which they have experienced isolation, exclusion,
othering or bullying. Our aim should be to prevent these ruptures, and ultimately to reduce the need
for remediation when a relationship between child and school breaks down. However, we need
backup processes in place for when these relationships are irrecoverable. Sometimes a child’s
wellbeing requires that we change educational settings.

Page | 4

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 70‬
‬
‬
‬
‬
‬
‬
 Make it Easier to Undertake Home-schooling and Distance Education
We must also make it easier for students to undertake home-schooling or distance education, and
support parents in this move, including increased financial supports for families, such as supports to
meeting cost of living, access to disability funding for education that would otherwise be paid to the
school, increasing the Assistance for Isolated Children payments and broadening eligibility criteria.
Many of us have a period of not being able to work while we attempt to re-engage our children with
school, but at this point, this supplement is not available to us and we may not get exemptions from
mutual obligations on social support payments like Job Seeker, not to mention those of us who have
ongoing financial commitments such mortgages and rent for which this scenario was completely
unanticipated.

End the Bias Towards Home-schooling
Many of us are discouraged from home-schooling by the overt bias of education and mental health
professionals, who feel that students are better educated in schools, when experience of school has
negatively impacted a child’s wellbeing, and therefore their capacity to learn. We can’t just keep
pushing through without appropriate supports. This is exhausting.  We are stressed, we burn out,
parents and children alike.

We must acknowledge that there are alternate pathways ways to higher education other than
school. Approximately 30% of students of first year higher education students are admitted to their
courses on the basis of their ATAR. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-
news/2021/jul/31/alternatives-to-the-atar-most-kids-dont-know-about-them

Another support for home-schooling, would be to have optional access to state provided learning
supports for children not in the school system, such as education hubs where children could sample
classes, or home visiting teachers or tutors, or interest based online classes, or to allow home school
students to attend public school for specific classes only such as PE or Art. There is a lot of creativity
and industry in the home-school community, as families and teachers try to build up suitable
educational and social networking infrastructure for home-school families themselves. These
industries must also be supported. The key to meeting the needs of our community are
collaboration, diverse offerings, flexibility, financial and organisational assistance.

Universal Design to Mitigate Undiagnosed Student Learning Needs
We must change our systems of school discipline. Our tendency to frame student behaviour in terms
of motivation is a barrier to understanding hidden disability and learning differences. PhD Candidate
Haley Tancredi from QUT has researched the prevalence of language and attention difficulties in
students, to test the notion that a universal design approach to teaching with respect to these
conditions will proactivity mitigate these student difficulties. She tested a sample of students in year
10 and found that a significant portion of the students had previously undiagnosed and potentially
unsupported language and attention difficulties, pointing to a need for universal design approaches.
This research is not yet published, but Tancredi prepared a short video presentation describing her
research and her findings. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0O9HT8g2j1U

While we’re busy thinking that these undiagnosed students are lazy and unmotivated, and while
these students are feeling bad about their capacity to meet adult expectations, and while we’re busy
searching for reading material that might interest the children or using reward charts to encourage
reading and perhaps feeling frustrated that a student isn’t meeting their potential, or perhaps
thinking that their parents haven’t read books to them or modelled good reading habits, there is an

Page | 5

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 70 underlying neurological reason for their difficulties which not one has yet picked up! And that
requires our support and compassion, not a judgement on the character of the parent or child.

Adult assumptions often get the way of us understanding how we can best support our children.
Many behaviours are symptomatic of an underlying difficulty. They are a signal.  We must lean in, dig
deep, and become curious. What is really going on for our children and young people when they are
not meeting adult expectations?

Collaborative and Proactive Solutions to Identify and Address Hidden Barriers

“Everybody is talking about the behavior. Behaviors float downstream to us. We need to paddle
upstream. The problems that are causing the behaviors, that's what's waiting for us. It's a crucial
paradigm shift.” -  Dr. Ross Greene

Dr. Ross Greene, author of the book Lost at School, has a beautiful model for identifying and
addressing problems impacting our children, with our children, both at home or at school. It is called
Collaborative and Proactive Solutions (CPS). In this model children learn to identify and to work
through the problems that are causing them difficulties, in a dialogue facilitated by an adult and
driven by the child. Together adult and child identify and acknowledge what is difficult, barriers that
can be removed and accommodations that can be put in place to support the child. Children learn
not only that they can be agents in solving the problems they face, but that they can call on their
grown-ups and peers when they need assistance.

We have schools in Australia using this model, such as Dynamic Alternative Learning Environment
(DALE) at St Philip’s Christian College in NSW, featured in NSW Education Department Magazine
https://education.nsw.gov.au/content/dam/main-education/teaching-and-learning/professional-
learning/scan/media/documents/vol-40/Scan 40-7 August2021 AEM.pdf  There a growing
evidence base for CPS https://link.springer.com/epdf/10.1007/s10567-019-00295-
z?author access token=vmOPHvbAaIJoksUgIPWH e4RwlQNchNByi7wbcMAY7VUkJRW2aYL2g6pY1
1SZOuB9gdQEBcF7ymn18DwZHo-o-hyyFUG50Dk0GPvv8-
vKCFoR1vlEb3Z9Bh2Q8IWRYMvMrB6hZhjPAUCBMEMyPaqw==&fbclid=IwAR1Q2yfUtsRGiEfhqbWBA
mmduiHuYDdgO8ltu4xJWu6t0u4O2k6krASJurI, including research from The Kidman Centre at the
University of NSW https://www.uts.edu.au/research/kidman-centre/collaborative-proactive-
solutions-clinic-certified-dr-ross-greene/collaborative-and-proactive-solutions-cps-clinic.

Collaborative and Proactive Solutions represents a huge paradigm shift in the ways that we
understand and respond to children’s behaviour, but it is a necessary one, to bring equity to our
schools. The use of Positive Behaviour Interventions and Support (PBIS) is widespread in Australian
schools and is promoted by education departments and in teacher training at universities across the
country. PBIS is a Multitiered System of Support (MTSS), built on an engine of Applied Behaviour
Analysis (ABA), a behaviourist lens for understanding and modifying behaviour. PBIS can be modified
to incorporate Collaborative and Proactive Solutions, as has been done in this paper
https://view.officeapps.live.com/op/view.aspx?src=https%3A%2F%2Flivesinthebalance.org%2Fwp-
content%2Fuploads%2F2021%2F06%2FCPS-and-PBIS-Paper-4-13-21.docx

You will find that CPS is a preferred model of addressing behaviours of concern, within the
neurodiversity community. It creates a space for the child’s feelings to be explored and validated,
building emotional literacy. By sharing perspectives, adult and child learn things about each other’s
experiences, that may not have been inferred previously. When adult and child are different
neurotypes this becomes especially important, due to the double empathy problem, a term coined
by autistic researcher Damian Milton, in reference to the difference in subjective experience

Page | 6

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 70 between people of different neurotypes. Adult set expectations that are full of assumptions based
their own subjective experiences. When it comes to the behaviours of neurodivergent children, they
are often jumping to the wrong conclusions about their behaviour.

Collaborative and Proactive Solutions will reduce a child’s stress load, by addressing the barriers that
are causing stress behaviours, and you do not add to their stress load with a punishment or a
withheld reward when they are already struggling. The Collaborative and Proactive Solutions model
honours the relationship between adult and child, leading the adult to demonstrate unconditional
acceptance and support for the child, without compromising the relationship with the child because
their stress behaviour is inconvenient.

Incorporate knowledge about the Autonomic Nervous System into Educational
Practice
Knowledge about the human autonomic nervous system increases our understanding of human
behaviour and gives us new strategies for helping children who are easily distressed.

 We learn that when a child’s nervous system is in a protective state, that access to social
functions such as socialising, thinking deeply, being playful and curious, and making
thoughtful choices is significantly dampened, as the body redirects resources into keeping
the child safe.

 We learn that the body and brain move into patterns of protection such as flight, fight and
shutdown, automatically when a person’s autonomic nervous system detects signs of
danger. A meltdown or a shutdown is not something that is chosen.

 We learn that the state of one person’s autonomic nervous system, can impact the state of



another.
A person with a calm nervous system, can lend their calm to another, and help a distressed
person return to a state of calm through coregulation.

A person with a heightened nervous system may inadvertently escalate another.
 We learn that capacity to self-regulate develops over time. Repeated instances of

coregulating with others via the medium of relationship, build the bran circuitry that will one
day be used for self-regulation. When a mother reassures and calms her crying infant, she is
coregulating with her child, helping her child to down regulate from a distressed state to one
of calm and felt safety.

These learnings come from Polyvagal Theory, developed by Stephen Porges. His work has been
translated into the parenting context by psychologist Mona Delahooke and to the education context
by educators Lori Desautels and Claire Wilson. Polyvagal Theory is built into many models of trauma
informed education, such as the Berry Street model.

With this knowledge we come to recognise that



Systems of rewards and consequence are not suitable for managing a child’s stress
behaviour. Instead, we must think about how we can influence that that child’s nervous
system, by reducing that child’s stress load, helping the distressed child to down regulate,
A well-regulated teacher can coregulate an entire classroom,


 Opportunities for regulation, such as play at recess or lunch, should never be used as



rewards or consequences,
Timeouts, seclusion and exclusion deny children relationship, which is to deny them the
bridge through which coregulation occurs and regulatory capacity is built.

Page | 7

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 70  When a child is overwhelmed and demonstrating stress behaviours, their cognitive functions
are not fully available to them, so discussions with children about their behaviour are best
left until they have calmed. (Neuroscientist Bruce Perry has proposed a sequential model of
engagement, that follows this principle, The 3 Rs – Regulate, Relate and then Reason.)

Chronic stress and trauma can sensitize our nervous systems, so that we go into these protective
states far more quickly. Due to nervous system differences, and experiential factors such as
increased risk of bullying, neurodivergent students experience high levels of stress.

Teach Models for Identifying and Addressing Stress
A stressor is anything that uses energy. Stress within our window of tolerance is important for
learning and growth. Too much stress and too much stress over and extended period, not only
depletes us, but sensitises the nervous system, reducing our tolerance for more stress.

Shanker Self-Reg is a model for identifying and reducing stress and for identifying practises that help
us recover from stress. We learn that to helping our children manage stress starts with all the grown
ups in a child’s life (e. g. their parents and teachers) learning how to address their own stress and
being supported in this endeavour.

Models of energy planning such as Spoon Theory, an informal model used in the disability
community, teach us to plan for our energy expenditure, to plan for rest and recovery, and how to
set boundaries that prioritise our wellbeing.

 Both of those models are very helpful in reducing stress and improving the lived experience of
children and adults.

Address Teacher Stress
It is vital to our children’s education that look after our teachers. Our teachers can only bring their
best selves to the classroom is they are well rested physically and mentally, well-regulated and
engaged. Teachers who are well-regulated have capacity to coregulate with children and young
people and down regulate their stress response. Well-regulated teachers are less likely to co-
escalate with stressed children and young people.

We must address the stressors in the system impacting teachers such as teacher workload, the
casualisation of the workforce, pay teachers more and show them that we value the work that they
do. Schools are workplaces, and they must prioritise the wellbeing of their staff. We must also fund
and resource schools appropriately, so that they that teachers have what they need to do their jobs.

Implement Interoceptive Capacity Building Supports in our schools
Interoception refers to our internal senses, sense that indicate pain or hunger or needing to go to
the toilet etc., or the physical feelings associated with an emotional state. If we are not aware of our
internal senses or cannot make sense of what our internal senses are telling us, then we have
difficulty meeting our needs and proactively managing our stressors. For example, if you cannot tell
that your hand is burnt, you will not remove it from the stove and could be much more seriously
injured.

Emma Goodall is Australia’s resident expert on interoception. She and psychologist Wenn Lawson
developed an Interocepetion Curriculum for the Department of Education in South that if freely
available from the department website. The practises articulated in these documents are designed
to build interoceptive awareness, and therefore empower students to manage their needs.

Page | 8

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 70 Teach Autism as a Neurological Difference, not a Behavioural Disorder
The diagnostic criteria for Autism diagnoses are observational, which has led to a mindset of
targeting autistic behaviours to change them. This is typically done with systems of rewards and
consequences, often ignorant to multitude of different underlying reasons for behaviour, or the
value of that behaviour to a person. Behaviour is information, but behaviour is not always volitional.
These systems may discount a child’s subjective experience, their feelings, their energy levels, their
skill to meet an expectation, the state of their nervous system, their maturity, or the physical
limitations of a child’s body to do what has been incentivised.

When you consider autism as a neurological difference, a multitude of different possible strategies
emerge to support an autistic child, and many of these strategies have to do with supporting the
regulation needs of that child’s autonomic nervous system. When we target a child’s needs, we
address the source of their distress; We will see fewer behaviours of concern.

My suggestion would be to teacher educators and aides working with autistic children and young
people in schools about these topics related to autism:

 Models of Autism such as Intense World Theory, Monotropism, Predictive Coding, Allostatic

Independent Oversight
We need independent oversight of education departments around Australia; channels for complaint,
arbitration and problem solving. All these things must involve persons with lived experience of
disability and other marginalised groups impacted by inequities in the education system.  We need
an organisation that can help ensure that our children are appropriately supported and to hold our
schools accountable.

Acknowledge Parental Stressors and Support Parents to Address These
Parents face enormous stress when their children are struggling at school. It is natural to be
concerned for a child’s wellbeing and for their education. We step in and advocate when things are
not going well. We spend hours on end waiting with them in carparks or hanging around school or
trying to get children ready and out the door or listening to them and attending to them in their
upset. We make multiple trips to and from school coming to pick them up early or to drop them off
late.  We organise appointments and meetings and assessments. We search for providers. We take
our children to therapies. We collect reports. We write carer impact statements and apply for
funding in education and disability support. With what we know and the resources at hand, we do
our level best to get our children appropriate supports. All this takes time and energy and love.

For other children, teachers act in loco parentis during a school day, when children are in
attendance. But often not for our children, because ours aren’t often in attendance, or aren’t in
attendance without us also being present. Between bureaucracy, worry, caring and the lack of
routine and predictability, many of us do not have consistent time available for paid work, and our
standard of living is impacted.

Sometimes the gap between what we need and what people think we need or what we are entitled
to is huge. Sometimes we have to give up things that we love or need, and we make compromises
and concessions to expectations we previously held, because our children’s need is so great that we
cannot see another way. Sometimes parents can’t do things, because our children can’t do things,
because the world is not so easily accessible to them. We must be creative and flexible and do things
differently because the world is not working the way it is supposed to, for our children or for us.

And then there are the social narratives, which paint children who struggle and their parents, as
dysfunctional and wilful and oppositional and lazy and all other words we have for people who don’t
make the grade. These are very one-sided narratives, that rarely considers that the other part of this
equation is a child’s experience of school.

School Refusal is isolating, heart wrenching, financially draining and exhausting.

Parents have limited impact to the school environment. We are usually only ever on the periphery of
that experience, as advisers to school on how to meet the needs of our children. We do have impact
to the home environment.

Our children are distressed, their distress impacts our adult nervous systems. We are distressed, and
our distress impacts our children’s nervous systems right back. We can get caught in a pattern of
stress escalation, reacting to each other’s dysregulation.

Page | 10

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 70 Once we learn a little about the way that stress states travel through groups of people, but that a
well-regulated person can lend their calm to another, we being to see that there is an intervention in
the home, and that is to reduce parent stress, so that we can lend our calm to our children.  Far
easier said that done.  Stressors accumulate, so anything that acts as a release valve will help. We
find a way to put on our own parachutes and start with bite sized self-care. But it’s not enough. We
need a community that cares and supports us.

Our stories and our struggles, set us apart from broader society and are not well understood by the
institutions and services or other people in our lives.  They are also hard to tell, in part because of
the shame and judgement felt by families, but also because these are not just our stories; They are
our children’s. And our children have a right to privacy.

I joined the school can’t group in 2018 and
 It is a wonderful
group of parents and primary carers, who support and learn from one another, as we support our
children. I found community and common ground in this group. I made friends who got it.  That
lifted an enormous weight from my shoulders. I began to make sense of what had happened.

Conclusion
School attendance difficulties are complex, and there will be different underling reasons for different
children. Whatever is going on for an individual child, we need to discover the things that are making
school attendance hard for that child, and work with the child to address them, prioritising that
child’s wellbeing over and above their attendance. A child’s learning is compromised under excessive
stress. No one can learn when they are dysregulated. As the old saying goes, we must Maslow
before we Bloom.

When a child’s needs are met, we will see less stress behaviour, we will see fewer calls to manage
their behaviour and we will see more attendance.

Human connection is a biological imperative. We need safe relationships with other humans for our
very wellbeing. Even the introverts among us! Universal inclusive education, practises that address
the barriers and stressors that our children experience, and practises informed by the neuroscience
of human relationships will go a long way to helping us prevent and remediate school attendance
difficulties.

“Both my children LOVED school – until they didn’t. I was a highly paid professional – now I'm not.”

School Can’t fundamental issue is:

 ‘I DON'T FEEL SAFE’

It is fuelled by:

Pressure – in school environment and when school can’t presents (a vicious cycle)

Competition – Australian schools are based on placing kids higher than each other as opposed to the
most successful education approaches in the world (Scandanavian countries) where competition doesn’t
play a part.

Bullying – students, teachers and parents

Negative feedback – student feedback is usually 10% you’ve done well and 90% this is how you need to
improve. It is teacher led not student led. Post school can’t the child is getting negative feedback from
teachers/parents/mental health professionals – a vicious circle.

Sensory overload – too loud, bright, too many kids, smells, not enough time to process, overwhelm etc

Not seeing the logic of what they are learning – seeing the one size fits all approach as filler, not seeing
how it fits into real life application.

Low self esteem (prior or post school can’t)

Anxiety – GAD, social anxiety, separation anxiety

Depression (prior or post school can’t)

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 72

 Inauthentic institutions and people – sensitive school can’t children sense when people are not genuine

Recommendations for Senate

-  Change language for School Refusal to School Can’t – most children want to go to school but
they just ‘can’t’. They are in flight (amygdala) and it is not a conscience thought. It is extreme
fear.

-  ALL schools to introduce flexible learning options – hours/subjects/remote – children from
younger age should be able to choose what subjects they learn. Fundamentals such as
literacy/numeracy are taught to certain level however other subjects are chosen per child
preference.

-  Make it illegal for ALL schools to pull a child’s enrolment due to School Can’t (unless broken a

serious rule like violence/drugs etc).

-  Make ALL schools have a School Can’t program that is based on National guidelines co-created

by mental health professionals/school can’t parents/school can’t children and federal education
representative so it is genuinely representative and effective. As soon a child presents with
school can’t they can have understanding, empathy, remote school option and therapies that
helps them through the process no matter how long it takes – child led.

-  A thorough research program is conducted to understand the triggers for school can’t and how
education institutions can make positive changes to circumnavigate these issues – eg. Bullying,
too much pressure, too long at school, negative teaching styles etc

-  Based on the above research plus research into overseas positive educational approaches (eg.
Scandavian countries) new type of school is created. Yes established schools can make positive
changes but a new school, genuine approach is required, where a child’s need for mental,
physical, emotional, intellectual and sensory safety is prioritised above the schools academic
scores, funding, enrolment numbers etc.
Support for school can’t parents – a support website is created where parents are instantly
directed and they can get all supports – therapies, emotional, mental and financial support.
Most parents (usually the mother) has had to give up work to support their school can’t child. It
is devastating financially, mentally, emotionally and their career effectively halts.

submissions.text:
Submission to The Parliament of Australia:

Inquiry into the National Trend of School Refusal

To whom it may concern:

I worked in a career within education for over 30 years.  Trained as a primary school

teacher, I continued my education to include two Masters Degrees. I also started a PhD

intending to examine the impacts of lack of school attendance (including withdrawal by

family) for young children with Autism. I ceased this study when I realised that I would

encounter significant blocking from both the school systems, and also to some extent by the

University.  Everyone’s funding is dependent on perceived ‘success’ of the individual

structure on a short-term basis. Nobody could afford anything that may resemble criticism.

At the time I was working as an academic at Queensland University of Technology, and also

undertaking some work privately under a program focussed on working with the families

and young children diagnosed with Autism.  Essentially it was to be an early intervention

program for both the children and their families.  I also undertook some work with older

students who were resisting school attendance due to other factors (mental health, family

situations, learning experiences, bullying etc).

Most of the children with whom I worked were experiencing reasonably significant mental

illness, though not severe enough to involve enrolment at a Special School environment.

Many were diagnosed with (sometimes multiple) neurodivergent conditions. Most had

numerous other (sometimes disconnected from each other) support workers and

professionals, including mental health professionals.  Most took some form of medications

for their condition.

During this period, I noted that many of the children I worked with withdrew from school for

various reasons.  With many of the young children, significant neurodivergence or mental

illness resulted in extreme anxiety and/or behavioural difficulties impacted from the day

they enrolled and commenced school.  They experienced failure from Day 1 or shortly

thereafter.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 75





 At the time the in-school additional supports were comparatively scarce.  Often valuable

resources such as Guidance Counsellors, School Chaplains etc were occupied with more

likely to succeed cases.

Once the students had left the school situation (often having trialled 3 or more schools

within a short period), it was common for their education to be undertaken by a parent,

who was given little guidance or support.  I was often asked to support the completion of

the required paperwork for home-school authority.  Alternately students who came from

more affluent family backgrounds often left the State School system to attend a private

school.  This had limited and varied success, as these schools often would not accept the

most difficult students and/or their attendance soon became problematic, though at times

the pastoral care component provided by some of these schools appeared to assist the

student. An individual teacher could sometimes make a big difference, but this was not

consistent and often difficult for the school to manage.

Based on my experience, and expertise I wish to comment on the ‘Impacts of demands of

the increasing load on service providers and schools’.

The area where I live and worked is classified as quite low socio-economic community, and

included many unemployed parents.  In general the State Schools were significantly

underfunded, leaving them having to apply funding where they might best achieve some

success.  For many of the children who I met, the easiest solution was to initially isolate

them in a Special Ed or Support unit, and then ask the parent to remove them from the

school temporarily.  Sometimes this started in their first week of school experience, so an

expectation was formed. I noted that there was a tendency to employ

underqualified/experienced support workers and experts.  Rarely did I see a School Chaplain

who was sufficiently skilled to work with the most complex of students.

Difficult school situations are not always conducive to attracting the most effective teachers

and support workers. Often, being in low socio-economic localities, they could not generally

attract significant funding through benefactors, fundraising activities and events.

Recommendation 1:  Ensure that schools are realistically funded according to the equity

needs of the students.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 75 Recommendation 2:  Due to the complexity of needs for some students, it is imperative that

the quality of staff is held and supported to highest standards.  Reward staff accordingly.

Their major achievements may not be academic, but in the longer term may be of greater

benefit to society.

Recommendation 3:  Create an independent monitoring body to ensure equitable

distribution of funds to education.

Recommendation 4:  Encourage and support teachers and others who are engaging in

support work for students with significantly higher needs to engage in further quality

training and education, and commensurate them accordingly.

Recommendation 5: Provide for diverse learning opportunities for all aged students, that

support the needs of students who are not succeeding within the current public system.

Investigate a range of alternate educational possibilities. Include greater diversity and

support for families/carers and students who are home-schooling.

In many cases with the students and families with whom I worked, they were experiencing

significant conflict outside of the school.  Many experienced a difficult family life.  Too many

were born to parents who had substance abuse and/or extreme mental illness themselves,

and were being raised by often over-traumatised and poorly supported grandparents.

Although I am aware of large amounts of money being spent in the community, it does not

appear to be gaining full and best benefit.  In many cases multiple services overlap, and

administration costs are a significant drain on what money is available. Service is often

inconsistent, due to the clients testing out various options, without committing fully to any.

Whilst I understand that choice must be available, I noted that often the result was

despondency on the part of the client’s family.  They struggled to find their ‘safe space’.

Many turn to various religious groups, who, whilst I believe they can provide some support,

it is not befitting of a holistic, inclusive and democratic support process.

Recommendation 6: Create diverse, inclusive, fully integrated and financially supported

support hubs within existing community for both the students and their families/carers.

Extend the provision of a safe space that is both secular, as well as inclusive of all

backgrounds.  Ensure appropriateness within the local community rather than uniformity of

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 75 provisions to differing communities. Minimise leakage through administrative costs by

requiring high level business management strategies in all cases. Some of this may be more

effective as a public service, as opposed to a private business.

Recommendation 7:  Ensure that as part of the planning process for all new housing

developments and communities, appropriate community hubs that include the provision of

secular and high quality support services suitable for the most vulnerable potential

members of a diverse population are provided.

Recommendation 8:  Integrate enhanced support services within new communities with

schools, medical facilities, community services etc.  prior to populating the development.

I thank you for your consideration and attention.

When school refusal is viewed as a behaviour problem,
then students are perceived as refusing to go to school.
The student is viewed as wilful or defiant and adults are
more inclined to respond with rewards and
consequences.  Clinicians and education professionals
are more likely to view the problem as residing with in
the child or the family.  In responding they are more
likely to make demands of the family or the student,
that either focus on remedying a fault within the child
or family or focus on gaining compliance with the
expectation of attendance. These lead the parents/
carers and student to feel judged, ashamed, and
experience increasing distress. This conceptualisation
of the problem does not lead to exploration or
identification of the issues underlying school can’t.

The risks associated with this conceptualisation include:

•  Increased feelings of stress leading to feelings of

helplessness for the student and/or parents/carers,
•  Continued and deepened student disengagement,
•  Damage to the parent child attachment,
•  Damage to the student – school relationship,
•  Student distrust of adults and withdrawal from

engaging with them to identify what is impacting
the student.

Figure 2: “Reframe the Behaviour” Visual by Kristin
Weins. Used with permission.  Source:
https://northstarpaths.com/

•  Worsened mental health of the student,
•   Failure to identify how to assist and support the student,
•   Parents / carers left with no choice but to exit mainstream schooling to protect the child’s

mental health and wellbeing.

Reframing school refusal as “school can’t” helps adults instead, to conceptualise school refusal as a
response to stress.  It leads them to be curious and to look for underlying reasons why a student
might be having difficulties attending school. Adults are more likely to identify and remove barriers
and to install accommodations and supports that meet the student at their point of need, reducing
student stress in the process.  Teachers and clinicians are more likely to work collaboratively with
students and their parents/carers to assist them.  Students and their carers feel understood,
supported and safe in their interactions with teachers and clinicians who approach school can’t in
this way.  Parents who join School Can’t (SPSR) Australia report that the change in the way the
problem is conceptualised empowers them: to connect with their child, to seek assessments that
assist them to understand the difficulties and to find solutions and supports enabling their children
to recover and thrive (see Section 7.2.3).

 It is, fundamental when considering school can’t that shared understandings are developed across
the community, in clinical, school, parent, and research contexts in order to effectively address the
issues that lead to school can’t.  Failing to do so puts our young people at risk.

7.1.1 Student Experiences:

Parents and carers share in our parent peer support group about their children’s experiences of
school can’t.  We have observed from the sharing in our group that those experiencing school can’t
may:

1.  Feel frustrated with themselves that they are unable to successfully meet expectations to

attend school,

2.  Either be able to tell us what the issues are, or they may be unable to communicate about
what they are struggling with. Their ability to understand and communicate about the
problem can be impacted by their limited life experience, and/or the state of their nervous
system or any communication disabilities they may have.  These factors can make it hard for
them to make sense of what is happening.

3.  Feel distressed, or even lose hope that the issues that led to them being unable to attend

school will be identified or addressed.

4.  Feel frustrated and angry that no-one seems to understand how to support them.
5.  Feel angry that their concerns are invalidated or dismissed.
6.  Feel frustrated with their school that understanding, accommodations or supports they

needed were not available or that the school lacked the capacity to flexibly meet their
needs.

7.  Feel judged, ashamed and confused from messaging that blames them for school can’t: “try
harder”, be “more resilient”, or “you just need to change your thinking” being common
messages.  This may lead to internalised shame and self-blame

8.  Experience adults (including: parents/carers/teachers/clinicians) who are unable to show
compassion, or curiosity, or to see things from the student’s perspective and who may be
focussed on behaviour management.

9.  Feel that adults are against them or that there is no hope or way to resolve their situation

and lose the ability to trust adults to assist them and may withdraw from contact with them.

10. Experience adults (including: parents/carers/teachers/clinicians) who are anxious about

them and focussed on “worst case scenarios” such as this child will: never get an education,
never live independently, never grow up, never be able to get a job, never be able to go to
university, never amount to anything, or is headed for prison unless we get them back to
school.  The anxieties of these adults lead the child to become increasingly stressed and
anxious.

11. Be aware of the adult community’s anxieties about completion of year 12 and doing well in

year 12.  This anxiety exacerbates the student’s own anxiety about themselves.

12. Experience stress and feel dysregulated for extended periods of time due to the lack of
resolution or relief from the people, situations, or things that are causing them stress.
13. Become socially isolated from peers.  This may be due to reduced proximity to peers, lack of

flexible options for engagement at school, and exclusion by peers both intentional or
unintentional in nature.  Even peers who are sympathetic to the student who would like to
connect can after a while struggle to find shared experiences around which they can
socialise.

7.1.3 The Autonomic Nervous System and School Can’t:

Viewing school refusal through the Polyvagal framework of understanding (Porges 2011) assists us to
understand what is happening for the child.  Seen through this lens school can’t is a symptom of
chronic unresolved stress.  Usually when faced with a stressor our bodies automatically (without
thinking) respond in order to attempt to resolve the situation and help us quickly return to a relaxed
and regulated state often referred to as a state of homeostasis.  This automatic response usually
results in either a fight or flight response.  If the threat is so significant or if a fight/flight response
has been unsuccessful in the past then a shutdown or freeze response in more likely.  A freeze
response sometimes occurs also after a fight or flight response in order help transition back to a
relaxed state.  When children/young people experience something particularly threatening or
stressful or they are exposed to repeated stress or stress that remains unresolved over a period of
time, this impacts their ability to return to a relaxed state.  Normally a stressor is resolved by some
action and we are able to quickly return to a resting state.  However, when students are exposed to
ongoing stress, then a trauma response occurs. This relationship between the ANS and trauma is
discussed by Levine (2015:43-46).  A trauma response leads the baseline resting state to shift from
one of low arousal to one of high arousal.  The student’s nervous system stays alert instead of
returning to a low arousal resting state.  This becomes their new normal resting state.  They seem to
escalate more quickly when faced with a threat and are often diagnosed at this point with anxiety or
PTSD.  When this goes on for too long then the Autonomic Nervous System becomes ineffective at
regulating and Autonomic Nervous System Dysregulation (ANSD) occurs.  There is considerable
research that links stress to a range of physical health impacts which require ongoing medical care.
(Please refer to Section: 19.1 for a more detailed explanation of the Autonomic Nervous System and
ANSD)

Use of rewards and consequences, continued expectations of attendance at school or increased
demands on the student can add more to the student’s stress load, further preventing the student
from being able to return to a “safe” state.  Over time this impacts the student’s mental health and
puts the student’s physical health at risk as well.  School Can’t (SPSR) Australia’s position is that it is
crucial to the wellbeing of the student that we identify and reduce stressors and support the
student’s nervous system to reset back to its default “safe” state as soon as possible.  Early
identification of and resolution of stressors is crucial to ensuring recovery and to mitigating
protracted mental ill health and prolonged experience of school can’t.  In the absence of being able
to work with a school to identify and reduce the stress the child is experiencing at school, parents
are left with no option but to remove the child from the source of stress.  This is both a sensible and
often a necessary protective response.  Options include removing the student in order to: Register to
home educate, enrol in distance education, attend an alternative school (such as Community
schools, specialist therapeutic education environments, private special education schools), or to
obtain a medical exemption from school.

Parents/carers are frequently limited in the choices available to them when they choose to leave a
school:

Recommendation 6: That DOE policies are reviewed to support students and parents/carers to take
time off work or time out of school, while parents/carers work with the student, school and
clinicians to identify underlying issues and address the mental health concerns of the student, in
order to facilitate recovery via an individualised plan.  This should be communicated to families so
that they understand that this is possible.  This will reduce parent/carer and student stress.

Recommendation 7: That state and territory DOEs provide positive messaging about forms of
schooling other than formal schooling and ensure messaging that normalises that there are many
different ways to engage with learning.  Such that families and students are aware that there are a
range of options available to them should they require them.

Recommendation 8: That state and territory DOEs provide positive and more frequent messaging
about the variety of pathways that exist to higher education outside of mainstream school.  So that
schools, parents/carers and students are aware that there are many options and successful
completion of year 11 and 12 are not the only ways to access tertiary studies. This will help reduce
stress in the final years of school if young people experience school can’t at this time.

Recommendation 9: That State and territory DOEs fund an on demand free health and wellbeing
check, with parents prompted about the service in year 1, year 4, year 7, and year 10, to identify any
previously unidentified diagnoses, mental health issues and support needs.  This service should
provide referral to funded assessments and supports. This will reduce barriers to accessing costly
diagnoses leading to more timely identification of childhood illness and developmental conditions
and ensure parent/carers support in their effort to seek help for their child.

7.2.3 Finding Help and building skills and knowledge:

When parents find themselves in a novel situation, they often find themselves needing new skills
and knowledge.  They refer first to prior knowledge, skills and understandings in order to try to
understand, and help their school can’t children. Parents often resort to the application of rewards
and consequences to begin with, to gain compliance with attendance expectations.  This approach
may work if a child has very mild or recent onset of school can’t, however if the difficulties the child
is having in relation to school are significant for that child, then this approach will not result in
enduring change. Parents may ignore early stages of school can’t, until the child is experiencing
significant distress.  Once they determine that they have exhausted all known methods of getting
their child back to school, parents and carers begin the search for more information to try to assist
their children.  The difficulties parents and carers experience in relation to finding help, and building
skills and knowledge are substantial and varied.

Anecdotally, parents new to School Can’t (SPSR) Australia, report that they have difficulty:

Identifying suitable supports at the school and in the community.

•  Making sense of what is happening for their child.
•  Understanding why their child is resisting going to school.
•
•  Finding resources and information.
•  Being an advocate at school.
•  Knowing what help to ask for and who to ask.
•  Knowing their legal rights and responsibilities.
•  Knowing how to repair their relationship with their child.
•  Knowing how to connect and collaborate with their child.
•  Navigating and applying for government supports.
•  Understanding how to apply new frameworks of understanding to their lives (e.g. learning how

to use Collaborative Proactive Solutions or Shanker Self-Reg).

•  Finding alternative education pathways.
•  Processing feelings of shame and blame.

In question 61 of SC Survey-22 we asked our survey respondents to indicate how much they felt
School Can’t (SPSR) Australia has helped them with a range of skills and knowledge.  91.9% of
parents/carers indicated that the group had assisted them to focus on their child’s mental health
and wellbeing.  Commonly parents are told by schools and clinicians that the focus should be on
getting their child to comply with the expectation that they attend school.  A shift to focussing on
wellbeing marks a significant change in approach.  91.6% of parent/carers indicated the group had
helped them with understanding that their child was doing the best they could, and 88.4% indicated
that the group had helped them “see school refusal differently”. Both these items testify to a
conceptual change that takes place when parents join our group.  School Can’t (SPSR) Australia’s
unique environment provides a place for parents new to school refusal difficulties to learn and
benefit from the experiences of those who have travelled the road before them.

7.2.7 Planning and managing unpredictable demands:

Typical parents/carers can usually predict how their day will go and expect that routines will be
followed, but this is not the case for parents/carers of a school can’t child. Parents/carers with
school can’t children are exposed to larger amounts of unpredictability. Consequently, they work
harder, from day to day, expending more mental energy having to consciously plan and arrange
logistics only to have to rejig those plans later if their child is unable to attend school. 49% of SC
Survey-22 respondents indicated that unpredictability of school attendance impacted their ability to
access and engage in self-care, we know it also impacts their ability to plan and manage day to day
life.

Anecdotally we know that at the beginning of the year parents/carers face the following unknowns:

1.  Will their child go to school or not when school resumes?
2.  What will their child’s capacity be like for full time, part time, distance, or face to face

schooling?

3.  What supports will be in place at school?
4.  Will the support personnel this year be the same or different?
5.  Will the support personnel at school listen and collaborate or will they make demands and

be directive?
 Will it be easy or hard to form a working relationship with the new team?

6.
7.  What will the child’s mental health be like once school is underway and pressure of school

returns?

8.  Will the parent/carer be able to work?
9.  Will the parent/carer be able to get some of their personal needs met?
10. How much energy will they need to get through the year?

It can be difficult to know whether a child will be able to go to school as planned.

On a day-to-day basis parents/carers often describe experiencing hypervigilance in relation to the
state of their child’s nervous system. Parents/carers describe a state of constantly waiting to see
whether:

1.  They will be able to get to work or to an appointment on time.
2.  They will be able to get a sibling to school on time.
3.  Their child will be able to get ready to leave the house independently or whether they will
need assistance or prompting to: eat, brush teeth, dress, pack a bag or even to get out of
bed.

4.  They will be able to accomplish a household task or not while their child gets ready for

school.

The parents/carers surveyed describe a state of being constantly on edge, waiting to see what will
happen. They are aware that if they become agitated themselves it will add to their child’s
dysregulation. They juggle expectations about their day, the expectations of others and the
expectations of the school. They may wait patiently in a car for an hour to see if a child will be able
walk through the school gate. They may sit outside a classroom to see if their child will settle and to
provide reassurance. They co-regulate and calm their child knowing that doing so can’t happen to a
schedule and can’t be forced.

Whether they finally get their child to school (or not) and return home, they collapse from the
exhaustion of the effort it took, pulling into the driveway they sit on their phones scrolling unable to
summon the energy to move on and adjust the rest of their day.

7.2.9 Regulating Parent/carer worries about their school can’t children:

Parents/carers frequently report feeling anxious about their children. They are exposed to messages
about the importance of attendance regularly in school newsletters and other communications from
school. Parents/carers feel anxious about things happening now and things that may happen in the
future including:

1.  their child’s mental, and physical well-being,
2.
loss of academic progress and keeping up with peers academically,
3.
impacts on the child’s social relationships and connections,
4.  the impact on their child’s future education opportunities,
5.  whether their child will ever be able to return to school/learning,
6.  whether their child will be able to one day get a job.

They are impacted by a range of narratives in the community which fuel anxiety such as:

1.  School to prison pipeline – they will be headed for a life of crime.
2.  Home schooled students don’t develop social skills.
3.  Every Day Counts: students who miss school won’t have a future.
4.  Non-compliant children are: lazy, manipulative, and no good.
5.  They will never be able to care for themselves or be independent.
6.  A high ATAR means you are a success, and your parents did their job successfully.

It is important that parents/carers are encouraged to maintain calm and optimism about their
school can’t children and are assisted to counter the negative narratives listed above.  Parent
anxieties about school attendance can:

1.

2.

Interfere with being able to work with the child collaboratively to identify the underlying
issues.
Increase the child/young person’s distress about themselves and their situation which can
lead to depression.

3.  Lead parents/carers and schools to push attendance at the expense of well-being.

Calm begets calm. Parents/carers who stay calm can connect and co-regulate with their child. Adults
at school who communicate calm, help the student feel safe at school. At School Can’t (SPSR)
Australia we frequently discuss “radical acceptance”. This is the act of accepting the child where
they are at now rather than communicating disappointment or frustration at their current situation.
Radical acceptance communicates safety, but is challenging for adults in the face of such negative
and frequently unfounded narratives about engagement with school and learning.

The study (Hancock et al 2013) underpinning the “Everyday Counts” narrative shows a correlation

38% of SC Survey-22 respondents access NDIS for their school can’t child. This number equates to

not mean you can access the funds you need to assist you to get back to school or recover from
school can’t. Barriers include not being able to access supports across multiple environments and
not being able to access psychological supports to assist with being able to access the school

Parents and carers of children with NDIS plans are told by NDIA representatives that they can’t use
their funds to provide a support worker to accompany their child to attend school or to employ
tutors to build capacity for learning reengagement in a safe and supported way. Parents/carers are
told these things should be funded by schools. Funding at schools is insufficient however, to cover
these supports and these supports often need to cross over between home and school.

Families report that they require supports that are flexible and able to be accessed in both the
home, community and school environments. Sometimes support workers or tutors who are privately
funded by parents/carers are prevented from attending the school site if a principal feels it is not a
necessary support, they may also find that there is a lack of a suitable room or space at the school.

NDIS does not cover supports for the mental health of those with a disability, even though their
mental health has deteriorated as a result of their engagement in contexts (such as schools) that are
not inclusive and understanding of their needs and even though anxiety is considered to be a
common co-occuring condition in some disabilities.

Meta analyses suggest that 39.6% of autistic young people under the age of 18 meet conditions for a
co-occuring anxiety disorder under DSM-IV (van Steensel et al, 2011). Rates of co-occuring anxiety
in people with ADHD are estimated to be at 25% (D'Agati et al 2019). Rates of anxiety disorders are
estimated at only 6.5% for non-autistic young people under the age of 18 (Polanczyk et al, 2015).

Access to psychology should be available on the NDIS to support autistic children with co-occurring
anxiety, as these children require support from mental health professionals who understand Autism.

with 14% of respondents accessing Carers Payment and 29% accessing Carers Allowance. Parents
and carers who have a student with school can’t that does not have a disability or is awaiting an
assessment for a disability, are currently unable to access support from Carers Payment/ Carers
Allowance. They are also unable to access Carers Gateway for counselling support. They financially
unsupported while waiting for assessments, having to pay privately for those assessments and at a

Access to the federally funded Assistance for Isolated Children (AIC) is restricted to those who live in

home schooled or attend Distance Education for medical reasons or whose child is unable to attend

8.3.3 Cost of accessing privately funded supports

Cost of privately funded supports was identified as a barrier by 55% of respondents. We have
reported earlier (see 7.2.2) about the impact on family finances of having a parent or carer unable to
work. This directly impacts their ability to afford services. The cost of psychological assessments for
ADHD, Autism, or Specific Learning Difficulties averages $1500 - $2,200 and are not covered by
Medicare.

A recent report evaluating the “Better Access Initiative” showed that “Affordability was consistently
raised as an issue by consumers and providers who contributed to the various studies in the evaluation.
In 2021, 65% of Better Access treatment services attracted a co-payment compared with 53% in 2018.
The median co-payment for these services was relatively stable at around $74 per session between 2018
and 2021 but increased significantly in the first half of 2022 to $90. (Pirkis et al 2022:14). This is
consistent with the experiences of our members seeking psychological care for their children or
themselves. Many state that with reduced income they struggle to afford the substantial co-payments for
fortnightly mental health care that they may need to access. They also worry about the number of
subsidised sessions they can access being inadequate.

8.3.4 Other barriers to accessing supports for the child:

48% of SC Survey-22 respondents indicated that they experienced difficulties in finding clinicians
who understand school can’t and 30% indicated they experienced difficulty in finding clinicians who
are trauma aware.  In relation to accessing re-engagement programs: 21% of respondents indicated
that had experienced lengthy wait lists to access external to school re-engagement programs and
19% indicated they were unable to access suitable re-engagement programs near them.

8.3.5 Barriers to School Based Support Access for a Child or Young Person

Many of our survey participants nominated barriers relating to difficulties in collaborating with
schools and school personnel. This is a point of some concern as School Can’t (SPSR) Australia
considers that collaboration between parents/carers and school personnel is essential in order to:

1)  identify and address the underlying difficulties contributing to school can’t,
2)  establish conditions that support a child or young person in their wellbeing, and
3)  ensure the student’s sense of felt safety and belonging such that they might be able to

return to school.

These factors are all critical in setting the scene for reengagement with education.

Parents rate parent-teacher collaboration and communication as one of the most helpful
interventions for supporting autistic children with anxiety a school (Adams, Young, Simpson & Keen,
2019). Difficulties collaborating and communication with school, are characteristic of a breakdown in
crucial supports for these students.

SC Survey-22 participants identified a range of difficulties that impeded their efforts to access
support at their child’s school (refer Table 13). 38% found it difficult to find supportive people at
their child’s school. Discussing school can’t is challenging for parents due to many narratives in our
culture that blame children and families for their distress (discussed Section 12). Parents can often
be dismissed or are given advice that is inappropriate or unhelpful. 36% experienced difficulties in
engaging their school in exploring underlying issues related to their child’s school can’t. This
frequently happens due to a widespread belief that the problem and therefore the solution lies
within the family or the child.

 Many of these stressors can be proactively addressed by adjustments to the way we do things in

•  Designing our schools and classrooms to meet sensory needs,
•  Adjusting timetables and attendance expectations,
•  Facilitating interest-based learning,
•  Reconsidering the use of competitive timed activities,
•  Use of Collaborative and Proactive Solutions, low arousal, and de-escalation approaches, and
•  Social emotional learning that is neurodiversity affirming,
•  Ensuring that learning support plans focus on accessibility by removing barriers, making

adjustments and providing support.

As you can see from Figure 14, there are many stressors impacting on children and young people.
School Can’t (SPSR) Australia’s lived experience knowledge and research has led us to have much to

2.  Recognition and acknowledgement of student stress by school staff
3.  Masking

10.1.1 Felt Safety

71% of survey respondents nominated a lack of safe people as a definite problem for their school
can’t child. The students in this cohort are struggling with relationships and connection with both
teachers and peers at school, and feeling safe. Usually this is because the child’s nervous system has
been sensitized to detect social threat as a result of poor experiences in the past. Students may
struggle to determine if a teacher or peer is happy with them or not and the effort of trying to
determine this makes them feel anxious. While not attending school itself could be a reason for a
lack of relationship, children have generally been to school before school attendance difficulties
began and we must consider whether a lack of those relationships in the first instance, or a
breakdown in relationship may be contributing factor.

Difficulty with a specific teacher was nominated as a contributing difficulty by 40% of parents/carers.
Bullying and social exclusion from peers were both nominated by 35% of parents/carers. Lack of
friends was nominated by 40% of parents. Physical restraint by a teacher and witnessing peer to
peer violence were also mentioned by parents in our free form text response to this question. One
respondent described a situation where a student was shamed by her teacher in front of the class
for struggling with a timed task, which resulted in bullying from students who witnessed the
exchange. While this will impact a student’s sense of belonging, and a student’s capacity to call on
peers or teachers when they need assistance, this also impacts the nervous system arousal state of
the student. Only when students feel safe will their nervous systems enable their brains to attend to
learning. Felt safety is a necessary precursor to learning.

Behaviour of peers was also nominated as influencing students’ sense of safety at school with 49% of
parents reporting that this was a factor in their child’s school can’t.

Misguided advice from schools on how to address school attendance difficulties is also problematic
for the recovery of school can’t students (See Table 25 on page 91 for further discussion. Attempts
to force students back to school negatively impact student – adult relationships and damage trust.
School can’t children and young people need to feel heard and supported by their grownups. They
need to feel like they have allies not adversaries.

50% of SC Survey-22 respondents identified a focus on behaviourist practises as problematic for
their young person. 47% identified school behaviour management as an issue. Exclusionary discipline
is also problematic (26%), with 16% nominating exclusion from school activities as contributing to
their child’s difficulties in attending school.

Focussing on behaviours of concern distracts staff from recognising and responding to underlying
student distress. Behaviours of concern should be treated as signals of student distress. Models like
Collaborative and Proactive Solutions draw attention to the antecedents to behaviour. Self-Reg aims
to identify and reduce a student’s stress load and thereby improve self-regulation. Both are of huge
benefit in assisting staff to understand and identify student distress and to create a sense of safety.

Collaborative Proactive Solutions helps school staff avoid misunderstandings and assumptions about
behaviour. It encourages adults to be curious about the student’s perspective and to collaborate
with the student to find solutions. Students feel heard and validated in response and
misunderstandings about behaviour are less likely. See our discussion about Milton’s Double
Empathy Problem (2012) in section 12.

10.1.3 Masking

Most children don’t like to stand out as different. Masking was nominated by 67% of SC Survey-22
respondents. Masking is the name given to the act of camouflaging one’s differences. It involves the
suppression on one’s natural tendencies and conscious modification how one presents in order to fit
in. Masking behaviour is more common in autistic people than non-autistic people (Jedrzejewska &
Dewey, 2021).

School Can’t (SPSR) Australia recommends that attention is paid to creating school cultures which
value diversity and make room for difference so that students can feel that the person they are is
valued unconditionally and that they have space to be themselves. In the past many aspects of
autistic presentation and ways of being, have been portrayed as wrong by our society. Research and
therapies have been aimed at normalisation of the autistic person. Cultural beliefs about disability
and difference have led to spoken and unspoken rules about how to be, and have been applied to
things like: the way autistic children play, the way autistics socialise, and the way they move. Neuro-
normative rules impact the way children are expected to be in a classroom: sit still, eyes on the
teacher when they speak, raise your hand and wait to speak. These all assume every student has the
same capacity for the prescribed behaviour. “Whole Body Listening”, is an example of a neuro-
normative set of expectations/rules about how children should conduct themselves in class. Its use
has led to shaming of autistic children in front of their non autistic peers for things like lack of eye
contact and difficulties sitting still. Whole Body Listening has recently been overhauled by its
creators as a result of input from neurodivergent people. The “Meet Bumper: a Whole Body
Learner” resource, from Autism Level Up, also offers an alternative more neurodiverse affirming
approach to the original “Whole Body Listening” resource (Fede & Laurent, 2022).

The need to mask impacts a child’s sense of belonging. As Brené Brown (2010) says, “Fitting in is
about assessing a situation and becoming who you need to be to be accepted. Belonging, on the
other hand, doesn’t require us to change who we are; it requires us to be who we are”.

include paying attention, working memory, self-control and the ability to problem solve. They impact
a person’s capacity to plan, organise and sequence ideas, tasks or belongings, to prioritise, to initiate
or complete tasks, control impulses and focus (Psychology Today Australia, 2023).

access the curriculum and demonstrate their learning.

require a program including structured synthetic phonics. Many students with executive
function difficulties benefit from step-by-step instructions. The “I do, We do, You do”
learning model is an example of an evidence based teaching model that includes explicit
instruction, modelling, scaffolding and repetition to support student learning (Killian, 2023).
2.  Difficulty with group work was nominated as another stressor by 45% of survey respondents.
No longer are many classrooms set up with rows of desks facing the front of the classroom
with students engaging in solitary study and receiving instruction from the teacher. Working
and collaborating in groups is something that is encouraged in many schools however, many
students struggle with group work. These students may benefit from more independent
work or increased support from the class being supported to learn how to help the child feel
included and valued as a group member.

3.  Processing speed is the amount of time it takes for someone to process and understand

some input prior to responding to it. 49% of respondents nominated processing speed as a
stressor for their children. These students find that timed tasks requiring them to think and
respond quickly are very stressful and pose a barrier to them being able to demonstrate
their learning. Many students with slower processing speed also find that the classroom just
moves too fast for them. They try to participate in classroom discussions for instance but by
the time they have processed what others have said and thought about what they want to
say or ask the discussion has moved on. They take longer to produce work and lament never
being able to finish things. They have lower output and feel frustrated that there is never
enough time. They frequently feel left behind and need the pace of instruction, and
discussions to slowed down in addition to being asked to do fewer tasks compared to their
peers.

ability to attend school. 61% of parents/carers indicated that the length of the school day impacted
on their child’s school can’t. 51% indicated that the number of transitions /periods in a day impacted
their child’s school can’t and 46% indicated that early start times were a source of stress. (See Table
17).
