15. Conclusion:

There are a number of popular narratives about school refusal. The two most often seen assert that
school refusal is due to:

1.  Parenting failure. Caused by parents who do not set appropriate boundaries or use “tough
love” to gain their child’s compliance. The cure is to ensure that parents are enforcing
rewards and consequences to gain compliance.

2.  Children/young people who have anxiety disorders. The cure is to treat the disordered

thinking and convince the child that there is nothing to be afraid of through use of Cognitive
Behaviour Therapy and Exposure Therapy.

School Can’t (SPSR) Australia takes a different perspective. The application of an ecosystems
framework of understanding, together with new understandings about the nervous system and the
brain-body connection, which lead us to see school refusal as a response to stress. The cure is
simple: if we identify the stressors and reduce the stress, then we can reduce the incidence of
school can’t and provide effective support to those who are experiencing it.

In the past, research has neglected to investigate school-based factors contributing to student stress
and the subsequent onset of school can’t. Psychologists have focused on within child and within
family factors instead. This failure to draw a connection between chronic stress and school can’t has
led schools to blame school attendance difficulties on parents, and psychologists to perceive mental
illness as a pathology of the individual. The result has been little interest in identifying school-based
stressors.

Society’s understanding of school can’t, is shaped by cultural beliefs about: education, parenting,
disability, mental health and behaviour. School Can’t (SPSR) Australia invites the Senate and others
examining this issue to consider the way these beliefs influence and shape understandings and
responses to school can’t. We must challenge beliefs about education: how, what, where, when and
why? We must embrace inclusion and listen to neurodivergent voices to do better. We must value
the voice and knowledge of parents, as they walk alongside their children year in and year out and
seek help for them. We must call out ableism and the role it plays in oppressing and ‘othering’ those
who are different. We must look at this problem through an inclusion lens! Mental health clinicians
must look upstream to identify sources of stress, leading to mental health break down, and join in
advocating for reductions in student stress to promote wellbeing. Schools need to rethink
compliance focussed behaviour management practices and instead focus on regulation, connection
and collaboration, to improve “felt safety”.

The data from SC Survey-22 is alarming. We must do better! The long-term financial and health
impacts on families are extremely concerning. The impact of long-term stress on students, and the
fact that so many are experiencing school-based trauma, should concern us all. Trauma that follows
them for years to come:

“I still sometimes struggle to pick up my siblings from school or go to their school recitals
because the fear of school buildings imprinted upon me has impacted my mental health
and relationship with the education system for the rest of my life” (Hayden:2022)

Reducing school-based stressors will also be protective of the teaching workforce. No doubt
teachers are also adversely impacted as they struggle to teach and support chronically stressed
children and young people. It’s important that teachers are equipped with knowledge about the
nervous system and are supported to meet their own regulation needs within the context of
education communities that care.

19.1 The Autonomic Nervous System:

19.1.1 Autonomic Nervous System Dysregulation

Our Autonomic nervous system helps us to defend ourselves. It comprises two systems of nerves
that facilitate communication between the brain and the body in order to help us to meet threats
and challenge.  When our brain perceives a threat, our Sympathetic Nervous System automatically
acts to release an adrenaline rush to increase the heart rate and respiration, increase tension in the
muscles and provides a charge of energy so that we are prepared to take action. The blood flow in
the body is changed and the frontal lobes and digestion are shutdown to speed up our ability to fight
or flee from the threat. If it is not safe to fight or after the fight is finished then freeze, submit
responses are triggered by our Parasympathetic Nervous System via the automatic release of other
neurochemicals that slow down the heart rate and respiration leading to physical collapse,
exhaustion, weakness, increased gastro-intestinal activity. This process allows the nervous system to
transition back to a “safe” state.

This is a biological response it does not require thoughts or intentional action and after the trauma,
threat or stress is over the person’s Nervous System would normally return to its usual level of
functioning and thought processes. However, when a person is exposed to the ongoing stress of
repeated threat and subsequent emotional dysregulation a trauma response occurs.  The nervous
system stays alert and is always prepared for danger. The down regulation to a ‘no threat’ position is
no longer achieved. This threat position becomes the “new normal”. If this goes on for too long the
Autonomic Nervous system which controls the involuntary bodily functions is damaged and this
interferes with the messages sent between the brain and the other areas of the nervous system and
the organs of the body: the heart, the stomach, the bowel, and the bladder can all be affected.
Common symptoms include: dizziness, fainting, urinary tract problems, sexual problems, digestive

When the “new normal” is in control of the brain it is constantly assessing threat. It is reacting not

Informed Consent Statement

This survey is anonymous and will cover your demographics,
your school can’t journey and its impacts on you, your child and
your family, along with what supports you have accessed and
how the school/s involved have responded.

The findings from this survey will be used by admin of School
Can’t (SPSR) Australia to inform a public submission to the 2022
Senate Inquiry into School Refusal / School Can’t on behalf of
the parent peer support group. The results of the survey may
also be used by the School Can’t administration team to apply
for grants, and to educate others about school can’t. This
includes using quotes from open ended questions or comments
made as part of the survey.

Often a distinction is made between School Refusal and
Truancy. School Refusal is when parents are aware that their
child or young person is not attending school. Truancy is when
a child is missing school without their parent’s knowledge, such
as when a child wags.

School Can’t (SPSR) Australia would argue that this distinction
requires further investigation as the key difference identified
above may not be related to the factors contributing to truancy
behaviour but may instead be related to the degree to which a
student feels they are likely to be met with adults who judge
their behaviour as a sign of failure rather than as a sign that
something is not going well for them at school, or where the
student has decided that the problems at school have no
solutions.

Signs of school attendance difficulties range from reluctance to
attend, physical signs of anxiety such as stomach upsets and
headaches, sleep disturbance, not wanting to go to bed or get
out of bed or get dressed or eat, or to get in the car, or to get
ready, anger, crying, begging, upset, late to school, missing
school, missing particular classes, avoiding or refusing work or
homework, hiding when at school rather than going to class or
out for lunch or recess, unable to move physically or to talk,
flight, fight, freeze, shutdown, absent from school for single
days at a time over many weeks, absent from school for many
days at a time, or extended absence from school.

We consider any of these presentations as manifestations of
School Can’t. For the purposes of this survey we would like to
collect information in relation to any of the above listed
presentations including what might be considered truancy.

The survey should take around 45 minutes to complete.

Definitions

For the purposes of this survey School Can’t refers to a child’s
inability to attend or participate in formal full-time education.
Children in our School-Can't cohort may spend time in different
educational settings, as parents search for an environment
where their child experiences belonging, engagement and feels
well supported. These settings may include mainstream,
specialist, distance education, remote learning, and even home
school environments. School Can’t can occur in the context of
any of these settings.

School Can’t has many different names and shows many
different presentations of varying impact. Some of the names
you might be familiar with include:
School Refusal
School Phobia
Emotionally Based School Avoidance
School Attendance Difficulties
Truancy

PLEASE READ THE FOLLOWING BEFORE PROCEEDING:

For the purposes of this survey School Can’t refers to a child’s
inability to engage with formal full time education including
attending or participating in:
●  mainstream
●

●

distance education
remote learning

School Can’t is experienced on a spectrum from mild to severe.
Please use the following descriptors to rate the severity of
school can’t for your child for each year that they have
experienced school can’t.

Mild school can’t: A child with mild school can’t might
express a desire not to go to school but is still able to attend
school most days. They might have several days a term where
they cannot go to school. They may be persistently late to
school because of their reluctance to go. They may report
feeling unwell (tummy ache or headache). They may feel
anxious on Sunday nights as the school week is about to start.
They may be unable to complete school work either at home or
at school.

Severe School Can’t: A child with severe school can’t might
be unable to attend school at all. Duration is often for more
than 6 months. They may not be able to leave their bedroom or
the house. They show signs of severe distress and or shutdown.
They may develop atypical sleep patterns often awake all night
and asleep during the day. They may show signs of self-harm,
clinical depression, or severe anxiety.

School Can’t often escalates over time. It is frequently episodic
in nature returning in subsequent years to varying degrees.

 19.3 Testimonies of School Can’t Parents/Carers:

The following testimonies were provided by
parents of School Can’t (SPSR) Australia in
2022 when we asked for their feedback about
how the group had supported them with their
child’s school can’t journey.

Response 1

When a child can’t go to school you lose all your support
and networks, often work becomes very difficult or
impossible, your child needs understanding, their needs
need to be investigated, they need strong support
personally and advocacy, school administrators become
demanding. Life becomes stressful but yet suddenly it
becomes impossible to share parent to parent support,
at the school gate, for a quick coffee and you often don’t
know what to say and how to protect your child’s
privacy but stay connected to school communities. In
short, you and your child become isolated at the time
you most need community support and understanding.
This is what this group provides- as well as practical
support, more than anything it’s the understanding and
support of others walking the same path. It helps us just
about keep our heads above water.’

Mum of ASD GAD 9 year old

Response 2

After many years of school can’t my son’s transition into
yr 7 tipped him into a mental health crisis and burnout.
This affected the whole family and we were spiralling
into a dark place.

I had never felt so isolated and alone, I had no idea what
was happening or how to fix it. Neither did any
professionals or school staff. I hadn’t found anyone who
understood and I had been searching for years. I found
this group and I feel like it literally saved our lives. I’m so
grateful to everyone here.

Single parent to school can’t autistic 15yr old boy

Response 3

With the support of this group I have been able to seek
the right professional help and advocate for my sons
disability. Prior to finding this group we were heading on
a path which I now have learned was further damaging
my school can’t child and adding to the trauma he
experienced at school from unmet needs.

I am so grateful for this support which has helped me to
find answers leading him on the right path and the road
of recovery.

Having a school can’t child is deeply isolating, has huge
financial and other major impacts to families. We
continue to struggle. This group was honestly our
saviour.

Mum to school can’t autistic (and pathological demand
avoidant) and ADHD 10 year old

Response 4

I felt so alone, isolated and such a failure as a parent
with regards to my school can’t daughter. She is the
youngest of eight children and prior to her I had never
experienced any issues with my other children attending
school. This really floored (sic) me. I constantly received
pressure and unhelpful advice from my extended family,
particularly my aging parents who felt it was a discipline
issue. But then I stumbled upon this wonderful site and
was relieved in the fact that I was not alone in this
journey. I have learn’t so much through other people’s
stories on this site and eventually sort assessment and
diagnosis for my daughter. If it wasn’t for this site I’m
not sure we would have got so far as we have in
providing the assistance and approach that my daughter
desperately needed. She is now attending 100% at an
“alternative” school, is far less stressed and a lot happier
with life.

Response 5

As a result of this group, when I enter difficult meetings
with school, I no longer feel alone. Instead I feel
informed, knowledgeable and supported. I am able to
use all I have learnt from this group along with their
strength to better advocate for my child and to improve
their outcomes. The leaders of this group should be
considered for citizens awards for what they have done
to support so many families and to shed light on this
debilitating and stressful issue affecting thousands of
Australian children. Without them we would not have
come as far as we have in advocating for the health of
happiness of these young Australians who are
experiencing debilitating distress just trying to attend
school like every other child.

Mum to 8 year old with GAD

Response 6

I found this group early in our journey, when I was
struggling to get Ms 9 to school, but still insisting she go
unless demonstrably ill. This was the rule when I was a
kid, after all. Reading the stories and approaches here, I
realised my error, and changed the way I parent. We
now work together to understand and overcome the
barriers, and if that's not possible, well, sometimes a
doona day is good for both of us.

Our relationship was suffering from my fixed idea of
what was 'acceptable', but a few months later, she is
relaxing and opening up to me again. She is far less
anxious about school and more open to learning, too.
We are also both now being assessed for ASD and
ADHD, partly thanks to information I learned in this
group!

Without this kind of peer support, I may have
permanently damaged my kid's relationship with both
me and with school and learning. Thank you for existing.

excellent information and sharing for people going

don't have the knowledge and skills to adequately

group has developed a wealth of expertise through lived

attend school (and sometimes other activities), and

all, not just to the lucky ones who happen to know

This is my submission on how school refusal is affecting young people and their families and the

impacts it is having on the employment and financial security of parents and carers.

In 2018 and 2020 I made seperate formal complaints to the Director Education Leadership where

my then

 (2018) and

 (2020) daughter who has a disability was physically

restrained, pulled and emotionally abused by Department of Education teacher and Principal. I

never agreed or authorised the use of physical restraints or the use of force full dragging of my

daughter. In both incidents she was never a danger or posed any risk to herself or staff or other

students.

Due to the trauma and abuse that occurred my daughter refused to return to school. Despite the

fact we obtained 2 medical certificates explaining that my daughter was suffering significant

mental health concerns given what occurred. The school was threatening to send around a

 and force her back to school.

There appeared to be inadequate safeguards to protect students with disabilities from abuse and

this caused my daughter school refusal as she did not feel safe at school.

I understand that the use of restrictive practices on a child with a disability is a breach of her

human rights. What occurred at school to my daughter has caused her long term trauma, fear

and anxiety and she refuses to return to school as she cannot trust that she will be safe. Schools

have a legislative and statutory responsibility to ensure the safety of students with a disability

and to all students.

My daughter did not feel safe at school and we have had to opt for home schooling to avoid

further trauma and abuse being inflicted on my daughter. I am my daughter’s full time carer due

to her ongoing school refusal and am not in paid employment.

I am very concerned around the limited transparency and independence around investigations of

a complaint made by parents of a child with a disability involving use of restrictive practices and

abuse of a child with a disability at school and the subsequent reasons for the child’s school

refusal.

I now understand that at the time Directors Educational leadership or even Principals are the

main arbiters of complaints. This is a serious conflict of interest where colleagues investigate,

review and respond to complaints about other colleagues.

 or now

procedural fairness or transparency.

 What

I read was very distressing and untrue and unsubstantiated allegations were made by DOE staff

that I was not informed of and these untrue and unsubstantiated allegations without evidence

and my complaints were closed off without even a conversation

with me as a parent or seeking third party independent witness to corroborate the parents

version of events.

What the DOE staff did to my daughter has caused her long lasting trauma, school refusal, PTSD,

significant anxiety and ongoing mental health issues which all affect her ability to return to

school and has significantly impacted on her learning and social opportunities with her peers.

School was not a safe place for my daughter. When I made 2 formal complaints both of my

I was never informed by the DOE of how to raise a complaint. I was given no support in making

Both of my complaints I was informed by

that the incidents did not meet the threshold of

misconduct and there was no evidence that the DOE Teacher and Principal have acted

Members of the public may think that a child who refuses to go to school is as result of parents

My families story regarding school refusal highlights that school refusal is a much more complex

issue. Children and their families are significantly let down by systems and institutions that have

School Refusal Submission

I am a parent/carer to a 14 yr old young person with Autism, ADHD and Anxiety. I also identify as having
a disability. Currently my young person is completely disengaged from school. This has been an ongoing
issue since the beginning of lockdowns, there have been periods of engagement however mostly short
lived. We are trying to adapt with the support of the school a way in which to reengage. The disruption
to life, education and social/community participation have been extensive.

During the pandemic, lockdowns, periods of isolation my child did not cope with the expected online
learning processes, no additional support was provided. It became my responsibility to support,
encourage, education and navigate the significant challenges relating to continued education without
any additional resources. After schools began returning, my child found it difficult, due to being behind
with her educational expectations, socially and emotionally withdrawn and unable to participate.

The impact on their mental health was evident early on and this only exacerbated as time went on,
episodes of depression, agoraphobia, and obsessive-compulsive tendencies. The pressure on myself as
the carer giver, sole parent was extreme, impacting my ability to participate in life, return to work or
study, socialise and at times even function.

Two years on this has only increased. It feels very one or the other situation, try to reengage in
employment, life, socialising, or care for my child. The mental health challenges making this incredibly
difficult as the ‘School can’t” comes with aggressive, impulsive, and difficult behaviours. I can not access
appropriate health or mental health support as I am required to be as available to my child as possible.
Whilst I have considered on numerous occasions to present to the mental health intake teams, they
have very little understanding of Autism and ADHD which creates the potential for further trauma and
distress. Remote of in person mental health supports are not only hard to access, long waitlists, my child
has disengaged so much that she won’t attend, or access appoints I make.

I am beyond exhausted and like many other parents in my community in a similar situation, I am out of
idea’s. The financial pressures have been extraordinary, the rising cost of living adding to this. I
attempted to make a significant change by moving from our regional centre to a city to access better
school/educational/mental health support but even this has made no difference.

I think more provisions are needed to assist with school reengagement, tutors, support staff, mental
health programs, support for parents that do not judge, cause intimidation, or fail to recognise the real
challenges families and young people are facing.

These last 2.5 years have been detrimental to social development, maturation, education, and the skills
required to successfully complete education post reengagement, the mental health of student and their
families.

It has placed excessive pressure on schools and teachers to support students either remotely or when
they do reengage.

At this point I have seen very little, if any, from local, state or federal government to address support or
reengagement for students, especially those with disabilities. NDIS does not allow educational
provisions and the education department doesn’t fund students without significant disabilities. Thus far

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 78 no support until recently was offered from the school and that looks like a relaxed return with few
demands and flexibility, short/half days or dual care education which I just can no longer do due to
exhaustion and the toll on my mental health. It feels like a trauma all of its own, opening compass to
notify of absence, trying to wake my child and work through the anxiety that today is the day to try
again only to not get out of the house, it fills me with anxiety.

I long for a break, to get a haircut, to go to the Drs, to selfcare just a little, to make appointments but its
all near on impossible when your day is controlled by a young persons inability to breakthrough the
return to school anxiety and the level of support that requires.

I read stories like mine in the online groups I am in, parents at breaking point, anxious, some are at the
point of relinquishing care, if they haven’t already. Most of these are parents with neurodivergent
children, who already have a difficult journey parenting. Students from these communities are self-
harming at alarming rates. Parents exhausted from having tried every strategy, support and means they
can to get their children back to school. Remote learning is not suited to many neurodivergent children,
whilst some thrive others require a classroom setting.

I have tried to reengage in work by becoming a sole trader however even that is challenging due to the
amount of energy and space taken up by my young person. I struggle to have the clarity, energy, and
cognitive functionality to undertake tasks in any sort of routine.

It is not just the families and children that are suffering now and ongoing, it will be an economic disaster
when these students age out of education or leave early without the skills to seek employment or
further education. They will not have the emotional, mental, or developmental maturity to engage in
healthy relationships or practices.

The mental health services are going to be inundated with these young people for years to come. It isn’t
as simple as school refusal, its an absolute consuming anxiety, existing in fight/flight and overloaded
systems. A sense of both doom and failure, fear for their futures and yet simply going to school is too
hard, being there is a sensory nightmare, exhausting, socially depleting and confusing. We need
practitioners to understand this, to not just call it behavioural, lazy parenting, it’s a mental health
condition of its own and its incredibly hard for everyone going through it. We are trying, every day,
trying. The answers are not simple, the situation isn’t simple.

To the Committee,

This is a personal submission of our family experience with “school can’t” and our 15-year-old
autistic daughter.

In late 2021, after several months of school refusal, our daughter was diagnosed as autistic. There
had been no sign of autism in primary school, but with high school, and then the lockdowns, and
then the return to school after lockdowns she really struggled to cope. We can only guess that the
relative peace and quiet of being home for an extended period during the lockdowns, followed by
the raucous nature of the return to school exacerbated her anxiety and sensory issues to a point that
she could no longer cope with day-to-day classroom experiences. We don’t think lockdowns
themselves were to blame, but the school environment post-lockdown.

state high school. Because she was diagnosed at age 14, and did

Our child attended a
not enter the high school already diagnosed, and because she presented as withdrawn and internally
acting, the school staff and teachers did not offer any supports to help her cope with school. We
approached teachers and the guidance counsellor multiple times to ask for ideas or
accommodations. There were none offered or provided. There was no follow-up with us when she
did not attend school for days or later weeks at a time (aside from the automatic school absence
reporting). There appeared to be no concern about our child missing so much school.

The school chaplain was and is not trained in supporting children with severe anxiety and depression
or other special needs. The school has no trained psychologist (who would be an appropriate person
to provide support). The school never once put us in touch with any staff who might be trained in
supporting autistic kids (though we asked multiple times). I am not even certain that they have any
trained staff. Or perhaps they only support the acting out and aggressive kids, rather than the kids
who present as my child did.

We tried distance education but there were also no supports provided despite us requesting them.
The distance ed school was overwhelmed with too many enrolments.

We now homeschool, which without support is not going well. But we have no alternative. There are
no other high schools in our regional area. The nearest other school is an hour drive away (each
way). There are no distance education schools that are specifically set up to support autistic kids. We
can only struggle to help our once straight A student to reach 16 where she will then be able to
move into TAFE or other options.

I have given up my employment to support our child in her homeschooling attempts. This has put
severe financial stress on our household.

What I would like this committee to recommend:

•  Employment of at least one full-time psychologist at each high school in Australia (redeploy
chaplain funding as we have found they are not at all helpful for truly difficult situations).
•  Have a trained unit of multiple teachers and support staff in each school who are trained to

support autistic and neurodiverse kids.

•  Fund specialist distance education schools for autistic and neurodiverse kids.
•  Ensure each school has a room/space overstimulated kids can go to feel safe.
•  Each school should have a process to contact families whose children are missing a lot of

school and reach out to them to offer support to help them get back to school.

•  Recommend each state education department work with groups like Yellow Ladybugs to find

ways of setting up school environments to support neurodiverse kids.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 79

attend school (and one of those options is knowing it is ok if your child is unable to school).

School policies and environments that are designed to support students’ self-regulation and
are responsive to individual need. Large changes are needed to the current education
system to achieve this.

early School Can’t issues arise, not being forced to attend the zoned school when it is
unsuitable for the child’s needs.

Our families experience of School Can’t

Sadly, our story is not unique but it is still an important story to be told to this inquiry. Our family
currently consists of Mum, Dad, Miss and our 2 pets and we live in the

easy to attend childcare/school. When she was younger at childcare/kinder, Mum & Dad assumed it

It didn’t take long for Mum & Dad to realise that unfortunately school was not going to be as easy

teachers raising their voices, and the class being evacuated due to a distressed child exhibiting

By the time we got to the end of Term 2 of Grade 2, Miss was no longer able to attend school at all.
Mum & Dad were working closely with her paediatrician and psychologist whereby a difficult

By this stage it was at least a year since Miss  had been identified as Autistic and Mum had been

similar issues. It was also identified by both her paediatrician and psychologist that Miss  appeared

Being the parent of a child who is unable to attend school is life changing. It affects the child and all
those around them for every second of every day. It is a stressful feeling that is there the minute you
wake up to the minute you fall asleep. My daughter,
Year 8, has been unable to attend school
regularly for the last two and a half years. This is her story, this is our story and one that I hope can
help to make changes so that maybe the pathway will be different for others.

In year 6, after covid lockdown in 2020, my daughter was unable to return to school. Whilst an
anxious child, she had always coped and managed in school. She had friends, she was a bright and
engaged student who loved gymnastics. My husband and I spent many days in 2020 communicating
with the school through meetings and emails, trying to get our daughter to re-engage with school.
We were ill-advised to get her into the school at all costs and leave her there. We dragged her in
kicking and screaming, we took away privileges, we offered her positive rewards, we went to
psychologists ( some better than others), we tried walking with friends, we tried everything but still
our daughter had very poor attendance. At the end of that year, we had a transition meeting to high
school which was attended by numerous staff from her primary school, staff from the high school, a
department representative, her psychologist and us as the parents. The very strong message to us at
that meeting was that there was NO WAY the high school would be able to continue the supports
that the primary school were implementing. Many of the suggestions recommended by our
psychologist such as relationship building with a staff member were seemingly impossible. My
husband and I left the meeting thinking the only option for us to get our daughter to high school
would be to medicate her. I am not suggesting that this was what the staff at the meeting
recommended however, we felt immense pressure to get our daughter there and then they would
manage the situation once she was physically in the school. The high school staff in attendance at
the meeting had no empathy nor understanding of the gravity of the situation. It was even
suggested that somehow miraculously her anxiety would disappear, and the high school setting
would suit her better. I repeatedly requested a contact person so that if there were issues I would be
able to contact someone and it could be dealt with early before the situation snowballed.

So at this stage of our story, you may be thinking oh she’s one of ‘those’ parents. The helicopter
parent, the anxious parent who is projecting onto their child, the bad parent, the parent who won’t
let their child speak for themselves, the parent with too much time on their hands, the parent who
needs to get a job, get a new interest, get a hobby, learn to show their kid who’s boss. When actually
I’m a
 teacher who would love more than anything for her daughter to be able to get
out of the car at the drop zone like all the other kids, catch the bus with her sister, walk with a friend
and get the joy out of school that I always had.  My husband owns his own business and works
around the clock. We are a normal, every day family cracking under the strain of having a child who
is unable to go to school.

SO back to our story. We medicated our daughter and she got into the school Day 1, Year 7. We
were so happy and proud and to be honest relieved. That was short lived. By the end of Term 1 we

adjustments made. To an outsider our daughter looks very ‘normal’ in the classroom- you would not
pick her as the ‘anxious kid’. It was very much let’s wait and see what happens, she’s fine, she’s
doing really well. Our daughter started to feel anxious over a pending maths test and as it drew
closer her anxiety increased. During this time, I had contacted the maths teacher with no response,
the year 7 coordinator and the learning and support teacher with no real support provided and no
one listening to me that the situation was snowballing. On the day of the test she couldn’t go to

Terms of Reference

On 27 October 2022 the Senate referred the inquiry into the national trend of school refusal and
related matters to the Education and Employment References Committee for inquiry and report
by 22 March 2023.

The national trend of school refusal or 'School Can't' – as distinct from truancy – that is affecting
primary and secondary school aged children, who are unable to attend school regularly or on a
consistent basis, with specific reference to:

a. the increasing number since the COVID-19 pandemic, of young people and their

families who are experiencing school refusal;

b. how school refusal is affecting young people and their families and the impacts it is

having on the employment and financial security of parents and carers;

We are University educated parents with two children who both have SLD and ADHD, eldest child is
also gifted. For this inquiry we will be focusing mainly on our eldest daughter who is currently 13,
grade 7 but is currently experiencing total school refusal for a large proportion of this year.  My
family also identify with being Aboriginal.

School refusal really started for us when our daughter (currently 13 years old) started school in
kinder in 2014. In the beginning this was just a few stomach aches during sport lessons but over the
years this has increased and accumulated into high levels of anxiety and full school refusal. Early
primary (k-2) was supportive and nurturing however when our daughter moved schools in grade 3
(due to her other school being an infant school) we soon realised that there were bigger challengers
for her, but we didn’t know where to start or how to start looking into these challenges.

Where do parents go for help if schools are not supportive? How do parents find out what to do?
These are questions we are still asking and trying to find out.

During her final few years of primary school (5-6) her confidence waned, and she became less
interested in schoolwork, she struggled to complete tasks, focus works and school expectations and
started to become disengaged. This year (grade 7) she has missed a large proportion of school and
since October hasn’t attended school at all.

Below I have summarised some of the issues we have encountered and are still dealing with. For this
review I have focused on a few key points that I believe have impacted on our daughters schooling
resulting to school refusal. This isn’t a singular incident or issue, its multifaceted and complex.

Learning plans:

She had an Indigenous learning plan from her previous school (K – 2) however at her new primary

plan. A learning plan was revised in 2018 (grade 3) during the first year at her new school but it
wasn’t updated again until 2021 – it took us three (3+) years to get them to update her learning plan
and to also include an indigenous learning plan. We spent numerous hours trying to reach out to the
school, offering to provide resources, resending assessments and reports only to be told the school
had never received these from the previous school. We know the school had uploaded them into the

 education department system and had spoken to the principle about them so don’t understand why
we were told this.  We feel that if her learning plan, which is a legal requirement, was actioned,
updated and used in the classrooms then she would have been supported in the classroom and
given the same chances as every other student. If her learning plan was implemented, she might
have had a greater sense of belonging and some of our concerns around her learning challenges
would have been noticed or picked up a lot earlier.  As a parent we often felt our emails and
concerns were ignored and there were not avenues to progress these in anyway.

At the end of 2021 (grade 6) we emailed to school to make sure they updated her learning plan
again, so it was ready for her high school. We believe that it was imperative that we devise a new

Unfortunately, this system had again failed our daughter. We reached out to her year 7 home
teacher in April this year (2022) and asked to discuss her learning plan, we didn’t receive an email
reply. We continued to email her teacher, the assistant principle and the year coordinator,
requesting a meeting to update her learning plan – this process took 5 months to organise a
meeting. Several times during this 5-month period, whilst waiting for the meeting, we expressed
concern about our daughters’ rising levels of anxiety and issues with understanding the schoolwork.
We also suggested she might have an SLD or ADHD so they understood it wasn’t just anxiety alone
that was causing our daughter to feel stressed at school. To date a learning plans for her SLD, ADHD,
sensory accommodations or indigenous requirements has never been done.

Learning accommodations:

She has had no learning related accommodations for late primary or high school, there has been no
evidence of any requested learning support such as explicit teaching and scaffolding of tasks, visual
supports and examples of work etc. We have asked the school on numerous occasions to work
together, to find solutions and for their input and recommendations – to date we didn’t receive any
replies. Our last and final email to the high school was pleading with the school for help because our
daughter was so disengaged and anxious around school that we really needed to work
collaboratively on an approach and way to support her, surely, she wasn’t the only student
experiencing this so they must have systems and processes of support in place already? At no time
did a learning support staff reach out to us, at no time did the school call us and at no time did they
reply to our emails. A few weeks later we pulled our daughter out of school completely due to the
recommendations of her paediatrician.

Impact on family, work and finances:

The last two years, 2021 – 2022, have been the most difficult for our daughter to navigate and the
impact has seriously affected her mental health and wellbeing to the point of complete school
refusal due to no support or accommodations for her anxiety, SLD, ADHD as well as being gifted (IQ
130).

I am now working part time from home – I have had to reduce my hours to half time to support my
daughter through this very difficult time.  It has taken me 8 years to build my career back up to post
childrearing days and I have recently received a promotion this year but now my career is on pause.

The school refusal has significantly impacted on my ability to work – before going part time I was
almost always late or having to leave early to collect my daughter from school or I didn’t work

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 82 because I have care duties. This has also impacted significantly on her father’s mental health who
doesn’t have the flexibility to work from home.

Struggles with navigating the Education department (Schools), finding help and costs of
assessments:

We have spent her schooling years trying to navigate the education department processes and
policies as well as getting numerous health and learning assessments done (at our costs) as well as
support for our child. We have had very little support from the schools and there has been no
guidance on what to do and where to get assistance. We have been navigating this blindly as there
are no clear pathways but also being told we are looking for problems in our child.

There doesn’t appear to be a system that parents, and teachers can follow regarding these issues.
Many of the teachers we have spoken to have no idea on what to do. Its like the blind leading the
blind.

There is a lot of information on the Department of Education website but in reality, these guidelines
and policies don’t hold up and are not followed especially if the people on the ground can’t help or
don’t know what to do.

Strain on personal finances:

Because we didn’t have any support or guidance from the schools (not for a lack of asking or trying),
we have had to pay for all the assessments ourselves. All the assessments that have been
undertaken (Cognitive, ADHD, SLD, Auditory processing/ hearing) have been done so privately and
not through the schools. We have spent thousands and thousands of dollars on assessments that
document her cognitive abilities, SLD and ADHD and now confirm diagnosis. In addition to the
assessments, we have decided that the current school and system has done so much damage to our
daughter that we have decided to enrol her into an independent Catholic school for 2023. The
ongoing cost of school fees for 2023, new uniforms, books etc plus the costs of the assessments has
and will create a long-lasting burden on our family’s finances.

This year (2022) we also engaged the services of a specialist learning support educator to assist our
daughter organise her time, assignments for school and workload. The idea was to assist her in these
areas due to suspected ADHD and the need for support because the school wasn’t assisting or
providing any help. This is an additional out of pocket cost for our family which added to the burden
of financial strain.

Strain on personal time:

We have also spent a large amount of personal time trying to work out what to do – there is no
support for parents trying to navigate assessments and diagnosis – where do we go for help, how do
we get help etc. for example, early this year was suggested to the school that we wanted to
investigate getting our daughter assessed for SLD, ADHD and ASD.  We had employed a learning
specialist to work out us and our daughter (again at our costs), this learning specialist advised we
seek and assessment for ADHD only after seeing her twice. We again advised the school of this and
suggested that she might have SLD and or ADHD. At no time did the school help, offer guidance,
information or provide contacts of staff within the school what could help with this process, in face
we were faced with the inappropriate comments of the educational psychologists who dismissed our
claims that our daughter has ADHD. Over and over again the system had failed our daughter –
learning plans not done or implemented, support systems and accommodations not applied and
integrated into her learning, parental feedback and concerns not taken into consideration or taken

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 82 seriously, no avenues to address concerns, educational psychologists dismissing our suggestions of
SLD’s and dismissing the reports from an external private clinical psychologist, educational
psychologists saying the assessment we had paid for privately is not supported by the education
department and not accepted.

The beginning of assessments:

Going back a few years to the beginning of schooling we initially got our daughter into seeing an OT
for sensory issues. By the time she was in grade 3 (new school) these sensory issues were completely
ignored, and the reports and recommendations were not considered or implemented by the school
in her upper primary years. Obviously, her sensory issues hadn’t gone away and with the lack of
accommodations she started to become overloaded easily and was struggling with emotionally
dysregulation (from ADHD that wasn’t diagnosed at the time). We had suggested that she might
have auditory and sensory processing issues or even ASD (grasping at straws), but the teacher
completely dismissed our claims. We knew she was very intelligent but was struggling with school,
some social situations and paying attention - we were trying so hard to work out what was going on.
We also requested our daughter be assessed for dyslexia (it runs in both families) but our claims
were again dismissed, we also requested an ASD assessment but again this was dismissed by the
school so we ended up going directly
did suggest we investigate her inattention.  We spent the last few years trying to navigate what
‘inattention’ means and have had no guidance or support from the school on what this might have
been and how this might be impacting on her learning – she has now formally been diagnosed with
ADHD (Nov 2022). Again, surely the school could have suggested getting an ADHD assessment done
based on this recommendation from the ASD report.  As parents we don’t know what to do, don’t
have experience and knowledge in these areas and are not trained health professionals so the path
to diagnosis was long and hard.

 and a private paediatrician. ASD was ruled out, but they

Recommendations for a better future:

I would recommend clear pathways (workflow map) to be outlined for parents and schools regarding
getting assessments done if parents raise concerns, this could be done for all types of assessments.
Schools require resourcing and good clear processes to enable these early intervention assessments
and screenings to be done. The two main schools my daughter went to didn’t give us any indication
of clear pathways for assessments or clear guidelines. This might be due to the lack of knowledge,
lack of staffing or resources etc. I would recommend all schools have inclusion officers, more
learning support staff to spend time with parents and children who have complex issues (or
suspected SLD, ASD, ADHD), more school psychologist and clear pathways to investigate and resolve
concerns. These would improve part of the systems but also school staff need to listen to parents
and take their concerns seriously – especially for gifted twice exceptional children or children who
don’t have disruptive behaviours.  Staff should have current training on how to manage and
accommodate students with diverse learning needs including students who are gifted. This training
should be compulsory for all teachers and should be renewed every two years (like first aid training).
Accommodations and resources for schools to be on hand to support parents and children rather
than trying to reinvent the wheel all the time.  This would provide useful if a parent suspects a child
had SLD and or ADHD (for example) and are waiting for a formal assessments – then a list of possible
accommodations and support can be ready to go and implemented in the day to day learning at
school whist the student is waiting for assessments and diagnosis.

Accountability needs to be implemented regarding learning plans, so they don’t fall through the
cracks. Who is responsible for doing these, signing off and making sure they are implemented and

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 82 updated?  In high school where there are multiple teachers its critical that they are aware and
understand these plans for each students in their care. Its not a case of set and forget. Timelines for
completing these learning plans also needs to be considered. It should be compulsory to have these
written and signed off by the end of Term 1 each year and then reviewed late term 3.  The evolution
of the learning plan has the possibility to work well if implemented and used by all staff and for the
students to know what their accommodations are and how they are being supported. They are an
aid to assist the teaching staff, to enable them to better understand they students’ requirements.

Parents who often raise concerns early are only doing so because they care for the welfare of their
child. Often this is dismissed or overlooked however if parental concerns were taken seriously, early
assessments were done, and the education department had clear channels of support many children
would not be in the current position of school refusal. Parents have been put in the position to be
the ones driving these processes and assessments, asking for support in schools – there is no
communications between different areas of the education department, school staff or external
health providers so its up to the parents to bridge the communication gap and drive the support.
Parents are having to be advocates for their children to even get heard.  I would recommend the
education department have ‘case workers or inclusion officers’ external to the school of enrolment.
They could take on the student’s ‘case’, assist with any processes of assessments or diagnosis, assist
with the implementation and review of requirements such as learning plans and accommodations,
navigate any other concerns or challenges that the student may have and assist to implement a care
plan such as getting assistant through school counselling etc. The ‘case worker’ could follow the
student’s education throughout their schooling. That way they can follow up the parents, teachers,
schools and other support persons.

Funding and support for school students who have either a formal diagnosis or have an imputed
disability should be made a lot easier for the schools to apply for NCCD funding and access. We
asked the school this year to impute a learning disability and ADHD and this should have given the
School enough evidence to apply for funding – this was following the guidelines set out from the
education department. The school never imputed a disability or ADHD and never applied for funding
however with our youngest daughter (currently year 5) there was a huge lag in the time between
assessments / diagnosis and applying for NCCD funding and then getting support – in our case it
ended up taking several formative years before she received any additional support. This
disadvantages students whose diagnosis falls outside the deadlines for funding and data collection. I
would advise this process is done twice a year to enable faster and more dedicated support for
students. To date our eldest daughter (year 7, 13 years old) has never had access to education on
the same basis as a child without disability. This is against human rights law and critically needs to be
changed to benefit all students.

Emotional impact:

As a family we are totally exhausted and broken by the system. There have been times that I thought
we would fall apart – that our family would break apart. The impact on our mental health, our
finances and our ability of live a ‘normal’ life has been so severely impacted by this systemic failure
by the school and education department. Our daughter’s life, her future and her entire sense of
worth had been destroyed by lack of support, disregard for her learning, her individual needs and
supports, the total disregard for her parents’ concerns (
another school in our first meeting, even before trying to work out a solution and a diagnosis) – the
school’s completely given up on her, disengagement from her as a student and their lack of support
and duty of care is horrifying. I consider myself a strong resilient person but when you spend years
and years struggling against a system that is also broken and doesn’t care then the impacts are felt

the children and families impacted by the failure of the schooling system and education department
will experience these impacts for life.

Submission:
Brief history of school can’t for my child
Our daughter, now 13 years began refusing to participate in online learning during the peak of the
pandemic in 2020. We were overseas
 and the pandemic was growing in the
community fast. In 2021, the family were fortunate to return to
 Australia. However,
lockdown and remote learning continued. Our daughter’s anxiety and refusal to participate in
learning were building. Since mid-2021, our daughter has been seeing a child psychologist. She has
recently been diagnosed with ADD, social phobia and clinical anxiety. She is currently on medication
to alleviate her anxiety. Our daughter’s ability to get to school is severe. She would throw up, have
headaches, scream, cry, have panic attacks and talk of suicide. She has missed approximately two
years of school (online and face-to-face). We believe this was directly due to COVID and the
lockdown overseas and in

 Australia.

Impact of School Can’t on my child, my family and myself:
Impact of School Can’t experience on my child:
The impact on our daughter’s social and academic life and mental wellbeing has been nothing like we
have seen before. Although with the medication and coping strategies provided by the psychologist,
our daughter’s life is slowly showing progress. However, she still does not want to socialise in large
groups or leave the house. She does not want to join any community clubs/groups. She used to play

with the local club, but her anxiety became too much for her. She does at times talk of suicide.

This has been the hardest part for us. She feels alone, afraid and inept to function in life outside the
home. She has lost friends from around the community and school. They have moved on with life and
other friends. Today, as I mentioned, life is slowly showing positive progress due to the medication
and psychologist visits. Our daughter is having sleepovers (only at our house) with a friend from

Page 1

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 83 school; she is getting out of the house with me at times; she is going for walks with our dog; her panic
attacks have reduced and she is talking about a plan to return to school next year.

Impact of School Can’t experience on our family and myself as a parent:
The impact on our daughter’s ability to participate in school life has been severe. About four months
ago, we needed to make a decision with regard to our jobs. I decided to work part-time (3 days/week),
while my husband works full-time
 Working full-time was causing a great deal
of stress, as our daughter was home alone every day. Some days she was talking of suicide and she
had self-harmed at one point. Therefore, I decided to work part-time. Subsequently, this has caused
economical hardship. We have had to reduce our mortgage repayments, request financial support
from the school our daughter is enrolled in and budget our weekly expenses carefully. In particular,
we’ve had to find the money to pay for our daughter’s psychology sessions, as she had used up all her
medicare claims quickly in six months. Medicare only allows ten visits within six months on a mental
health care plan! Our daughter has used all of these within two months!  If it were not for having
private health care, we would not be able to claim anything. At least we are claiming some money
back.

My relationship with my husband and I was strained for some time. When I was working full time, my
husband, and I were not communicating very well at all with regard to our daughter and the situation.
When our daughter had self-harmed on one occasion, we were at work. To find this out at the end of
the day was mind-blowing. This was one of the significant factors that made the decision for me to
quit my job and work part-time. I saw myself as a failure when it came to being a mother. This is the
same for my husband. There was a point where my husband was going to leave me and my daughter
because he felt like a failure.

Our daughter currently is still not participating in school life. She will do the occasional homework
that’s assigned to her but overall she is not attending school. We hope next year to be different and
that she will attend. As her mother, I’ve decided to continue part-time work so I can monitor and
support my daughter’s transition to school next year.

Access to supports:

We have been fortunate enough to find a child psychologist who has taken on our daughter’s case.
Our daughter sees this person fortnightly. We access the Mental Health Care Plan funding, but those
funds ran out very quickly, so we claim rebates through our private health insurance. The school that
our daughter attends (private school), helped us to access this psychologist. If our daughter was not
attending a private school, I honestly think our daughter would be placed on a long waiting list.
The school that our daughter is enrolled in have been extremely supportive. Her teachers send our
daughter emails at times regarding feedback on her work from home and to check in to see how she is
going. The coordinators have also been supportive. We recently had a meeting with the coordinators
and the principal of the school. It was a relief to hear that they will continue to support our daughter
into 2023. We are not under the illusion that our daughter is struggling academically due to not
attending classes, but we all agreed that we will push on and try again next year.

Monitoring and identification of School Attendance Difficulties:
As far as I’m aware, my daughter’s school has been logging my daughter’s attendance per the internal
school-based system they use. Initially, I was calling every day to log my daughter’s attendance, but
after some time, I stopped. The school understood that my daughter was not going to attend.
The school responded positively. I met with coordinators (ie. Wellbeing, and Academic coordinators)
earlier in the year to discuss our daughter’s issues. They were supportive. They wrote up an
agreement that our daughter signed. This detailed what our daughter could do if she ever required
support at school (i.e. who to see, where to do).

Page 2

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 83 Periodically, the school (Teachers, Coordinators) have reached out via email and phone calls to
discuss our daughter’s needs. They would ring to check in with our daughter and see how she is
going.
The school reimbursed all of the Term 3 and Term 4 fees, which was a relief for us. This showed us
that they supported us and wanted to help us.

Barriers to attendance.  Things that have worked and things that haven’t:
Thinking about treatment/responding to school can’t:
Initially, when our daughter couldn’t get to school earlier this year, she was seeing a social worker via
Zoom. This was once a week. However, this was not going well. Our daughter wasn’t engaging with
the social worker. Some sessions were very short and our daughter wouldn’t respond well, other
sessions our daughter refused to sit in. When she didn’t attend school completely, the school helped us
seek a child psychologist. Our daughter responded extremely well to these sessions. I’m not sure what
the difference was between the two specialists in the sessions, but our daughter responded a lot better
and continues to see the psychologist to this day. Our daughter is currently on anxiety/depression
medication. This seems to help her. I’m not against medication for children if it will help her.
My husband and I respond to our daughter’s mood swings and meltdowns differently today. Speaking
with the previous social worker and psychologist has helped us learn new approaches and strategies
that have helped build a stronger relationship with her. Different communication skills, body
language, and tone of voice have all helped.

Our daughter does lie a lot and is oppositional, so we had to find other approaches to managing her.

Thinking about proactive strategies to prevent school can’t:
We were all overseas when the pandemic first hit and when our daughter first started withdrawing
from school. At this time, the school was online. To be retrospective, perhaps we all should have
returned home together. Instead, we decided that my husband return home and I and my daughter stay
overseas. It was a difficult and complex situation. One that has impacted us for a long time.

When we returned to Australia, I enrolled her in the local school. Lockdown and remote learning were
on and off. Our daughter continued to respond negatively to this, as she had a great deal of time with
remote learning. When our daughter decided to not attend her school last year, we contacted the
school and reported our experiences from overseas, so they knew the entire story and our daughter’s
needs. The primary school support was fabulous. They worked hard to help our daughter by assigning
a wellbeing coordinator to her and checking in with her periodically.

How has your relationship / conceptualisation of education changed or been challenged
as a result of your parental lived experience of school can’t?
Today, I have a much clearer understanding of what ‘school can’t mean compared to ‘school refusal’.
I have heard teachers/principals say, ‘the best thing for school refusers is to come to school.” I would
refer to my daughter as a ‘school refuser’, but I now refer to her as someone that ‘cannot get herself
to school’. My husband and I would engage in conflict and frustration that our daughter wasn’t
attending school. We didn’t understand our daughter’s mental health and the world she was living in
her head. We now understand: this ‘school can’t’experience’ is serious and very real for children. As
parents, we have taken a huge step in another direction to understand our daughter by talking to
specialists, educators and reading research articles and listening to podcasts. We believe that our
daughter’s education is not a priority anymore. We believe that her mental health: happiness,
self-confidence and social skills is the priority. Academics will fall in place eventually and she will
find her own pathways to success. As long as we are there to support her. She needs our support.
