SUBMISSION TO THE SENATE EDUCATION & EMPLOYMENT REFERENCES COMMITTEE’S INQUIRY INTO SCHOOL REFUSAL

Senate Standing Committees on Education and Employment

PO Box 6100

Parliament House

Canberra ACT 2600

Submitted online

Dear Senator O’Sullivan

I write to the Committee in my capacity as a parent with lived experience of the situation referred to
as “school refusal”. I appreciate the Senate’s interest in this increasingly common experience and
note the Terms of Reference that have been given to the Committee.

My submission relates specifically to terms b and e, though in opening I would like to use our story
to illustrate what I think may be a fairly typical experience for families who have parented through
the pandemic and who now find themselves dealing with a child unable to attend school on a
regular basis.

Our story

Our daughter, who is now 13 and in year 7 at high school, experienced high levels of separation
anxiety from toddlerhood. Separating from me at childcare and pre-school was often very difficult
for her and we were referred to the Circle of Security parenting program, which we completed and
put into practice with little to no improvement.

She was a brighter than average child, though she seemed to find it difficult to connect and engage
with other children. We received support at pre-school from an early intervention service designed
to support her to build social skills, but she seemed happy enough at play and was well-adjusted at
home and with family. The early childhood educators adored her, and said she was clearly one of the
brightest kids they had had through the service. At their suggestion, we had her cognitively assessed,
and her full-scale IQ came back as in the above average range.

As early as kindergarten, when she was 5 years old, there would be days when she would not leave
the car when we arrived at school. These situations were accompanied by tears and significant
distress, on both our parts. On these days, I would return home with her and try to fit in freelance
work around caring for her. Enquiries with the school revealed no concerns about her fitting in, no
instances of bullying and that she was meeting or exceeding expectations academically for her age
and stage.

However, she did not make friends easily, was often left out of social events such as parties and
group activities and felt the sting of correction or criticism sharply. Her early primary school years
were relatively stable; however, around the age of 8 or 9 school began to be a difficult place for her
to be. Teachers criticised her lack of organisation and while she had a few friends, the relationships
were characterised by power imbalances that often left her feeling left out and excluded. By year 4,
school refusal began to become an issue and she would regularly miss two or three days in a row
every two or three weeks.

1

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 86 SUBMISSION TO THE SENATE EDUCATION & EMPLOYMENT REFERENCES COMMITTEE’S INQUIRY INTO SCHOOL REFUSAL

 systemic school. Her existing friendships had begun
In 2020, our daughter was in year 5 at a
to break down, homework was becoming more demanding, and her school attendance became even
more patchy. Tears, tantrums and anger occurred every morning. We engaged assistance from a
psychologist as her anxiety about school seemed to be increasing. Though the early days of the
pandemic were confusing and worrying for all of us, we were in fact relieved when we were able to
keep her at home. She struggled to engage with online learning though she was notably calmer and
more relaxed at home. We undertook telehealth counselling to try to address her anxiety, though
online therapy was extremely difficult for her.

When school resumed as face-to-face attendance, we were unable to get her to return to school.
We met with her teacher and Assistant Principal, who were kind and encouraging of her return, but
the school was unable to provide us with any structured support to return her to full attendance and
her anxiety grew. Eventually, we withdrew her from that school and enrolled her at the local public
primary school.

At this school, our problems continued, though we received a much more considered, thoughtful
and engaged response from the school. We also saw a paediatrician, who diagnosed anxiety and
began her on medication. Psychological support continued. The school made many accommodations
relating to attendance, uniform and classroom participation to try to make attending more
comfortable, but her school refusal persisted. She had a few friends, but no close connections and
this was exacerbated by irregular attendance.

Her psychologist suggested we aim to just get to the school gate every day – so that became our goal.
Each morning, we would manage to get her dressed, fed and out the door though this was not
without tears and anger, and feeling ill. We reminded her that we were just going to the gate, and
we would see what happened from there. We would leave the house at 830 and drive the two
minutes to the school (we are within easy walking distance of the primary school, but school refusal
made walking impossible). We would pull up to the gate and sit there for five, ten or fifteen minutes
as she tried to work up the courage to go. We would drive around the block. There were tears, angry
words, ultimatums, bribes, promises and pleading until eventually, around 40 minutes later we
would return home and I would try to begin work for the day with a distressed child to also comfort.
And we would repeat this the next day.

I would receive phone calls from the principal, school counsellor and her teachers trying to support
us, but we were very much alone with the fact that our child could not bring herself to walk through
the school gate, and on the days she did – was likely to need to come home early.

‘If we can just get her to high school’, we thought, perhaps naively assuming that a wider variety of
potential friends, more interesting curriculum and a more ‘mature’ environment might help.
However, high school has only served to bring into sharp relief what we might have seen earlier if we
had not had the experience of the pandemic.

Two months ago, with no signs of her anxiety being under control despite 18 months of
pharmaceutical treatment and psychological support, we undertook a full cognitive assessment, and
she was diagnosed with ADHD, predominantly inattentive. We are also in the process of having her
assessed for autism, at the suggestion of a psychologist and our general practitioner.

We are now approaching the end of year 7 and school refusal for our daughter is at an all time high.
She attends approximately 2 to 3 days a week. On the days she is there, I receive multiple text
messages asking if she can come home or telling me how unbearable the situation is. She spends

2

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 86 SUBMISSION TO THE SENATE EDUCATION & EMPLOYMENT REFERENCES COMMITTEE’S INQUIRY INTO SCHOOL REFUSAL

time in learning support or in the calm area daily to cope with the intense experience of school
attendance.

This would be difficult enough for any parent. I work in a senior role in
with supportive management and flexible work practices, but the emotional toll of school refusal
leaks into my working life every single day and I am frequently in tears at my desk as I struggle to
balance caring for my daughter’s psycho-social, physical and academic wellbeing, my professional
commitments and my own health and wellbeing. Her father also works full time, and commutes 50
minutes to the office three days a week, meaning most days I am managing school refusal from 6.30
in the morning, right through the school day (whether she makes it there or not) and through to
5pm by myself.

At a recent meeting I attended, I listened to a senior executive from the Catholic school system
talking about school refusal and poor attendance. He claimed that “parents are telling their kids not
to bother going to school”. My heart sank.

Here are my learnings and the points I would like the Committee to understand about school refusal.

It is real, it is traumatic for the child and the family, and it has an impact on everyone in the family
unit every single day.

Daily arguments, pleading, cajoling, bribery and feelings of failure, inadequacy and hopelessness
accompany the sanitised term ‘school refusal’.

As parents we carry an awareness that missing school means missing opportunities to learn – not
just academically but socially. Well-meaning messages from educators and experts that equate one
day off a week is the equivalent to 2.5 years of missed schooling across the course of their schooling
are unhelpful to a parent or family struggling with school refusal and do not help the child who is
very aware that they are not doing what is required.

Meanwhile, we are endeavouring to perform at a standard expected by our employers and
colleagues. While, in our case, we are fortunate to be at a senior enough level that we have some
agency around our time and inputs, the Committee might like to consider the impact on a casual or
part time worker, who is reliant on their child being at school (and potentially before or after school
care) in order to earn a living.

The idea that this is a problem generated by parents who are too relaxed about their children’s
attendance is fallacious and should be discouraged.

My husband and I are both tertiary educated. We both struggled through social difficulties in high
school but are committed to our daughter’s education. We know that education is life changing.
What we are equally committed to, though, is her mental health and wellbeing. I see the impact that
a full day in a mainstream school environment has on my child and am not surprised that after one
or two days in a school environment, she is exhausted and unwilling to face another day in the
classroom or in the school grounds. This leads me to my next point.

Our school system does not value inclusion and diversity in practice.

Our school system is highly industrialised in its structure and operations. It requires adherence to
strict timetables, one-size-fits-all learning, and the ability to learn in crowded and often inadequate
spaces. It was designed for a time when most students left school at 15 or 16 to get a trade or enter
employment. It was designed for a time when we were less cognisant of (or less willing to
acknowledge) difference, disability and diversity.

3

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 86
 SUBMISSION TO THE SENATE EDUCATION & EMPLOYMENT REFERENCES COMMITTEE’S INQUIRY INTO SCHOOL REFUSAL

Today, we expect children with cognitive and physical disabilities, neurodevelopmental divergence,
and a range of other needs to fit within a very prescriptive model and mode of education. It causes
severe stress for many of these children and young people.

Further, schools do not have the cultural maturity, resources or programs to create the necessary
shifts to ensure that children and young people who are somewhere outside the ‘norm’ are not
subjected to exclusion, bullying or social isolation. Students with diverse needs are often teased or
hassled which can contribute to feelings of anxiety, difference and reluctance to attend school.

While our daughter’s high school has an excellent learning support team who have been responsive
to her needs, since being diagnosed with ADHD she has been told multiple times to “learn to focus”
by her maths teacher, teased by peers for wearing headphones to muffle excessive noise in the
technology space, and told to read a novel for an entire period in class. My child has an amazing
vocabulary and is an imaginative and effective storyteller. When she had a brief period of private
tutoring for maths, her instructor had her completing year 9 and 10 maths problems in the first half
of year 7. I remind the Committee that her full scale IQ was assessed at Above Average before
primary school.

But her ADHD means she struggles to process long blocks of narrative text, excessive noise
overwhelms her (and in a class of more than 20 students, it is always excessively noisy) and her
working memory and processing speed are so low that she can’t hold numbers in her head for long
enough to perform the manipulations required (and in year 7 they may not use calculators).

No wonder, then, school is not a place she feels able to be if the timetable for the day has a double
maths period, followed by English and metalwork before she has a ‘break’ in a playground with a
thousand other young people.

The pandemic meant that a lot of children who might have been identified as requiring
assessment and support went un-noticed and un-observed for the best part of two years.

We wonder what might have happened if, when school refusal began to be a real issue for our
daughter in 2020, an educator or learning support specialist had been able to work with us to
identify the root of the problem and refer us for assessment and support. Perhaps nothing. But
perhaps we might have been able to engage in assessments earlier and understood that at least
some of her school refusal was related to the environment she was in being unfriendly to
neurodiversity.

A psychologist I spoke to about this said that, from their perspective, there was a huge cohort of kids
who had been holding on to school attendance by their fingertips. When the pandemic hit, and they
were removed from the pressure cooker of school, the grip was lost. She said, “they have seen what
it’s like to not be in that environment, and they are not going back again”.

This is what has happened: kids who were under extreme pressure but were holding on because
there was no other option, now cannot face having to go back to that environment.

4

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 86 SUBMISSION TO THE SENATE EDUCATION & EMPLOYMENT REFERENCES COMMITTEE’S INQUIRY INTO SCHOOL REFUSAL

Health system pressures mean that obtaining appropriate support to correctly diagnose and
address issues is an onerous and lengthy process…meanwhile, our kids are at home or struggling
to remain in learning environments.

We waited three months for a cognitive assessment – we went through the private system and paid
$1500 to have it done. Wait lists for public assessment clinics are formidably long.

We know that our child’s experience of school may be more positive if we can address her ADHD.
We are unable to investigate and begin medication without a paediatrician’s assessment. We were
unable to find a paediatrician in our local area able to see our child within the next year. We have an
appointment in March 2023 with a paediatrician in
 – that will be more nearly 6 months since
she met the diagnostic criteria for ADHD. By the time we get her established on medication (which
we hope will help, but there is no guarantee), she will have been struggling with schooling for more
than three years.

We have an autism assessment scheduled for the week before Christmas. Again, we will pay $1,500
for that assessment in the hope that we will then have evidence to advocate for accommodations
for our child’s neurodiversity in the mainstream school system. In the meantime, we will limp
towards the finish line of another wasted year of schooling.

The Committee is encouraged to consider the cause of the problem, not just the effects.

Again, I appreciate the Committee’s interest in this issue. However, focusing the terms of reference
primarily on the effects of school refusal on employment and workforce participation, and the ability
of the education system to monitor and respond to school refusal will not achieve better outcomes
for children, young people and families.

There are committed and passionate teachers in our schools who see and value our children. But
there are more (both at the school level and at the systemic level) who seem to believe that children
who ‘refuse school’ are lazy or unmotivated, or that their parents do not care about their education.

Until our education system is revolutionised to consider the student first and to create a model and
system of learning that is truly inclusive, the number of young people missing out on the
opportunities provided by education will continue to grow.

For our family, we are holding on to the hope that medication and a definitive assessment of
whether our daughter is autistic or not will provide us with answers and options. As we have done
for the last three years, we will continue to try to get her to school each day. We will take each day
that she makes it as a win. And we will persevere with trying to balance her formal education with
supporting her emotional and psychological wellbeing, all the while trying to manage our own
careers and keep our family home as peaceful and loving a place as it can be. We intend to seek
enrolment in a Big Picture school, where her neurodiversity will be seen through a ‘strengths’ lens.
Unfortunately, this is not an option until year 9.

I thank the Committee for considering my input. I will look forward to reading the Committee’s
report on this issue.

5

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 86

Brief History of school refusal for my child:

at high school

School refusal started for my child towards the end of
had not experienced any difficulties with my daughter’s school attendance, nor had I experienced
any attendance issues with my other children. At first it seemed to be triggered by the fact that
several of her friends had left school, mainly due to their families needing to relocate due to a local
housing crisis (lack of available and affordable rentals). However, as my daughter’s school refusal
became worse, and her mental health deteriorated it became clearer that there was a lot more
going on.

 Prior to this time, I

At first my daughter would request days off school, usually using the excuse of “I haven’t got any
friends”, “I’m feeling too tired”, or that she “wasn’t feeling well”. When she was at school, she
would continually text or ring me on her mobile pleading with me to come and pick her up because
she just “couldn’t stay”. You could hear the distress and absolute desperation in her voice. Initially I
simply refused to pick her up and informed her “that we all have to do some things that we don’t
like” and told her that “school was compulsory” and that “I’d get in trouble if I kept her home”. But
she would continue to ring and text wanting to come home and it got to the point where I had to put
my phone on silent and ignore her pleas. Society taught/pressured me into believing that this was a
disciplinary/parenting issue, and I initially treated it as such. She then started taking herself to the
school’s “well-being” area and was missing a lot of classes, particularly the ones she found stressful.
Then she started taking herself to sickbay where she knew that the school would ring me to come
and collect her. She requested to change to another school and so an out of area application was
made for another high school and she was transferred there, but this was unsuccessful culminating
in her return to her original school.

My daughter’s school refusal graduated to the point of me being unable to get her out of bed to
attend school, despite trying to employ multiple different strategies. She then completely stopped
attending school and withdrew from life in general. She stopped going to her
 classes (which
she had been attending since the age of 5), she quit
and stopped communicating with her
remaining friends. She stayed in her darkened room, under her bed covers and completely withdrew
from life.

My daughter was eventually diagnosed with ADHD and as having autistic traits, as well as anxiety
and depression. She was commenced on medication and attended Headspace for counselling and
CBT. She enrolled into a small local independent “alternative” school for term 4 of this year and has
been successfully attending.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 87 Impact of school refusal on my family:

The entire school refusal journey has had a significant impact on my daughter’s life. Her personality
has changed through this experience. She has lost confidence in herself and has developed anxiety
and depression. She is not as happy and outgoing as she once was. Her future aspirations and goals
have changed, and she is now setting much lower expectations for herself and has altered her
planned career path. She had always wanted to be a schoolteacher or social worker (IQ testing and
her teachers have indicated that my daughter is bright and is more than capable of attending
university and achieving these aspirations), but now she is looking at a more vocational pathway.
She is stressed by the mere thought of anything resembling schooling in any way.

My daughter’s relationship with extended family members has also altered, particularly with her
grandparents. They don’t understand her “school can’t” and believe it’s a disciplinary or behavioural
issue and they are very dismissive of her diagnosis. Her older adult siblings hold similar beliefs and
feel she is being “spoilt” and that she is being “naughty”. She has lost her previous close bond she
had with these family members.

This experience has had an economic impact on my family. I’m a single parent with limited financial
resources. I’ve had to spend more time at home to support my child through the crippling effects of
her “school can’t” journey. There is a lot of time expenditure required to seek the relevant
resources/services to assist my child, and then there’s the cost of attending these specialist services
and the of obtaining assessments. I’ve also had the expense involved with changing my daughter to
different schools (uniforms, school fees). I’ve had to access a portion of my superannuation to assist
with the resultant financial hardship.

Access to supports:

I reside in regional
found myself having to do all the legwork, and a lot of the supports I found “by accident”.

and have found accessing the right supports very difficult to navigate and

Starting with the mainstream high school. Whilst they were friendly and approachable, and didn’t
hassle us about my daughter’s absenteeism, they didn’t really offer any practical support. I
instigated a meeting with the deputy principal to discuss my daughter’s school refusal issues. At this
meeting some basic strategies were planned to try and assist my daughter with her school
attendance, however, none of these were followed through. Despite a lengthy discussion with the
school counsellor about my daughter’s attendance issues and a promised meeting for my daughter
to attend counselling, this never eventuated. The school refused to provide any work for her at
home (despite being both a face-to-face and distant education school). Their reasons for not doing
so were that this would not support her return to school. Hence my daughter went through a period
of time not receiving any form of education.

My daughter had a good rapport with our GP and he proved very supportive, arranging weekly
appointments with my daughter when she was at her worst. He monitored my daughter’s mental
health closely and made referrals to free allied health services where available. Even though our
medical centre charges for GP services he arranged bulk billing for my daughter’s appointments,
which helped. Unfortunately, the medical centre where our GP worked closed without notice. We
then had trouble trying to find another GP as all other GP practices in our local area (5 of them) had
closed their books. Eventually we found out that our GP had relocated to a large medical centre an
hour away and were able to reconnect with him.

counselling services, and whilst waiting my daughter’s mental health deteriorated dramatically and
she became unable to attend school at all. Then when she finally accessed the counselling service
there, they felt she required the services of their psychiatrist which entailed an eight-month waiting
time. Our GP ended up referring my daughter for a Telehealth appointment with a paediatric
psychiatrist located interstate
our GP commenced my daughter on a low dose of an antidepressant whilst waiting for further
guidance from the psychiatrist. Thus, there was a lot of waiting involved with accessing specialist
services.

 which involved a three month wait. In the meantime,

Equine therapy has been useful for my daughter, but it was difficult to find and is quite expensive.

We were fortunate enough to locate a small, independent “alternative” school for my daughter to
attend. The school’s clinical psychologist conducted extensive diagnostic testing for my daughter. I
would have otherwise been able to afford the access of such services privately. My daughter now
has a diagnosis and is commencing stimulant medication for ADHD. My daughter has been
successfully attending this school for the whole of term 4 this year. This school offers a completely
different approach from the mainstream schooling model. My daughter feels heard here, she has
more autonomy and feels better supported at this school. The school has developed a personal
support learning plan for her, and my daughter’s anxiety has reduced significantly.

The best source of support, I stumbled onto by accident has been the “School Can’t (school
phobia/school refusal Australia” Facebook group. It has offered unconditional support and until I
joined this group, I had felt very alone in my daughter’s school refusal journey. I didn’t realise how
many families were experiencing similar problems. There is a wealth of information on this site.

I’m currently in the process of trying to find an OT that supports teenagers with ADHD but have yet
been unsuccessful because the OT’s I’ve contacted only treat children up to the age of 12years.

What strategies have or haven’t worked:

Suggested strategies of utilising a reward and punishment system at home didn’t help and only
caused more distress for my daughter and myself. My daughter was totally unmotivated by
punishment (such as removal of devices) and there were no rewards that would entice her.

Changing to another mainstream school didn’t help, it led to worsening attendance.

In the initial stages counselling via Headspace wasn’t useful because she refused to attend.
However, after a period of being medicated with an SSRI her anxiety and depression decreased
enough for her to be receptive to attending the services that Headspace offered. She required
several changes in therapists until she found the right fit for her. She is successfully receiving CBT at
Headspace now.

The consultation with the paediatric psychiatrist led to a diagnosis and appropriate treatment.
Having the diagnosis provided my daughter and I with a better understanding of what was
contributing to her difficulties with attending school.

Transferring my daughter to the “alternative school” has made a huge difference. My daughter feels
no pressure at this school, finding it has more flexible and that it provides better for her needs.

When my daughter was in a complete state of mental exhaustion, we found a period of total
deschooling was necessary to allow her to recover. This helped her to be in a better space which led
her to be able to be able to later accept the assistance she  required.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 87 How my conceptualisation of education has changed as a result of lived experience of school refusal:

I now see that mainstream schooling is not a good fit for some children and doesn’t or is unable to
provide the necessary supports for these children. I am now more open to more alternative forms of
education (including homeschooling and access to “alternative” schools), I previously held the
opinion that these weren’t proper or adequate forms of education.

I have had to lower my expectations and allow my daughter to be the guide as to what she can cope
with and what her education future looks like. I have had to completely alter my ideas of what
school actually looks like for my daughter and have also had to let go of previously held study and
career path aspirations I held for her. I now accept there are alternative career paths and ways of
transitioning into tertiary education (if she desires), and that she doesn’t have to attend mainstream
schooling to attain her goals.

Recommendations for the committee:

Encouragement for a change in the perception of school refusal as being a disciplinary or parenting
issue. Parents really want their children to be attending school and are completely baffled and
heartbroken when their child refuses to attend. Parents exhaust all available strategies to try and get
their children to attend school, and the last thing they need to be told is that their child’s non
attendance is due to poor parenting or a lack of discipline. There also needs to be a change in the
view that “school can’t” children are being “naughty”. There are lots of reasons why children can’t
face school and a number of them don’t even know themselves why they can’t go and would love to
be capable of attending.

Remove legal threats and consequences for families experiencing school refusal and instead provide
a more supportive role.

Accept that ABA (Applied Behaviour Analysis) is not suitable for some children and can be quite
detrimental. Rather utilise CPS (Collaborative and Proactive Solutions) which can be a far better
approach for all involved. Provide education for the utilisation of CPS.

Provide more flexible learning options. Provisions for partial attendance or options for a
combination of online and face-to-face learning. Be more flexible by providing some work that can
be done at home by school can’t children. A blank all or none approach doesn’t give the child the
opportunity to re-engage with their school if or when they are better able to. This also assists the
child to maintain social connections at the school.

Easier access to professionals to be able to obtain assessment for possible underlying diagnosis and
having affordable options for low-income families. People are on lengthy waiting lists for
assessments and support, and this is a longer time where a child is unable to access the specific
supports they require.

Education for teachers on the specific signs for ADHD, and autism in girls and of how girls often
mask.  (The teachers at my daughter’s mainstream school didn’t think she could possibly have ADHD
because she wasn’t hyperactive, and that she was quiet and co-operative).

Easier access to information pertaining to all services available to assist these families. Also, easy
access to information pertaining to home schooling and a site listing all “alternative” schools and
their location.

Establishment of more “alternative” schools as there is an increasing demand for these types of
schools, and not all families have one accessible to them.

Thank you for conducting this inquiry and for giving us a chance to share our stories. I am
the mother of an eleven-year-old boy who is experiencing school refusal.

My child’s difficulty attending school began after a prolonged period of bullying by an older
student when he was ten years old. He was reporting daily physical and verbal intimidation
– hitting and shoving, threats and insults – but it took his school several months to take it
seriously, by which time serious damage to his mental health had been done. Initially the
teacher and principal told me that my child was being too sensitive and needed to “move
on” from these incidents. When my child started to talk about suicide and struggled to
attend school, the principal dismissed this as a lack of “resilience”, rather than a sign that he
was feeling unsafe at school. It was only when I suggested I would contact the other child’s
parents that the school took more proactive steps to address the bullying.

By that point it was a daily struggle to get my son to school. When he did attend, he arrived
in a very anxious state and his behaviour was often challenging. He became withdrawn in
class, was rude and wary towards teachers, and reacted angrily to any perceived threat or
slight. The punishment for this was often exclusion from the classroom: if he spoke
disrespectfully or did not engage with a task, he would be sent to sit outside by himself. On
some occasions he spent the entire six-hour school day sitting alone outside the classroom,
doing nothing. This is not a healthy way for any ten-year-old to spend a day.

Teachers do a crucial and demanding job and have been among the heroes of the pandemic.
I am loathe to criticise them because I know how hard they work. But my child’s experience
this year has highlighted a lack of understanding and compassion in our schools. When he
began experiencing bullying, my son’s school attendance dropped suddenly from over 95%
to less than 50%. He started being hostile towards teachers where previously he had warm
relationships with them. The change was swift and dramatic, but nobody at the school
expressed curiosity about what might be behind it – the school’s focus was entirely on
disciplining the challenging behaviours he was suddenly displaying.

My child is autistic and experienced domestic violence when he was younger, both of which
may have made him more sensitive to perceived threats. However, neither of these things
should have made school refusal inevitable. He loved school until he stopped feeling safe
there. Children who have experienced trauma and/or who are neurodiverse are more at risk
of school refusal. The current approach is to shift the blame for this back onto these
children and their families. We need instead to be helping teachers and other school staff to
ensure that school is a safe place for all children. Shaming or punishing children and parents
does not work. Students can’t learn when they don’t feel safe. We need to listen to children
who are struggling and take them seriously when they say that they don’t feel safe at
school.

I don’t believe the situation will improve until bullying is taken more seriously, until schools
adopt a trauma-informed approach to behavioural challenges, and until schools have the
resources and training to accommodate neurodiverse students.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 89

 The effects of school refusal on our family are ongoing. I am a single parent and work full-
time. My work can be done remotely, and my employer has been accommodating, but it is
not sustainable for me to keep working full-time while my son is at home. I am waiting to
see if he is able to return to school in the new year. If his difficulty attending continues, I will
need to reduce my working hours and educate him at home. I love my career and am not
sure how we will manage financially if I am not working full-time, but currently this seems
the only alternative way for him to access education.

On a practical level, I believe we need:

 Better training for all teachers and school leaders in responding to bullying, mental

health, trauma and neurodiversity.

 More options for students who are experiencing school refusal or who are at risk of

it to ensure they can still access education, including flexible attendance options (e.g.
shorter weeks or shorter days), resources to learn from home some of the time,
genuinely child-led individual education plans, and early intervention to help with
mental health.

 An urgent response to the exodus of experienced teachers from our schools. In the
six years that we have been at our local public primary school, every teacher and
school leader over the age of 40 has left. The remaining staff are dedicated and are
doing their best, but they – and our kids – need more experienced principals and
teachers to stay in our schools. We need to pay teachers more, make their
workloads manageable, and listen to them when they tell us what it would take to
retain skilled teachers.
Increased funding for child and adolescent mental health services, so that kids can
more easily and quickly access the support they need.



 Greater accountability in our schools. Principals and administrators who fail to

address bullying should be held responsible for its effects on their students, just as
employers are accountable for workplace health and safety. Principals who are not
willing to take on this accountability should not be in such an important role.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 89

Summary and recommendations for the committee

In summary, I believe that school refusal in children is an increasing problem that can have long term

I recommend specific funding be allocated to each school to develop “in house” options for children

submissions.text:
I am a parent of an autistic primary-school aged child with school refusal, currently home schooling
due to mental health problems exacerbated by school.

Summary of recommendations:

•  Ensure all schools have a way to record lateness and absence due to school distress. This
data should go to staff that support wellbeing and mental health, so that changes can be
noticed and support put into place early. It should also go to the Department of Education so
that schools with more distressed children can receive extra support.

•  Ensure there is always a safe quiet space available for children who need it; ideally one that

doesn’t require the child to walk unsupervised across the school to reach it.
•  Quiet spaces should be available at lunch and recess as well as during class times.
•  Schools need to move away from the ‘rewards/punishments’ for ‘behavioural choices’ style
of behavioural management. If a child doesn’t want to sit on the carpet or do the maths
exercise etc, it will be for a reason, and they need help to solve the problem they are having.
If a child raises their voice, it’s because they are feeling unheard or they are upset and losing
the ability to control their volume, and a red sticker against their name and/or a lecture on
speaking mindfully to others won’t help. Instead they need co-regulation (help to calm
down). Teachers will need training and support to use this approach.

•  Teachers need training in neurodiversity and helping children with additional needs.
•  Neurodiversity should be recognised alongside cultural diversity to create an inclusive

environment in schools; there are many great books for children of different ages that could
be read in class.

•  Recognising the role of attachments/relationships in children’s ability to feel safe at school,
and that autistic and anxious children may need more time and effort put into establishing a
relationship with their teacher.

•  Extra support staff in schools to assist with mental health concerns, available at the first
signs of a problem, rather than after the child has lost hope and completely disengaged.

This is our story of school refusal with my second child. My eldest child has never had a problem
attending school. I hope this case study makes it obvious that while school refusal is a major
problem for families, it’s not the case that ‘just getting the kids to school’ would solve everything –
the refusal is a logical outcome of a school system that cannot or will not adapt for children who
need something slightly out of the ordinary.

In prep, my child enjoyed school and did well academically. School refusal started in grade one
(2018), with a teacher they didn’t like. We would frequently be late to school as my child would hide
when it was time to go, refuse to get dressed or in some cases take off their school uniform. We had
a visual schedule for what needed to happen when, packed lunch the night before, etc but none of
these helped with the morning attacks of refusal. I eventually learnt that we would get to school
earlier if I gave up trying to get to school on time, and sat with my child until they felt comfortable to
tell me what was the problem with school today. I raised my child’s discomfort with the teacher, but
all they had noticed was that days we were late were often days when my child was less able to
focus in the classroom. They assumed that my child was unfocussed or easily upset because we had

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 92
 been late (not late because my child was upset!), and thus their only solution was to tell me to make
sure we got to school on time. This was not helpful.

A missed opportunity here relates to the way schools record attendance difficulties. In the program
our school uses (a common package used by multiple schools), the options for recorded lateness or
absences are ‘sick’, ‘medical appointment’, ‘parent approved’, or ‘truant’. There is no way to record
a child’s distress at going to school as the reason they are late or absent. I believe that had there
been the option to record my child’s distress at this stage, it might have been noted by the school
and we might have received a diagnosis and support at 6 years old instead of 8. Certainly I would
hope that the school administrators would have realised that a child who showed zero separation
anxiety during prep, and did not have any changes in their home life, suddenly starting to exhibit
distress at attending school needed some assistance.

In grade two my child had a teacher they really liked, and this helped them have less morning
anxiety around school. However they would still get upset when there were issues in their friend
group, or changes to the usual schedule like a relief teacher. By the end of this year, with my child
aged 7 and 8 months and still not able to regulate their anger and distress at times, I thought there
must be something more going on.

We sought help from a psychologist at the start of 2020/grade 3. Initially I had thought my child
would be diagnosed with some sort of anxiety disorder, however the psych picked up some other
symptoms and my child was diagnosed as autistic. This made a lot of sense in hindsight – I just wish I
had known earlier that a child can make eye contact, be physically affectionate and interested in
social interaction, and still be autistic. My child was having difficulty with sensory input and following
the increasingly difficult social demands at school. Their grade 3 teacher was great and used several
strategies like a visual communication system so my child could let them know when they were
feeling overwhelmed, and some quiet time just outside the classroom to settle in at the start of the
day. These were fairly successful. Of course 2020 was the year of the first long lockdown

 which made things very difficult. Engaging over class video call was unpleasant for my
child – all those faces up close seemingly looking right at you! And they had difficulty knowing when
and how to ask for help when the teacher wasn’t visibly available. When I wasn’t able to supervise
them directly I would often find them watching videos instead of doing the learning task. We were
all glad to get back to school.

2021 started well as the grade 4 teacher kept up the successful strategies from the previous year.
Finally having received an official autism diagnosis from a paediatrician as well as a psychologist, the
teacher and the assistant principal created an Individual Education Plan (IEP) for my child. By this
stage they were having difficulty with engaging with six entire sessions of schoolwork per day, so we
encouraged them to choose which sessions they would concentrate on. During the second long
lockdown at home we concentrated on maths and English tasks, so my child did not fall too far
behind in these subjects. They were able to return to school in term 4 with the teacher commenting
on their positive attitude and ability to use the strategies in their IEP to communicate when they
were starting to get upset and needed a brain break.

Unfortunately this did not continue in 2022. A lot of things changed at school all at once, which for
an autistic kid is very difficult to deal with.

-  Rather than being in a single classroom, they were in a portable building with two classes
sharing the space and no sound barriers in between. This was convenient for the teachers
when lessons needed to be shared due to illness etc, but made it very noisy. There was no

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 92
 -
-

quiet corridor to escape to if a break was needed. I assume my child was placed here
because the third year 5 class was in a similar open space but with four classes. (I don’t
understand why the Department built a new building, opened in 2019, open plan with no
quiet spaces. This does not seem inclusive.)
Two specialist teachers were replaced, including my child’s favourite specialist teacher.
There wasn’t one consistent classroom teacher, but two teachers job-sharing, which meant
readjusting to a different teaching style twice a week. Plus one of the teachers went on
maternity leave at the end of term 1, and was replaced with a teacher coming back from
maternity leave. There was no effort by the school to introduce the new teacher to my child,
and I’m not sure if she was even given the information sheet I had prepared and given to the
two teachers at the start of the year.

-  One of the key strategies to reduce uncertainty and anxiety was a timetable for the day on
the board at the start of the day. This was frequently not updated, and the usual weekly
schedule was frequently rearranged due to staffing issues resulting from the pandemic.

It soon became clear what an enormous effect an engaged, trusted teacher has. No disrespect to my
child’s teachers, they were doing a difficult job in a difficult environment, overworked, undertrained,
stressed, possibly burnt out. But none of them seemed to bother actually getting to know my child,
or using the strategies that had worked in previous years. It was obvious when we met for the first
IEP meeting in term 2 that they had no idea of how to prepare an IEP, of the difference between
intentional misbehaviour and behaviour that signalled my child was becoming overwhelmed, of the
difference between a goal and a strategy to achieve a goal, of even what appropriate goals should
be. For example, my child had a goal in their plan to engage more with lesson introductions. At the
end of 2021, this was successfully happening for most lessons, with the grade 4 teacher using the
strategy of allowing my child to draw at their desk while listening – while the teacher was initially
concerned that my child would not be concentrating and would need extra help to understand the
lesson, not having to sit on the scratchy carpet with other kids in their personal space allowed my
child to concentrate better. In the 2022 IEP the grade 5 teacher complained about ‘pushback’ when
asking my child to sit with the class for lesson introductions (when sitting with the class wasn’t even
an agreed goal). Their comments indicated resentment at having to deal with this difficult child, and
of course my child picked that up. When I and my child’s psychologist suggested a low arousal
approach might assist with continued anxiety, they seemed to take that as permission to not bother
asking what my child was finding difficult in a task, and just left them alone.

This year my child had completely disengaged from school by halfway through term 2. They didn’t
want to go, and often complained of stomach aches and headaches and sore throats. When they
were in the classroom they often sat reading instead of doing the allocated task. School tasks
seemed incomprehensible and pointless, and they had lost all the enjoyment they formerly had in
going to school. They were constantly under sensory assault, unable to concentrate, no relief at
break times as 600 kids on a tarmac playground with a single grass oval is even noisier than 50 kids
in a double classroom. They had difficulty eating lunch at school, even when I packed their favourite
foods. After school they appeared listless, exhausted, like a zombie. They felt that they were stupid
and a burden to everyone.

The school started the process of engaging with the Education Department’s psychologist to obtain
extra funding for next year. They observed my child in the classroom and did a cognitive and
behavioural assessment. The psychologist was lovely, and wrote a thorough report, but the process
was long and I think made my child feel even more like a freak. If we had psychologists embedded in
schools they could pick up problems much earlier, and work with teachers to prevent children from

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 92 getting to the stage of disengagement and depression that my child reached before the school could
even start the process to get help - which wouldn’t even have arrived until 2023.

My child was prescribed an anti-anxiety medication in August. I was deeply dubious about the idea
of medicating a child for what was clearly a mismatch of person and environment, but the school
and my child’s psychologist suggested we should try all options. It didn’t seem to have a lot of effect.

In term 3 we trialled part time school, with days off on Tuesdays and Thursdays, to see if rest breaks
helped. My child was able to engage in home learning activities (created by me, not the school) on
our days together, but remained completely disengaged and depressed on the days they had to go
to school. I paid for my child’s speech therapist to observe them in class and they provided
recommendations for the teachers on how to better engage my child, but I don’t know if the
teachers attempted any of these ideas. At the end of term 3 I met with both teachers, the principal
and assistant principal, and my child’s psychologist. We all agreed that continuing school was
harming my child’s mental health, and I am now completely home schooling. My child is slowly
recovering, but they are so traumatised by their experience this year.

The main factor in the disaster of my child’s 2022 was their classroom teachers putting them in the
too hard basket, so a key recommendation should be for teachers to have more support, and for
there to be flexibility in cases of a teacher/student mismatch. It stuns me that teachers are expected
to deal with all sorts of individual differences without any training in what to expect from these
students, which strategies are usually helpful, and how to write and carry out an individual
education plan; or even apparently any extra time to read reports about a particular student and
plan with their needs in mind. One of my child’s teachers had to attend IEP meetings via videocall on
the days she was at home with her baby. I don’t blame her for resenting this imposition on her
personal time.

Another key factor was the lack of an accessible environment. It shouldn’t be up to kids with
auditory sensitivities to have to wear headphones the entire time to cope with school, any more
than it should be up to kids in wheelchairs to provide ramps. Quiet spaces are just as much a
necessity. Due to the lack of quiet space next to the classroom, my child was given the option of the
library (but only when it was staffed, not at lunch) or the assistant principal’s office (but only when it
wasn’t needed for a meeting) when they needed a break. They would often find both spaces
unavailable and end up wandering around the campus because outside the buildings during class
time was the only quiet place. This is ridiculous and unsafe.

The impact on my life, as a carer, is considerable. I was constantly getting calls from sick bay to pick
up my child as they weren’t feeling well. I had to turn down a promotion this year because my child’s
increasing difficulties with school meant I couldn’t be available for more days. Currently I work one
day in the office and one day from home; if the person who does fill the manager’s role is unhappy
with this arrangement, I will have to quit my job. I am also trying to investigate occupational therapy
activities we can do at home, as all the OT waitlists are full. We are lucky in that my husband earns
enough that we don’t need my income, and we can pay privately for speech therapy (social skills
coaching) and psychology sessions. NDIS doesn’t cover much of it. I know how difficult it is for us,
and it seems impossible to imagine how people manage if they can’t afford to home school.

It’s very difficult emotionally to be the parent of a child who can’t attend mainstream school. People
don’t understand the level of distress my child was in, and they assume I must just be a bad parent
with no boundaries, or one who doesn’t value education. It’s also socially isolating. I used to be
highly involved in volunteering at our school; I was a class parent representative twice, on the

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 92 reading roster for five years, helped run the uniform shop for a couple of years and ran several
community events for the Parents & Friends committee. I loved being part of the school community.
Now it feels embarrassing to talk to the other parents whose kids are all coping just fine with what
my child found unbearable. The only people I feel I can still talk to are the mums of my children’s
closest friends – who each have a neurodivergent child themselves, and ‘get it’.

The terms of reference of this inquiry talk about how school refusal affects young people and
families, financial security and careers, case loads for service providers… but it doesn’t ask why this
is happening. My child’s ‘school refusal’ is impairing their social life and connection to our local
community. That’s depressing; it’s still a better option for them than attending school. The mental
health impacts of this trauma may be life-long. And my child is not the only one – the mainstream
school system is broken.

I don’t think my child needs a ‘special school’. They have no specific learning disabilities or
intellectual impairments. They just need a mainstream school which can cater to their needs: quiet,
supervised spaces; minimising demands which aren’t actually necessary for learning; and teachers
with enough energy and support to accommodate individual differences and build a relationship
with each child so they feel safe enough to attempt difficult tasks. I can’t tell you how heartbreaking
it is watching your child go from ahead of their class, helping others, and being proud of their
achievements… to hating school, feeling that they are no good at anything, and wondering whether
it would be better if they didn’t exist. (Yes, my child has said that to me more than once this year.
They are ten years old.)

All children deserve to feel safe, accepted, and competent. Children need us to assume that they are
doing the best they can at that moment, and that there is some reason beyond their behaviour
other than ‘poor choices’. I would like to throw out the ‘traffic lights’ and star charts and the
assumptions that they could do the work if they ‘chose’ to. My child would love to be like their
peers, able to process instructions as the teacher spoke them, able to navigate the dynamic social
currents of group work, able to ignore sensory distractions, able to read what’s not written and hear
what’s not said. Unfortunately they can’t. And with both their strengths and their weaknesses being
ignored while their teachers and other kids subtly disapproved their lack of ability, of course they
gave up in despair.

An alternative approach is offered in the Collaborative and Proactive Solutions model by Dr Ross
Greene.  The focus is on identifying the lagging skills that cause problems, and working together to
solve problems, sometimes acknowledging that it is not possible for the child to meet that
expectation at this time. This is how we now parent, and it is also possible to use in schools. I believe
this model or similar approaches would have much more success in enabling all children to receive
the education they deserve. We just need, as a society, to decide that all kids are worth it.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 92

submissions.text:
Submission to the Senate Inquiry into the National Trend of School Refusal and Related Matters.

Committee Secretary
Senate Education and Employment Committees
PO Box 6100
Parliament House
Canberra ACT 2600
eec.sen@aph.gov.au

7/12/2022

Dear Committee,

Re: Senate Inquiry into the National Trend of School Refusal and Related Matters.

Introduction - I am a mother of two children who have both experienced school refusal or school
can’t. I am writing this submission on behalf of myself, my husband (the children’s father), and my
children. Our eldest child has experienced severe school refusal which intensified over time. Our
younger child has experienced school refusal to a lesser extent over a shorter period of time. Both
children are now home-schooled by myself. My husband runs his own business, and, since
September 2017, he has had
that our eldest son was diagnosed with Autism in 2020, and I was diagnosed with Autism in 2021.

 I will also mention

I am making this submission to present to the Committee our family’s particular experiences of
school refusal, to attempt to address the terms of reference of the inquiry, and to illustrate how our
family has been affected and impacted by school refusal financially and emotionally. I aim to indicate
a number of factors that contributed to school refusal in our family and whether the COVID-19
pandemic played a role in our personal situation, and what has been the greater influence.

The first part of this submission attempts to address the factors that played into the school refusal of
our children. The later part of this submission presents our family’s experiences in some more detail
in case this is useful.

Terms of Reference –

“The national trend of school refusal or “School Can’t” – as distinct from truancy – that is affecting
primary and secondary school aged children, who are unable to attend school regularly or on a
consistent basis, with specific reference to:

a.  the increasing number since the COVID-19 pandemic, of young people and their families

who are experiencing school refusal;

Our children were already experiencing a level of school refusal before the COVID-19
pandemic. This was due to a number of different reasons, which I will attempt to explain in
this submission. From our family’s point of view, the pandemic pushed our children’s school
refusal over the edge, but it was not the main reason the children refused school.

In many ways, the pandemic lockdowns of 2020 and 2021 were a positive for our family. The
time spent during lockdown highlighted that our children were able to learn at home. We
had space and time to think about aspects of school that were difficult for the children. It
provided us with a break from the stress that we had been going through every weekday

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 93 morning, struggling to get distressed children to school. We were able to stop and question
the things in our life that were causing so much distress, fear, stress and tears, such as
school, and question why these things were stressful, and we were able to start seeking
support or other options.

I do acknowledge that COVID-19 and the lockdowns added demands to teachers and staff at
the school, taking up more of their time and energy. This seemed to affect the
communication at the school somewhat, but by and large, the issues we experienced and
observed were already apparent in the school environment before the pandemic, and, as
mentioned, so were our family’s struggles with school refusal.

I submit that there are a number of factors, beside the COVID-19 pandemic, that have
played into our children’s school refusal.

1.  Anxiety within the child, later diagnosed as Autism.

Many things in the school environment elevated our children’s anxiety, for example,
noise, people and crowds, unreasonable demands, and change. The environment and
people at the school quickly became too much for our children to cope with.

2.  The school’s lack of understanding of the actual needs and individual

accommodations required for children with disabilities, and a lack of support for
disabled families, (in our case, Autism - neurodivergence and giftedness).

A staff member at our school demonstrated a lack of understanding or sensitivity to
neurodivergent children when, in trying to encourage the child to join the class one
day, exclaimed that the classroom seating had been completely rearranged and how
exciting that was. Surprise changes can greatly distress many neurodivergent people.

Additionally, if the school had a better understanding of Autism and anxiety, they
might have been able to point our family in the direction of seeking a diagnosis
before the school refusal became severe.

3.  The fact that a Key Performance Measure for schools in

 is student attendance

rates and the way that this appears to affect the culture or atmosphere at the
school, and the attitude of the staff towards children and their families struggling
with school refusal or attendance.

Some school staff were welcoming and encouraging when engaging with us, but I
often felt guilty and pressured when our child was absent. Comments like, “they’ve
missed a lot of work” or “I can’t write their school report properly because I haven’t
been able to assess them”, although probably well-meaning, often made me feel like
I was doing something wrong, when I was actually doing everything that I could to get
our child to school.

Towards the end of our time at the school, school newsletters began including a
section titled “Every Day Counts”, pushing the importance of attendance. I found the
statements and attachments (i.e.,

 Compulsory School Attendance – Information for Parents two-

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 93








 page document) that were sent sounded quite harsh, and were without sensitivity for
families struggling with school refusal.

Comments from school staff, counsellors and other professionals such as, “you need
to be tougher on your child, you are too soft on them” did not help. “You need to
make home more boring and take away their fun so they want to come to school”
was advice given that we felt was ridiculous and unreasonable. We were being asked
to sacrifice our home life and family relationships, on top of our children’s mental
health and wellbeing to accommodate school. This might also be evidence of people’s
lack of understanding of the difficulties faced by families experiencing school refusal.

4.

Inappropriate and insensitive means used by school staff to get a child into the
school or keep them at school.

Using any level of physical force to drag a child to school and then dragging a child
from a parent to have them at school, or instructing a parent to leave the child at the
school when the child is in extreme distress should never be appropriate. We were
encouraged to do all of these, and had staff members take our child’s hand and drag
them into school or class at times. I also remember our child being held to stop them
running off from a staff member. None of this helped our child actually want to go to
school or be at school. I believe it did the opposite and permanently affected our
child’s feelings about the school. It also placed strain on the parent/child relationship
and affected the child’s trust.

5.  The school’s lack of real, genuine connection and engagement with the parents of

students, a lack of holistic care, and a lack of continuity of care.

Issues we noticed or experienced included the fact that it was clear that, on more
than one occasion, there had been no handover of information about our child and
our family hardship (due to illness) from one teacher to another when our child
moved up a grade. Also, my husband, in the school playground one day, greeted one
of our child’s past teachers, and while this teacher appeared happy to see my
husband and was keen to ask how his health had been, she told my husband that she
had once asked a senior staff member about how our family was doing, only to be
told that it was none of her business and she should not ask. At another time, a
different staff member indicated that they wanted to be able to talk to my husband
about our situation but wasn’t able to chat near the school.

6.  The impression that the school had an issue with doing some things that required
additional effort in order to help support or provide accommodations for children
and families who needed them, particularly if it fell outside the scope of the day-to-
day running of the school.
This became evident to us when our child was diagnosed with Autism and we asked
the school if there was a way to get additional supports for our child at school. We
felt we were being given the “brush-off” more than once. The principal once told my
husband that “there is nothing here for you”. Two other families we have spoken to,
also with neurodivergent children, said that they were told the exact same thing by

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 93





 the same principal. We were not given any guidelines or ideas to explore and were
given the impression that extra support at school was just not an option.

Additionally, the school’s executive staff never communicated with us, as a family, in
writing. Emails were not answered. Front office staff had to chase up executive staff
for us. Teachers did not answer emails, but occasionally answered messages on a
school messaging service, but this was actively discouraged by the school.

7.  Slow or poor communication between school staff about children requiring extra

support.

This appeared to be an issue we noticed when reporting to us that they would be
meeting to discuss our child’s situation or putting together a tailored plan for our
child to help bring them back to school and to help them communicate in the
classroom. This was said to have been partly due to meetings being postponed due to
COVID-19, staff leave etc. At times, this also felt like a “brush-off”.

8.  The school not taking into account the real effect of school refusal, family

illness/hardship on the child and the family.

I feel that some staff at the school took advantage of our emotional state when we
were at the peak of our school refusal issue. The stress, guilt, etc. that we were
feeling left it hard for us to push back, advocate for ourselves, and request that the
school do what they are required to do for all children, as prescribed by the Disability
Standards for Education (2005) that is – “to ensure that every student is able to
participate in the curriculum on the same basis as their peers through rigorous,
meaningful and dignified learning”. Instead, we walked away crying, giving ourselves
a hard time, trying so hard to figure out if we were doing the right thing for our
children.

It felt like, behind all the box-ticking guidelines, there was a culture or an attitude
that students with different needs or neurodivergent brains were in the way,
distracting the class, or holding other students up. Unless the child had a really strong
advocate, they were not going to get any necessary accommodations if they fell
outside what was already being provided in the classroom.

9.  School environments, as they exist at the moment do not suit all children.

Very careful, thorough, and considerate thought needs to be put into any physical,
professional, and cultural changes and adjustments in schools and this needs to be
done in discussion with people and families with disabilities. Any sort of “band-aid”
solution will be unsatisfactory.

b.  how school refusal is affecting young people and their families and the impacts it is having

on the employment and financial security of parents and carers;

School refusal has had a heavy effect on our family in many areas of our life. We have been
affected emotionally and psychologically, socially, and financially. In particular, school

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 93







 refusal affected our employment and financial security, especially as we were already
experiencing hardship due to the children’s father’s life-threatening at the time. That
diagnosis initially had a fairly short prognosis and this in itself was taking a great emotional
toll on us. I was a stay-at-home mother who was starting to consider moving back into the
workforce or further study as our youngest child was soon to start Kindergarten. I was
unable to return to work or study as I always had children at home and, at times had to take
my husband to medical appointments.

My husband runs his own business and was unable to work full-time for a while due to his
illness. Also, the school suggested that he should try being the main person to bring our
oldest child to school because he was tougher or stricter on them. I believe this has had a
lasting, negative effect on the relationship between our children and their father.

Meetings with the school, time spent sitting with our children, counselling them, dropping
children to school late or collecting children from school early etc. all took time.

As the school was unable to present to us any useful suggestions and seemed to push
everything back on to us (i.e., change the child, rather than change the school environment)
we found that we had no choice but to withdraw the children from school and home-school
them. Without the safety net that my parents have been able to be for us, we would have
probably found ourselves homeless.

Even now, after being away from the school for some time, the emotional trauma of school
refusal, coupled with Autism and anxiety, have left my children more anxious about leaving
the home. Often one parent must always be at home to look after the children if the other
parent needs to go out. We have difficulty getting our children to come with us to do simple,
everyday things like grocery shopping or going for a neighbourhood walk.

c.  the impacts and demands of the increasing case load on service providers and schools to

support these students and their families;

We were called to a meeting at the school with the
Truancy Officer when our child was at the peak of their school refusal with many days
absent. I assume that if more are children experiencing school refusal, then there are more
meetings for these people to attend and more families to support.

Liaison Officer and the

At one point in time, after COVID-19 prevented parents entering the school grounds,
teachers began meeting students at the gate. Whether the teachers would have waited for
our child at the gate if there had been no pandemic, I can’t be sure. This would take teachers
away from their prep time etc.

We saw counsellors, psychologists and doctors but I cannot say whether we would have
ended up needing the help of these service providers if there was no school refusal issue.
One of our children is Autistic and so it is likely we would have used such services anyway.

d.  how relevant state, territory and federal departments are working to monitor and address

this growing school refusal challenge;

Unable to comment.

 e.  any other related matters.

I ask that the Committee takes into consideration how families and their young people, who
have experienced school refusal, are affected by having to choose home-schooling. For
many, home-schooling does end up being the right choice for their families but it is a choice
that comes with employment and financial sacrifices. A two-parent family is limited to one
income while one parent home-schools the children. For a one-parent family, it may not
even be an option. There are costs associated with educating children at home, and
although these can be flexible, they can add up. Learning how to prepare an education plan,
understanding the curriculum, and keeping the appropriate records presents a steep
learning curve for someone who isn’t trained as a teacher. I suggest that home-schooling
families could benefit from having the option to use materials and resources provided to
them by the education department or the local primary school, as they would be provided to
any child in a government school, particularly if the child has a disability and is entitled to
enjoy the same opportunities and choices in education as any other child. This would save
time, stress, and money for a family who is likely going to be struggling already.

I feel that schools and education departments should pay more heed of the Disability
Discrimination Act and provide environments that any child, disabled, neurodiverse,
disadvantaged, will gladly come to each day. A pile of pillows or a play tent in the corner of a
classroom where a child is allowed to go, as long as they don’t disturb the rest of the class, is
not enough. Just because it is in the classroom does not mean it is inclusive. Because of the
way a classroom is traditionally run, some children will always “disturb” the class just by
being themselves. I would love to see every primary school have a room or unit, with
permanent support people, for children with Autism, ADHD, intellectual and physical
disabilities, children going through traumatic events, or children just having a bad day etc.,
where they children are free to come and go. This unit would be staffed by more than one
support person, and they would be trained in child psychology, specific to disabilities, special
needs and trauma, and perhaps they would have some teaching training. Students in this
room would be able to self-direct their day, whether it be learning about their current
special interest, or playing a video game to regulate their emotions and prevent overload,
supported by the teacher/psychologists and possibly by parent helpers. They would have
access to one-on-one attention when necessary, and be allowed to “spin around in the
middle of the room” for a few minutes, for example, without getting into trouble. These
children would feel a sense of belonging, or know there was a place where they could be
themselves when they need it, whether that be every day of the year, or only once. This unit
and support person would always be available at the school, no matter the number of
children with a “diagnosis”. The staff in the unit might be able to communicate with the
parents, sharing their observations, offering actual, constructive advice. I cannot picture any
school that has absolutely no children who could find comfort in a space like this.

The “Impacts and demands” on schools and service providers would be eased with proper
teacher training, proper environments that are built to fit around children with additional
requirements and adjustments rather that forcing every child to fit into a single classroom
model.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 93




 In Conclusion -

Before continuing below with our personal family story, I acknowledge that there are certainly more
issues that contribute to school refusal than what I have indicated here. For us, a combination of
diagnosis and its treatment, a lack of
anxiety, Autism, family stress and trauma due to serious
genuine interest from and connection with the school, gaps in the education and training of teachers
and staff, a lack of support or guidance for the less-experienced teachers, a lack of understanding of
what Autism and neurodivergence is and what accommodations disabled children need, and an
unwillingness to get involved in the situation in a way that would provide actual concrete support
are all factors that contributed to the school refusal our family has experienced.

I ask, how can a parent really fix a child’s problem that occurs in a classroom or playground, where
the parent isn’t present? It is very difficult, sometimes impossible.

Better awareness, education, and more importantly, actual understanding of Autism and other
disabilities is needed. Families need options that all have supports in place, for example, home-
schooling where parents are actually supported with provided materials, and resources. More
flexibility in the education system is going to be essential now and going into the future. Teachers
need more training before they hit a classroom. Teachers need less box-ticking and more concrete
support from the Education Department so that they can give their students more time, actually
engaging with them, rather than pushing them along a conveyor belt and out the school door. Why
should a teacher miss their break worrying that a child hasn’t finished their work in the allotted
amount of time? As a parent, I honestly never cared if my child’s schoolwork was unfinished. I can
see how much child is progressing or struggling just by engaging with them myself.

The atmosphere in society and in schools that implies that children must all perform at the same
level as their peers or there is something “wrong” with them is sometimes subtle but is particularly
damaging for children who don’t “fit” or can’t “perform” or participate in a prescribed way. They
learn that they don’t belong… so why would they want to go to such a place, day after day?
