 Our Family’s Experiences with School Refusal

Both of our children attended preschool for a couple of days a week during the two years before
they each started school. Initially, both children were fairly happy to attend preschool and
sometimes didn’t want to leave at the end of the day. Over time, they both occasionally showed
anxiety and expressed that they did not want to attend. Some days we were able to leave them in
the hands of a caring childcare worker, and sometimes I would have to take them straight back
home as they could not be settled. At that time, I felt that they were both anxious children who
didn’t always want to be away from home, like many children of that age. In hindsight there were
other signs indicating that neither child was comfortable in a preschool setting.

Our first child was not particularly interested in starting school but, in the early days, went along
without much fuss. They were never a child who happily ran in the school gate to start the day. In
the first two years of school, they only really showed signs of school refusal when returning to school
after school holidays or after they had been at home for a few days due to illness. They
demonstrated signs of anxiety during various school activities including performances in front of an
assembly of parents, or when having to line up with classmates in a noisy environment. Our
experiences and observations continued to suggest they were an anxious child.

Our first child had the same teacher for Kindergarten and Year 1. This teacher was caring and
engaged. During these two years, she noted that our child struggled with anxiety and with
handwriting. She gave helpful, practical tips and was never pushy.

At the end of Term 3, 1st Grade, my husband was suddenly diagnosed with a life-threatening
Emergency surgery,
 treatment, and (initially) a short prognosis left our family reeling.
Although our children didn’t express any stress outwardly, we informed the school of the situation
and asked them to keep an eye on our first child and let us know if they seemed to be struggling so
that we could do what we could to help. (Our second child was still at home with me as they were
not yet two-years-old.)

 surgery appeared successful and his treatment extended into our

The children’s father’s
child’s 2nd Grade year. At the beginning of the year, we had assumed that the school would have had
some sort of conversation or handover with the new teacher to inform them of any issues our child
(or any other child) might have, family situations etc. It wasn’t until late in Term 3 of 2nd Grade that
we realised that our eldest child’s teacher had no knowledge of the
stress in the family even
though we had referred to the situation in conversations over the year. Also, more disappointingly,
the teacher, who was young and new to teaching, approached me at the end of a school day at the
classroom door, (in a fairly public situation), to tell me that our child had been refusing to work for
some time, was being very defensive at times, and that they weren’t forming friendships as children
their age “should”. He said that this was important and if they didn’t form such friendships, they
would have to repeat a year of school. I was shocked as we had regularly checked with the school
and teacher and asked them to let us know if there was anything we needed to work on. In addition,
I believe this kind of conversation should have occurred in a proper, private meeting environment
with the head of the stage present, not as an off-the-cuff “chat”. I wasn’t able to respond very well
as I was caught by surprise and was trying to keep an eye on my two children in the busy
playground. I was left feeling extremely upset, disconcerted and disappointed. When my husband
heard about the conversation and saw how upset I was at how it had occurred, he approached the
school office for further explanation. He met with the principal who admitted that what had
occurred was not proper process. The principal arranged for our child to be assessed by learning
support to gauge their progress, and for some ongoing counselling which only occurred after we

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 93
 chased it up, and it was not ongoing. The school’s assessment of our child indicated that our child
was achieving at or above the level of his peers.

School refusal became more of an issue as this 2nd Grade year wore on. The teacher had been keeping
our child in at  lunch or recess  breaks  to  get  them to  finish  their  work. We  already  knew  our child
struggled with handwriting. We never felt that it was necessary to keep them in at break times to
finish their work though and were surprised when we learned that this was happening. We knew they
were  a  bright  child  who  was  not  struggling  academically,  even  with  their  handwriting  issues.  The
choice to keep our child in at break times put stress on the teacher/student relationship, and took our
child away from the other children at play times, hampering their ability to socialise, even though we
had been told they needed to socialise more. It felt like the teacher wasn’t prepared to put in place
any useful, thoughtful accommodations and that the teacher was asking us, the parents, to fix the
child’s  behaviour  in  the  classroom  and  playground,  even  though  we  weren’t  in  the  classroom  or
playground with our child.

Our first child began 3rd Grade in 2019. They were in a very large class. (I believe there were 32
children in the class by the end of the year.) This teacher was new to teaching but had previous
experience in early childhood care. Initially, the teacher was thoughtful, and would report to me
some afternoons about whether our child had had a good day, or had struggled.

Our child’s school refusal escalated during this year. Sometimes I was able to accompany them into
the classroom through a back entrance, and I would leave them with a teacher, or I would sneak
away. Sometimes, our child’s distress would be amplified by the head of stage trying to encourage
them to stay. At times, our child would be held, or physically dragged to the classroom and I would
be told to “just go” and leave the child in distress. I would walk home in tears. I would sometimes
stay with my child (often with our toddler in tow) in the corridor outside the classroom.
Occasionally, we would be given some work to try to do in the corridor. Our child was so fearful of
other children looking at them that they often just hid behind a door, or slowly pick up their own bag
and try to leave. My instincts told me that what we were doing wasn’t right for our child. I feel the
head of stage didn’t have any bad intentions, but as soon as you have to physically force a child to
enter school or remain in school, that is not right.

As the year wore on, the class grew and I suspect the teacher was tired. We heard directly from her
less and less.

We got the feeling that the school was encouraging all options to get our child out of the school e.g.,
encouraging them to try out for OC (opportunity classes) which would mean more change for a child
who doesn’t cope well with change due to their disability. Our child did not want to take the
entrance test.

Our child’s Year 3 NAPLAN results were exceptional, above the school and state scores. It was clear
they weren’t struggling academically even though they struggled when it came to writing and
completing written exercises in the allotted time. They once got scolded for not doing their work
when they were staring into space, but they were actually calculating the answer to a maths
problem in their head. Here and there, we were noticing that they weren’t being given the space
and time to learn and complete their work in the particular way they needed. Their interest in
learning was being extinguished as they were often being told or shown that the way they did things
was the “wrong” way or was not good enough.

 All evidence and comments suggested they were a child who was well-liked by other students of all
ages and teachers. Bullying from other students never appeared to be a problem. We had been told

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 93 that they were the child who would stick up for others, even if it was a teacher who was seen to be
the “bully” treating someone unfairly.

We began taking our first child to see a counsellor in early 2020 to try to get help with anxiety,
outside of school, the same year that the COVID-19 pandemic took hold. The counselling didn’t
really help with the school refusal issue. We could see that our child understood all the tools and
ideas being taught during counselling sessions but it was clear this was not the solution.

Our child refused or was unable to go to school very much during this year, their 4th Grade Year.
When I could, I would accompany them into the corridor, sit with them there or encourage them
into the classroom. Our child had two different teachers this year, making communication more
difficult. One of their teachers commented that she was missing out on her lunch or recess breaks
because she had to stay back with our child while they finished their work. Again, this was never
something we expected of them.

This was the year we experienced the first COVID lockdowns and schooling moved to online for a
time. I was able to work closely with our child when they were learning at home. With one-on-one
attention and lots of encouragement, we were able to continue their learning with some success.
Our family were able to relax a bit and get some perspective on what our biggest stressors were.

School returned and so did the school refusal. I was no longer allowed to accompany my child onto
the school grounds, making it harder to get them to go to school.

We decided to seek an assessment for Autism from a developmental psychologist. Nobody had ever
suggested that this might be the problem or might be worth looking into. I believe we would have
been very grateful if someone had pointed us in that direction earlier on. It would have saved us a
lot of time and stress, and probably prevented our child experiencing trauma, caused by the school
refusal struggles.

The teachers and staff met with us and school spoke of developing an individualised learning plan
for our child. We never saw this plan and are unsure if it was ever completed.

 liaison officer and the

Our child’s absences had become so numerous that, even though the school were well aware of the
situation, they called in the
 to meet with us. Our
child came to the meeting with us because they would not, or could not leave our side. They spent
the meeting, hiding under a chair, curled up in a ball. During the meeting my husband and I were
emotional explaining our situation. I was in tears. The liaisons seemed emotionally moved by what
they saw and heard too and were very kind and understanding. During a later conversation, the
home school liaison officer offered to escalate our situation to her boss in order to find some way to
help our child come to school, but she basically indicated that there might not be much they could
do. She came to the school again, specifically to spend time with our child and see if she could help
them into school. I remember she was able to get him to the classroom that day, but there was no
ongoing change to his school refusal.

It was obvious that our child was not going to go back to school willingly if the school environment
remained as it was. That, and our disappointment with the way the school had failed to support us in
any effective, tangible way meant that we were left with only one option. We chose to withdraw our
child from the school at the end of Term 3 and register them for home-schooling. Over the next few
months, our child returned to being a happy, interested, talkative child. Their mental health
improved so much that it was obvious we had made the right choice.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 93 Just before Christmas of 2020, my husband had to have further surgery

 Some side-effects
over the first few months of 2021.

 meant we had many medical appointments

Our second child started primary school in 2021, a few months after we had started home-schooling
our first child and not long after their father had his latest surgery. They had signs of anxiety and
they had seen us go through the stress and turmoil of the first child’s struggles with going to school.
Term 1 was ok, with only small signs of anxiety but also, the child expressed some stress caused by
other children hiding their belongings etc. In Term 2, our child was ill for a number of weeks and was
unable to return to school very often due to COVID-19 safety guidelines and their illness. When we
started feeling the pressure from the school regarding attendance, plus a phone-call from the

 liaison officer, and after a lot of emotional struggles trying to decide whether to keep trying

to send them to school or not, we decided to withdraw them from school to home-school with their
sibling after only two terms.

What did school refusal look like for us? Our children demonstrated their refusal to go to school by
refusing to put on their school uniform, telling us they didn’t want to go, hiding under their blankets,
hiding far under their bed, being distressed, crying and sometimes shaking. Sometimes there would
be very slow walks to school, not always making it all the way there or refusing to go in the school
gate.

We tried many tactics to encourage our children to school. Long, deep conversations about the
importance of education and school, bribing them with treats, taking a special toy or belonging to
school, distraction on the way to school with videos or games, driving to school instead of walking.
Our child couldn’t be bribed or convinced because none of our tactics actually changed the source of
the problem, which was the school environment and the way the staff engaged with our child.

An additional note - My brother and his wife and their children have also had experience with
 and, although are unable to compile their own submission to the
school refusal
inquiry, asked that their main observation be included here. This observation was that it appeared
the school, or some staff at the school, had an issue with any “behaviour” difficulties that would
require them to make any additional changes or to do any actual work or paperwork in order to
assist the child and family with the issue. It seemed that as soon as work on their part would be
required, the school, and particularly the principal, would be very quick to push the problem back on
the parents, expecting the family to solve the problem, even when the school themselves might
have described the problem as being with socialising within the school or how the child acts in a
classroom.

Thank you for allowing people the opportunity to submit their experiences and thoughts to this
inquiry. It is something that has deeply impacted our family in recent years and has, at times, left us
feeling isolated. Just the fact that someone is asking to hear about our experience feels validating
and reassuring.

Yours sincerely,

Brief history of school can’t for my child
I am the mother of a 14 years old daughter who has been on a School Can’t journey for the last 1.5
years.

My daughter has always been an excellent student and seemed very happy in long day care and
primary school, although occasionally struggling with anxiety issues. She continued doing very well in
year 7 and got into the year 8 extension classes at our new local high school after we moved house.
She was always very engaged in class, a keen learner, a good friend, a rule follower and all the
teachers loved her.

During the long covid lockdown that started in July 2021, in the middle of her year 8, we realised our
daughter was struggling with severe OCD, anxiety, self-harming and depression. Despite her severe
mental health issues, she continued engaging with schoolwork remotely for the duration of the
lockdown. However, she struggled going back to school at the end of the lockdown.

While engaging in therapy with a team of psychologist and psychiatrist, she tried a gradual return to
school, only going for a couple of mornings per week. The plan was to increase attendance
progressively. However, it became harder and harder for her to attend school. In particular, she
developed School Contamination OCD, which meant that her brain considered school or anything
that had been in a school as highly “contaminated”. She was also experiencing social anxiety, phobia
of vomiting, panic attacks, etc. She would come back from school extremely stressed and exhausted,
would take very long showers to “decontaminate” herself and would struggle - and even later down
the track refuse - to touch her homework, books, stationery, etc once at home. Her OCD and anxiety
became so severe that going to school became impossible for her. We decided to stop sending her
to school at the start of term 2 in 2022 (year 9) when we realised going to school had become
literally torture for her.

We immediately made a request for Distance Education. However, it took 1.5 terms before her
application got approved, even though I had shared all the required information and was following
up regularly.

 In the meantime, my daughter stayed home, continuing to engage in therapy but hardly doing any
schoolwork. As soon as she started Distance Ed, she got accepted into the

 program at

 This program is designed for teens with depression, anxiety and school

can’t.  She is currently doing an 11-weeks residential stay there where she is engaged in intensive
therapy and is happily attending school in the small, specialised

school.

Page 1

We were lucky that, as part of her admission at
a neuropsychologist who understood girls’ presentation of autism, as we and her psych team started
suspecting she was on the spectrum (girls are very good at masking their autism so are too often
undiagnosed). Our daughter was diagnosed with ASD Level 1 and this was a game changer in the
understanding of our daughter’s issues: in addition to her OCD and anxiety, school is also difficult for
her due to her autism. We have realised that, while she has been masking her autism until now, it
has come at a great cost to her mental and physical health and it is exhausting for her to attend a
big, mainstream school – especially a high school where social demands are high.

She was also very recently diagnosed with POTS (Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome) by her
paediatrician. This is causing her dizziness, extreme fatigue and intolerance to exercise on a daily
basis.
Impact of School Can’t on my child, my family and myself:
Impact of School Can’t experience on my child:
My daughter used to love school and learning. However, going to school became so difficult after
the lockdowns that even going for a couple of mornings per week was a real struggle that in many
ways impacted her mental health even more: her OCD became more severe, she was self-harming
and had suicidal ideation.

We were initially told by her psychiatrist to continue sending her to school no matter what as it
would otherwise be extremely difficult for her to ever go back. We now regret waiting so long to
withdraw her from school as it was so terribly stressful for her, and she could not focus during class
due to overwhelming anxiety anyway.

 Her local public high school was supportive and understanding of the situation, however we were
disappointed that teachers mostly did not post work for her to continue learning from home. Since it
took 1 term ½ to get her approved for Distance Ed, she missed out on lots of learning in year 9. She
is still motivated to do well at school as she wants to go to university to become a psychologist, but I
feel she has not been given the chance to keep up with schoolwork this year.

Our daughter is very social, and she became very isolated at home, not being able to see her friends
much and not being able to make new friends. This impacted her depression and self-esteem
negatively, as well as her physical fitness as she stopped exercising.

Being at home all the time and often in crisis mode put a lot of pressure on our relationship and the
family dynamics. Too often, I had to play the role of a therapist or of a teacher instead of just being a
mum and this impacted our relationship.

Impact of School Can’t experience on our family and myself as a parent:
My daughter’s mental health issues and School Can’t and have been impacting our family life
tremendously.

As her primary carer, I have had to be home every day to look after my daughter, educate myself on
her mental health issues and conditions, manage crisis, be her advocate, find her medical team, take
her to her bi-weekly therapy and medical appointments, find schooling options, make applications,
help her practice her ERP exposures, keep her safe from self-harm and be her supervisor for doing
school from home/Distance Education. This has been extremely time consuming, often taking a good

Page 2

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 94 part of my days. Fortunately, I have a job in IT that allows me to work from home. I work part-time 4
days per week and my job provides flexible hours. Without this flexibility, I would undoubtedly have
had to quit my job. However, I have not been able to give my work the focus I should have, limiting
my career advancement and even putting me at risk of losing my job.

My husband works a high demand managerial role and works very long hours, so he has been unable
to provide as much support as he would have liked, and we would have needed. Both sides of our
extended families live overseas and have not been able to visit for 3 years due to covid.

I have felt very isolated and unsupported during the whole period, and this has impacted my own

that I have been able to get a break, do some self-care and spend more quality time with my

 after over a year of daily struggles,

My younger daughter has also been impacted by her sister’s issues. Even though she loves school

After our last trip to the ER for suicidal ideation, we got support for 3 months from a Care
Coordinator through The Way Back Support Service (Beyond Blue). This was very helpful in providing
a different, non-clinical perspective, on my daughter’s situation. The Care Coordinator was very
helpful in suggesting activities and support groups that could help improve my daughter’s mood. She
also supported me through informal chats and made suggestions of things that could help the whole
family. The Way Back service provided financial support for 6 sessions of equine therapy, which were
very beneficial to my daughter.

After this trip to the ER, we also got access to additional free psychologist sessions through

 which really helped financially as our daughter had been having weekly psychology sessions for
the entire year and we had already reached the end of Medicare and private health insurance covers
so had to pay her psychologist sessions out of pocket ($260/week). Sadly, outside of the 10 sessions/
year partially covered by Medicare (that went up to 20/year during the covid pandemic), there is no
financial support for children suffering from severe mental health issues like severe OCD and who
require intensive therapy treatment, unless they attempt suicide.

Finally, the main game changer was my daughter’s stay at
following a referral from her
psychiatrist. While the whole process for her to get admitted took months, and my daughter had
started stabilising by the time she started at
and School Can’t. She has been very happy with the program and has made significant
improvements during her stay.

 it really helped a lot with her OCD, depression

Overall, we found support was either inexistent or difficult to find and long to access.

Monitoring and identification of School Attendance Difficulties:
My daughter was attending her local public high school when her problem started. I communicated
almost exclusively with her year advisor, who herself coordinated with the school. They were very
understanding and keen to accommodate whatever would work for my daughter. They were ready
to work with us to get my daughter back at school, without pressuring us.

I am not sure how her school attendance was recorded but we had a couple of medical certificates
done by my daughter’s GP and sent to school to justify her absences.

Barriers to attendance.  Things that have worked and things that haven’t:
Thinking about treatment/responding to school can’t:
As mentioned earlier, I wish we had not forced my daughter to go to school for so long when this
was obviously so challenging for her. Her psychiatrist told us we should keep trying a gradual return
or we would really struggle getting her back to school in the future. However, continuing to go to

Page 4

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 94
 school only increased her mental health issues and has now caused her to not want to go back to her
old high school because of the trauma. In retrospect, we have also realised she was certainly not
learning much anyway due to her high level of anxiety being at school.

My daughter had weekly sessions of therapy with a psychologist all year long, doing Exposure
Response Prevention therapy to help with her OCD and CBT and talk therapy to help with the
anxiety and depression. This was obviously critical for improving her mental health and giving her a
chance to ever go back to school. However, when my daughter’s OCD was at its worst, she would
definitely have benefited from a specialised, intensive therapy program (in-patient or out-patient),
like they do have in the US in places like Roger’s (https://rogersbh.org) or McLean’s
(https://www.mcleanhospital.org/ocd ). To my knowledge, such places to treat severe OCD in
children and teens do not exist in Australia.

The Way Back Service was very helpful in giving another non-medical perspective. The Care
Coordinator helped us look at my daughter’s interests and activities she could do outside of
psychology/psychiatrist appointments like Equine therapy and walking rescue dogs. It helped with
her moods and to improve the family dynamics.

was the most helpful as my daughter was able to connect with children going through
similar struggles and do more intensive ERP therapy with the help of a psychologist and nurses.

also allowed her to go back to school in a smaller, more casual setting that was

understanding of her challenges and needs. We would need more schools like this one.

Thinking about proactive strategies to prevent school can’t:
I am not sure my daughter’s School Can’t could have been prevented in the context of the covid
pandemic. The lockdowns tipped things over the edge and the onset of my daughter’s severe OCD
was so rapid that we hardly saw it coming. The only thing I wish was that her psychologist at the
time was more knowledgeable about OCD and would have warned us about the risks of the OCD
escalating when we started seeing the first signs. I also wish her autism was identified earlier by any
of the psychologists and psychiatrist she saw since she was 6 years old.

 much earlier in the process, somewhere
I also wish we had the support of a place like
where children can do intensive therapy while doing schoolwork if they are able to. If there was
more support for helping children and teenagers with mental health issues, they would have more
chance to stay at school or to get back to school earlier. Instead, I was left for over a year having to
manage my daughter on my own even in the worst of crisis.

Whilst my daughter’s school was understanding, they were not equipped to provide much support
when she started not attending school. I wish they had a proactive process in place to discuss the
issues and possible solutions in a formal way, between the child, parents, year advisor and school
counsellor. I also wish teachers would have posted the work online like they were doing during the
lockdowns so our daughter would keep up with her year. My daughter, who had been so motivated
and engaged doing online learning with her school during the lockdowns, ended up completely
losing motivation and hardly did any work for almost 3 terms.

For year 10 next year, my daughter would like to go back to an onsite school but, unfortunately, we
cannot find any school that will cater for her needs so it is likely she will have to continue doing

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 94 Distance Education or a private online school. This will impact her ability to socialise and put a
burden on our family having her at home all year long. We would need more specialised schools that
cater for children with autism (including those who are “high functioning”, which does not mean
they are not struggling) and/or mental health issues. Alternatively, we would need smaller classes in
bigger schools that let the children have the support of a counsellor and more flexibility in terms of
attendance, duration of days, academic expectations, sensory needs, etc while they are going
through a difficult time. All the autistic schools/schools with autistic classes I contacted had high
volumes of demands and were targeted to children who are non-verbal, have mild disabilities or
have lots of additional learning support needs.

How has your relationship/conceptualisation of education changed or been
challenged as a result of your parental lived experience of school can’t?
I often tell people that I did not really question the education system until my daughter started
having problems. I then realised school was designed for children who fit in the box. If they don’t,
parents are left on their own to find solutions and often have to home school their children, at a
great financial and mental health cost for the family.

Both my husband and I have been to university and have master degrees. Our daughter is very
smart, and we always thought she fitted perfectly in the school system. We now realise she does not
fit in mainstream high school due to her autism, yet we have not been able to find alternative
options for her.

I have also realised schools have become extremely competitive and are causing parents and
teachers to put so much pressure on children, often starting from a very young age and culminating
in years 11 and 12
 where teens are overly and unnecessarily stressed about achieving
high ATARs. This is contributing to children and teens’ poor mental health. When you experience
School Can’t, you realise the common definition of “success” is very materialistic and unhealthy. At
the end of the day, what is the most important is for children to have good physical and mental
health, which will then allow them to achieve to the best of their abilities.

Summary and recommendations for the committee:
I am a strong believer that, when children can, they try to do the right thing. When they don’t do the
right thing, it’s because they can’t or don’t know how to. Adults should try to understand why and
get these children the help they need.

My daughter can’t go to school, although she wants to, and here are the things I wish we had had to
help her during her School Can’t journey:

Submission on School Refusal
For the Senate Inquiry into the national trend of school refusal and related matters to the
Education and Employment References Committee for inquiry and report by 22 March 2023.

Committee Secretary
Senate Education and Employment Committees
PO Box 6100
Parliament House
Canberra ACT 2600

SUBMISSION
Date: December 2022

OUTLINE

Introduction

1.
2. Our story
3. Recommendations for the Senate Inquiry

Introduction
I am the parent of a long-term School Refuser (SR). Our story is still very relevant to the
Inquiry, despite taking place from 2005-2016. It still describes the current situation in most
schools as they have not had the time to change nor the monetary support to implement
programs to assist with SR students despite the increase in numbers. I hope that by sharing
our story, and providing recommendations to the Inquiry, that those with SR and their
parents do not have to suffer as we did.

Hopefully after the Inquiry it can be recognised as a Mental Health issue rather than a
behavioural issue and receive monetary and advisory input from Government sooner rather
than later. As an increasing issue with so many children and teenagers finding it hard to
return to school after the COVID lockdowns, I hope that this will also allow for a better look at
our schools and how they operate, and what it is about our school system that either causes
this or perpetuates it. I believe our schools need to re-look at catering for ‘all’ students and
thus making the more sensitive student, the Social Anxiety student, the Generalised Anxiety
child, and those on the autism spectrum not feel excluded.

Our Story
School Refusal started several weeks into the first year of Primary School. We never learnt if
there was a particular trigger or whether everything just became too overwhelming and the
expectations too great.

Almost every morning I had a distraught child, screaming, crying hysterically, almost
vomiting, physically fighting against going to school. Saturday was the only day of reprieve
as by Sunday afternoon, the fear returned. There was at least 1-2 or more days absent
every week, and some whole weeks, that added up to months in total per year. We were

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 95 ‘spoken to’ by the School Principal but offered little to no support. I was constantly told ‘you
know you have to get your child to school, don’t you?!’ As a teacher myself, I found this
comment particularly condescending. The School Principal told me he had never come
across anything like this in all his teaching career. They blamed me for being ‘too soft’ and
this same attitude and relentless judgement came from others outside the school as well. I
was definitely not being ‘soft’. I was exhausted from trying. Blame, however, was the result
of a lack of understanding of what SR is.

The Primary school was not equipped for students facing any mental health issue and the
school psychologist that visited the school intermittently was of no help.

It was only when I sought assistance outside of the school that I discovered this had a name!
I located an SR unit (run by Catholic Education). My child was ‘too young’ but at least we got
counselling there. I also discovered an online Forum for parents and despite being based in
the UK – it was my saviour.  I later became the official support person/modifier on that
Forum and helped many desperate parents find help or just have someone who listened
without judging. This was before the Facebook group formed in Australia.

As it was not addressed at Primary School – the issue remained when starting Secondary
School. In fact, it became magnified. I was treated as if it was only my child who had this
problem, yet the statistics indicated that there would have been others in this one large
school. I was told by the Welfare Coordinator that they had more serious problems to deal
with (not surprising given one Welfare Coordinator for 1000 students!). I was told by the Year
Level Coordinator that it was my fault for not being strict enough! I was made to feel very
small. Again, I had to seek private help from psychologists for my child outside of the school
system.

My child was then placed in a new class with no-one they knew. The school refused to hear
my complaint. The days missed increased. The Year Level co-ordinator threatened to report
me to the Education Department re absentees. My child begged to go to a new school. I
knew the SR would go with them, but I was willing to give it a go. We ended up choosing a
smaller government school. The staff at this school were supportive but it was hard to make
new friends, so although attendance was better, it was still sporadic. My child asked to return
to the first school, as at least they had friends there. Reluctantly but not knowing what else to
do, I met with the Year 10 Coordinators (with my child) to ask if they could return with
support this time. They turned the whole request on its head and instead of saying they
would do more to support, they told my child that they would have to repeat Year 9, and
when I informed them that Year 9 had already been passed, they said due to  ‘behavioural
issues’ ie. non-attendance –they were not allowed back! I suspected this was illegal, but I
had no fight left!

Through my own teaching I had known about Distant Ed, so I contacted them and this
became the choice for Year 10. They were most helpful and communicated well, as they
evidently get several SR students. But isolation and motivation was becoming a concern and
my child requested trying somewhere else for
add that Home Schooling had been tempting throughout this ordeal, but I wanted my child to
interact with others, especially because of the anxiety.

 rather than working from home. I might

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 95 Year 11 was completed at TAFE. They had an excellent Welfare Coordinator. Attendance
improved greatly, partly because of being treated like an adult with a mental health issue,
and not a naughty child.  Unfortunately, the
Long distance travelling became too much and so Year 12 was eventually abandoned. It had
been an exhausting journey for 12 years!

Year 12 class was then moved elsewhere.

I was interviewed for

 TV to hi-light the problem of School Refusal

 (a School Refusal student from another school we had met was also

interviewed) and also interviewed for an article
. There
was obviously more awareness that SR existed but this still had little effect or influence on
governments or schools in relation to how they handled the issue.

Due to my child’s poor attendance, I was unable to take on full time employment. I managed
to find part time work from home and also had to rely on government support. SR and the
lack of support totally disrupted our lives.

RECOMMENDATIONS

The following are recommendations from our experience, and are the same issues faced by
the parents I supported via the online Forum and are the same kind of issues faced by
parents today.

1. Change the name to reflect Mental Health: That the name be changed so that it

does not have the stigma of a behavioural issue that it currently has. School Refusal
is a mental health issue. The name ‘School Refusal’ is therefore a misleading and
unfortunate term, as it trivialises what the problem is, and leaves schools and even
some psychologists thinking it is merely a ‘refusal’ to go to school and thus a
behavioural issue. This was a constant setback we faced. Until it is taken seriously
as a mental health issue, as severe anxiety, then these children will continue to be
treated as if they are ’misbehaving’ in some way and the parents will continue to be
blamed. I do not believe that ‘School Can’t’ is a suitable replacement as it also does
not specify this as a Mental Health/Anxiety issue. I believe that we need to remove
the total focus on just being ‘school’ and support the underlying anxiety. Whether one
leads to the other or not, it is hard to tell, but SR students often avoid other situations
as well. They might be reluctant to join a local sporting team, or go to a family social
event, or interact with peers. They tend to withdraw from ‘life’.

2. Educate all teachers about SR: That all teachers, in schools and training courses,

be educated about School Refusal as a Mental Health condition and provided with
steps to help them to help the student as an individual teacher, as well as part of any
program the school sets up. The lack of support from individual teachers was such a
lost opportunity but could also be because teachers have too much paperwork to fill
in. But unless they know what it is, then it is hard for them to get to know a child who
is so often absent. Yet is could be the individual teacher who makes all the
difference.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 95 3. Referals: That Schools that cannot help the student – refer them to School Refusal
Units, Headspace or any other outside support and then work with that outside
support to implement a return to school.

4. SR parent support: That Schools put ‘SR ‘ parents in touch with other SR parents to
form a Parent Support Network ‘within the school so that they can talk or help each
other and thus ease the stress. And perhaps this can extend to the SR students
meeting with other SR students at the one school or including nearby schools.
Perhaps initially or regularly off campus in a non-stressful situation. This might be
informal via the Parent network or via the school but be supported by both. This
could address the isolation of the student at home and also build friendships of young
people supporting each other.

5. Peer buddy: Introduce a possible peer buddy system to assist School Refusers, so
that they are not facing being on their own when they do return to school. This could
be a friend or someone they know or someone they request.  Friends were never
seen to be part of the support solution but I think had they been aware then they
would have helped out. If this is not possible – a teacher of the child, could volunteer
to be the ‘go to’ person. Someone at the school needs to connect with the child
regularly.

6. Welfare Coordinators: Increase the number of trained Welfare Coordinators

employed in all schools and have an on-site equivalent trained person in Primary
Schools.

7. Home Support: Schools directed to Create an ‘At Home Support Program’ that

supports a child who might be at home for periods of time and send school work or
topics home. Refusing to do this, which happened at both our Primary and
Secondary Schools – with the mistaken belief that it will create complete non-
attendance is counter-productive to the overall education and welfare of the student
and leaves many SR sufferers under educated, lacking motivation, and completely
left behind when they do manage to return to school, which results in more time
away! They need to keep up.

8. School Refusal Units: Increase the number of School Refusal Units and the number
of trained staff involved in them (still few and far between!). Models that exist or did
exist, where groups of students from the local area who have dropped out of school
or have behavioural issues were brought together in a classroom (somewhere in the
community) is not the answer as those students are often on a completely different
road than SR students. They need their own specialised help.

9. Transition from Primary to Secondary. A support team or teacher from the Primary
School should meet with the parent and the support team/teacher at the Secondary
School to discuss the history and options for the future. Try to have consistency.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 95

 10. School sizes be decreased, not increased. Large schools pose more problems

with SR and other students in regard to mental health and physical disabilities. This
also allows for a better Welfare Coordinator-Student ratio. It also allows students to
get to know other students more easily and teachers to get to know the students
better.

11. Support research: Research units such as the

 need more support to continue and maybe take in more than just those who

have missed at least two months in a row. More research is needed.

12. Changes to Education system: The Educational System needs to scale back the
‘accountability’ that teachers are required to carry out in order to teach to certain
requirements or goals. Sometimes a teacher needs to diverge from the usual
curriculum in order to provide an SR student (or other students that don’t fit the
system) the chance to succeed (eg. a similar work requirement, a different approach,
talk to small group not the whole class, acceptance of some late work or work sent in
via the Internet, send work home etc. The current system is way too rigid and the
reporting system means that SR kids don’t fit into the ‘tick the box’ approach and fall
through the cracks. If work is also not sent home – then an SR student has no hope
of having those boxes ticked.

The expectations of students these days are far too great. Acknowledgment of differences
seems to have been overlooked in recent years in education and now teachers have to
teach ‘the same’ rather than ‘catering for individual differences or differing abilities’ as it was
in the past. There is also too much emphasis on a child’s performance…their ability to
confidently engage in all activities!

I hope that our story, which was one of sadness, anguish and at times despair – is not
something that parents have to keep going through. I hope that the fact that School Refusal
has now been noticed enough to be part of a Senate Inquiry, that recommendations are
made – and acted upon to get help out there as soon as possible. These current SR
students need help now – and their parents need as much support and understanding as
they can get.

I hope our story and recommendation helps. Thank you for holding this valuable Inquiry.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 95

Our family continues to suffer the consequences of a school system that does not have the resources
to support children who are struggling with neurodiversity and mental health issues, and where the
behaviours associated with these issues are turned inwards, impacting the individual and their family.
The resources are assigned to those projecting their distress in the classroom and onto others. I was
told that the school psychology resources could only address the children at the “pointy end”. If the
resources had been available in school when we first recognised my daughter’s signs of distress, not
only would her educational outcomes have improved, but her significant use other public resources
would have been avoided. Instead, over the last three years, she has required considerable use of
public  hospital  and  emergency  service  resources,  has  ongoing  need  for  functional  support  in  the
community, and because she wasn’t supported to reach her education potential requires long-term
financial support from the government due to her inability to work or study. I have given up my career
and now identify as a carer, impacting our family finances both now and into my retirement. My own
mental health and well-being has been impacted and I am isolated from friends, family, and career
networks.

Suggested solutions
These suggestions are supported by commentary in my daughters’ stories on the following pages.

1. Scheduled  and  regular  wellbeing  check-in  with  a  mental  health  professional/youth-
worker/social-worker  for  every  child  in  school.  If  every  child  has  the  same  opportunity  to
check-in, the stigma in seeking and needing help is removed, and children can be taught how
to ask for help. These regular reviews would enable early intervention for identified children.
2. Encourage and empower teachers to identify children who they believe are not reaching their
potential;  and  have  trained  mental  health  professionals  on  staff  with  whom  teachers  can
discuss concerns, knowing that the resources are available to follow-up their concerns.
3. Autism  Spectrum  Disorder  (ASD)  and  Attention  Deficit  and  Hyperactivity  Disorder  (ADHD)

assessments for all children in early primary school, especially first in family and girls.

4. Wrap-around  services/case  management  for  all  identified  children  (neurodiverse,  mental
health,  school  can’t)  –  working  on  an  early  intervention  model,  and  including  support  for

1

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 99 families,  planning/negotiating  adjustments  within  the  school,  investigating  and  arranging
educational alternatives, and instigating referrals into other services.

5.  Provide  a  ‘safe  place’  at  school  for  children  with  neurodiversity  and  mental  health  issues.
These children feel vulnerable around other children and seek out quiet safe adults in times
of  distress.  These  adults  should  be  trained  mental  health  professionals,  not  teachers  with
classroom responsibility. Professional support should be available, in this ‘safe place’, at all
times during school hours.

6.  Develop and fund alternative school environments for children experiencing school can’t. It is
unhelpful  to  mix  this  vulnerable  cohort  with  children  who  have  wilfully  disengaged  from
education. The environment needed by children who have disengaged from education due to
neurodiversity and mental health issues must focus on safety and recovery. Re-engagement
should be student led, not time limited, as each failure accumulates and prevents recovery.
7.  Use the experience of online learning during COVID-19 to create a government funded online
learning environment for children who can’t attend school. This online school could provide a
real alternative for isolated children, whether they are learning alone in their bedroom or in
hospital. Schools around the country approached the pivot to online learning with innovation,
this must provide a plethora of material and ideas that can used to provide an amazing service
and real alternative to the school can’t community.

The impacts of the school can’t journey
I  have  been  managing  the  impact  of  school  can’t  and  ongoing  mental  health  issues  for  both  my
daughters for six years. The initial stress of managing a demanding full-time job, which I loved, with
the ongoing uncertainty of each day, and the trauma of coping with the self-harm and behavioural
issues associated with my daughters’ decline in mental health have impacted me, my husband, and
our family circumstances.

My views of public education are tainted by experience. I had always considered myself an advocate
for public education, I supported my daughters’ schools on committees and P&Cs, ran and attended
fundraising  events,  provided  help  in  the  classroom,  and  made  financial  contributions.  Due  to  the
inability of the school system to provide the services needed to support my children,  neither have

makes me very sad to acknowledge that.

Our school can’t journey began
benefit of  hindsight  I  can trace  the  issues  back  to  primary  school, and  the  lack  of  recognition  and
support  for  children  who  are  internalising  their  distress.  Those  children  who  are  not  thriving
academically or socially; and yet they turn up every day, sit quietly in class, don’t bother the teacher,
and instead of being included in groups they sit alone at breaks or play with younger children. These
are the children who fly under the radar in the school system. How do families know that their child is
not  thriving  at  school  unless  they  are  told  by  the  teacher?  Teachers  must  be  empowered  and
supported  to  voice  their  concerns  about  these  children,  knowing  that  there  are  robust  support
services  and  trained  staff  who  can  follow-up  their  concerns  (suggestion  2).  The  decline  in  mental
health that kick started our school can’t journey could have been avoided if wellbeing support was a
routine part of primary and high school. Teach children what it might look like to need help, that it is
OK to ask for help and where to go to get help; provide a robust support system within the school that
includes a scheduled and regular check-in for every child (suggestions 1 and 3).

- - -

Unfortunately, once the school can’t journey begins it feels like you are driving a bus with no steering
wheel and dodgy brakes, you have no map, and your eyes are closed. What happens next is potluck
and depends on the school’s reaction, the supports they have available, and other local services. On
top of dealing with school can’t day by day, the burden of advocating needs into the education system,
and  researching  alternatives  and  other  local  services/supports  falls  to  parents.  When  students  are
identified at risk of or experiencing school can’t, the school should have access to a co-ordinated/wrap
around  support  service  (operating  on  an  early  intervention  model,  not  responding  to  crisis).  The
service must work with families, as well as provide support, referrals to other services, and suggest
and negotiate education alternatives (suggestion 4).

My eldest daughter (D1) went through school until year 11 with undiagnosed ASD and ADHD, only
receiving these diagnoses following a mental collapse at the end of year 10, when she became non-
verbal, depressed, started self-harming and was unable to attend school due to severe anxiety and
panic attacks. There is considerable evidence showing that this decline is quite common for teenage
girls  with  ASD  as  the  techniques  they  use  to  fit  in  with  their  peers  become  too  hard  to  maintain
(suggestion 3). At the time of her collapse, we discussed options with the school and their advice was
let her rest, she has done enough to pass year 10, try again next year. Within a few weeks of starting
year 11 D1 was hospitalised following an overdose, her anxiety over attending school was too great.
However, her desire to learn and future ambitions were intact, and we battled to get her to school
every day  for  three  years. We negotiated part-time  attendance,  developed an ILP, applied for ISP,
attended regular meetings with teachers, drove her to school, sat in classes. Each day would end with
words of encouragement, then a largely sleepless night worrying about tomorrow. Each day would
begin with the battle to get her up, encourage her to get dressed, eat something, gather her things.
As the morning ticked by negotiations would begin between me and my husband, who had the most
flexible morning schedule at work, who could be late again? Even though D1 wanted to learn it was
hard to get her in the car (sometimes we didn’t), she would turn in on herself on the journey and in
the carpark be unable to move. On a good day, with encouragement and time, I could walk her to
class. On a bad day we would turn around and go home to study. On a really bad day we would go
home, and she would collapse into bed exhausted, to try again tomorrow. Depending on her mental
state this meant one of us needed to stay at home too. When she was at school one of us was on call
to collect her either at the end of the day or an urgent dash because she was hiding in the bathroom.

 The school and her teachers were aware of and accommodated her issues, but there was nowhere
safe at school to go when she was overwhelmed. No place where a friendly face would be available to
just sit and recover or plan what to do next. Escape was her only option. The needs of children with
neurodiversity  and  mental  health  issues  must  be  considered  when  providing  student  supports  in
mainstream environments. These children feel vulnerable around other children and seek out quiet
safe adults in times of distress. For these children the ‘safe place’ must not be the same ‘safe place’
used by loud, disruptive children. From experience student support staff are usually ‘cool’ teachers
who have a connection with difficult children, these outgoing adults are not the right fit for children
operating in fight/flight/freeze mode. The staff in student support areas must be trained mental health
professionals (suggestion 5).

If we had known that D1 had ASD and ADHD when she was in primary school, and accommodations

D2 had an ILP in year 5 and 6 to assist her transition to high school, she had the same teacher for both
years, the teacher was great, but at no time was any additional support offered or discussed (I suspect
that D2 also has ADHD, but events have overtaken this diagnosis) – (suggestions 1-3). When I went to

created by the primary school (a feeder school) and said they would keep an eye on her progress.
Reports and conversations with the teachers during year 7 indicated while not thriving, she was “doing
ok”. As D2 started year 8 her sister was in hospital, I approached the school to let them know about
the situation at home. The year co-ordinator took my daughter aside for a chat, no additional support
was offered. During the year we had reports from teachers informing us that D2 no longer appeared
interested in their class, and her marks dropped. Despite expressing my concerns to the school and
them knowing what we were dealing with at home, the school was not able to offer support, in fact I
was told they only had resources to support children at the “pointy end”. And that is the problem, the

(their families too). The children who are internalising their distress, quietly self-destruct and their
families implode around them (suggestions 1-4).

D2 always went to school because she liked seeing her friends, and with hindsight, it got her out of
the house and away from the stresses of her sister. By the end of year 8 she was totally disengaged
from learning yet started year 9 excited to see her friends. In the first week of year 9 she was assaulted
by two girls in the playground, the assault was filmed and put on social media. The impact of this event
and  the  appalling  mediation  processes  enacted  by  the  school  began  an  intense  period  of  school
refusal,  which  coupled  with  the  situation  at  home,  led  to  behavioural  issues,  significant  self-harm
requiring  emergency  service  management,  hospitalisation,  mental  illness  diagnosis  and  family

There are several things which may have helped on this school can’t journey.

Immediately following the assault, D2 was required to face her assailants in a mediation, we were not
allowed to attend. She had to do this twice. Following failed mediation, she was told that she could
just come to school, sit in the student support area have a cup of tea and go home. As discussed above
there are significant issues with ‘student support areas’ – the loud, disruptive kids hang out there too,
the teachers are usually outgoing as well, and they are teachers – they need to be on class by 9:15
(suggestion 5). For a school can’t child, this means that when you get to school late after struggling to
get up, eat something, get dressed, and get into and out of the car; the support teacher is no longer
available. You (and your Mum)  have to sit in the  school  foyer, in view of other  students,  until the
teacher is available between classes to say “Hello, I’m busy for the rest of the day. Try and be on time
tomorrow”. We did this for two weeks. The day D2 did get to school on time, she sat with her cup of
tea in the student support room, expecting to have time with the teacher for support and planning
next steps, then at 9:15 was told to take herself to class. At 9:30 I got a call to collect  her, and she
refused to go back - ever. She felt totally betrayed by school staff, the school community, her friends,
and her family.

Unlike her sister, D2 disengaged from her education, she was not interested in learning. In fact, she
was not interested in anything much at all. Halfway through the term, I arranged a meeting with the
school, on their advice we had sought private therapy for D2 and had a medical certificate for the rest
of the  term.  At  no  time  did  the  school  proactively  check  how  D2  was  going.  At  the  end of  term,  I
arranged another meeting to discuss plans for next term, the school said they couldn’t accommodate
D2 and suggested that I pull her out and register for home schooling. I agreed on a joint enrolment
and spent the holidays completing the paperwork and planning what we could do. It seemed like a
good idea; however, again with hindsight, the family stress created by us all being at home together
was too much. D2 refused to do anything, didn’t want to get up, didn’t want to leave the house, didn’t
want to spend time with the family, didn’t want to live. We needed a co-ordinated wrap around service
to help us navigate these difficult circumstances, there wasn’t one (suggestion 4).

Using the personal network I established managing D1s school can’t journey, I was able to secure a
referral to CAMHS who agreed to engage D2 in the local return to school program. This program runs
for  one  to  two  terms  with  the  intention  of  re-engaging  with  school,  it  provides  a  very  low-key
atmosphere in which to recover, regain confidence, and make some friends. This environment is good,
however it isn’t permanent. From the start of the placement families must work out what comes next

5

 and there are limited options (suggestion 4, 6 and 7). It was obvious that we were not going to get D2
back into mainstream school, she needed an environment with more support, our only option was an
independent  school  providing  education  in  a  supported  environment  for  children  who  have  left
mainstream school for a variety of reasons, mental health being mixed with discipline and behavioural
issues. Starting this school
 gave D2 some hope, but the kids were not what she expected, they
made her anxious and afraid. She did get some comfort from the staff (teachers and youth workers),
and the high staff to student ratio (1:5) meant that they were available during and between classes.
Then COVID changed everything. Suddenly the little routine D2 had established, attending school and
therapy, was gone and she was stuck in her room again, with the stress of her sister ever present. In
with a significant period in
hospital due to declining mental health, and her symptoms escalated as the year progressed. By the
middle of the year our family unit was at breaking point and D2 has spent most of the last 12 months
in hospital. Her cohort are graduating
 this year and I suspect that she will not be able to re-
engage with her education until she is a mature age student. D2s entire future has been impacted by
school can’t.

 D2 was in year 10, she did not graduate. D2 began year 11

The  school system is failing many of our young people, it  does not  provide  for the complex  needs
associated with neurodiversity and mental health. To be able to learn our children need to feel safe
and understood, therefore schools are responsible for more than the education of our young people.
Children with neurodiversity and mental  health issues need an environment that  is supported and
safe, this vulnerable cohort has different needs to the children who wilfully disengage from school,
they do not mix. Priority must be given to develop and fund alternative school environments for school
can’t children that concentrate on safety and recovery, increase the staff to student ratio and have
youth workers in the classroom. Take the pressure off learning, make it practical, include activities,
cooking, excursions, have dogs in the class. Support each student to work at their own academic level,
help them to make friends, and improve their self-confidence. Recovery and engagement should be
student led, not time-limited, each failure to achieve accumulates and makes it harder to try again
(suggestion 6). There is an amazing opportunity to use the knowledge gained about online learning
during  the  COVID  pandemic  to  develop  a  robust  online  government  funded  learning  platform  for
children who can’t attend school (suggestion 7).

Imagine if …..
Our lives have been forever changed by our school can’t journey and its ongoing impact on the mental
health of my family. Imagine if ….

Imagine if D1 had been assessed as ASD and ADHD in year 1, she would have had the support she
needed to thrive at primary and high school. We would have learnt how to support her when she was
little, when her issues were small and contained.

Imagine if there had been support available for the quiet, confused year 8 girl who was worried about
her sister and her family and struggling to stay interested in her classes.

Imagine if when school can’t happens, families can access a wrap around support service, providing
case management, advocacy, support and referrals.

Imagine if when school can’t happens, there are educational environments available to enable children
to remain connected to learning; and feel safe to turn up, knowing that someone is there to help them
with their work, their questions, their problems, their fears.

We continue to live with hope for our daughters’ futures.

Senate inquiry - The national trend of school refusal and related matters

School refusal is a complex issue and needs a nuanced response. Just because the number of children
refusing school may have increased during the Covid – 19 pandemic, it does not mean that the COVID
-  19  pandemic  is  solely  the  cause  of  this  correlation.  In  our  circumstances,  as  parents  of  a  school
refusing child, we consider it was just: “the straw that broke the camel’s back”.

he generally went to school but as he
Our son has never been enthusiastic about school
reached the end of his primary education it became increasingly difficult to encourage him to attend.
In his 2nd year of primary education we were overseas and he did
Distance Education (now
 The experience of distance education was not a pleasant experience for the student
known as
and my wife the person supervising him (I observed on a daily bases how dysfunctional this was).

His secondary school education commenced with the onset of Covid (2020). In
 “in person”
education stopped and started a number of times. During Covid lockdowns education was provided
online but this proved to be a disaster, with little engagement and increased anxiety and stress.

During periods of “in person” education, it was almost impossible to get him to school. Being parents
who  had  a  conventional  education  and  two  older  children  that  did  not  have  any  problems  with
education  (both  university  educated)  the  school  refusal  was  difficult  to  understand.  However,  we
persisted with every trick at our disposal, resulting in the exhaustion of both child and parents and a
child that remained frequently at home. The process of trying to get him to school was generally a 1.5
hour  emotionally  charged  process.  On  the  rare  occasions  that  he  did  attend  we  would  often  be
contacted  by  the  school  requesting  that  we  collect  him.  As  a  result  of  the  additional  stress  he
developed a phobia for wasps that made it more difficult for him to feel safe outside. On reflection I
would  now  consider  the  schools  inadequate  response  and  our  ignorantly  going  along  with  their
approach bordering on child abuse.

Our child had first been diagnosed with mild Autism and then towards the end of 2020 with ADHD.
In the book: The ADHD Explosion Myths, Medication, Money, and Today’s Push for Performance by
Stephen P. Hinshaw, Richard M. Scheffler the authors comment on education and ADHD, saying
(Page 28)

“ Two crucial points are that (a) the initial trigger for ADHD in the 19th and early 20th centuries was
compulsory education, and (b)  the recent press for academic and job-related performance has
propelled rates of ADHD to new heights.  The huge variation across people in terms of attention
span, inhibitory control, and reward sensitivity is strongly related to genes, yet such differences were
not terribly salient or impairing until society decided that all children needed to sit still in classrooms

“

Part of the complexity of school refusal is the interactions of  neurodivergent students with the stress
of Covid pandemic and a school system that is insensitive to the needs of neurodivergent students.
Hinshaw and  Scheffer  in  their  book states that in Australia  over 10% of the  school  population  are
estimated to have ADHD and hence are poor fits for the so called education system that results in
school  refusal.  However,  my  observation  is  that  little  effective  facilitation  for  these  students  is
implemented and what is offered is purely perfunctory.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 100 After much consideration we withdrew our son from the school (the school seemed relieved) in May
of this year and we commenced home schooling. He had been significantly adversely effected by the
school experience and has taken some time to get to a state of mind that has allowed progress. We
have since discovered by associating with others in the  home school community that there are many
families who have had similar issues. Many are struggling with the addition challenges of their new
role. Home schooling is not an easy choice.  It takes commitment and sacrifice to be able to offer an
education to a child which will equip them for a future as an adult.

I'm retired and my wife works part time. We share the roles eg my wife mainly doing the written type
  science
work  (her  choice)    and  I  doing  workshop    activities  such  as  woodwork,
experiments etc.  Our son is now happier to learn, is curious and increasingly self-motivated to explore
areas  of  interest,  has  a  great  social  life  with  other  home  schooled  children  of  his  age.    We,  as  a
household, are also much happier.

With the benefit of hindsight, I could see the issues developing in grade 2 but the education system is
not responsive; in fact they unwittily stymied his education eg In his early primary years I could see
that he was falling behind so as an incentive I would offer him computer time for topics that needed
extra attention eg writing, times tables, analogue clock reading etc. This was working very well until
the school introduced a IPad (computer) based education and stopped any incentive I had to offer, as
a motivation for learning.

All things considered I think Covid was only a small component in school refusal. It was only the last
item  in  a  long  list of  previous  factors. It took many small  stressful  factors to  accumulate (not only
educational but the cultural induced stresses that children should be protected from) to reach this
breaking  point.  In  many  cases  home  school  is  the  answer  to  an  inadequate  and  dysfunctional
education system for many students and should be encouraged when appropriate.

Applying  pressure  to  a  refusing  student  to  attend  school  only  adds  to  the  stress.  The  so  called
“experts” ie educational consultants, psychologists and OT etc are a  blight on the system, costing the
government  via  NDIS  huge  amounts  of  money  on  unhelpful  and  in  many  cases  counterproductive
measures.  The  money  saved  can  be  used  much  more  productively,  just  ask  the  child  expert;  the
parents. They have observed the child for most of their lives and intuitively run dynamic, real time
experiments,  with  real  time  feedback  loops  that  optimizes  a  child’s  welfare,  that  includes  their
education.

school. This is not a case of our parenting being ‘lax’ or us not being committed to our
children’s educational outcomes.

•  During COVID ‘home learning’ where local schools were closed, during periods of

lockdown, my youngest child became aware that he could learn in an environment that
worked better for him (ie not in a school environment), and that he could complete his
work in a focused way, in a timeframe that worked for him, and then have time to follow

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 101






 his own areas of interest. He became aware that he could complete his education
without going to school, which caused him significant distress – so why would he go
back?

B. How school refusal is affecting young people and their families and the impacts it is
having on the employment and financial security of parents and carers;

This has been the hardest aspect of this for our family – the impacts have been huge and far
reaching. These include:

•  As parents we have been forced to relinquish work hours and job security through

reduced capacity to attend the workplace and increased need to be at home educating
and supervising our son. Currently I am facing the difficult decision to potentially give up
my full time paid position to be at home full time to educate him. This will potentially have
wide reaching financial implications for us – I am the primary income earner for our
family so we are not sure how we will be able to continue to pay our mortgage. Having to
make a decision between traumatising our disabled child by forcing him to attend a
schooling model that does not work for him, or losing our home due to financial distress;
this is an awful position to be in.

•  Further to this, if I am essentially forced to give up paid work to care for and educate our
son, this will have significant impacts on my superannuation long term. It is likely I will
not be in a position to be self-funded at retirement age and therefore more reliant on
government pensions and supports.

•  As workers, our availability and productivity at work has been impacted. Because our

this impacts service and program delivery for our community.

work is
We are not the only parents in our workplace who face this challenge, making it an
organisational issue as well. For a community that has been impacted by bushfire, flood,
pandemic, now experiencing major issues with housing availability and affordability
impacting on staffing, this is significant.
Increased social isolation, for our child and for us, and the negative outcomes of this,
which are well documented in research: evidence has linked social isolation with adverse
health consequences including depression, poor sleep quality, impaired executive
function, accelerated cognitive decline, poor cardiovascular function and impaired
immunity at every stage of life.

•

•  Health (including mental health) has suffered in our home due to school refusal, without

a doubt. The stress of the situation has impacted my husband’s
management, with poor health outcomes (he is less able to exercise due to needing to
supervise and support our child at home, and increased stress levels have increased his

 Concerns about financial security have increased my own anxiety

levels, resulting in needing to seek psychological support.

•  Access to accepted forms of education – longer term implications of our son not being

part of the mainstream school system and the impacts on his future.

We have concerns about this more broadly also, as this applies to many other families
beyond just our own:

•  Parents acting as teachers, potentially reducing the quality of education
•
•

Increased anxiety for families due to decreased financial security
Increased levels of anxiety and mental health issues throughout the whole community as
families can’t work etc, having to make huge lifestyle changes.

•  Children being left unsupervised while parents attend work can be a safety issue.
•

Impact on other (neurotypical) siblings who do attend school, creating dissatisfaction,
rivalry and disharmony within the family unit.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 101
 C. The impacts and demands of the increasing case load on service providers and schools
to support these students and their families;

•  Despite our son having an excellent classroom teacher, the school seemed to have very
limited capacity to understand our child’s needs in real terms, and provide practical
support. Despite us having numerous reports from qualified professionals (psychologist,
occupational therapist, psychiatrist) stating his challenges and requirements, the
education system seemed to be incapable of providing real supports to help with these.
For example, despite multiple reports that stated that his comparative age range for
social skills was aged five or under, and his social challenges were significant, making
playground time extremely difficult for him, the school said he did not qualify for any
support because they “did not see evidence of those challenges at school”. Respectfully,
they are school staff, not health professionals trained and qualified to diagnose the
difficulties or understand the nuances of his disability (eg masking). This resulted in him
essentially pretending to cope all day at school, and completely falling apart at the end of
the school day, with huge meltdowns and distress (ie aggressive behaviour at home,
harming himself, other people and property, and needing to be medicated to survive
this).

•  This experience has left us to believe that there is systemic and institutionalised

exclusion of children with additional needs / disability. This is after seeing school staff
making decisions about supports that should be made by qualified health professionals,
and further, ignoring the advice of qualified health professionals.

•  All of the above has placed significant additional demands on other providers and the
government generally. We have had to utilise some of his NDIS funds to manage the
negative impacts of his schooling experience. As parents trying to manage this we have
had to access additional medical support for
(Medicare, NDSS); many additional appointments with family GP, referrals to other
services and providers (eg psychologist), financial counselling services, additional
requests of Carers

management due to stress

 and Carers Gateway etc.

It would be a great improvement if there was a better understanding from government
generally, education department, and other services and agencies, of the complex
dynamics that play out across these areas when working with people with additional
needs / disability.

D. How relevant state, territory and federal departments are working to monitor and address
this growing school refusal challenge; and

It is very heartening to see an inquiry into this.

Possible ways to improve the current situation:

Involve neurodivergent people / people with disabilities in the dialogue to find solutions.

•
•  Financial support for parents who need to stay home to educate their children that

reflects costs of living (Assistance for Isolated Children Payment of around $4K per year
does not at all reflect the real costs of educating children from home).

•  Additional social supports put in place for families with young people refusing school –
these need to be financially supported as many families are not in financial positions to
pay for additional services.

E. Any other related matters.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 101

 •

I believe COVID has highlighted a pre-existing need for a new model which better
supports people who are neurodivergent and or living with disability.

•  Parents know their kids best – schools and the system need to recognise and

acknowledge this.

Thank you for taking the time to read this.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 101
