The national trend of school refusal school can’t and related matters

I am the mother of a

daughter who has struggled to attend school for the past 2

years.  Whilst her peers

 my

daughter is currently unable to leave the home except for fortnightly visits to the

psychologist.  In this submission I will describe the impacts that school can’t has had on my

daughter and our family, assistance that we have received over the past two years, and

recommendations that may assist my daughter and other school can’t children and their

families.

Background

At the beginning of 2020 my daughter started

at our local government primary school.

She was a happy child who enjoyed school, loved learning, had a close circle of friends, and a

teacher that she really liked.  In March of 2020

went into the first of what became

many long periods of lockdowns, due to the COVID19 pandemic.  Since that time my

daughter has been unable to set foot in a physical classroom with other children.  She has

now been diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), misophonia, and social anxiety.

Her sensory sensitivity is heightened in most circumstances outside of the home, and she has

also been diagnosed with depression.

Impacts of school can’t on my daughter

School can’t first began for my daughter when schooling was forced to transfer to the online

world in March 2020.  At first, my daughter really tried to engage with the teacher and her

friends/peers online at home, however it soon became evident that she struggled to learn or

feel connected to school that was conducted online.  By the time we were nearing the end of

the October 2020 lockdown period my daughter was not engaging with online schooling at all

unless I sat beside her and encouraged her to engage with the work.  Throughout much of this

time my daughter spent her days drawing, painting, playing Roblox, watching Netflix and

Disney+, listening to K-pop on Spotify, teaching herself Korean, playing board games, and

playing with the cat.  My daughter’s entire social life transferred to the online world.  After

the long lockdown period of 2020, when my daughter was eventually permitted and able to

physically attend school, she became so agitated at the thought of school that she could not

get out of the car at the school gate in the morning.  So began the 2 years of school can’t!

1

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 102 On a very good day, my daughter may be able to go for a short walk in a local park or visit

her grandparents for a very short period.  On a good day, my daughter will play a game of

Chinese Checkers with her sister or take the cat for a walk around the garden.  On an average

day, my daughter will get dressed by midday, get herself a simple breakfast, go back to bed

for a few hours, and then spend some time reading Korean children’s books or listening to

music on Spotify.  On a not so average day my daughter won’t eat very much, won’t get out

of bed (except to go to the toilet) and will sleep a lot.  On a very bad day my daughter’s

mental health is severely impacted and she may lie awake all night.  Thankfully, we have

ridden the waves of those very dark times and my daughter is slowly making small steps

towards reengaging with the world and school.

My daughter is currently enrolled in the local government primary school but is yet to be able

to attend classes there this year.  She is also enrolled in the local government

college for 2023, however she can’t attend the orientation day, with almost 300 new students,

next week.  My daughter longs to attend school and have real friends, like her older sister,

however she is currently unable to make this happen.

Impacts of school can’t on our family

I am a single parent and I care for 2 daughters.  The impacts of my

daughter’s

school can’t status has greatly impacted my personal, social, and working life.  It has also

impacted on the life of my

daughter.  As a single parent I must work for money,

and this has meant that I have not always been able to give the time and attention to my

daughters as much as I would have liked.  Both of my daughters are diagnosed with ASD.

My eldest daughter has managed to continue to attend school despite the difficulties of

lockdowns over the course of the past few years.  Her mental health was not good in 2020,

however music, art, books, and sessions with a psychologist, have helped her to navigate to a

happier place.  She has also experienced short periods of school can’t where she has had to

take a day off here and there to avoid what we now know as autistic burnout.

In our small household we never have people, including my parents and extended family,

visit our home as this is too anxiety provoking for my

daughter.  We have had

one 3-day holiday in the past 3 years.  We went to an isolated part of

where my daughters were able to take short walks, observe the wildlife, and enjoy the natural

environment.  Unfortunately, my limited time and finances meant that we could not stay

2

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 102

 away any longer than 3 days.  I work as a

 and I am fortunate that I can

frequently work from home, however I feel torn when I am sitting at the computer giving

attention to my colleagues

 all the time knowing that my youngest daughter is

cocooned in her bedroom.  Most of my colleagues do not know the extent of my daughter’s

school can’t status, and few of my family and friends truly understand the impact that it has

had, and continues to have, on the three of us.

Assistance with school can’t

Over the course of 2021 and 2022 my

 daughter has regularly met with a

psychologist, an art therapist, a speech therapist, and a paediatrician.  We have received, and

continue to receive, invaluable assistance through the NDIS to fund these services.  I believe

that the Assistant Principal at our local primary school, and the Regional Disability Liaison

Officer have done their best to assist us with my daughter’s school can’t status.

For some of 2021, and for the first half of 2022, my daughter attempted schooling with

  Initially this worked well as my daughter connected

reasonably well with the allocated teacher, as the teacher was trained and had experience with

ASD students.  Unfortunately, the

teacher in 2022 did not connect well with my

daughter and we were encouraged to leave and try the local primary school again.  Initially

we made some progress in getting my daughter back into the classroom to meet with the next

new teacher in July of this year. However, her anxiety levels soon escalated, and she became

paralysed with fear at the thought of going back into a classroom filled with 25 other bodies.

In term 4 of this year, my daughter was referred to the Child Youth Mental Health and Well-

being Service (CYMHS) by the Regional Disability Liaison Officer.  We met with them on

one occasion, however I decided that we would not participate in their school can’t program

as it would mean that my daughter could no longer connect with her current psychologist

whom she has developed a strong trusting relationship over the course of 3 years.

Additionally, my daughter would have to work with a different CYMHS team again when

she starts

 school in 2023.  My daughter requires consistency, patience and

stability, and less focus on timeframes and outcomes, in order to develop trust in people and

gradually take the steps that she needs to reengage with the world and school.  In the past few

months, I am grateful that I have discovered an online support network of school can’t

parents/carers that have shared similar experiences of their own children’s stories.

3

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 102
 Recommendations

I am aware that all families, children, teachers, schools, and students are different.  I am also

aware that what works for one person and one situation may not work for another, but these

are some of the thoughts that I have that may assist those impacted by school can’t.

1. All States and Departments of Education need to rethink the purpose/s of school/s in

their current format.  Large schools, large classrooms, busy and noisy environments,

are not conducive to learning and teaching for many neurodivergent children.  There

are currently not enough alternatives and options available for children that struggle to

survive, let alone thrive, in our local government schools.

2. Educate teachers, school workers and school communities about neurodiversity.  This

is particularly important for girls with ASD as many people do not realise that girls

are frequently “masking” their true selves at school.

3. Provide greater support in all schools for all children with a strong network of

psychologists, speech therapists, art & music therapists, animal therapy, and anything

or anybody else that will assist the mental health & well-being of all children.

4. Provide support for schools and teachers to encourage children that are experiencing

school can’t to remain connected to school communities through engagement in

online social and curriculum activities, as well as providing hard copy packages of

schoolwork that may be regularly sent to the home.

5. Ensure that schools have a category for school can’t on their attendance records as

school can’t is not the same as school refusal or truancy.

6. Provide support to the parents/carers of school can’t children.  A weekly phone call

from a case worker would be invaluable, particularly for single parents.

7. Provide financial support for parents/carers (particularly single parents) of

neurodivergent children to enable them to work part-time, in order to give more

attention to the needs of a school can’t child.

8. Develop a National Virtual School Can’t Service that exclusively deals with school

can’t children so that expertise is created and developed in this area.

9. Develop a national framework for schooling during lockdowns/pandemics, as this is

bound to occur again in the future.

10. Provide research funding for investigating the extent of the school can’t situation in

Australia, in order to better understand how we can develop solutions to assist

children, families and schools in the future.

4

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 102

I  am a
educator  of  a  twice-exceptional teen  (known  online  as

Autistic (PDA Profile) with ADHD and Generalised Anxiety Disorder (diagnosed 2015). She is
clinically identified as profoundly gifted. I am also Autistic with ADHD (formally diagnosed in
2018 after self-identifying for two years). My husband has ADHD and has an online business
run from home. A note about PDA – rather than “pathological demand avoidance” it is FAR
better described as Pervasive Drive for Autonomy.

  is

An initial point: this is not about “school refusal”. That term is a dismissive misconception. It
is akin to a slap in the face to all of the families who are navigating the rollercoaster of school
attendance difficulties. This is not a new phenomenon for neurodivergent children. But, since
the Pandemic, it’s affecting more children (including neurotypical), drawing more attention.
As Dr Ross Greene says, “kids do well when they can”. Parents do too – no-one would choose
this journey.

This will be a short submission regarding our own story. Its relevance is largely restricted to
Term of Reference b. I support more comprehensive submissions from bodies such as The
Autistic Realm Australia, and the Administrators of the School Can’t [School Phobia/School
Refusal Australia] Facebook Group, which have been lifelines for our family.

Our school can’t journey has spanned two states and three schools.

Pre-School

After an uneventful and very enjoyable two years in an excellent long day care setting,
spent  much  of  the  2012/13  holidays  playing  “schools”  with  her  toys.  She  had  attended
orientation  at  our  local  school,  which  had  an  excellent  reputation,  and  connected  with  a
couple  of  children.  She  was  very  excited  to  go  to  school  and  learn  new  things.  We  did
everything right according to what we knew. She had already taught herself to read aged two
years (which was unremarkable to us, as I did it too), could write and do some maths, had
strong  interests  in  Ancient  Egypt  and  medicine.  She  devoured  St  John’s  first  aid  manuals,
comparing what had changed from one issue to the next.

I had met with the Deputy Principal to fill her in, so the school was aware before she started.
Turned out that Deputy Principal left before the start of school and that information was not
passed on. We had a transition statement from her early childhood teacher at long day care,
which  wasn’t  referred  to.
  was  sociable,  very  funny,  highly  communicative,  and
charismatic, with some hypersensitivies (mostly auditory and olfactory) that weren’t unusual
to  us,  as  I  had  them  too.  She  drew  people  to  her  wherever  she  went,  from  the  bank  to
supermarket, to the park. She absolutely loved life.

returned from school and flew into a rage like I had

and  that  learning  would  come.  But  it  didn’t.  These  meltdowns  continued  every  day.
Sometimes she would go to sleep and then wake in the wee hours, only to have a meltdown.
I recall sitting on the bathroom floor with her at 2am as she screamed and cried about school.
I quietly read her favourite poem to her, over and over, until she calmed down. At school she
was  compliant  and  eager  to  please,  despite  having  to  sit  through  jolly  phonics  and  basic
integers.  This,  for  a  child  who  was  reading  chapter  books  and  understood  binary  aged  3.
Turned out she was petrified of getting a “red ticket”, so she internalised all her distress until
she was safe at home.

An early meeting with the teacher left us feeling like poor parents, she had no trouble with
her  at  school,  and  all  this  was  because  she  was  an  overindulged  only  child  (with  no
explanation for having no issues at long daycare). That teacher actually said, “if she wasn’t so
intelligent, I’d think she had an attention disorder” and “I can’t just put her in a group of one,
even though she’s ahead of all the others.” But we didn’t know anything much at that point,
so we trusted this very experienced teacher at a very good school. We did a lot of critical
reflection  about  our  parenting  and  felt  awful  that  we  had  apparently  failed  this  little  girl
whom  we  loved  so  very  much.  With  what  I  know  now,  I  would  have  set  her  straight  very
smartly.

was  gifted,  but  we

elementary parenting strategies that we had tried many times, to no avail. Of course they
weren’t going to work – they weren’t strategies that would EVER work on an Autistic child

Recommendations for acceleration were made, but not followed by the school.

All behavioural issues completely disappeared over school holidays, only ramping up when

High School

We began transition meetings with the High School halfway through year 5. This high school
is very well known for supporting “out of the box” students, particularly Autistic students.
Because of
 anxiety and executive functioning challenges, it was thought best to start

when  asked  the  reason for her  success  with

None of them responded so I figured I’d been cast as one of “those” parents. She struggled

school.

100%, then still be expected to do all the exercises and post-assessment as well. Why? She

She did her best to demonstrate what she knew, so that she could get some more appropriate
work set. One or two teachers were fantastic, and flexible with their assessment when
emailed to negotiate alternatives. But that wasn’t enough to overcome the work expectations
of the other teachers. Her maths teacher told me in an email that “most bright students go
through and do that work quickly and then they can be set some more challenging work”. My
reply (having lost all patience by now) that “appropriately levelled work should never be a

 was able to achieve results that were slightly indicative
Still, in a calmer environment,
of her capacity, with teachers saying they had never seen anything like it. With an accessible
environment,  she  was  able  to  at  least  do  some  of  the  work.  With  her  level  of  executive

 6

Most of her work was still way too easy, so we spoke with the Deputy about skipping year 8.
The  school  executives  agreed  immediately,  so  that  was  one  plus.  They  also  agreed  to  her
continuing to work remotely, even after school returned to face-to-face learning.

With zero effort, she got the Maths and SOSE awards in semester 1. She didn’t care at all;
she’s never been motivated by rewards; she is motivated by learning in her interest areas. It
was like dragging a bulldozer up a hill with a bicycle to get her to complete the set work. My
own  workplace  was  extraordinarily  flexible,  allowing  me  to  continue  working  from  home,
knowing I was trying to support
 at the same time. She needs creative scaffolding with
her “busywork”, and my husband found that very difficult (despite trying his utmost), so it
was largely up to me. We engaged a tutor to come to her twice a week for an hour each time,
out of our own pocket, to try and take some pressure off.  We still have that tutor, but only
once a week now, and she is fantastic.

 continued into semester 2 of year 9 (2021), with increasing difficulty engaging in her
work. She was attending the Drama elective in person, which she really loved. The Drama
teacher was the head of Student Wellbeing and is an extraordinary educator. I can’t speak
highly  enough  of  him.  She  was  also  in  the  rock  band  program,  once  a  week  as  an  extra-
curricular activity. Every other subject was done remotely.
 was able to do less and less,
and we removed all pressure from her. She lost herself in gaming and her main interest of
music production, and we allowed her that space.

Her NDIS review was coming up (her package is tiny, only a few thousand dollars, which we
use for psych support). We had to provide her Individual Learning Plan. She didn’t even have
one, so I emailed asking for a meeting to formulate one. The only time it had been mentioned
was at the start of Year 7 when the Inclusive Education Executive emailed wanting a copy of
her previous one and said she would get back to us. Then COVID-19 happened, and everything
fell by the wayside.

In the meantime, I met with the Home Education Team and felt very reassured about the level
of flexibility and options open to us. I can’t speak highly enough of the
 Home Ed Team –
they are experts in the education of unusual children, and very supportive.

The final straw came when
 was doing a maths exam. She had already achieved 98% in
the pre-assessment in Mathspace. I emailed the teacher and said she would not be doing any
of the other tasks in that unit. He asked if she could just do the post assessment.
 agreed,
to try and please him. All her post assessments were done on paper – her teacher would email
me the exam; I would print it out, she would sit beside me, and do it while I was working, I
would scan it and email it back to him. She started off okay, did all the questions on the first
page,  turned  the  page  to  find  a  list  of  similar  style  of  questions,  slightly  harder,  and  just
collapsed on the floor. She was enormously distressed; I would call it a breakdown.

That day I emailed the school and said that we were going to home educate but would like a
part time arrangement so
could continue Drama and the rock band program. The school
readily agreed and that has been our path since August 2021. She has just now finished her
time at that school and there is no way she could go to years 11 and 12.

 7

We  are  focusing  on her mental  and  physical  health,  and  letting  her  lead her own  learning

our girl back; the one who was all but destroyed by mainstream schooling.

What would have helped?
It’s hard to know the answer to this, without trying possible strategies, but:
-  Teachers and School Executives believing what we told them about
-  Understanding or at least respect of different sensory experiences;
-  Meeting her where she was at, instead of trying to box her into the curriculum;
-  Awareness of internalised presentations of Autism;
-  Connection with her teachers before each school year commences (we were able to

do this in our

 primary school and it made a huge difference)

-  Smaller group settings in high school
-  Project-based, interest-based learning focused on skill outcomes rather than content;
-  Awareness of how highly gifted children learn (and the results of lack of appropriate

differentiation)

-  Professional development from those with lived experience
-  Core undergraduate study in gifted education and twice-exceptionality.
-  Ability to access a funding pool to support home educators. The Allowance for Isolated
Children is a drop in the bucket compared to the loss of income sustained when forced
into home education.

To whom it may concern

I am writing to express my concern in relation to the Department of Education and its lack in support
and identifying the increase in School Refusal that has existed prior to Covid-19 but has now
exasperated since Post Covid19 Pandemic.

School Refusal is when our children cannot attend school due to the complexities of the school
environment and therefore cause anxiety to rise to debilitate the child whom then avoids school due
to the impact it has on their mental well being.

This is particular concerning for our children who are neuro-divergent. Neurodivergent describes
people whose brain differences affect how their brain works from neuro-typical.

This means these children have different strengths and challenges from people whose brains don’t
have those differences.

There are no measure or statistics at current from the Department of Education that collect statistics
for school absenteeism due to mental disorder separately to those who are physically sick

Such school refusal has accelerated even more post Covid-19 due to society and the school
environment encouraging avoidance tactics like school shut downs, due to pandemic break outs,
school shut downs due to Le Nina and multiple cancellation of events due to weather.

Children who are neurodivergent have additional challenges and impacts on them 10 x more then
neuro typical children but what has the department of education provided to support these
children?

BRIEF HISTORY OF SCHOOL CAN’T FOR MY CHILD

My daughter is
and Selective Mutism which is a symptom of her autism.

 who is

 years old. She has always presented with symptoms of Social Anxiety

We have always had to advocate with her school from Kindergarten to implement Independent
Learning Plans each calendar year. They are meant to rollover from year to year but unfortunately
her current school do not do this well and we have had to remind each year, the new teacher about
modifications required and continually follow up the current school in relation to implementing ILP
and constant reminders about issuing an ILP.

She was formally diagnosed with Autism Level 2 earlier this year in March 2022. I advocated to get
her formally diagnosed due to witnessing whilst in lock down, her melt downs had escalated and
refusal to complete required tasks whilst learning from home that were beyond/unreasonable.

Upon multiple complexities and changes in her school environment and lack of understanding/lack
of support from her school this year since post Covid-19, her condition accelerated due to the
environment causing her anxiety to accelerate. This is due to a number of reasons, and her school
can’t started as mild in 2020 and 2021 with random days of school can’t/anxiety but refusal went
from Term 3 2022 as moderate to now Term 4 2022 as severe (non attendance).

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 105  As various teachers/leaders continued to single her out in front of her peers not understanding
appropriately her condition or being appropriately qualified/experienced in understanding how
children should be supported in main stream schooling with her diagnosis.

 did show signs of attending difficulties at preschool and school prior to Covid-19 but never

refused to go, just showed resistance. It has now accelerated since post-Covid and resulted in School
Cant.

IMPACT OF SCHOOL CAN’T ON MY CHILD

 has suffered immensely socially and mentally. Due to her school can’t, when we were in

moderate phase struggling to get her to go, often I would find her on the school morning withdrawn,
curled up in bed refusing to move, disengaged at home.

With multiple attempts to obtain support from the public education system whilst my daughter was
attending 50% of the time, the school failed upon each of the opportunities we addressed with the
school to collaborate with implementing appropriate supports.

Teachers are only required to study Disability Act 2005 to provide appropriate adjustments to create
equitable education for all children.

My child is now isolated from her peers to be able to connect socially due to her unable to attend
main stream school.

I have attempted to create external opportunities for her to connect to her peers but these are not
on a daily basis and are limited. As she struggles socially with new surroundings, by attending other
external programs, even though it exposes her to new environments, she still struggles with
unfamiliarity environments/people.

 Academically she has missed 50% of schooling this year.

I have commenced an external tutor 2 times a week for an hour as that is all we can afford to at least
create some form of habit of education this term so she is not entirely missing out, however, she is
still not being provided equal opportunity to her peers.

We have been focusing on providing support for her mentally so we can transition her back to school
environment and have seen a positive change in her when she has no pressure to attend her existing
school due to the trauma she was exposed to.

IMPACT OF SCHOOL CANT EXPERIENCE ON OUR FAMILY AND MYSELF

School can’t has had a huge emotional impact, mental impact and financial impact on the family as a
whole.

As myself I am self employed/sole proprietor and operate my own micro-business, due to my hours
of work being restricted since my daughter has had to be home 24 hours in my care. My capacity to
earn my required amount of income to remain afloat has SEVERELY declined.

I have lost opportunities of new work due to my limited hours of work and delays in responding in a
expected time frame due to my capacity to care for my daughter taking priority.  It is the first time in
my 16 years operating my business Ive had to request extension of time for work deadlines.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 105 My husband has attempted to pick up additional hours at work to try to cover decline in income,
however, his support at home is needed so lack of him being present, has severely impacted on
support I require at home to give me respite. I feel my work/family load as tripled since she has
suffered severe school can’t and now I have less capacity to continue the work that I am required to
do when Im not supporting my daughter at home in my care and minimal, if any opportunities to
look after my own mental health/well being.

The mental fatigue is exhausting having to constantly switch roles throughout the day but financially,
we would not be able to survive without me working due to increase in living costs.

There are no appropriate supports for families and siblings suffering from children who school cant/
There are some local non-government organisations but they are scarce and long waiting lists.

Society still have a long way to understand school can’t as do our public education school system.

I am constantly judged so often avoid responding that she cant do school but use other sayings such
as “we are just home schooling “ or “ having a break”  to minimise any additional stress/judgement.

Our family has suffered immensely we have had to seek out our own couples therapy due to
tension/stress existing managing our daughter. The sibling and our
and has required days off school due to the existence of his sister not attending school.

 year old son has also suffered

We constantly have to make adjustments whilst out socially for our daughter and leave when she
needs to go to avoid additional meltdowns or reduce her anxiety when it accelerates in social
settings with friends, family and professionally.

I feel constantly judged and have felt numerous times as a failure as a post graduate qualified parent

We have sought unschooling due to my mental health suffering and it impacts on my parental

I have sought out a home tutor professional twice a week for this term as well as we are using

We have sought attendance one day a week for
qualified professionals in a child led outdoor environment. However, due to her trauma from prior

. There is a lack of support for families to help maintain a

The schools are not equipped in managing children psychologically and often their treatment has

However, the current education system fails to support this and does not have appropriate support

Due to already accessing NDIS before the acceleration of refusal occurred, we had already

There is no government agency to provide support for these families within the school environment

There is a lack of not for profit organisations that also assist families at home as a third party to work
with the families to help build and trust back with the school community.

Children on the Spectrum are known to avoid difficult situations. In the UK this has been funded to
be researched but not enough studies/research in Australia and NSW.

Pathological Demand Avoidance (PDA) which is a trait of children on the spectrum doesn’t present in
all but is on the increase.

MONITORING AND IDENTIFICATION OF SCHOOL ATTENDANCE DIFFICULTIES

The school has no separate system to monitor school attendance difficulties. The school failed in
acknowledging or identifying the substantial decrease in school attendance. I the parent was the one
who initiated the phone calls with the school due to increase in absenteeism when it got to 60%
school attendance rate.

The school had no other options to identify the school difficulties and the data seems to get lost in
statistics for the other children with physical illnesses.

I had to initiate a call to the local area of Department of Education once I found out by multiple
errors/misses, Department of Learning and Wellbeing to help navigate with the school about
assisting us with her school cant. No direct support is offered to families by the department but
more directing the school on what to do and leave the principal to talk to us. This is not ok.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 105 The regional area for wellbeing only reached due to myself wanting action to be taking and initiating
the calls. The school never initiated anything. They failed my child.

BARRIERS TO ATTENDANCE

Covid-19 and children forced to learn from home has accelerated school cant/avoidance. This has
enabled our children and programmed them to avoid things when it gets too hard. Those with
additional obstacles like autism, social anxiety this has exasperated and has collaboratively assisted
in increase in school refusal/cant.

No appropriate supports provided at the gate of the school /kiss and drop to help with transfer from
parent to the school and warmly welcome to settle children in before joining main stream classes

School did not implement an updated amended learning plan within reasonable time to navigate
appropriate adjustments.

School was not equipped nor school counsellor in helping the child or families in building resilience
for her return.

Once the child was exposed to trauma 3 times with various meetings held on the school grounds
within space of 4 – 8 weeks, no one in the meeting appropriately addressed my daughters welfare as
she sat there for an hour for one meeting whilst they spoke about her which further humiliated her
and traumatised her.

By allowing the child who school cant to partake in her learning plan/solutions to re-integrate on
how they would like to attempt to any form of returning to school by what they felt comfortable or

she had feelings of overwhelm instead of the staff expecting her to “suck it up “ by the failure of
appropriate actions of the staff for suppressing how she felt.

The school refused to allow us to incorporate a part time attendance whilst we handle the
debilitating anxiety due to reasons that the application would take too long to be approved.

School cant then quickly escalated to non-attendance due to the failure of responding in a timely
manner and forcing her to do more then she was able.

The school dismissed her autism led anxiety complaints by our
sore tummy but due to no signs of physical illnesses, the deputy principal dismissed her request of

her back to the class room.

There has been no real support from the school to help us with transitioning her back or engaging
her back into the school system.

Due to the teachers and learning support team unable to understand autism in girls, they are not

For example, dismissing how she was feeling, not acknowledging how she was feeling and expecting

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 105 The only helpful thing the school implemented for the selective mutism, was have the whole class
hand signal gestures which helps by incorporating some adjustments for the whole class to not
single out the school cant child. By signalling out in front of her peers any appropriate adjustments
caused further anxiety. The school failed and did this at least 5 times in the period of this school
cant.

Any acts of support by the school further damaged my child requiring us to remove her from the

No at home learning packs were provided to keep a connection whilst she was at home with the
school cant.  They expected her to keep connected by coming to school but provided no
link/emotional support/contact whilst at home.

PROACTIVE STRATEGIES TO PREVENT SCHOOL CANT

For independent learning plans to be implemented with inclusion/input by the child and a
spokeperson representing the child that is not the teacher or parent but has relationship with the
child.

To allow child to seek safety in a place they choose to de-sensitise in the complex school
environment

To encourage and talk about neurodiversity within schools by the teachers and staff and celebrate it
as a strength not deficit.

To apply short term strategies with an urgency with appropriate supports in place with immediate
part time attendance without penalty by the government. Government to allow Dept of Education in
times of stress to allow a quick process for part time attendance.

HAS MY RELATIONSHIP/CONCEPT OF EDUCATION CHANGED/BEEN CHALLENGED?

100% has changed. I have to come to realisation the education system which has been built on a
1950’s industrial revolution system now applied with bandaids. We live in a complex society and we
need to have smaller class room sizes or have 1 – 2 teacher aids in each class to help with complex
children with or without formal diagnosis. My daughter had 8 complex boys in her class. Due to her
not being disruptive, the school viewed her as not complex as she was compliant at school. This is
called masking.  The melt downs happened at home due to the school not making adjustments for
her as requested.

The school, teachers, learning support lack understanding of autism in children particular girls.
Schools need people/professionals who are formally trained and should be mandatory to have a
team of experts working within each of the schools.  My daughters school was not pro-active at all
and only re-active to my calls of help after multiple attempts.

We have always had to advocate with her school from Kindergarten to implement Independent
Learning Plans each calendar year. They are meant to rollover from year to year but unfortunately
her current school do not do this well and we have to remind the new teacher about modifications
required and continually follow up the current school in relation to implementing ILP and constant
reminders about issuing an ILP. It is not what the parents are not doing at home, it’s a school system

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 105 that needs to co-exist and collaborate together for a unified solution. The school system failed in
acting swiftly.

SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDATIONS FOR THE COMMITTEE

I strongly advocate and suggest the following measures are undertaken:-









Separating absenteeism from normally illness to separately account for school cant/school
refusal based anxiety/informal diagnosis/formal diagnosis
Implement appropriate support/aids within our public education system to have an
allocation of trained psychologists with understanding/experience with children with autism
to assist children not only within school but to assist in helping those families get the

To allow for funding for a system for support to happen for short term immediate response

The national trend of school refusal or 'School Can't' – as distinct from truancy – that is affecting

Why have I started this tale way back here? Well because frankly,

digress. Chronic not attending school despite best efforts doesn’t
develop overnight. To my way of looking at it there are significant

Now that we’re talking about it I’m going to skip right to the COVID

12 months following this. My children saw me extraordinarily ill and two
family friends died at the time I was sick. So COVID arrived while we
were still quite raw from severe flu illness and we were naturally very

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 107 During lockdown, my work, despite having ‘flexible covid hours” refused
me the chance to work the extended covid hours of 5am to 10pm
(normal workday within these hours), so I was attempting to work full
time 9am to 5pm with two children homeschooling who needed
significant supervision and assistance.  They of course did not get this
from me during the day, so they missed any scheduled online lessons,
and I made futile attempts to homeschool at 5pm having finished work. It
was a nightmare that didn’t work. But peers, the media were all saying
“don’t worry, it’s the same for all of us” I now know how much of a fallacy
that was. My kids were seriously dysregulated by the whole thing and
the very first thing I would go back and change if I could would be the
dedication I made to my work. I wish I had not. But it seemed at the time
there was no other option for me. My kids needed the regularity of
school and without that they needed close and intense support to access
their education, which I was not able to provide. There was no support,
no one from school reached out to assist, everyone assured me doing
absolutely no school work for the duration of lockdown would be fine.
They were wrong. They were also not psychologists and should never
had made such claims.

Knowing how disruptive lockdown had been, particularly for my son, I
attempted to reengage him early in the return to school, however he
already displayed anxiety at this point, it was quite profound.  My
daughter managed to mostly attend at this point, but had many
concerns.

During the period following COVID, it became obvious my two youngest
were not coping as expected and over a period of time in 2021 were
both diagnosed with Autism and my daughter with ADHD.

I am afraid I will run out of time and energy to write this. As I write the
situation is unresolved. My son is so disillusioned he does not want to
engage in school at all. My daughter wants to attend, but was told just
yesterday by the Principal “*name*, you are welcome to go to your
classroom” when she arrived.   I remind you that my  daughter has
significant anxiety, ADHD and Autism and is entitled to ‘reasonable
adjustments’ to enable to her access her education.  Yesterday she was
offered NO ADJUSTMENT at all.  After two
years, the Principal could not see fit to provide ANY support to including
her on that day.  We waited for over an hour for any space to be made
available for my daughter, or a person to support her and none were

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 107 made available (my daughter had brought her own craft and simply
wanted to engage in activities in the school environment, a support
which was provided in term 2 but suddenly removed in term 4).

As a parent advocating for two children with School PTSD, wishing to be
participating but instead being excluded I cannot stress highly enough
the following solutions are needed: (I know this isn’t what was called for
in the terms of reference but it is the only way I can gather my thoughts.
Think of it as a list of barriers that made it harder)

Proposed changes to assist students

1. Accountability similar to Grants returns demonstrating how funding for

disability has been allocated and used in individual school that is
available to the public.

2. Smaller class sizes in all schools
3. Improved amenity in classrooms e.g. air-conditioning, used,

refrigerators in primary school classrooms

4. School principals and deputies listening to students and parents

advocating for students

5. Total removal of arbitrary, paternalistic restrictions on students self-

regulating including timers.

6. Staff who are qualified and experienced in specialised areas of
disability widely available. A short course in Autism is not a
qualification.

7. Parents and students who are engaging in flexible plans not being

excluded from freely accessing all staff normally available to students

8. Principals and deputies not promising one action and then not

following through

9. An avenue for parents and students experiencing difficulty accessing
their education to seek resolution that does not begin and end with
the Principal.

10. Education providers need to trust that parents know their children
11. Consistent recognition that it is not the student or the parents who
are failing to fit into the system, but the system is failing our young
people.

12. Gender bias

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 107 13. Make inclusive adjustments not accommodations. Change the

system not the individual.

I would dearly like to extrapolate on the points 8 to 13 however I can’t
write further today.

Rationale

1. Accountability similar to Grants returns demonstrating how
funding for disability has been allocated and used in individual
school that is available to the public.

Our current school receives a significant amount of funding for my two
enrolled children (some estimates suggest in excess of $60,000) due to
their diagnoses as ‘verified’ by
 which I was not obligated
to agree to, but did not readily so that school would receive more funds.

It is abundantly apparent that although this funding is received, as well
as ‘regular child funding’ for normal class attendance, my children have
received only a tiny fraction of the overall monies they contributed to the
school’s budget.  As it stands, the funding received is pooled and used
to ‘generally support’ students, but this system is intrinsically flawed as
there is no accountability for money to be allocated in a way that even
remotely supports the children whose disability have generously
provided the extra funds.  I am not suggesting that individual funding is
necessarily allocated to individual children, but that schools are required
to make publicly available the cost of programs and supports received
by ‘verified’ children and the funds received applied against their
allocation in a way that is similar to existing grants funding returns.

This would provide families with some understanding of how funds are
used as well as a significant amount of accountability for schools to
allocate funds appropriately.  It would also potentially become a useful
tool in evaluating what the real cost of adjustments are compared to
allocated funding, which I would hope schools would use to lobby for
additional assistance for individuals who need it.

2 Smaller class sizes in all schools

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 107 Making a significant reduction in class sizes obviously has a major
funding and facilities impact for educators.  However keeping class sizes
under 20 or even better under 18 students has been proven beneficial.
Aside from all the peer reviewed research that demonstrates worldwide
that smaller class sizes has a significant positive affect on educational
outcomes I have also observed the following in my own children
suffering from school can’t / school based anxiety / school refusal.

 My  children have repeatedly found themselves comfortable

working in small peer groups as well as small groups of adults
despite not being able to enter a classroom for over 12 months.
 It is my observation that managing behaviour in a larger class size
takes up more time as the class size increases. My children’s
inability to attend school happily often stems from a view of
negative adult management of behaviour. Smaller class sizes
allow more individual and individually appropriate management of
behaviour of students.

3. Improved amenity in classrooms e.g. air-conditioning, used,
refrigerators in primary school classrooms

Similar to smaller class sizes, improving amenity for students makes it
more comfortable, more like both a work and home environment and
may produce a greater sense of well being and safety.  I know that both
my children have significant sensory processing issues and that
attempting to obtain decent nutrition from a school lunch box is almost
impossible with children who believe hot food needs to come directly
from the oven/warmer/microwave and that cold food should be cold from
the fridge. Also when students with heightened sensory needs are over
heated in classrooms 30 degrees and over, or humid sweaty
classrooms, they are entirely unable to learn under those conditions.
Increasing amenity makes an improvement for all students. Again,
research supports this.

4. School principals and deputies & all staff listening to students
and parents advocating for students.

Use the ATP system – ask the person what they need. Then do NOT put
barriers in the way of delivering it.  Also just listen to students, actually

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 107 hear what they say, make genuine inquiries of them if they are brave
enough to speak. And listen to parents who are more than likely
speaking word for word what the student has expressed to them. And
keep listening, don’t assume because you listened once that you’ve now
‘heard’ any individuals issues, sometimes things change, and when they
do it can be rapid and dramatic so assuming you’re familiar with
circumstances is unhelpful. Again, there is everything to gain from this
approach and very little to lose. Listening actually does not cost any
money, it is free. No huge budget nightmare will be borne from actually
listening to people and making sure you are really understanding what
they are saying, not making judgements or assumptions along the way.

Total removal of arbitrary, paternalistic restrictions on

5.
students self-regulating including timers.

Children who need ‘time out’  or time to reset / recover are managing
their bodies very real reactions to stimuli. They are attempting to
regulate and to be told that  they have a time limit to do so is harmful, it
erodes their capacity to self-soothe (some children spend  the  entire
length of time a  timer is near them in a state of panic!). It sets an
arbitrary adult boundary, quashing the child’s autonomy.

Self-regulation is something that can’t be measured or timed.

Put into words better than I can explain is this:

The reason I think timers can be an issue is because it's putting a time length to something
that doesn't necessarily take a specific length of time. For example, I don't always take the
same amount of time to drink a glass of water, and if someone hurts me it doesn't always
take the same amount of time to recover or feel better.
When you put a certain time to it, you're telling the person "You should drink water for a
certain amount of time" instead of "Drink to quench your thirst and to prevent
dehydration". So, by the time the timer is up, you might still more water. Or you might fill up
before the timer is up. Then the consequence is that the person doesn't learn to drink when
they're thirsty, they learn to drink when they're told, or when they're allowed. They might
not drink enough because there's not enough time. They might drink too much because the
timer wasn't up yet. They might feel like they can't drink unless the timer is on. They might
drink too fast because they're worried they'll run out of time. They might feel rushed or
pressured. They might not figure out it works better for them to keep a water bottle with
them to drink throughout the day instead of waiting to do it all at once.
This happens with other needs too, including more abstract needs, or needs that are harder
to articulate or access. Putting a timer to it is telling the person their needs aren't what
really matters, that what actually matters is doing it on someone else's schedule. It doesn't
teach how to recognize when you need something, or how to make sure you get as much as

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 107 you need. It can create anxiety. It can tell someone that the timer dictates what they need, or
what they deserve.

6. Staff who are qualified and experienced in specialised areas of
disability widely available. A short course in Autism is not a
qualification.

In all the time my children have struggled they have not been able to

and willingness of Autism
officer in regional office this week and he advised the principal has to
request services of the autism expert.  There are systemic barriers to
accessing supports, and underfunding (apparently) of all of these areas
of allied health. If schools can’t support kids with high needs they need
to stop making excuses and start bringing in genuine assistance so that
all students can access an education.

School said the right things, and even put some support in place for child

On multiple occasions, with catastrophic affects on our household. In

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 107 worked really well, however child 2 wasn’t getting any engagement with
education. His OT wrote to school and recommended he spent one

SCHOOL HAS CLOSED for the preceeding term. E.g. 4pm or 5pm on

school can’t.  Back to 2021 and the history situation. My son, child 2 was

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 107 in a 1:1 class with chaplain).  The deputy for inclusion however didn’t

My other gripe is that child 2 applied to be part of the school leadership

Child 2 my son was able to secure himself a job, but due to the extreme anxiety of school
can’t he could not go to the first day of work. He feels like a failure. He wanted to be a doctor
and he is intelligent enough to be one. He may still become a doctor, and be a better one for

I can’t even begin when it comes to child 3. It has affected how I parent, how much capacity I
have for parenting. Which in turn affects how both children manage with their llves moving
forward. It is a  terrible situation that is very hard to resolve. Both children WANT to be at
school.

I already mentioned that child 1’s ATAR was adjusted a full 2.5 points
based entirely on the anxiety caused to her by the disruption that school
can’t caused in our household. It has cost us thousands and  thousands
of dollars in therapy, in creating diversions and extra activities to try to

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 107 support the children, and more thousands in lost income. I have no
career now to speak of as my work were entirely not understanding of
the situation. They were incredulous at how hard it was for us with the
school. I spend so much time now supporting child 2 and child 3 in their

now less independent and less capable in many ways than they were 4

Submission

My

year-old, son lives with Autism (level 2) and has struggled with school since starting

five years ago. He is what is commonly described as ‘high-functioning’ and very intelligent.

He has always found the classroom and playground environment overly sensory stimulating

and chaotic, which would often lead to meltdown and overwhelm when he came home

from school. Peer interactions and social situations were a cause of great anxiety and stress

and he always felt left out or different, weird, and bullied. As time went on the anxiety

increased, but then came COVID-19. Everyone was worried. Then came the lockdowns and

we had to stay home. My son loved being home and being ‘home- schooled’. He finally felt

safe and comfortable. Eventually he was made to go back to school. Which didn’t go well.

He was very anxious. He was very unhappy. He begged me to go back to home schooling

him. When things weren’t working out for him at school, I thought a change might help. So, I

moved him to a private school, with the promise of more support, he was there less than a

year.

As a single mum, working part-time and studying full-time, I was trying to balance it all. I

was getting called up to the school regularly for meetings or because staff had concerns

about my son.  Or I was calling them up for a meeting because I was having concerns about

him.  My son was regularly saying he was sick, he was often refusing to go to school, or he

would ‘breakdown’ at the school gate when I was dropping him off.  I was lucky to have an

understanding employer.

Going out shopping for school supplies at the beginning of this year, triggered a panic attack

for him. It was really distressing. He experienced symptoms such as a sore and tight jaw, he

got hot and sweaty, then shivery, his chest got tight and hurt. He felt like he couldn’t

breathe and thought he was dying. He had a headache, blurry vision and felt like vomiting.

Thankfully, as a

 crisis supporter, I knew exactly what to do to help him in that

moment and was able to do some grounding exercises and reassure him that he wasn’t

dying, and it was a panic attack and it would pass. After experiencing several more panic

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 108 attacks in the following weeks, I took him to the paediatrician, and he began on anti-

depressant/anxiety medication.

My son was increasingly ‘getting in trouble’ at school which was out of character for him,

and he would often say he wanted to be suspended or expelled so he didn’t have to go.  I

was constantly advocating for him to the school and asking for more support. He

experienced bullying and there was so many interruptions and changes to the classroom

routines with teacher shortages and absences, that he struggled more with each day. Like

most people on the Autism spectrum, my son didn’t cope very well with lots of unexpected

changes and upheaval and the pandemic brought about so much uncertainty for him. At one

point, to my despair he even expressed suicidality.

Finally, after a particular incident that occurred at school involving my son in September this

year (in which I believed the school over-reacted, knowing the difficulty my son was having

and chose to take a punitive approach), I made a radical decision that has a huge impact on

my family. I pulled him out of school immediately and with the support of my parents, made

the decision to home school him.  A decision, I don’t believe I would ever have considered,

nor would my son have needed or begged me to do prior to the impact or experiences of

the pandemic.

Financially, it’s devastating for me as a single mum and carer. I have just about finished

studying at university and had been thinking, I would be able to work full time next year,

finally with a decent earning potential (approx. $100k). I have spent the last 6 years trying to

recover financially, having experienced (and escaped) two domestic and family violence

relationships, in the preceding 20 years that also included financial abuse, meaning I don’t

receive any child support. My goal for full-time employment is no longer viable in the

foreseeable future.

I consider myself to be one of the lucky ones as I have family support. My parents, both

 years old, also live in

.  My dad not yet retired still works casually as

 Both my parents are assisting me home school my son, which allows

me to continue to work part-time to maintain an income of around $50k.  I am also very

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 108 lucky to live in a modest 3- bedroom townhouse that

 am very aware is drastically under the current market

rental rate.  If I did not have this level of family and financial support, I don’t know how I

would be able to manage this situation financially. I am very fortunate to be in this situation

with the cost of living and housing crisis that we are currently experiencing as I would be

further marginalised without my family’s support.

I am aware of a payment of $1000 per term that is available to me, and I do intend applying

for this next year to assist. $4000 although helpful, will not go far with today’s high cost of

living.

At this point, we are not yet formally registered through

, as I admittedly, stalled this process due to being overwhelmed by my

personal circumstances at the time I pulled my son out of school (change of employment,

trying to complete my theory subjects in full time uni study, dealing with the issues at the

school at the time, not to mention the impact on my own mental wellbeing). This has now

been actioned and I am awaiting the outcome, which I expect will be positive, having taken

the time to research and understand the process, expectations, and opportunities.

There are a number of community led small groups across my local region that I have come

across that are helpful in offering opportunities for socialisation, activities, outdoor project

based learning and support.  It has been eye opening to realise just how many families are

making the switch to home education for various reasons. Perhaps it could be of benefit if

there were some subsidy or grants to support such community networks? Or perhaps if

there was some sort of community-based learning, that could be engaged on a part time or

collaborative basis for those students struggling to re-engage in mainstream education?

Next year, I am required to do placement (unpaid) to complete my degree, which will

require me to do two days a week while I continue to work (3 days) to maintain living costs,

for a period of six months. During this time, my parents will have to manage the home-

schooling full time. I am very concerned at the impact of this on them. My dad is in great

physical shape for his age and still very active, my mum not so much. Both my parents are

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 108

 not as patient as they used to be, and my son can be a challenge. For example, he can’t sit

still to self-regulate, he needs to move his body around constantly and this can be irritating

to older people with more traditional ideas. When my dad finally retires, they should be

able to travel, enjoy their senior years. They have worked very hard all their life they live

comfortably as self-funded retirees. Instead, their plans have now changed they are now

restricted, home-schooling my son.

Home schooling is exhausting. As a single mum I am very fatigued. I don’t get any breaks

now. I used to get plenty of breaks when I could leave my son with my parents for some

respite. Now, they have him for home-schooling 3 days, I can’t expect them to help me

anymore than they are. I can’t imagine how tiring it must be for them at seventy! We are all

exhausted. My mum is worried that she won’t do a good enough job of teaching my son and

I am worried that it is just too stressful for them and all of us.

We need more support to do this as parents, as single parents, as grandparents, as carers.

The schools and the system need an overhaul to be able to handle these traumatised kids.

subjects.  I asked for support from the wellbeing team and met with senior
teaching staff.

His mental health deteriorated again.  I sought help from Headspace.  They
agreed that he needed assistance but there was a waiting list of a few months
for their psychology program.  All they could offer was 6 weeks of phone
support from a social work student – not a fully qualified clinician but a
student.  Our paediatrician was supportive and informed me that many of his
other patients were also struggling with school during lockdown but had no
other suggestions.

units in 2022.  At no point were we encouraged to seek special provision on
the basis of health.  Later I learned about the

3

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 111 4

but we were never referred to this program or any other specialist program for
school refusal.

Eventually due to non-attendance the school insisted that I complete an “exit
form” approving his formal withdrawal from the school.  And sadly that was
the end of his education.  My child who is intellectually gifted and full of
potential would not be completing school.  The exit form I signed stated that
he planned to enter the workforce, but he has not been able to find any
employment.  He is lost to the education system and to my knowledge this
isn’t counted in any figures or statistics.

This has had a huge impact on his self-esteem, and he is now socially isolated
as he has lost contact with the friends he had at school.

SUMMARY AND RECOMMENDATIONS

Prior to the Covid-19 pandemic, my child was engaged in school and attended
regularly.  I firmly believe that my child would have successfully completed
year 12 if his schooling had not been interrupted by Covid restrictions.  He was
vulnerable to disengagement from school as a result of ADHD.  The structure of
school provided scaffolding that allowed him to achieve alongside his peers but
when that structure was removed he was unable to manage.   Schools should
have been given more resources to assertively follow up the children that were
struggling.  Teaching staff in general do not seem to understand the factors
behind school refusal and are therefore not placed to assist when it occurs.
Professional development for teachers and wellbeing staff is critical to address
this issue.

In our experience mental health care was virtually impossible to access.  We
had great difficulty finding any support and felt that no-one knew what to do.
Although school refusal is not a psychiatric diagnosis, it is strongly associated
with mental health disorders, autism and ADHD.  If we as a society want to
reduce the rate of school refusal, we need greatly expanded resources in the
area of mental health care for young people.  This must be guided by research
into the factors that drive school refusal as well as effective interventions.

Submission:
Brief history of school can’t for my child

My experience with school can’t has been through two children of mine, with marked differences
between both in age of occurrence, causes, duration. What brings them together is the marked
similarities in the affect on the family.

The first experience was in the transition from primary to secondary school for an almost teenage
 and the choice of high school is limited. This child had been
girl. We live in a regional city in
consistently attending school through out primary, never had unusual absences or difficulties, and
had easily moved from one primary school to another without concern when we moved. The
transition to high school was difficult from the beginning, and although she had firm friends moving
with her through from primary to high school, the anxiety and depression took hold in the early days
of Year 7. It began with not wanting to go to school camp at the beginning of year 7, and at first we
thought it was just the change to a large high school. It continued getting worse and she was unable
to leave her room, and would shake and cry at the idea of school. We cajoled, bribed, bullied, all
types of encouragement, and as it was a new experience for us and we didn’t know where to start
getting her help or support and even what the issue was about. As parents we were able to work
shift so someone was home, and when her mental health really dived we luckily were able to get
some medical and psychological help. I was able to take some long service leave, and spend
concerted time looking for support and advocating for her with the school. I rang around so many
agencies and support services, school wellbeing, hospital, teen mental health, and none was able to
assist aside from encouraging us as she wasn’t triaged for support as she wasn’t suicidal. Through
our GP we got into a psychiatrist who treated children, and after months of medical and

Page 2

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 113



 psychological care she recovered enough and with amazing strength somehow  returned at the start
of year 8, meaning she had a full year off school.  During this period away from school the family
underwent significant stress as we learnt about school can’t and how to navigate supports and
processes.  To describe it as a year long crisis would be fair. Her brother and other family and friends
didn’t understand, and the general attitude was ‘ just make her go’.  In our souls we knew she
needed to recover and be nurtured back to strength.

The school tried to be helpful but did not really understand.  This was pre COVID and the focus
wasn’t so much on mental health.  They did have supports available with wellbeing staff, and offered
any return to school timetable we could make. However for her even to get to the school building to
access any services was asking too much most of the time. She would literally be shaking when we
parked the car, and having panic attacks walking to the office.

For the parents, we ended up asking for the texts sent each day by the school saying she was absent
to be paused, as every time the text arrived we ourselves were traumatised by our feelings of failure
to get her to school.

When asking the teen (4 years later) about this experience their thoughts are they felt overwhelmed
by the number of students in the school (1000+) and the volume of noise in the corridor,  and made
to feel vulnerable by being singled out by other students. A smaller more nurturing environment
may have made a difference.  The factors that helped her return were missing her friends, receiving
medication and support, school being flexible with her days and not pushing or too much pressure.

From the parent point of view we used any resources that we had to hand, paying thousands of
dollars in medical fees to see specialists, using long service leave and any other leave available to be
available, and looking for services to assist in our area. It was a desperately lonely time for all of us,
and the number one support I found was the peer support on the School Can’t Facebook group.

From my point of view there is a deficiency in the high school model, where high schools have
become so large they are overwhelming. If you think of a school as a workplace, we are offering our
kids the only options of going to a huge workplace with a 1000 workers on a small site, or the other
option is a special school for intellectual disability.

-------------------------

The second child experiencing school can’t is now
, was a prep child in Feb 2020. His cohort have
been effected by the school shutdowns throughout his first 2 years of schooling, and his first term
without a lockdown interruption was in 2022.

 This has had a major impact on our lives, as he is too young to be home alone and we are yet to re-
engage him with school. His presentation of school anxiety in prep (2020) has been crying, shaking,
hiding his school clothes, running away when asked to get dressed and hiding in a cupboard. We
tried lots of techniques, bribery with lunch orders, half days, being strict, and walking him to school
swinging him between us to he would be distracted from the journey. His distress escalated and he
began ripping clothes off in the street, and breaking free and starting to run out on the street where
cars were driving. Being sent home from school so often during lockdowns I think has made school
seem an unsafe place whereas home was safer.

Page 3

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 113

 At times teachers have been not able to understand. There have been instances where teachers
have said ‘you’ll get mum and dad in trouble with the police’ or ‘the dept will be onto you soon’. This
isn’t helpful, and causes immense pain and suffering.  If there was anything in my power that I could
utilise to get him to school I would have done this.

We have been able to change from a larger school to a smaller arm of the same school which proved
successful for a time, with smaller classes and play area.  He has struggled with keeping up with the
work and as his peers also have been educationally interrupted by COVID the learning support is
spread thin across the class.

I have again used any leave available to me, and we soon must decide whether I or my husband give
up work unless we can get the child re-engaged again. It isn’t a great option to home school as it
isn’t in our patience or aptitude, but if that is the only option we will do that. Financially what is
means is that again we have used any resources available for assessments and medical and
psychological support and our future financial stability is eroded. I have used any long service leave
and bought extra leave through salary swap. The leave was hoped to be a rest and recharge for me,
but now I have used all the leave I can’t take a break.

Working out what to do next is tricky. The school has tried anything it can think of, as have we. The
experience of school seems to have been so difficult and stressful for the child that he can’t even
look at it out the window if we drive past. He has run across the road away from the school at times
when we have tried to get there, and hidden in the foot well of the car when a teacher has tried to
come and chat. We are getting assessments for neurodiversity, but these too are expensive and the
waiting list is long – bookings are 6 months ahead.

One aspect that may have helped (COVID happened and we couldn’t change that) is that the support
for learning within the school. He may have had a different experience if there were more aides or
help, especially for the younger children - covid kids who missed so much.  Now he is so far behind I
don’t know how to help him, and where to go for assistance.

I am not sure what is next, but my child is less traumatised now and slowly recovering. I asked if he
went to school that same small size but with more support would that be good, and the answer was
yes. Not sure if that will happen, but diversity of choice is good.

Impact of School Can’t on my child, my family and myself:
Impact of School Can’t experience on my child:
The impact on the teen has given them empathy for mental health struggles, and the
understanding that you can be unwell and can recover. The impact on the   year old is more
severe, his literacy is behind, and also other areas of learning. He considers himself in a
poor light and is aware the stress of his school can’t on all of us though we try and hide it.

The impact on our family is one of resilience, we support each other and I feel lucky my
husband and I are of the same understanding about supporting school can’t kids rather than
getting angry. That said the chronic stress is a concern to me in relation to my health, I am
aware every minute I am home that there is a problem for my child that I can’t work out how
to fix. It would be so simple if he would just go to school, I could go to work, and everything
would be easier. But that isn’t happening at the moment unfortunately, and I despair about
how to fix it.

Page 4

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 113

 Impact of School Can’t experience on our family and myself as a parent:
Financially it is a bit of a disaster, as we are renters and were hoping to save to buy a house after the
youngest started school. It may be that this may never happen now, or it feels like that. I can’t plan
with any surety about the future, and we struggle getting through each week with childcare, working
from home, and trying to keep him engaged in things other that screens.

I rack my brains in the middle of the night to think of things I may have missed or supports I could
put in place, it feels as though we are the failure as parents not able to provide our child with an
education.

Access to supports:
We live in regional
 and have been lucky to have some professional supports available. The
school initially was not sure how to react with both children missing school, and started out on the
discipline route. Then slowly both schools worked to offer supports, alternative days, hours, and
anything really.  I think they have been at a loss too, and need more resources to manage the large
number of kids experiencing this school anxiety.

We have put any resources we have into paying for specialists, and have consulted paediatricians,
psychiatrists, occupational therapists, psychologists, neuropsychological assessments, and speech
therapy. I would think this would add up to at least 10K a year, with ongoing sessions. We have no
NDIS or diagnosis aside from anxiety to work with at the moment so all is self funded.

Barriers to attendance.  Things that have worked and things that haven’t:
Thinking about treatment/responding to school can’t:

What didn’t work was physically trying to get the child to school – he and we were traumatised and
he tried to run on the road in a blind panic. We have discovered patience, support, and care work
slowly, and trying different environments to see what might help.

Medication has been useful for one child, and has reduced their anxiety considerably.

Thinking about proactive strategies to prevent school can’t:
Connection above curriculum

Summary and recommendations for the committee:

•  Treating the issue as a core mental health crisis, and provide help even without a

specific diagnosis

•  Having a Team of supporting clinicians
•  Having a variety of different and alternative learning environments/options
•  Have support workers available even for a child without a diagnosis
•  Provide education to teaching staff about children’s mental health
•  Providing a respite care service, or a way for the parent to be able to have a few

hours without needing to be a carer
