Our Story:

I am a

 year old solo parent of a

 year old school refuser. My darling “just in time” baby.

 My boy has never been easy to parent but he has wonderful strengths

and is much loved. Unbeknown to me the
ADHD, hypermobility, anxiety, dyspraxia and verbal giftedness. It took me a while to work through
what was going on for my active boy, and I am still learning. So, when it came to choosing a school I
had no reason to be concerned about the nearest school. My boy was bright, he would be fine.

 passed on the genes for autism,

He was not. Without knowing it I had sent my son to a school on the “problematic schools list” in the

Education system. The Principal was considered “problematic”. I learnt this when I spoke
to a community engagement officer, who was an ex-principal, when I complained about the school
and asked to move schools. This was when my son was at the beginning of Grade 4. The following
are some events that led up to my request. They will give you an idea how school refusal comes
about:

His prep teacher was dismayed that he could already read before he came to school. I was accused
of some form of hot housing. Nup! My son spent his early days rolling around the floor and helping
other kids to learn and he was often sent to stand in the classroom of the next door teacher as a
punishment for his “bad behaviour”. School was boring to him and he was required to sit still so
much more than his kinder/childcare. At the end of Prep I gave the school the results of a WISC V (IQ
assessment) I had done showing my son was bright and verbally gifted, with significant differences in
scales, and major problems with processing speed and some with working memory. They did
nothing with this information. The Principal was only concerned with how much my report cost me
because it was so much more detailed than the ones she pays for. Instead of understanding and help
in Grade 1 he was separated from all his Prep friends and was given a sweet new grad teacher with
an old school behaviourist mentor. My son was often punished. He was sad. He tried so hard but just
couldn’t do what they asked of him. He liked break times and played footy with other kids. Nothing
changed for him at school when he was diagnosed with ADHD (combined). I had a medical certificate
requesting my son use a fidget device in class. The Principal did not allow it. In Grade 2 his
experienced teacher told me “you don’t want one of those” when I asked for an individual learning
plan for my son. Instead, she spoke to me regularly about my son. In her classroom there was a
massive poster on the wall where the kids results for “timed tests” in maths were recorded for all to
see. My son’s anxiety and slow processing speed prevented him from doing well and he felt
ashamed. I recall with horror that one of the lower levels was called “plodders path”. In Grade 3 my
son had a caring teacher who was willing to implement a few basic accommodations for kids with
ADHD in the classroom that I taught her. I recall her light bulb moment “He’s easier to teach when I
do this!” It was a revelation to her. She had to be taught accommodations by a parent, she had not
learnt them anywhere else. I asked for an individualised learning plan. She did one, but it wasn’t a
formal one. In spite of this helpful intervention my boy was still sent to the Principal’s office for
discipline with a “good” child where the Principal yelled at him until he cried. He was ashamed of
himself and worried about what the other child thought of him (it was never the same child). While
this happened to my boy a “goody good girl” emptied the contents of her pencil sharpener onto my
boy’s head. She was not disciplined, he was a “naughty” boy and somehow this behaviour was
acceptable. The injustice upset my boy. Then my boy was diagnosed with moderate level autism. I

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 114


 asked the Principal to apply for support for my son. She told me there was no use as he was too
bright. The only way I got them to provide him with accommodations for his Naplan was to threaten
to keep him home if he wasn’t provided accommodations AND I provided them with the legal
accommodations in writing. I asked for the regional disability advisor to consult and learnt about and
formally requested the visiting autism teacher to consult. The Principal directly told me “We don’t
want that” and she needed to be pushed by the Education Department disability advisor to give me
the documents to complete. I later realised that this assistance for my son was a perceived threat to
the Principal. All the while my son begged me to stay at the school because that was all he knew and
that was where his friends were. In Grade 4 in 2020 my son was placed in the grade of a teacher who
was a family friend of the Principal and had known her since her childhood. This teacher had my son
in constant flight, fight, freeze mode. She held him back in class after school on the days he went to
after school care and even hit him with a ruler. At times my son would be lying on the ground frozen
and mute. She thought this was good because he was quiet and still. But mostly he felt like running
home to me, scaling the high fence with barbed wire top. He felt like jumping over the external fire
stairs from the first floor, which were right next to his classroom onto the concrete of the ground
below. An after school meeting with the teacher and year level coordinator informing them of my
concerns made no difference to their treatment of him. Then we went into lockdown 1. I heard first
hand how the teacher treated my son. When she had him in tears, I told him to close the computer
and she never taught him again. We had 3 months of no school. I wrote to the Principal formally
outlining my concerns and requesting another teacher. She declined. It took three requests before I
managed to get him into another school, with myself, the disability advisor and then the boss of the
Regional Principals (through my formal complaint) having success.

When he began at this new school, my boy was so overwhelmed that his brain shut down. He lost
the ability to word find, didn’t know the word for “bed”, lost his balance and ability to walk unaided
and became photo-sensitive. I put him to bed and I was shocked. Because of the extra demands
school has on his brain, especially with few accommodations his brain can begin to shut down. He
refused to go to after school care because it was different to his other school, much smaller and
attended by one of the two boys who “bashed” him on his first day at the school. This school takes
the children other schools don’t want, which meant my boy was fearful of other students at times.
Worst was when school went into lockdown and the police were called due to the actions of an
older boy. This new school had one (now two part time) welfare staff who have worked hard to keep
my son engaged with school. The welfare staff operate in a kind of silo and while they do good work
they engage to “fix” the child. The welfare staff successfully applied for state Education Department
level 3 funding for my son, which applies this year in Grade 6 and next year in Year 7. He has an aide
to help him, but they don’t understand the problems he has associated with executive functioning
difficulties well although they do help. My son is too ashamed to be seen to be using the aide. While
this school is better it still has teachers who take a behavioural/reward/punishment approach to
their work. This has resulted in my son being unable to attend school at times due to burn out from
lack of accommodation. There is a general lack of understanding about autism and ADHD. Standards
are ableist and neurotypical. An example of this is that my son last year was judged on his verbal
presentation by his teacher and another student for his ability to look at the audience and for his
voice modulation. Now these are diagnostic features of autism and largely means that my boy is
being marked down BECAUSE he is autistic and rated poorly by his peer BECAUSE of his autism only.
(The teacher also rated the quality of the content of the presentation). The teachers engage in
“whole of class punishment”, which resulted in a classmate yelling at my son “My mum is going to
kill me because of you!” when the class was held back at the end of the day because some children

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 114 (the neurodivergent ones) were unable to sit still and not call out. This sets my child up to be vilified
by other children because of his disability.

With all this trauma at school there are times that my son just can’t go to school. He is filled with
dread each morning and is almost always late to school. I have to coax him to get ready, set
everything up for him, limit demands as much as possible. If I push too much he can crumple and
refuse school for that day. Sometimes he knows first thing that he won’t be able to manage school
that day. The system says he refuses school, like he is “naughty”. No. He can’t manage school that
day. He is overwhelmed by expectations he can’t meet. It doesn’t help that my boy has the PDA
subtype of autism, which is poorly understood in Australia (known in the U.K.). He is driven by
anxiety and is the best at masking and social skills of all autistics so people frequently assume that
he doesn’t need help or that nothing is wrong. But he comes home and melts down.

During 2020 and 2021 I was able to work part time from home and managed my appointments so I
could collect my boy from school and then come home and keep working (when we weren’t in
lockdown). However, my sons inability to go to school meant that he was at home while I was
working. He would make appearances in my meetings, which my colleagues thought was funny,
although at times it was very distracting for me. My son appeared long after the other children had
returned to school, and he was more disruptive. His school “refusal” made work very difficult for me.
His school attendance was 60% on average, so every week he would be home one or two days. In
late Feb 2022 I was made redundant. I am burnt out by my employer expecting 7 days a week work
from me in my 0.6 EFT position during the pandemic. I was offered several roles when people heard I
was leaving that I could not take up. I can’t consider a private practice as yet, although this is my
plan in the future. I am now on the carers pension. I am an experienced
 and
people are crying out for my help. My son needs me most. My son is about to start high school and it
feels like we have one shot at keeping him engaged in the mainstream education system. I want to
end, or at least greatly reduce, his school can’t.

What Do I Suggest:

I hope that reading my story gives you an insight into how school can’t occurs, at least for my boy.

I hope you are motivated to make some real and significant changes.

Nothing short of a change in the thinking styles and models used in the school system will work. We
need to move away from behaviourism and models based on rewards, punishment, and external
motivators. We need to use current research to inform what we do in schools. We need to be
informed by people with lived experience. We need to realise that when you focus on helping the
hard to engage, the anxious, the disabled, you actually help ALL children. We actually need to
properly support inclusion in our schools rather than separating some children. We need resources
in our schools and to train our teachers better.

I have done so much reading and research and advocacy for my son. The two academic clinicians
who make most sense to me and I see as at the forefront of positive change are both American
clinical psychologists. They offer models that provide a map towards a better school system.

Using Dr Ross Greene’s Collaborative Proactive Solutions model is stopping the education system to
prison pipeline in the U.S. and actually closing juvenile detention centres because they are no longer
needed. Imagine what using this model could do in our schools.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 114
 Visit www.livesinthebalance.org as an amazing resource explaining and supporting Dr Greene’s
model.

Dr Mona Delahooke translates Dr Stephen Porges polyvagal theory well in her work and offers great
descriptions of how to work with children in schools. Her model teaches parents and educators to
use neuroscience to engage with children and to frame their approach to teaching/parenting.

Below is my description of some of the changes in thinking that need to occur in the education
system. They are largely based on the work of Drs Greene, Delahooke and Porges:

Train teachers better. Think differently. What we are doing now isn’t working.

 I was not taught the most helpful strategies of working with children, instead I was
As a
taught behavioural models. Teachers are taught the same. Behavioural models are easy to teach and
are step wise and seem clear and safe. But they don’t work and create harm.

So many teachers use fear, which makes children anxious and school an unsafe place. Stop using
behavioural strategies. Kids do well if they can. If they can’t it is because they lack the
developmental skills to do well. They can’t. Behaviourism infers kids do well if they want to.
Behaviourism tells us kids just need to be motivated to do well. Thus, teachers use rewards and
punishments. All these do is shame children. Teachers can use all the rewards they like but if a child
can’t do something they can’t do it. Getting a sticker won’t help. The kids getting stickers don’t need
them because they can already do what is asked of them, and kids do well if they can. Giving
rewards to some and not others leads to some kids thinking they are better than the kids who don’t
get rewards. Some even feel entitled to tip their pencil shavings on top of another kid’s head.

Providing children a safe person is most important at school. Relational safety. This needs to guide
teacher’s thinking. If a child is dysregulated at school they are having a hard time, they are not giving
their teacher a hard time (even though the teacher may think this). The child needs help, not
punishment. Teach teachers to use co-regulation skills to help kids in schools.

Teach teachers child development and about common disabilities/different abilities.  Please learn
that children develop at different rates and have different characteristics. Allow/embrace difference
in school rather than conformity and ableism.

Collaborate! Actually speak to children about what is wrong, rather than assuming you know.

Listen to parents – they are often not included when decisions are made by schools. Parents know
their child/ren best.

And finally – these ideas come from my personal experience rather than the researchers above:

Follow the experience in Finland and increase the amount, and especially frequency, of play time in
primary school.

Ban homework except reading for all primary students. There is no evidence that it is helpful in
learning and creates difficulties at home and prevents children playing and engaging in social
activities, which are more beneficial for them.

Children should never be kept back from recess/lunch breaks as a punishment for their “behaviour”
in the classroom.

Please ban “whole body listening” – my son’s school introduced this across the school this year and
attendance got worse across the school! This model has even been discredited now even by its

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 114 original author, but somehow a lead teacher thought it was a good idea. Why? She takes a
behavioural approach to teaching. Some kids can’t sit still and look at the teacher and learn. It takes
too much conscious brain power, so they focus on sitting still etc rather than the lesson content.

Start recording school can’t correctly so we can know the true extent of the problem. There is no
category for this in
“parent choice” either. It is not medical illness. It is an inability to manage the demands of the school
system as it is currently.

 state system). It is called truancy. It is not this. It is not

My son’s first Principal was allowed to put herself nominally into the welfare officer role in a school
of 750 students, which is effectively not funding this position. This should not be allowed.

And for the tired, burnt-out carers: Please increase the amount of carer’s payment so we can afford
to live while we support our children.

Thanks for reading and working to make things better.

SUBMISSION:    Senate Inquiry into School Refusal / School Can’t

Page 1

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 115








 Summary

Our
-year-old son rarely attends school. For him, school has become a stressful,
punitive and highly distressing environment. He wants to attend, both for the social
and learning opportunities, but has psychological and physiological responses that
often incapacitate him when he tries. When he is successful in attending, he is at
severe risk of psychological trauma, and comes home elevated and distressed.

His condition was first noticeable in kindergarten and has worsened over the years.
We have watched as our child’s mental health, self-esteem and academic potential
have eroded so severely we are extremely worried about his future.

The schooling system has not provided any support and only limited
accommodations. In fact, some experiences at school (including with teaching staff)
have actively and significantly worsened his condition.

Our son’s school refusal has had significant emotional, mental health and financial
impacts on our family. And, as of writing this submission, the situation is as dire as it
has ever been and there is no end in sight.

We have learned through online forums that our child and family are not alone in
this. Within our local community in
similar schooling challenges, though they are not necessarily aware of how seriously
things can deteriorate.

, we also see others who are facing the

We don’t know what happens next. At best, our child will find a way to return to
school in a sporadic capacity. At worst, they may never attend school again, have
their substantial academic capability wasted, and have lifelong mental health
challenges.

We will do whatever it takes to avoid the latter. But we can’t do that alone.

Page 2

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 115




 History of my child’s “school can’t”

The following is an abridged timeline of the difficulties our now
-year-old son has
had with school to demonstrate the progression of his condition, the lack of support,
and the way in which school responses have actively contributed to his deterioration.

Pre-school

Our son has always been intellectually very capable and gregarious, but has
struggled with some social situations. He coped with the early childhood environment
relatively well, though this is in no small part due to the lucky support of a learning
support worker who was employed to provide full time support to his best friend in
class.

Kindergarten (prep/reception) and Year 1

In kindergarten our son suffered extreme separation anxiety. This manifested in
screaming and clinging to his parents, and he needed to be physically separated
from us each day. We received almost no support with this no matter how extreme
this became, beyond generic (and ineffective) advice about how to handle anxiety.
This separation anxiety response lasted well into year 1.

Although our son took to the academic requirements of the early years of school in
his stride, he struggled with the school environment and found the social experience
at times overwhelming. He also seemed affected by some sensory issues (such as
loud noises and large groups), though they did not impact his academic
achievements and thus were not considered important by the school.

In fact, the school viewed his distress as a lack of resilience and his self-soothing
behaviours (such as humming or sitting back from group time) as disruptive and anti-
social. They offered no support to co-regulate or help to establish a strong
relationship with a safe adult to help him build resilience. His issues were described
by teaching staff as a character flaw that we, his parents, should fix. Over time, our
engaging, gregarious child became increasingly anxious and mistrustful of peers and
staff.

Year 2

In Year 2, our son became increasingly agitated and miserable about school. I
approached his teacher, but was told our son was ‘catastrophising’.

We didn’t know at the time, but our son was being mistreated at school. He was
being used by teaching staff to manage one of our child’s friends, a kid who was
dealing with significant trauma and had related behavioural issues. The school would
regularly isolate the pair, use my son as a reward/distraction for the other child, and
spread punishments and negative outcomes to both. My son was regularly
prevented from spending time with other children so he would be company for the
other child.

Page 3

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 115

 My child started exhibiting more serious outbursts and meltdowns, and we received
semi-regular calls from executive staff about his behaviour. Our child’s classroom
teacher described our child as problematic and spoke of him in derogatory terms,
including in front of him (for example, describing him as “disturbed” and “incapable of
friendship” in his presence). At the same time, during a private discussion with the
school’s executive about his behaviour, the school again suggested I was a cause of
my child’s behaviour and recommended I personally seek psychiatric help.

The issue culminated in an incident where the other child was directed to go the
principal’s office due to his behaviour. Teachers were called to attempt to physically
move him. Our child attempted to protect his friend from staff by slamming a door
and yelling

We didn’t know this at the time, but the severity of his treatment at the school and
the way he was responded to was traumatic for our son. During sessions with a
psychologist in the years after the event, it became clear our son’s future behaviours
in the school environment were impacted by this traumatic experience and
exacerbated his “school can’t”.

We managed to convince the school to move our child to another class with a more
tolerant teacher. His behaviour improved, but his relationship with school has never
really recovered.

Year 4 and COVID

Our son continued to find school challenging and distressing, and had increasingly
severe reactions to negative interactions with teachers and other students. His “fight-
or-flight” response was constantly close to the surface, and others saw him as a
problem, which only exacerbated his anxiety and negative self-view.

He attempted to moderate the environment for himself by removing himself from
difficult situations (such as running away from teachers who yelled) or not taking part
in activities when distressed, but again these were seen as signs of defiance and
disruption. His reactive and self-protective behaviour badly impacted relationships at
school, leading to lost friendships, isolation, and a sense of complete mistrust
between him and school staff.

In 2020, children were sent home for several weeks to isolate from the COVID
pandemic. Although this home schooling certainly had challenges, our son must
have found a relief in not having to go to school. His behaviour and outlook
improved. However, when he was forced to go back to school, his anxiety spiked
significantly. He started having panic attacks at the mere mention of going to school.
His reactive fight-or-flight issues worsened. The school singled him out as a problem
student that had to be dealt with.

He was also being bullied by others at school because he couldn’t cope. We
mentioned this possibility to the school, but they dismissed it, holding the view that
he couldn’t be bullied (or if he was it didn’t matter) because he was a problem

Page 4

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 115


 himself. Again, later sessions with a psychologist demonstrated the impact this
bullying had on his psyche and self-esteem.

Eventually, a minor incident in the classroom led a teacher he had previously had a
strong relationship with to yell at him and corner him in the classroom. Our child
physically lashed out at the teacher and ran away. He never went back to that
school.

Years 5 and 6

During his absence from school our son received some support from a private
psychologist. He was prescribed low-level anti-depressants that he continues to use
to this day. His behaviour and demeanour slowly started to improve due to this
treatment, a major change in our parenting approach, and due to being absent from
school.

We moved our son to a new school in 2021. We hoped he could develop trust with
new staff through some proactive communication to explain his needs, sensitivities
and traumatic school experiences. Our son seemed to respond very positively to the
change and attended semi-regularly for some period.

However, after a short while several factors derailed his progress and longer
absences began again. He also had two incidents

which led to extended

absences, and he found it increasingly difficult to return from those. His teacher also
changed after his first term, and then five more times since. His new teachers were
less accommodating of his needs than his first, and our child lost confidence in the
school environment once again.

Our son began to feel exposed to the negative attention from peers and teachers,
and began acting in a self-protective and defiant manners. He displayed signs of
anxiety, stress and overwhelm from sensory issues. He felt minor incidents very
heavily and began to feel as though he was not safe at school. The school permitted
part-time attendance, but in reality any attendance was rare. On the days when he
did attend, we anxiously awaited a call from the school to explain how something
had gone wrong and that he was in trouble again. Even when nothing did happen he
would return home agitated and edgy and takes days to calm down.

Last week, our child was suspended from the school. He retaliated physically against
another student who verbally and physically abused him about his absences. The
principal chose to suspend our child without due process, likely because it was
considered the easiest course of action as our son rarely attends anyway. The other
child was not suspended. This action once again significantly impacted our child’s
self-esteem and further degraded their sense of safety at school.

Our son is unlikely to return to the school before he graduates year 6.

Page 5

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 115




 Impact of School Can’t on my child, my family and myself

Our child

My son’s experience of school has shattered his self-esteem. Over time, he has lost
his engaging, gregarious, funny spark, isolated by a system that doesn’t understand
him and doesn’t care to (or doesn’t have the time or resources to). He is increasingly
anxious, depressed and convinced he has no value. He perceives – not incorrectly –
that not only is no-one able to help and that they blame him for his struggles.

He has lost friendships due to his “anti-social” behaviour. He has lost trust in adults
in positions of authority due to their blaming and controlling responses to his ongoing
distress. This only compounds these issues when he reacts with fear to their
approaches and has extreme fight-or-flight responses.

His academic results are poor, despite the fact official cognitive testing has placed
him in the top 2 per cent of children his age. He has never achieved anything like his
potential at school and has started to question his abilities at all. The system’s
response to him as a problem to be controlled stole his confidence to dream for his
future.

Throughout his school career we have also noticed the impact school has on his
nervous system. The clever, engaging, helpful, loving kid we knew at home was
jittery, aggressive and very, very sensitive to perceived disapproval. His nervous
system is extremely elevated after an interaction with school, including the
anticipation of school. We see his nervous system become calm and capable on
holidays and again, now that we have removed the demand to attend school, we see
that he benefits from the absence of school in his daily existence.

The one benefit from my son’s “school can’t” experience is that he has been able to
work one-on-one with a private tutor that we personally pay for. At first this was to
cover the curriculum gaps due to his long-term absences, but he has quickly moved
on to curriculum well above his age group. His love of learning is palpable in these
sessions; he is energised by them. We see those glimpses of happiness and we
regret all the years we have limped through school in a system which cannot meet
his needs or even his psychological safety and has done untold damage to his self
image, health and sense of security.

Work and finances

In some ways we are lucky that the pandemic occurred and has provided some
employers the confidence to allow work from home. This is the only way we would
be able to meet our family’s financial needs as well as provide a welcoming and safe
home environment for our son throughout the week.

We still often have to take leave to meet with schools, take him to mental and
physical health appointments, and provide emotional support when he is struggling
badly. For two years my husband worked part-time to manage the additional time
and effort required to manage our unwell child. This has had a significant financial

Page 6

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 115

 burden, which has compounded the effects of the costs of additional health care,
psychological care and other support.

My husband has also had to put aside aspirations of a new career, or to further his
current career. He has turned down promotions as he does not have the capacity to
take on the additional stress and workload, and has to prioritise flexibility over
everything else.

He has also encountered the worst of an inflexible and punitive

 employer. When his son’s health impacted his ability to work with the same

productive intensity as usual, he was punished and bullied by his supervisor. Poor
performance processes were initiated. This further impacted his ability to support our
son and his own ability to feel safe and valued in the workplace himself. Worse, it put
pressure on him to put pressure on his child to attend school so he could be free to
work. It also impacted on his mental health and in turn on his relationships: including
with me and with our children.

He sought support from the union, but it never materialised. His only recourse was to
resign and find a new, more supportive and understanding employer. He has now
done so, and this has improved our family wellbeing significantly.

Our health

This is exceptionally stressful. Advocating for a child who is misunderstood by 99%
of school staff and other experts we have encountered, providing intensive
psychological and educational support for him, providing sufficient time and attention
for our two other children and holding down two jobs. The juggle is intense and our
health is suffering as we cut away our “self-care” (exercise, medical appointments,
social activities, housework, showering) to achieve the impossible.

I, his mother, have become very anxious. I am paranoid about what the world thinks
of my beautiful child and that he is judged on the construct of a failing system and
not on his value as an individual. I feel increasingly isolated as the only people who
seem to understand our experience are those I’ve met online. I also feel intense guilt
for not recognising his distress, for not rescuing him before it became this bad, for
believing all the bad faith advice of “experts”, for wanting to continue with a job I love
rather than home-school.

My husband has also dealt with significant health issues. He has had severe stress-
induced physical symptoms, such as collapsing/fainting, blood pressure fluctuations,
headaches, and heart palpitations. He has sought mental health support from his
local GP on two occasions, but ultimately does not have the time to take care of
himself. That space is dedicated to ensuring his children’s well-being.

I don’t talk openly with friends or peers about what is happening for us. It is too
distressing for me and their experience is too far removed from ours. I feel like a
failure as a parent but, intellectually, I know we have moved mountains to be the
parents our boy needs us to be. I am actually proud of the internal work – and
intense research – we have done (and continue to do) to become the parents we are

Page 7

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 115


 now. But the parenting our son needs doesn’t look like the traditional authoritarian
model (a suspected ASD with Pathologically Demand Avoidant profile child doesn’t
need a stronger hand) and I know we have encountered judgement of that from a
range of sources.

Access to supports

Health care support

 We have found it almost impossible to find support which meets

We live in
our needs. We do currently have a welcoming and gentle GP and a psychologist
who has worked well (but sporadically) with our boy over a number of years. We
have also had some success with a wonderful physiotherapist who has developed a
trusting and constructive relationship with him.

Currently we are not accessing any other care as our son cannot handle another
introductory session where we lay out all the negatives, everything that is “wrong”
with him. This is distressing to him and us, and even more distressing when help
never eventuates. It only exacerbates his mental health issues and reduces his
ability to attend school. We do want to access assessment for ASD and ADHD but
we have not found a provider who wants to look beyond his eye contact and
reciprocal relationships.

The wait for support can also be extensive. We have been on the waiting list for a
range of occupational therapists for almost 3 years now. The waiting list for an
ASD/ADHD assessment, paediatrician and the like are from months to over a year.
The psychologist he attends has long waiting lists, too.

Cost is also a factor. We have private health insurance and receive some rebates
through Medicare, but we are out-of-pocket for thousands of dollars a year to attend
these appointments.

The impact of regular health appointments should also not be underestimated. His
difficulties attending school and the treatment he receives at school have severely
impacted his self-esteem. He now sees health appointments as further signs that
there is something wrong with him and that he needs to be fixed. At these
appointments he is extremely withdrawn. Afterwards, he displays the same defiant,
self-derogatory, and agitated behaviours we observe after he has attended school.
We cannot keep putting him through that for no gain.

Schooling

school system has only in the last month managed to assess our son’s

The
needs for additional support (and funding for said support). We have participated in
these assessment sessions, but receive no insight into how or when this funding is to
be used at the school.

Page 8

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 115


 We have not found a model of schooling for high school that in any way reflects a
structure and environment our son can thrive in. I am loathe to limp our way through
four more awful years of traditional, discipline-focussed school.

The availability of alternative government schooling environments is extremely
limited. We had hoped to take advantage of the Big Picture program at a nearby high
school, but the program has been scrapped for Year 7 next year. The school has
also disbanded its virtual schooling option
these programs had the potential to meet our son’s needs but both are suddenly,
and disappointingly, unavailable for next year.

 for 2023. Both

There is also no communication between elements of the system (school or health).
We have to carry those messages and re-tell our story over and over again. This is
damaging. There has also been no support to find opportunities or alternative
programs; this is something we have done through our own research, or discovered
by accident by talking to others who are also struggling in the same way.

Communication with schools has been generally unproductive (or
counterproductive), with the specific exception of a very small number of teachers
and executive staff who have made an effort to understand our son’s unique needs
and not apply a standard lens to the issues in front of them.

Monitoring and identification of School Attendance Difficulties

My son’s first school took a punitive and judgemental approach to attendance
difficulties: snide comments (to parent and child) about school starting after 9am;
demands to fill in forms with explanations for growing absences without any attempts
to understand the challenges we faced; simplistic and off-hand attempts at solutions
that quickly gave way to punitive responses when schooling staff ran out of patience.

At his first primary school, teachers disbelieved the distress he was expressing to
them. They refused to call his parents when he expressed difficulties, refused to let
him go to sick bay
refused to let him access the toilet
behaviour destroyed any chance he could trust them to have his back, to support
him, to meet him in his distress and provide comfort and support.

 and
 Their

At his current primary school, we were more proactive stating that we supported him
going to the front office as needed and them calling us any time he asked, which
they have followed through on. This has enabled them to build his trust and
supported his confidence to attend. We have been open about his physical and
mental health with the school and they have been broadly understanding of his
absences. When relevant, we get supporting documentation from his psychologist,
GP of physiotherapist. Thankfully, the school does not have unreasonable
expectations of attendance or of a linear return to attendance as things improve
(though they have tried).

Page 9

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 115


 Legal issues

We have not received any legal notifications for our son’s absences, for which we
are extremely grateful. If there was to be legal involvement, this would be highly
detrimental to our son’s sense of safety and our ability to give him the home care
that he desperately needs. The thought that even his parents are not able to keep
him safe from the distress provoked by school would be overwhelming.

Keeping him psychologically safe is paramount. The level of stress and distress is
substantial without unreasonable bureaucratic legal proceedings impacting on our
ability to meet our boy’s needs. We have participated willingly in

 processes to obtain funding and put in place supports and have

maintained a positive and constructive relationship with staff at all times.

Home schooling

We have had no real plan for home schooling. We ensure that our son keeps up with
any work uploaded to his Google Classroom. He keeps in touch with schoolwork and
what is happening with his peers this way. It would have been very helpful to us if the
school had been willing or able to place more work online for him to complete, but
this was not something they felt able to do.

We also provide additional projects and direction, and hire a tutor, though there is no
direction or communication from the school to support these.

Thinking about proactive strategies to prevent school can’t

Schools

If there are to be two takeaways from this submission, this is the first: a
psychologically safe school environment is the most important factor in
preventing and responding to school can’t.

This is not about bullying (although bullying becomes a factor, as described above).
It must extend to how a school operates and how teachers interact with children.
Prioritising strong relationships and relational safety over compliance would have
made a significant difference for my son. Mutually respectful and trusting
relationships should be built and valued, rather than one’s based on authority and
dominance.

This leads to the second key takeaway is this: the current education system will
not meet our child’s needs.

I previously had a strong ethical commitment to public education but, having seen
how incapable it is of meeting my child’s needs (and in fact how unconcerned it has
been with the untold damage it has done to his mental health), I no longer trust that
the education system has the best interests of children at heart. I see the love of

Page 10

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 115




 learning my son still has and I know that school has only diminished this love – and
will likely continue to do so if we leave him in a mainstream environment.

It is not simply a matter of simply increasing supports. Serious consideration must be
given to how suitable the current model of education is, not just for kids who have
difficulties, but for all children. A homogenised education model that attempts to drive
children towards a median point through the use of learning by rote and discipline is
not in anyone’s interests. Reduced resourcing plays a role in this, as motivated,
capable teachers lose the ability to drive such an approach, but ultimately the system
itself is flawed and needs to change. This needs to be a cultural thing as much as a
resourcing thing.

Other proactive factors to prevent school can’t in schools include:

•  Proactive investigation of our challenges earlier in their education would have

potentially stopped the slide toward school refusal. This should have started with
listening to our concerns, even when we didn’t know what they may be pointing
to. For a long time we simply accepted the school’s denial of our concerns and
simplistic efforts to satisfy the issues we raised. It took a very long time for us to
be empowered to support our child in the way they need.

•  Specific supports are needed. Appropriate investigation by the school

psychologist, may have uncovered his giftedness and need for extension and
may have illuminated the underlying reasons for his apparent defiance. School’s
no longer have nurses and the school psychologist is part-time. These are
fundamental resources for helping kids thrive mentally and physically.

•  When a child can’t attend school, their options for doing schoolwork at home is
limited. A hybrid model is necessary when a child starts exhibiting symptoms of
school refusal. However, except during the COVID pandemic, there are generally
limited or no options for online learning that mirrors the activities of the child’s
peers in their school. Essentially, there is no guidance on what they should do if
they can’t come to school.

•  Specific accommodations to school refusal should be tolerated. For example, one
tool we implemented to help our child attend school was to provide him with a
kid’s “smart watch” which he could use to contact us directly at any time he felt
unsafe. This was necessary as, as described above, we couldn’t trust the school
to contact us when it was needed. The school agreed to this accommodation. It
helped somewhat, but despite the school’s agreement our son was regularly
reprimanded for simply having the watch, and, on some occasions when he felt
the need to use it, was actively punished.

Healthcare

The healthcare system does not seem well set up to identify the underlying physical
and mental challenges that can lead to school refusal, or to provide support to
address the symptoms of school refusal when it emerges. Specific issues include:

•

It is hard to get appointments with specialists

Page 11

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 115

 •  Specialists are rushed and prone to give generic advice or fixate on specific

issues

•  There is limited communication between professionals (and between schools and
professionals), and thus a holistic assessment and response is not possible.

The most success we have had is where we have personally built a relationship with
a generic provider (such as a GP) over time so they can start to see the pattern of
issues and behaviours and draw more detailed conclusions. Their support has been
the most valuable and empowering. Some specialists, conversely, have been
actively detrimental (such as giving incorrect and dangerous advice about
medicines).

Education and community

There is limited information about school refusal in general. It took us years to realise
it was even a thing, and to understand that we were not facing a simple issue of
school reluctance, but a complex interplay of mental, physical and social challenges
that ultimately culminated in school refusal. Most of what we have learned is from
our own research and investigation.

The online community has also been fantastic: if not for that, we would not have
been aware that we were facing such a serious issue, we would have felt alone, and
we would have doubted our own ability to respond. It is paramount that parents know
they are not alone, that they can be a major force in helping their child. Such a
community—and associated resources to assist parents in understanding the issues
and how to work with schools and healthcare providers—are fundamental in
facilitating that.

History of school can’t, impact on the child and contributing factors:
Now finishing year 8, my daughter has suffered from varying degrees of school
can’t for eight years.  Usually mild but occasionally at the severe end of the
scale.  Severe symptoms of school can’t have been accompanied by very poor
mental health.  My daughter is autistic (diagnosed in kindergarten).  Our
primary school failed to flag that my daughter had a learning difficulty
(Dyslexia and Dysgraphia) or that she had inattentive ADHD.  These diagnoses
were only discovered because of parental investigation while trying to uncover
the reasons why she was not happy at school.  Delays in discovering these later
two diagnoses have severely impacted her mental health, her self-esteem, her
confidence as a learner and contributed to her experience of school as an
extremely stressful and unsafe place to be.

My daughter’s learning difficulty meant she had great difficulty learning to
read.  With hindsight I wish I had removed her from primary school in grade 1
when it first became apparent to me that she was struggling.  She was not
diagnosed with learning difficulties until she was in grade 2 and was not
diagnosed with ADHD until year 7.  During her early primary years, she suffered
from a range of stress related illnesses including migraines, hives, and anxiety.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 116
 Her migraines were so severe and frequent that the paediatrician requested an
MRI to rule out anything organic.  In grade 1 she begged me to home school
her and I recall telling her we had to trust the teacher because she had lots of
experience.   The teacher however, believed there was nothing wrong, and told
me during a parent teacher interview that my daughter just needed to try
harder, stop talking to her friends in class so much, and stop being lazy.

Once diagnosed with learning difficulties the school did not offer the evidence-
based reading instruction she needed.  The principal recommended I take her
to see a tutor who she had observed to have had good success with dyslexic
students to learn to read and spell.  The principal seemed to believe that due
to the diagnosis my daughter needed specialist care.  We enrolled her in
weekly sessions with a reading intervention specialist which cost
approximately $100 each week.  It was thanks to this private instruction
outside of school that my daughter learned to read.  Sadly, the Balanced
Literacy instruction offered at the school, which encouraged children to guess
words rather than decode them, prolonged the need for private instruction.
Balanced Literacy instruction is not recommended for students with dyslexia.
Structured Literacy is recommended.  Structured Literacy involves explicit and
systematic instruction in synthetic phonics and explicit instruction in
morphology (DFS Literacy Services 2022:20).  Structured Literacy is a suitable
tier 1 program for literacy instruction under a Response to Intervention model
(RTI).  It is also considered as a suitable Universal Design for Learning (UDL)
literacy instruction program meeting the needs of all learners but particularly
essential for students with learning difficulties or learning disabilities.

Each year I struggled to communicate with teachers about how to support my
daughter and accommodate her in the classroom.  My daughter only ever
completed a handful of pieces of work in the whole of primary school.   When I
tried to discuss this with teachers, I was told that she could either complete
her work later or she could take it home, but there were never enough hours
in her week to complete work at school and she came home exhausted every
day.  One teacher told me he wasn’t concerned because the purpose was to
practice a skill not to complete work.  Teachers seemed repeatedly to not be
able to understand the impact this had on my daughter.  The lack of
opportunity for dopamine hits obtained from completing work and the effort
of trying both contributed to her experience of stress and declining mental
health.  At the end of each year the students would paste examples of work
they were proud of into their student portfolios and my daughter’s portfolio

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 116 would come home almost empty.  She refused to paste in work that was
unfinished as she was not proud of it unless it was completed. Her self-
reflections in relation to schoolwork, over time became increasingly negative.  I
paid for an education consultant to provide the school with advice, but the
teachers did not have adequate training in making adjustments for my
daughter to make use of the advice.  They did not appreciate the need or
understand how to adjust work so that my daughter could complete it and feel
successful.

When my daughter first showed signs of declining mental health, I got a
Mental Health Care plan and took her to see a psychologist.  During primary
school she saw 3 different psychologists in the search for support.  She
received lots of Cognitive Behaviour Therapy (CBT) but this type of therapy put
the responsibility back onto her to change her understanding of the problem
instead of reducing the stress that was causing her distress.  It felt like I was
patching up her wounds but sending her back in to do battle every single day
at school.  Once I found School Can’t (SPSR) Australia I realised that we needed
to identify the source of stress and reduce it rather than try to change her
response to the stress.  Unfortunately, while the adults at school determined
that the problem lay within my child, they were absolved of doing anything to
help and did not see the need to reduce her stress levels.

Due to chronic stress my daughter’s mental health deteriorated to the point of
being suicidal in grade 6.  She missed several weeks of school and then
attended part time in term 3. She commenced taking medication for
depression.   Her nervous system still today has an involuntary trauma
response to school which frequently disables her in the classroom causing
shutdowns.

6.  We live in

She started high school in 2021 (another year with covid lockdowns).  Her
catholic high school seemed to have a better idea about accommodating her
learning needs, however managing so many subjects with so many teachers
has been challenging.  School this year has involved lots of absences due to
physical illness both COVID and non-COVID illness, lots of teachers absent due

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 116 to COVID or other illness, and a lack of continuity of care at school.  Teachers
have seemed stressed.  My daughter’s mental health again deteriorated, and
she was unable to return to school for 6 weeks following term 3.  Attendance
for 2022 currently sits at 42%.

Impact on family and main carer:
Our struggle has lasted 8 years.  My other two children have felt neglected, the
youngest has required way more attention and care than the older two ever
had and have often been met by an exhausted mum when they needed
attention.  My husband works full time and had great difficulty understanding
the nature of the advocacy work I was doing trying to support our daughter.
Thanks to COVID and now working from home and spending more time with
me he has a much better understanding.  Our relationship has been at times
strained as I have invested so much energy in keeping our daughter alive.  For
much of the past 8 years I was chronically exhausted and chronically stressed.
I was unable to work as I never knew when I might be required to support our
daughter and how intense this support might be.  I have only just returned to
work a year ago.   I am currently working casually, from home (~12 hours a
week) in an arrangement that is very flexible in relation to when I work and
how many hours I work.

My career has been impacted.   My 3 autistic children have required the full-
 shortly

after my first child was born.  I would have entered the workforce when my
youngest started primary school, however, the emotional labour required to
support her while she engaged with the education system was such that I did
not have capacity to work.  We were frequently late to school due to her
reluctance to attend.  It would have been very stressful to be worried about
making it to a workplace on time.  It was not until my daughter was enrolled in
a more trauma informed high school and the ability to work from home
(thanks to workplace changes due to COVID) became a possibility that I was
able to commence casual employment in my profession.

As I have not been able to work full time for a minimum of two years in my

Access to supports:
We have struggled to find clinicians who understand school can’t.  A
psychiatrist recently refused to provide a medical certificate to cover absence
believing that if she provided a medical certificate for a number of weeks it
would disincentivise me from encouraging my child back to school.  She did not
recognise that school can’t was occurring because my daughter’s nervous
system was in shutdown and part of the solution was to take time to rest and
restore – the psychiatrists only solution was to medicate.

Schools constantly broadcast the expectation that children are to be at school
every day and when a child lacks capacity to attend the expectation weighs
heavily on the child and the family.  Parents frequently feel that their parenting
is being judged when they can not get their children to comply with the
expectation to attend school.  Advice from school included use of bribes, and
taking her to see a psychologist to learn coping strategies.  My daughter was
once reprimanded in front of me by a teacher for not displaying “resilience” (a
school value).

Medical care has been expensive.  Waitlists for care are long.  My daughter has
NDIS funding, but it will not cover education or mental health related expenses
even though her needs for funding in these areas are as a direct result of an
education system that has failed to accommodate the needs she has because
of her disability.

For the past 8 years since school can’t started, we have funded medical costs
including psychiatry, paediatricians, educational psychology (for assessments
to determine diagnoses), psychology (for counselling), and a private specialist
tutor.  Following Medicare rebates the total cost to us has been in excess of
$38,000.  All this has been funded while we live on one wage, living a very
modest lifestyle.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 116
 Advocating at my daughter’s school has been stressful.  Once it was so stressful
that I spent a whole weekend unable to get out of bed and unable to sleep.

 meetings were usually restricted to 30 minutes
(which was never long enough) and they were held at times of day (before or
after school) that were difficult for me to attend.  At primary school it was
difficult to get meetings with staff and these meetings frequently felt
combative.  My daughter’s needs were not considered severe enough to
warrant a learning plan until she was suicidal, despite my requesting assistance
repeatedly.  Once my child was suicidal then the school were keen to have
regular meetings that lasted for more than 30 minutes, and I finally felt like I
had their attention and interest in helping.

The struggle to obtain resources and support was significant.  It once took 10
weeks for a piece of assistive tech (funded through the school) to be linked to
the school Wi-Fi so it could be used by my daughter in class.

Over the years I have developed strategies to help make communication with
school less stressful.  Developing a communication strategy which involved
interviewing my daughter about her difficulties, discussing with her different
potential solutions, and discussing these solutions with her therapy team and
then communicating these potential solutions and the justification for them in
writing to the members of the
could consider things prior to the meeting.

before a meeting.  This way the school

I slowly developed a team of supporters around us including a psychologist
who understands school can’t, a music therapist and a tutor who has provided
substantial support.  I wish I could fund the cost of the weekly private tutor
through NDIS or the education system somehow because my daughter would
say this is her most significant and helpful support.  Her tutor is a disability
trained educator who has consistently been in her life for 6 years and provided
1:1 support through consecutive years of schooling.  The tutor has been a
valuable asset often helping explain to my daughter’s teachers the kinds of
supports that are helpful or coaching me to know how to explain this to
teachers.

It's my experience that schools do not provide information about the supports
available with in a school and how to access them.  This information should
form part of a parent handbook so that parents understand what they can
expect from their school in terms of support.  I spent a lot of time wondering if

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 116
 my daughter was even eligible for a meeting to discuss a learning plan during
primary school.

Things that have worked for us to support our child when
experiencing school can’t:

1.  Viewing school can’t as a stress behaviour has transformed my perception
of the problem and how I respond to my daughter’s struggle to attend
school.  Prior to this shift in thinking we had been led to believe that our
daughter’s inability to consistently attend school and enjoy it was
because of some defect in her: poor resilience, poor ability to manage
anxiety or worries, or due to poor parenting.  School Can’t (School
Phobia School Refusal) Australia played a major role in helping me shift
my thinking.

2.  Identifying learning issues and neurodivergence has helped us obtain

information about supports and accommodations so we can advocate
for these supports at school and reduce stress for my daughter.

3.  Drilling down to identifying underlying sources of stress and seeking ways to
reduce stress to preserve or increase capacity has helped but this is
frequently limited by teacher knowledge about inclusive teaching
practices and how to make appropriate adjustments to the way
information is delivered or to the way my daughter demonstrates her
learning.

4.  My daughter and I being considered equal collaborative partners together
with the school.  When we work together to identify, understand and
find solutions to problem then we find better solutions to problem.  Not
all school leaders are equipped to do this with many preferring to use
“power over” parents and students rather than work collaboratively
with parents and students.

5.  Utilising the power of interest.  Harnessing student interest by allowing
engagement in passion projects has helped my daughter return to
learning in the past.  This has been dependent on the school’s capacity
to provide support.  Our current school has said that they can not
facilitate this as part of their re-engagement program as it would not be
possible for the teacher to be across subjects for the 10 students in the
re-engagement program.

6.  Continuity of connection from one year to the next is helpful.  Starting

over each year with new support staff, new teachers and new

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 116 classmates is difficult.  For next year I have insisted that our high school
commits to having the same learning diversity leader work with us until
my daughter graduates.  I have also requested that they appoint a
mentor who understands curriculum adjustments and supports to check
in with my daughter fortnightly to adjust her load if needed in a much
more active way to manage her stress levels across time.

7.  Helping students connect with each other around shared interests and

passions alongside re-engagement.  This helps students build
relationships with peers and connection to school.

8.  Teachers who can co-regulate and have authentic relationship with students
helps.  My daughter feels very vulnerable in a classroom and needs to
know that her teacher likes her and cares for her.  Without a sense of
safety and connection she is like a kayak in the middle of the Pacific
Ocean.

Recommendations:
1)  That the government fund a program which seeks to remove barriers to

assessment and diagnosis of neurodiversity such as: Autism, ADHD and
Specific Learning Difficulties (Dyslexia, Dysgraphia, Dyscalculia),
Developmental Language Disorder.  This could involve free in-school
screening by a social worker, psychologist, or speech therapist at the end of
the first year of formal schooling.  Screening would involve use of parent
and teacher screening questionnaires along with suitable screening tests to
flag children who may benefit from referral to a suitable clinical pathway
for assessment commencing with a developmental paediatrician consult.
This would reduce the delay in receiving vital information that could help
parents and teachers support a student to have a positive experience of
school, thereby reducing the chance of the student experiencing learning
failure or chronic stress.  Many neurodiverse children are not being
identified through the current Maternal Child Health pathway.

2)  That education about Universal Design for Learning and Inclusive schooling be
prioritised for schools to ensure that in a Response to Intervention (RTI)
framework at Tier 1 we are meeting the needs of more students resulting in
fewer students requiring Tier 2 and Tier 3 supports.  Schools should be
required to report what they are doing to actively implement Universal
Design for learning and inclusive learning practices across the curriculum
and across year levels. They should also regularly collect feedback about

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 116
 how they are doing in this regard from those with lived experience
(including the parents of students with disability) and regional specialists.

3)  A review of the help that can be access through the health, and education

systems, as well as the NDIS be reviewed to identify gaps in support. Parents of
school can’t children currently incur the following costs in addition to the
cost of lost income:

i)  Cost of psychology, speech therapy and occupational therapy

assessment.   Sometime multiple assessments are required and there
is not time to wait on public lists for these services.

ii)  Cost of psychology support for the school can’t child, parents and

siblings.

iii) Cost of in home or out of school tutoring to build the student’s

confidence as a learner even if they can’t set foot on school grounds
due to a trauma response to that environment.

iv) Cost of paediatrician or psychiatric care to manage medications if

required.

v)  Cost of case management / advocacy support if trying to return to

onsite learning.

vi) Cost of carer support often required in home because they can’t

leave a child unattended, and the child won’t leave home. (This may
include counselling, support work to allow the carer the ability to go
for a walk or visit a gym, or practical support like house cleaning)
vii) Cost of support workers to attend school with the child or to support

the child to leave the house.

viii)  Cost of parent education courses to learn how support the child.

Frequently parents whose children have NDIS funding are told that school
supports are funded by the education departments, however suitable
supports seem to be unavailable in the education system.

4)  That messaging around attendance at schools be reviewed and consideration be
given to including education about school can’t alongside messages about
attendance.  So that parents who are having difficulty with their child know
how to seek help and they feel better understood and supported.  Strong
messaging about attendance compliance causes parents of school can’t
children significant stress.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 116


 5)  That School Can’t (SPSR) Australia be funded to produce resources for parents, as
well as resources for educators and clinicians around school attendance to
communicate lived experience knowledge about supporting young people
who are experiencing school can’t and to help reframe school refusal as
“School Can’t” a manifestation of stress behaviour.  Too many schools and
clinicians give advice that prolongs suffering and damages the parent child
relationship.  Causing increased stress for students and carers.  As a

 I would like to refer families to psychologists and psychiatrists who

are educated about school can’t but I struggle to find such people and when
I do find them their waitlists are closed.

6)  That School Can’t (SPSR) Australia be funded so that the organisation can continue
providing an ongoing parent-based intervention in a way that means it is less
dependant of volunteer labour and is able to expand and sustain it’s
activities.  Currently the organisation is vulnerable to collapse.  School Can’t
(SPSR) Australia has provided significant support to me.

7)  That School Can’t (SPSR) Australia be consulted in relation to or be tasked with
selecting research projects to recommend for funding to further develop
understanding about school attendance difficulties.  Lived experience
insight is very valuable.

8)  That each state and territory consider funding schools to receive training in and

coaching to implement Collaborative Proactive Solutions (Greene 2014:xi-xv) in
schools as an intervention which is highly successful in helping adults shift
from focussing on behaviour management to working together
collaboratively to identify the difficulties students might be facing and find
solutions.

9)  That each state and territory prioritise building institutional level awareness about
the nervous system.  Especially as we emerge from the collective trauma of
COVID.  Class regulation and student regulation has teacher regulation as
it’s foundation. Student regulation is also impacted by parent/carer
regulation.  When teachers are under pressure then they are less likely to
feel regulated and less likely to be able to help their class be regulated.
They are also less likely to be able to build relationships of warm regard
with students which promote feelings of safety and connection.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 116




 Recommend seeking training by Dr Lori Desautels1 for more information
about this.

10) That we shift from focusing on attendance to focussing on wellbeing and

encourage schools and families to be responsive to student capacity.  The
expectation that every student fronts up to school every day with the same
amount of capacity as every other student is not realistic.   School Can’t
children and young people need adults around them who are curious and
compassionate, who are responsive to the young person’s “felt safety”.  The
need to rest and restore is vital to wellbeing and permission to take time to
rest and restore is important.  The narrative that “attendance matters” is
detrimental to the wellbeing of vulnerable students.

11)  Condsideration be given to supporting parents of school can’t children with

indpendent advocates (preferably with lived experience as a parent or child)
who can attend meetings with them.  An independent advocate can make
recommendations for ways that students can be supported at school,
supported to return to school or support families to find alternative ways to
access education for their children.  Meetings at schools are often very
stressful and few people can afford to take professional help with them to
meetings.

12)

Provide positive messaging about forms of schooling other than mainstream

schooling.  For many students distance education, home-schooling, or
flexible alternative schools provide what they need either temporarily or for
the long term.  Too many times parents are discouraged from exploring
these options by professionals with the warning that the child will never
develop social skills if you don’t send them to a mainstream school.  This
fear is not founded and frequently prolongs the experience of suffering.

13)

Improve teacher training in how to create quality learning plans that meet
students where they are at.  They need help to understand how to build
learning experiences that promote feelings of success for diverse learners.
They need support to understand how to make adjustments to curriculum
and how to choose appropriate accommodations and supports.  Too many
learning plans look more like behaviour management plans than learning
support plans.  Professionally I’ve seen many learning plans that are a

1 Lori Desautels: https://revelationsineducation.com

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 116




 laundry list of the things the student is going to do differently or better,
rather than being a list of things the school will do to support the child to do
well.

14)  Review financial supports for parents who are caring for school can’t children.
The financial strain of trying to juggle work and sometimes unpredictable
caring responsibilities places strain on families that is passed on to students
and delays recovery.  This is particularly difficult for single parents who
must work. The cost of therapy and assessments and the loss of wages is a
substantial impost on families with single parent families very vulnerable.

15)  Review financial supports for parents who home school due to disability or

school can’t.  Current financial support for parents educating a child at home
does not come close to reflecting the cost of educating a child in a
mainstream school environment.  The funding for a student with disability
or school can’t enrolled in a mainstream school should follow the student
to home education or in home support if that is what the student has
capacity for.

16)

That a review of literature about the benefits of interest based learning be
conducted in consideration of the needs of school can’t students.  I have seen
the benefits of interest based learning for my own child when seeking to re-
engage her in school based learning and have also witnessed the impact
following this approach has had on many other students.

are Falling Through the Cracks and How We Can Help Them, Scribner, New

Submission:

Senate Inquiry into School Refusal/ School Can’t

16th December 2022

Brief History of School Can’t Journey

Our school can’t journey began at the age of 5 (Kindergarten), our son had struggled in
preschool at times but for Kinder to Yr2, at least a third of the time mornings would range
from tears and eventually go in with support from Mum, to extended periods where
teachers aids would meet us at the car and gently restrain him until I was gone.

Yr3 was the only year where I would say 80% of the time he managed to get to school
without at least tears. I attribute this successful year to his teacher at the time who
understood his struggles and worked intensely to make him feel safe at school, adjusted
assessments such as speeches and allowed him the autonomy at school events such as
assemblies, school performances etc to participate at a level he was comfortable with.

During the first covid lockdown he still partially attended due to my work commitments, still
struggling but at a lower level, I feel as at this time there were less students, no assemblies
to be expected to get up in front of, no performances etc., so school wasn’t as
overwhelming. The second lockdown he remained at home and following this his school
refusal was severe, with little to no attendance from term 4 of year 4 and into year 5 (2021).

He has a diagnosis of anxiety and with school threatening court action compounding this
anxiety by term 2 we applied to home school and have been home schooling since. His
anxiety has also led to an additional diagnosis of depression because of the struggles he
faces due to his anxiety.

Negative impacts on our son:

•  At the point his school refusal became severe, physically he lost 5kg, was nauseous,
declining meals, had diarrhoea every day, was struggling to get to sleep, having
nightmares and waking 5 times per night. Mentally, his anxiety became worse, and

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 117























 he became depressed, voicing suicidal ideation and stopped enjoying and
participating in activities he had previously loved.

•  Students seeing him upset and in turn bullying him for the same causing further

trauma, adding to depression and anxiety

•  The trauma of getting to school and the physical and mental impacts of this
•  A lack of validation and trauma from principles and a support teacher – “you got

here yesterday, why can’t you get here today”, being dragged out of the house by
school staff, comments such as

 as well as telling him he needs to come to school or school

liaison, then police get involved then your Mum has to go to court.

•  His own negative self- image as he views himself as weird or strange, as he wanted

to get to school but can’t.

•  The negative impact on his self-esteem because of the schools’ behavioural

approach, feeling like he had failed each time he didn’t meet an attendance plan
they had made him sign

Negatives that have impacted the family through school can’t include:

•  The emotional and mental trauma of seeing his level of distress to us as parents and

his siblings

•  Loss of income – My capacity to work has reduced by half
•  Loss of contact with family and friends that have opinions such as ‘you just have to

get them there’ and that mental illness isn’t a thing

•  Loss of time spent with other siblings as like any other illness there is extra support

required, appointments etc.

•  Cost of alternative education, for example
•  Stress of constant phone calls with the school, I was required to call daily and

provide doctors certificates for all days absent

•  The time and emotional energy lost to getting him to school, fear of court action

etc. when the focus should have been on our sons health and well being as opposed
to ticking a box that he was at school.

•  Frustration at the stigma and judgement when a child has a mental illness
•  Anxiety affecting other areas of our life from family dinners to holidays etc., where

we must consider his window of tolerance when planning these things

•  A lack of respect from the school for both my opinion as a parent but professional

opinion also.

Lack of validation was a major issue

•  When deputy was asked if we would be having the same conversations re court etc if
the child had cancer and was too tired to attend school – response “that’s different
they are sick”

•  Being asked for doctor’s certificates then being told that even with these the deputy

was not going to ‘justify’ the absences as questioned our sons’ mental illness
diagnosis

 •  Email to the Director of Education for our region stating concern at the practices of

the school such as:
  Bullying to the point I allowed them to drag my child from his home,
  Advising parents to isolate their school can’t children to force them into

attendance without being professional psychologists and the risks this poses
  A behavioural approach to managing a mental illness eg. We think it may help if
he is in a class with his teacher from yr.4 who is now teaching yr. 5 – ok we can
trial this - managed 4/5 days but as he didn’t attend the 5th day was sent back to
previously assigned teacher

  Comments from support staff and deputy to my son (aged 10 at the time) that he
had to go to school or there would be police involvement and I would have to go
to court if he did not attend

  Recommendations that this practice be reviewed to prevent further trauma in

the future for other children

  Request for more psychological support in the school and further training of staff

This email was replied to with the director pretty much saying the principal refutes
my claims of any wrongdoing from the school, that the deputy apologised for his
comments re police and court involvement, that I assisted in the removal of my child
from the home so that’s on me and that all has been done to assist my child. No
phone call or meeting just an email – case closed. More upsetting was that I
highlighted in my email that it was not written to blame anyone but more to seek
out discussion on how this could be improved so that the next families experience
isn’t so negative

Positives to school can’t experience

•  My son had an ILP for each year of schooling that included learning more about
hunting, fishing, mountain biking etc, the school could not accommodate these

around these topics.

book work for maths, Science, English, geography and HSIE, I use these interests to

•  The relationships we have established with other home-schooling families

With his

Access to Supports

what support was available, and how to access this, although there are wait lists for services
of at least 6 – 12 months in our area. The school initially was not aware of my work.

 for 10 years, so I knew

Within the school we were never once offered counselling at school, only the advice from
the deputy that we had to make home as boring as possible, not to allow him out with
friends to play, ride or any other extra-curricular activities.
