 Initially trying to get support in yr 5 I had contacted the school voicing my concerns and it
was 6 weeks before I had a meeting. Then suddenly it was all about how we were failing by
not getting him there. It was frustrating that I was aware of strategies such as partial
attendance, school liaison etc., but had to fight for these things to occur and despite the
psychologist and myself recommending that enforcing increasing attendance when the first
level was yet to be met was detrimental and creating expectations increased the anxiety this
was ignored.

When trying to assist our son in getting to school his psychologist contacted the school,
though the deputy principle questioned her advice and as she stated was very difficult to
communicate with.

Our request for Distance Ed on special circumstances was refused as he didn’t have a letter
from psychiatrist when school was aware there was an 8 month wait to see the psychiatrist.
At a later meeting and the final before moving to home-schooling, where the Health and
Wellbeing officer attended, she asked why the school counsellor could not have approved
this? I questioned why then the psychologist couldn’t have completed the necessary
paperwork and was made aware that this could have occurred.

We also requested work from his teacher to complete at home, this was denied by the
deputy, yet we were the ones being accused of educational neglect. Stating that teachers
can’t be expected to teach in the classroom and from a distance point of view also. At our
final meeting the Health and Well Being Officer also asked why this could not have occurred
and the deputy replied this had not been implemented as the teachers are too busy and he
doesn’t see a need as our son just needs to come to school. The deputy also stated that “I
don’t see what
won’t as the child has an internalised illness, not a behavioural issue”.

 see’s” to which the Health and Wellbeing Officer replied ,“you

Within our area there is also a 6 -12 month wait in our area for Occupational therapy,
another option explored in his treatment and $160 - $200 out of pocket for each visit.

Home-school and School Can’t Facebook pages have been a great source of info for
additional support, alternative learning environments, resources for learning and the
information regarding the Isolated Child Payment.

Barriers to attendance what worked/ what didn’t work

What worked?

A supportive teacher who removed expectations and didn’t enforce participation in anxiety
inducing activities was what worked best. He felt safe, heard and validated with this
teacher.

What didn’t work?

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 117







 Creating plans that had rewards and consequences for attendance that had to be signed by
our son – increased anxiety and lowered self-esteem when he was unable to meet the
expectation

Dragging him to school - he would internalise his anxiety while there then explode or
breakdown once home. He later voiced on these days he wouldn’t be able to concentrate
and learnt very little

Threats regarding police and courts – increased anxiety and reduced trust of staff and
school itself

Teachers that feel they know best and enforce participation in events such as book week
parade, end of year concerts etc, despite requests that this was not to occur, including a
letter from his psychologist.

Are there any proactive strategies to prevent school can’t - what could school have done?

Linking children who have anxiety in with the school counsellor early in their journey and
having a plan that all staff are aware of to provide support and enforcing staff stick to the
plan, leaving their personal opinions aside.

An increased awareness within staffing bodies at the complexity of mental illness and how
to better respond and that mental illness is exactly that an illness not a choice.

Early intervention to focus on skills building as opposed to restraining children

Has my conceptualisation of school changed because of our ‘school can’t’ experience?

I have always been aware of the many different pathways for the later years of high school
and now strongly believe that this should be replicated through infants and primary school
in the mainstream system also.

As we have moved through our home-schooling journey our younger son is now also home
schooling. We decided this as he also began struggling to get to school and we could see
how positive home-schooling had been for our older son.

I hadn’t realised until this point the autonomy and power of each individual principle/
deputy principle has dependent upon their view of the situation. For example, when I
advised our older son would be home- schooling we were forced to continue developing
attendance plans, advised that due to the wait time for registration the issue with non-
attendance may be escalated toward meeting with further external bodies in the interim.
However, when I advised the school (same deputy) that my younger son would also be
going to home-school the response was thanks for letting us know, please forward your
registration certificate when it becomes available. It would have been helpful in the first
instance had they been supportive and placed less demands on us at a time when our son
was suicidal and in crisis, where obviously as the later shows it was the deputy’s choice as to
how he managed this.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 117
 I find this ability of senior staff to make decisions based on their assumptions, beliefs and
values quite frightening.

I still feel the school system works for those children it works for but when a child does not
fit the box there is not much room for flexibility. Schools are great for those who are
academic, sports stars etc but for those who aren’t I feel the system fails to acknowledge
their strengths and value as a person.

Summary

Our school can’t journey has been quite traumatic for all involved, when senior staff can
accuse us as parents for not getting our child to school, as failing them in relation to
education I ask the question – Is a child sitting in a classroom with internal turmoil really
getting an education – no, their attendance is simply ticking a box.

Recommendations

A focus on a child’s strengths not deficits, what is the child doing well, how can the school
continue to support them at home to maintain that relationship, build trust and respect.

That schools have knowledge of all possible pathways and discuss these with parents such
as home-school and partial attendance, as this would reduce the pressure on the child and
the family as opposed to the stress of being threatened with police and courts which adds to
an already stressful situation.

A move away from focusing on what children are wearing as if the child is at school and
comfortable is this not more important than how they look.

A Health and Wellbeing Officer available in all schools to assist and support school can’t
children and their families, as opposed to a principle/ deputy in a position of power with
KPI’s in the back of their mind addressing the situation.

That teachers aides supporting students with mental illness have qualifications in this area
to adequately support the student.

That principles and deputies no longer have the power to override a medical certificate and
deem an absence as unjustified based on their own opinions, beliefs and values.

That if work is requested by parents, this is accessible so the child can continue to complete
work at home on the days they are well enough to do so.

That all teaching and senior staff in schools are given further training in mental illness,
including seminars where school cant families have the opportunity to share their journey of
what has worked  and what has caused further trauma.

That when children in the early years of school show signs of anxiety there is a program
available with the focus is on building skills to manage their anxiety for both parents and
students to attend, as opposed to the practice of having support staff take them in, with a
view of you’ll be ok now.

Submission:
Brief history of school can’t for my child: risk and protective factors across all ecosystems

School can’t is complex and multi factorial. There are risk and protective  factors across the
child and parent ecosystem, the peer group ecosystem, the school ecosystem and our
broader society. Conceptualisations and understanding of schooling and education reflect
on how children experience schools and learning.

We are a family of four and both parents have university level qualifications. The sole
income earner works as a senior executive at one of the largest global
companies. Both of our children have had school can’t for varying reasons and suffered a
range of sequelae as a result of having school attendance difficulties. With much learning,
healing, patience and time our two children are now happy, healthy and thriving young
adults.

We have come to understand that children who have school attendance difficulties
accumulate different risk and protective factors  across the ecosystems that students are
embedded in and moreover that it is vital to manage those risk and protective factors in
order to reduce the prevalence and negative impacts of  school attendance difficulties.

Significant risk factors for school attendance difficulties for our children included:

•  our son has ADHD (inattentive) and dysgraphia. He was premature and also has an

eating disorder.

•  We moved states just as our son commenced year 7 and our daughter started year 5.
•  Our daughter has ADHD (inattentive) and dyslexia.
•

In the current school system, neurodevelopmental disorders can be considered to be
a risk factor for school attendance difficulties given the lack  of systemic
misunderstanding, knowledge and skills within schools.

•  Another risk factor is that as parents we were not aware of the phenomena of school
attendance difficulties until they occurred. We did we know how to manage, and yet
nor did the school or schooling system.

•  Another huge risk factor was that both children suffered degrees of bullying at

school. My son suffered image based abuse published on social media. Our son was
also the target on a campaign of gatekeeping by a senior teacher that resulted in him
feeling persecuted and alienated.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 118










 •  Our daughter was bullied by her peers due to her dyslexia and certain teachers who
did not understand dyslexia implied she was simple minded and lazy. The response
by the school was adhoc and neither child felt supported.

Suggested solutions from the school and first psychologist comprised of punishment, blame
and shame. Parents should be able to trust that schools and mental health clinicians
understand school attendance difficulties. However our trust was misplaced when our
relationship and attachment with our son was damaged and he became further traumatised
by the professional’s recommendations.

Likewise, it’s important for parents to learn about protective factors for school attendance
difficulties. We developed problem focused coping strategies to deal with the stress and
distress associated with school attendance difficulties and furthermore so we could assist
our children to manage their own difficult emotions around school can’t.

We spent many hours researching the scholarly literature surrounding school attendance
difficulties, child development, attachment and relational neuroscience. We came to
understand that there are evidence based ways to reduce barriers to learning for children
with learning difficulties and neurodevelopmental disorders and that these in turn assist
with student engagement in school.

We relied on the support of our General Practitioner (GP), a psychologist, a speech therapist
and specialised education tutor.  We focused on developing and increasing our own healthy
social supports which in turn helped managed our stress cycle, modelled other healthy
behaviours, we underwent a lens change, focussed on wellbeing and non-pathologising
views of our children, accepted and supported where they were at and remained hopeful of
positive change.

Impact of School Can’t for our children

Both of our children’s self esteem and self concept suffered as a result of school can’t. They
received many negative and traumatising messages from a public school in

 from  peers and teachers.

From a relational neuroscience view,  the negative social messages our children received
and stigma around school can’t did not help solve the school attendance difficulties and
contributed to increasing  trauma and anxiety around going to school. Stressful and
distressing school environments are not conducive to learning and children require
environments that are relationally safe.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 118










 Impact of School Can’t experience on our family and myself as a parent:

We found the school can’t journey to be very lonely. As parents we did the heavy lifting,
particularly myself as a mother. My mothering was constantly critiqued and this was very
distressing. We were blamed and shamed by other friends, family and particularly by the
school. The school were very upfront about the fact that they believed it was an issue that
belonged to us as parents and that there was  something wrong with  our children. The
school told us that “they knew of no other children with school attendance difficulties”and
that there was not much could do to help. We found out through an online group that this
was patently untrue and the school had multiple families in the same or similar situations.

Experience of supports

We were required to constantly advocate for our children and ask for supports.  We
initiated meetings to request learning supports and to ask for help around making school
feel like a safe and belonging environment.. When our daughter was diagnosed with
dyslexia in Year 7 the school wanted to offer our daughter coloured overlays in the
misguided belief this helped dyslexic learners read. As coloured overlays are not an
evidenced based solution for dyslexic students it was a waste of precious time and money.

The school actively tried to discourage our son from participating in his
him passing and sometimes in excelling in his subjects.

, this was despite

We have paid many thousands of dollars to access professional supports. We estimate it
amounts to $10000 to $15000 a year for both children. And due to these demands I was
unable to do paid work during the years of school attendance difficulties.

Our most effective source of support was the School Can’t Facebook group.

Monitoring and identification of School Attendance Difficulties

Neither of our children experienced school attendance prior to high school. The school
attendance difficulties remained unaddressed by  the school level until the end of Year 10.
The school’s contact with us for the senior years consisted of mostly of updating us on
attendance statistics and informing us about the possibility of failing
 based on not
meeting attendance requirements. We now question if given the lack of other supports that
tnis may have been a type of gate keeping for students who are at risk of performing poorly
 reducing g the risk of reflecting poorly on the school’s performance statistics.
in

We believe that had the school level risk and protective factors been better understood and
addressed, particularly prior to the senior years, that this would have been a significant
ameliorating factor to both children’s school attendance difficulties.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 118








 Summary and recommendations for the committee:

Key recommendations include:

•  The cultivation of calm schooling environments using the latest understanding of
child development, relational neuroscience and all schools being trauma informed
•  The implementation of truly inclusive schools where all learners are welcome and

belong

•  The utilisation of praxis in schools: teaching and school culture is embedded in

reflective and evidence based best practices

Family, social, cultural, educational and political environments all play a powerful role in
shaping our children’s behaviour. Attention should be focused away from blaming and
shaming children and their families and also look towards aspects of the environment that
on the one hand have powerful opportunities to protect, nurture and empower students
and on the other hand can also psychologically damage students and contribute to school
can’t.

There has been over 80 years of research into school attendance difficulties with very little
change. We cannot continue with our current conceptualisations and paradigm around
school attendance difficulties and expect positive and real changes. I have no doubt that the
senate enquiry will show that all ecosystems have a role in managing risk and protective
factors and they will need to be examined, evaluated and actioned at all levels.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 118

that is affecting primary and secondary school aged children, who are unable to

•  My son is bright & quirky- he is neurodiverse/ Autistic and has attention with

significant executive function difficulties (diagnosed with ADHD inattentive) yet he is
also gifted his Full Scale IQ is on the 99.5th percentile /extremely high and
generalised ability index is on 99.8th percentile /extremely high. He fulfills the
definition of twice exceptional- gifted with a disability/ies, these children are least
likely to be identified and/ or supported adequately.

•  Under the Disability Discrimination Act 1992, and Disability Standards for Education
2005, my son should have all necessary provisions to allow him equal access to
education- put simply, this does not occur.

•  Schools rarely offer flexibility, and often have many imposed rules, routines,

structures, and sensory stimuli that are not in the best interest of all students, some
aren’t in the interests of any students.

•  My son benefited from the reduced extraneous stimuli of the classroom that remote
learning offered – be that the pressure of having peers around him, the need for
certain behaviour – direct eye contact to “show listening” and paying attention, noise/
sounds, smells, people encroaching on his personal space, less direct attention and
need for eye contact and set behaviour (e.g. a good learner looks like – everything
most neurodiverse children struggle with).

•  Schools use a behaviourist approach, looking to modify behaviours rather than

looking at behaviour as the sign of an unfulfilled need or a lagging skill. This results
in outdated approaches that can be harmful for students that merely force a child to
suppress the said “undesirable” behaviour, sometimes simply to confirm to a
neurotypical view.

•  For the first 18 months or so of Australian’s pandemic response, there was a

collective focus, led strongly by state government and enacted by education, health
etc to actively reduce Covid-19 transmission and protect everyone.

•  Since “opening up” or “let it rip”, the absence of any real mitigations for a level 3
biohazard, is well evidenced by the ongoing significant Covid-19 transmission in
schools. This reality, has forced children and their families to choose between in
person school attendance and continued forced infections, or forgo in person school
to learn remotely either via distance education/ online or home schooling, this is
particularly pertinent with the child/ren/ family have higher risk/s.

•  My son has a better understanding of how Covid-19 spreads via aerosols produced
when we simply breathe, talk, laugh, sing, cough etc than most in the education

 On the first day of Term 2, my daughter was hesitant to go in to class. I didn't push her,
feeling that if given time she would choose it freely and in a more relaxed way. Her
psychologist and occupational therapist agreed that a slower approach to separation was
best for her.

I didn't want to leave her with the feeling that she would have to stay there regardless of
how much of a fear state she was experiencing. More so because of the teachers' opinion
that reducing demands on a child during times of overwhelm simply reinforces avoidance.
I couldn't trust them to decide at what level of overwhelm to call me. The level of
overwhelm in a particular moment needs to be the key for whether we either challenge a
child to grow, or focus on helping them to feel safe. I didn't feel heard on this point.
Without trust between family and school staff, it was impossible to give my child
confidence in the environment.

I sat with her for a few minutes outside the classroom after the bell had gone, and soon
there were support staff, teachers, and the principal saying my daughter needed to go in.
She immediately stopped working up to walking through the door, and shut down. This
pressure continued over the following days, with the principal allowing only short times
for my child to try to settle before saying it wasn't working; blaming my child for the
problem

and calling us in for a meeting, in front of her, showing us how many

absences she'd had over those first few weeks of term.

Teachers also tried to use happy, confident momentum to call her in, but this didn't address
her concern about feeling trapped when I left. It genuinely wasn't intended as emotional
manipulation, and they wanted to help her feel welcomed, but it was adult-directed and
non-collaborative.

Compliance culture wasn't the right answer. Despite the care, it also felt like dominance, a
threat to both individuation and individual needs.

In meetings with my child's teacher, the head teacher of Kindergarten and the school
psychologist, they told me that she was 'normal', that my anxiety was the problem, that
attendance was not negotiable, and that it was traumatising her that I wouldn't just make
the choice for her.

I agreed we couldn't let that continue, but forcing her into an environment that felt
controlling wasn't an option. Ignoring her opinion without being there to see the dynamics
also doesn't seem right. She really wanted to try to attend.

I also knew from experience with her that, given choice and much less pressure (no time
limit for normalising attendance), she could have loved school and engaged with it. I wish
she could have felt safe and made it through the transition, choosing it for herself.

I think the ideal situation would be a homeschooling arrangement, where I am responsible
to
attend school by choice as well. Schools could also have more staff and systems
specifically devoted to keeping track of content students haven't learnt (whether due to
absence or not understanding classwork), and working as an intermediary between
teachers, families and students, to help them catch up using a flexible, streamlined
sequence and approach with a needs-led timeline that students feel genuinely receptive to.
I see some of the value in scripted lessons and term-based planning, but it shouldn't always
be about keeping up with the class.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 120 To regulate her sensory system, my child needs time to wander, to build, to dig in the dirt,
to play with water, to talk about her interests, in and around her ability to focus with
engagement on syllabus learning. She enjoys group work, but gets burnt out by too many
hours of adult-directed learning. Chronic stress doesn't make people stronger; it can create
negative ways of coping. She needs to be able to choose to take time off. But she still
needs the supports that are mostly channelled into schools.

She needs more intrinsic motivation, more talk about the reasons (and possible options) for
behaviour boundaries. Less of the praise/reward economy, which only works because kids
internalise the need to please the adults in power. This isn't 'positive' behaviour
management; it's essentially the flip side of shame and punishment. It leaves some kids
behind, while causing others to 'succeed' anxiously.

My child needs adults to guide and support her, but less of the sense that adults are
choosing the emotions kids should be feeling. Less competition on particular tasks; more
open-ended collaborative learning, even while explicit instruction and meeting of
standards are woven through, with a focus on pathways through literacy and numeracy.
This is even more so for Middle Schoolers, while they grow through a mostly social focus.

Schools need enough staff to create effective teams for planning and replanning. And
children, all children, need a foundation built on curiosity, reciprocal and receptive
relationship, and sensory/emotional regulation.

Regarding post-lockdown increases in school refusal, I've also heard a lot of families who
started homeschooling after Covid lockdowns, just because they saw how much their
child's mental health improved when they were learning from home.

There are certainly many cases where lockdowns created anxiety, too. The school system
still needs to look carefully at the overwhelm caused by attendance pressure and by the
long hours in a compliance-based, mostly adult-led environment. Not everyone can engage
with this without it affecting their mental health, yet schools won't support students unless
they commit to (or quickly work towards) full time attendance.

Thanks for considering all these things with us.

Introduction

I am a mother of two neurodiverse children. My youngest child has experienced school refusal
(which is better described as “school can’t) since Year 3. I would like to share my family’s
experience of school can’t within the public education system in

My autistic son attended a mainstream public primary school from Kindergarten to Year 2,
where he made friends and achieved very well academically. However, in Year 3 (2019) he
started to resist attending school. I believe there were two reasons for this. Firstly, his new
teacher was inexperienced and underestimated my son’s academic potential (due to believing
that if a child is autistic, they must also be intellectually impaired) and he also did not meet my
sons needs in the classroom. Secondly, my son's physical disability was also not appropriately
catered for and he was not offered realistic alternatives to participating in sport.

Despite actively engaging with the teachers, support staff and principal at the school, the school
was very inflexible in its approach to meeting my son's needs and my son became more and
more anxious and distressed about attending school. By Term 4 of Year 3, my son had stopped
going to school altogether. His school-based anxiety was so overwhelming that he could not
attend school at all.

I therefore requested that our primary school make an access request for my son for an autism
class. The
 Department of Education was unable to offer us a place in an autism class, but
we were offered a place in a multi-categorical class at another primary school, some distance
from our home. As I was so desperate to have my son return to school, I accepted the
placement. However, despite assurances from our new school that they understood autism and
school refusal, my son's school attendance did not improve.

The new school was equally unsupportive as the old school. Both schools made me feel judged
as a parent and that they blamed me for my son's school-based anxiety. Their view was that he
seemed fine at school, so it must be a problem with the environment at home. My son, like
many autistic children, would mask while at school. He was obedient and did what he was told
and never had any behavioural issues at school. However, as soon as he got into our car at the
end of the school day he would break down, angry and crying and overwhelmed. I understand
that this is a common experience for autistic children.

As the specialist class was not meeting my son's needs, we made the difficult decision to
withdraw him at the end of the year. To our great disappointment, his original mainstream
school advised that they could not allow him to return. We were an out-of-area family and they
advised that they were oversubscribed and unable to offer us a place. However, we had only
agreed to try the multi-categorial class at another school on the promise of the principal that we
could return to the original school if the new placement did not workout. In fact, my son would
not have agreed to try the new specialist placement if it were not for that promise from the
principal. I believe that the principal did not want us to return to the school due to my son's
autism and school-based anxiety. I believe that she felt that our situation was too difficult for
her to manage. My feelings were reinforced when the principal refused to even put our son's
name on the school's waiting list

Needless to say, the principal never contacted us about this.

impaired or just average, have a right to a public education. All children should be valued,
included, understood and accepted at public schools. Children with a disability should have the
same opportunities as children without disability. They have a right to a future. Because this is
not the case we have a rising tide of school can’t.

Terms of Reference

a. The increasing number since the COVID-19 pandemic, of young people and their families
who are experiencing school refusal

The COVID-19 pandemic and the related online learning due to lockdowns did not affect my
child’s school can’t experience.  In fact, both my children hated online learning and largely
refused to participate in online lessons.  Participating in Zoom lessons caused them great
anxiety and they both prefer face-to-face learning.  For some children there is a perceived divide
between school and home: school is where they go for lessons and home is their safe place.

b. How school refusal is affecting young people and their families and the impacts it is having
on the employment and financial security of parents and carers

As outlined above, school can’t has had an overwhelming and negative effect on our family.
Additionally, as I now homeschool, I am unable to have paid employment and this is causing our
family ongoing financial difficulty. For example, we have recently had to forego important dental
treatment because we cannot afford it.

c. The impacts and demands of the increasing case load on service providers and schools to
support these students and their families

d. How relevant state, territory and federal departments are working to monitor and address
this growing school refusal challenge

 Department of Education at all levels (from classroom

My experience with the
teachers to the Minister) has been an overwhelmingly negative one. I do not believe that they
are working to address the school can’t challenge in any meaningful way. They simply continue
to blame parents and to engage in threatening and punitive actions towards families
experiencing school can’t. My experience is that they are completely uncaring, unsupportive,
uncompassionate, ill-informed, unkind and ableist. They do not practice their own policy of
inclusion and have effectively abandoned school can’t families. I believe that schools and the
Department of Education would just like the problem to disappear.

e. any other related matters.

Australian Senate Committee Enquiry into School Refusal

Thank you for the opportunity to share my experience as a parent of a child who would be classified
as a ‘school refuser’, based on his limited attendance at school / online, and submission of
schoolwork. I started writing this submission in November 2022. I have been updating it to reflect
delays and progress in my son’s year level completion, the agreement of his school to allow him to
proceed to Year 12
, and diagnosis results in late December 2022 from a
new psychiatrist’s review and testing. I mention these points partly to explain the delay in providing
my submission to the Committee and partly as an example of some of the ways that school refusal –
including attempts to try to work out why the school refusal has been occurring - impact our ability
individually and as family members to plan, to readjust, to complete projects, and to support one
another.

This brief submission focuses on Point b from the terms of reference:

how school refusal is affecting young people and their families and the impacts it is having
on the employment and financial security of parents and carers

The reason I am drafted this submission is to stress how difficult it is to know how to address the
issue of school refusal, even for parents with sufficient knowledge and enough resources to seek
support for their child from many education experts and mental and physical health professionals.

My husband and I have not found the causes simple to identify and we’ve found the solutions very
challenging to identify.

Our son’s experience of school refusal

I realise there must be many different circumstances in which teenagers refuse to attend school. In
my son’s case, he did not start refusing to go to school on a regular basis until he reached Year 9.
This started occurring significantly in mid-2020, and my husband and I initially attributed this to the
impacts of the lockdowns
schools (he had been accepted into

 a select entry government school in

 as well as changing

 which commenced in Year 9, in 2020).

For context, my son had exhibited signs of anxiety prior to 2020. For a couple of years in primary
school he had been seeing a psychologist for OCD (particularly related to hand washing / germs), and
then later, social / generalised anxiety. Part of this treatment had involved a couple of sessions with
a psychiatrist – and this previous experience was in fact the reason he was able to become a patient
again with his current psychiatrist, at a time (2020) when it was so hard to get appointments as a
new patient. One of the reasons he changed schools in 2020 was to address his desire for an
environment where he was better able to focus and learn at his local government secondary school.
He had found it hard to focus at his previous school. We put this down to the fact that, while he had
friends, they did tend to muck about (as can often happen in Year 7 and 8) and that
School was more likely to have more focused students. However, although the new school had
positive aspects, it also meant that, when Covid 19 lockdowns were introduced after only six weeks
at a new school, he did not have a friendship group to support him through what turned out to be a
long period of remote learning.

Page 1 of 5

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 123



 In 2020 and 2021, my son outwardly changed from someone who had been an active participant in
at least two, and up to four, sporting teams on the go at any one time (most recently including
, as well as school bands and leadership roles, to someone who

would not get out of bed, who lost weight, couldn’t concentrate, and would not communicate. From
the start of Term 3 in 2020, he refused to turn on his screen for classes, and soon stopped attending
all together. My husband, son and I had numerous online meetings with his school’s wellbeing team
and year level coordinator and attempted (unsuccessfully) different time management and work
strategies. My son was also fortunate to be able to be seen by a psychiatrist (again, online) as well as
a psychologist, and together with the school, we all tried to work out what might be able to help
him.

Fortunately, Covid 19 restrictions were lifted for a few weeks before the end of 2020 and he was
able to reattend school in person. While he found it difficult to get to school on time (anxiety kicking
in), he was much more comfortable once he made it to school. He managed to complete Year 9.

Year 10, however, continued with more lockdowns and the challenge to maintain momentum.
Students in Years 7-10 had the longest period of remote learning compared with other school levels,
and I do not believe they really returned to school prior to end of year exams. My son found the
same difficulties as in Year 9 and exhibited more extreme reactions and opposition to remote
learning. He was becoming more and more isolated as he withdrew into his room.

My son tried meeting with different psychologists with different approaches, his psychiatrist was
looking for different causes and techniques, but for reasons we are still not clear about, my son
could not apply the approaches proposed. The challenge was two-fold – we had a son who insisted
he wanted to be at the school he was (in theory) attending (although rarely logged on), and we were
trying to work out if the covid lockdowns were solely the cause – and if so, if there was a better way
for him to navigate through – or whether something else was at play. The lockdowns continued. Our
son managed to scrap through Year 10, with some grace on behalf of the school in terms of
deadlines, and we hoped for a more straightforward Year 11 in 2022.

Late December 2021 – January 2022 appeared to demonstrate that, if Covid lockdowns were the
reason, the recovery would not be quick. Our son spent a large portion of the school holidays in bed,
online or asleep, and was extremely irritable. He started the school year reasonably positively but, as
he had not developed good study techniques and started slipping behind as he did little to no
homework. And then he started resisting attending school again. The support systems remained -
psychologist, psychiatrist, wellbeing support at school – however he was very resentful of having to
attend (to his parents, certainly, and lashed out verbally when reminded of appointments, regular
taking of medication, and application of the systems that were recommended and that he had
verbally committed to). We could see that there appeared to be something else occurring but could
not work out what was going on. His psychiatrist was also puzzled and referred him as an inpatient
to a private mental health hospital
 for a second opinion regarding medication, to
determine whether there was another underlying issue, and also to enable 24-hour oversight.

This period in hospital may have helped from a diagnostic perspective, but it also led to some weeks
lost to schooling (not possible to maintain as an inpatient with both medication changes, psychiatric
appointments and a program of therapy classes and sessions), slipping behind in his subjects in Term
3, as well as more weeks after leaving the hospital as he adjusted to the impacts of a varied medical
regime (for instance, medication which takes 9-10 hours to leave the system and therefore makes
one sluggish in the mornings – when needing to get ready for and leave for school, as well as the
first couple of periods). This created a very challenging process of trying to catch up in Term 4.
Thanks to his school providing a lot of support and extra time, he scraped through technically

Page 2 of 5

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 123
 completing this year level (eight subject units assessed as an unscored ‘satisfactory’), and he is
enrolled to undertake four Year 12
more enthusiastic.

 subjects in 2023. He is still tired, but slowly appearing to be

He had also recently seen another specialist, who just prior to Christmas has provided a verbal
diagnosis of high functioning autism. We will be provided with a written assessment in mid-late
January 2023, so are yet to properly understand what this means. We have been advised that our
son may also need to see an Occupational Therapist to assist with some other underlying issues
identified as part of the autism diagnosis.

Direct impacts of school refusal

I have outlined the school performance issues above, but for us, these are not the biggest challenges
of school refusal. The more significant impacts relate to perceptions of self-worth and competency,
the way so much of our family focus is on the school refuser and trying to change him, and how this
impacts his relationship to us as parents (and vice versa), to friends and others, and the impacts to
our other child.

There is an intense feeling of ‘wrongness’ that comes with school refusing, which has coloured our
relationships with our son, with each other, with our other child who, despite our efforts can be
neglected in the quest to address this ‘problem’ of school refusal, and more broadly with family and
friends who try to assist but cannot understand why it seems so difficult to solve. School refusal
presents a particular problem when the refuser insists he wishes to be at school and does not want
to choose a different pathway but becomes overwhelmed at the thought of attending school.

I cannot speak for our son, other than to report on his verbally articulated frustrations with his
slowness / challenges in getting ready / getting to school / focusing on work. I can say, though, that
for me, I was confronted with the same dilemmas each day (or several times a day) when I watched
him not doing what he says he wants to do:

•  Do I stand back and leave him to try to sort it out?
•  Do I intervene and become too controlling (not to mention, take on his problems and take

his autonomy)?

•  Do I treat it as a phase?
•  Do I try to help solve and fix (in the short term – or in continuing to search for diagnoses or

similar?

•  What am I trying to fix / solve – whose decision and to what end?

There is a constant sense that everything is wrong:

•  My son is wrong in being unable / unwilling (we are never quite sure) to get out of bed and

go to school, do homework, or (during lockdown) to work online.

•  My husband and I are wrong in not knowing how to support him and not being able to find
the ‘right’ psychiatrist / psychologist / therapist / medical specialist to diagnose what the
cause of the refusal is, not finding the right medication, right way to coach him, right way to
motivate him.

•  The school he attends is wrong for him – maybe – so should he change, or should he do

something else? But he insists on attending, and (particularly during lockdown), would any
other school be any better?

Page 3 of 5

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 123
 •  The ‘specialists’ who cannot find / fix the problem – why not? How do I know they are right?
When it comes to mental health, it does seem that the professionals come to treatment
with an pre-existing presumed approach and apply this, whether it is effective or not.

Living life as if everything is wrong is not a way to live life. My husband and I feel we are constantly
focused on negatives, partly because we continue to proceed along the standard track of one school
year following the next school year. There is limited scope, if this is the path we follow, to stop and
allow for adjustments and treatments. At the same time, when we do stop, it seems our son doesn’t
know how to start again. It means we don’t really know what we should be doing – and it seems that
no one else does, either.

Also, by focusing on the problem, we are obscuring our son. He has become a problem to be solved
rather than a person to love, who should have autonomy and responsibility of his own.

Indirect impacts of school refusal

In listing the activities of the past few years, I have referred to many specialists, as well as medical
treatment and hospital admissions. This approach to trying to address school refusal has been
expensive financially and very time consuming.

Getting our son to school, and school meetings (which for large parts of 2020 / 2021 – and towards
the end of 2022, were held fortnightly, or even more frequently) has often eaten into our working
days, requiring flexibility from our employers. As a result, there has been some impact on our
effectiveness at work, and certainly for me, career opportunities and progression. For my husband,
who works in
 the added pressure at work during the peak of covid outbreaks was
compounded by the challenges at home.

Having said that, both of us are fortunate to be employed by organisations

 where there is a level of flexibility that other workplaces may not provide. This would be

considerably worse for people who do not have the relative job security we are fortunate to receive.

A significant impact has been felt by our daughter, who is going into Year 10. Like her brother, she
started a new school in 2020 (Year 7) however did not have the same level of resistance to remote
learning. While she didn’t love it, she attended more, and has integrated back into in person
learning. She has, however, been impacted by the focus we have given her brother and the tension
that has existed within the household. We have been aware of the tendency to overlook the ‘non-
problem’ sibling(s), which in more extreme cases are referred to as ‘glass children’ (because you see
right through them and don’t notice themi), and, while we have tried to avoid this, we have not
completely managed it. We are managing an easily triggered level of resentment as a result, and
while we hope this will be overcome over time, it has been an impact that I want to ensure that the
committee is aware of.

Summary

This submission has been provided mostly as an example of the experience and implications of
school refusal. Unfortunately, we are not at the other side of this yet (and may never be) and so are
not able to provide any significant solutions for your consideration.

One element which we would encourage you to investigate, particularly if anyone with expertise
could comment on this, is some clearer way of being able to navigate the mental health system for

Page 4 of 5

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 123


 support. As noted, unlike others, we have been fortunate to have relatively short waiting periods to
see psychologists and psychiatrists and have been able to see them within a couple of months at
most. I know this is not everyone’s experience.

However, it does feel as though whoever we see has a narrow focus on the problems and solutions.
For instance, our son’s recent diagnosis of autism came through a referral from our psychiatrist to
another psychiatrist who specialises in autism diagnosis. This specialist said in passing that virtually
everyone referred to him has been found to be on the spectrum. Our son has had many diagnoses
over the past few years, and while this latest one may be correct, it also brings to mind the saying: ‘if
your only tool is a hammer, everything looks like a nail’.

It would be very helpful if there was some greater assistance in navigating the system, beyond the
directives of General Practitioners who are currently so overstretched, and who have such short
time periods to meet with patients. It would be very helpful if there was an intervening triage
system, for instance, after a GP referral but before meeting with a mental health professional, which
was focused less on prioritisation and more on pointing towards a useful direction in finding more
specialist assistance. I am not sure how this could operate, but as mentioned, I would hope someone
who has more intimate knowledge of the system may be able to assist.

In addition, the Committee is encouraged to consider whether some appropriately qualified
counsellors may be able to also assist in the provision of services. In addition to the psychologists
mentioned, we had met with a couple of counsellors who seemed to be able to provide useful
assistance but, as no Medicare rebate was available, they were too expensive for us to continue to
meet with (when added to the psychiatrist / medical costs). Given the shortage of appropriate
services as well as the assistance that counsellors could provide (if meeting the right training
standards), we encourage the Committee to consider whether extending access and rebates may be
beneficial.

Thank you again for providing the opportunity to make this submission.

School can’t began for my child in April 2021, when she was 8 years old and in Grade 2.  This started
Brief history of school can’t for my child
because of a health experience that she experienced as traumatic at school.  She was completely
unable to attend school, aside from periods of online learning until October 2021.

She returned to school with support from a particularly kind CRT and from our own psychologist.

She attended school quite happily for 3 terms but in term 3 this year this became more difficult due
to disruptions due to Covid and other illnesses disrupting her own attendance and that of her
teacher. My daughter is autistic (level 1) and changes to routine and teachers/caregivers are very
difficult for her. Her school also removed the support of an aide to help as she entered school in the
morning at this time, without consultation.  We persisted through term 3 with considerable support
from me, my child was able to enter school and wait in reception for up to 45 minutes before feeling
able to attend classes for the rest of the day. At the start of this term the school once again changed
her routine and on day 4 a teacher failed to follow her support plan and call me when requested.
This triggered my daughter’s trauma response about being trapped and she has been fully unable to
attend school this term, aside from spending 10 minutes before school each morning with her teach
and 10 minutes as the class arrives. As soon as roll call begins she has felt trapped and needed to
leave.  After applying considerable pressure to the school, the school then put an aide in place to
support her until 8.45am. This means my daughter can attend roll call but at 8.45am each morning I
get a call to collect her.  We did have a positive experience at camp as the school worked closely
with us to provide flexible support and my daughter was able to attend 2 of the 3 days of the
program, however the school has declined to provide similar support to access school. My daughter
has now missed seven weeks of learning and counting this term.  We have requested work to be
sent home from the school but we have received very little aside from the standard homework
which each student receives.

Impact of School Can’t on my child, my family and myself:
My daughter has missed a whole term of learning in Grade 2 and now also a term in Grade 3.  Her
Impact of School Can’t experience on my child:
experiences of wanting to go to school with her friends but being unable and being publicly anxious
and struggling have diminished her general confidence and her mental health, making her flat, and
lethargic.  She feels she is a failure because she cannot fit in with a system that was not designed
with her needs in mind and which will not flex to meet her.  She deeply misses her friends and the
fun shared experiences they shared and their comeraderie and feels shame she cannot join them.
She is also falling behind in social skills – as an only child who went through the lengthy
lockdowns of 2020 and 2021 she is now missing even more social time.

It has been tough on our relationship and I am her primary carer, trying to find school work /learning
for her to do and get her to do it, seek the mental health support she needs, and advocate for her
with school, all while pushing her out of her comfort zone every single day.

We have no family support in our state and the impact on my mental health has been tough at
times, and I have had to seek help from my GP and counsellor. I did not return to work in 2020 or
2021 due to the increased support my daughter needed in learning through lock downs and school

 attendance problems in 2021.  I returned to work this August for the first time in over 11 years,
given a great chance to re-enter the workforce and re-start my career. Due to my daughter’s school
attendance difficulties I had to resign in November.  My workplace were very supportive and I know
have a more junior role, only 2 days a week and an exemption to work from home. My pay has
halved and my work performance is severely impacted, but at least I still have a job.  This is
particularly important as we are having to privately fund a tutor to try to catch up on maths, and co
payments for GP, psychologist, paediatrician.  As my daughter is level 1 ASD we receive no NDIS

School can’t has been tremendously isolating for me.  I lost my community of parents and social
contact and struggled to be able to leave the house due to caring for my daughter. It’s hard to know
what to say to other parents as you don’t want your child to be judged or to share their private
information.  You also never know when things are going to get better, or if they will.  At its worst
my daughter could not leave the house at all and thus neither could I.  Even getting groceries was
impossible.

It has caused a strain on my relationship with my husband as we are essentially co-workers in a very
tough situation – with enormous pressure, stress and uncertainty.

In addition to the above comments I spend all my spare time reading about how best to support my

,

traumatised at school in 2021 and it was a terrifying time for our family as her mental health was so
bad that she was saying she didn’t want to be alive any more. It look us several weeks to find a

did an ASD assessment (which we paid for privately) but this needed to be validated by a

recommended social groups which we can’t yet access due to wait lists and equine therapy that we

 The school (private) have behaved appallingly and we will be leaving, even though change is
incredibly hard for my daughter and she wants to remain in a familiar school with her friends.  Last
year, at the start of our school can’t journey they were very well aware of her mental health
challenges but started a conversation with me with “How would it be for [child’s name] if she didn’t
come to [school name]  any more?’. In the same meeting they threatened to get the Department of
Education to fine me if our child couldn’t attend.  They wanted us to physically force her in, which
we had tried early on but it compounded the trauma and our psychologist was strongly against it.
Despite her diagnoses – ASD (1), GAD, phobias they have continued to be difficult to deal with,
unwilling to acknowledge her needs and unwilling to provide sufficient flexibility to meet them.  We
believe that they are failing to meet their obligations under the Disability Discrimination Act and
Standards for Education but have neither the time, money nor emotional bandwidth to fight them
any longer. We have to put our focus and energy into moving forward positively for our daughter.

My daughter does have an emotional and social support plan with school but it is treated as a form
filling exercise and little practical support has been forthcoming. Her needs vary depending on what
has happened recently at school and her generalised anxiety levels but the school just doesn’t belive
that these needs are real, much of the time and certainly does not react quickly.

The School Can’t facebook group and Yellow Ladybugs
providing a sense of not being alone, not being judged, and providing avenues to support – for
instance the School Can’t facebook group put me in touch with the ACVD which is an amazing
service and helped a lot with understanding my daughter’s rights and what can be done practically
to help her.

 facebook group have been invaluable in

none the less the school threatened to report us to the Department of Education, however, when I
spoke directly to the department they were very supportive.

In the second period of school can’t this year my child has attended every morning for 10 minutes
with the teacher but panics and asks to leave at roll call. In the latter part of the term the school has
provided an aide to cover until 8.45 am and my child leaves after that.  The school hasn’t told me
how they are reporting the absences but they aren’t making threats any more which is something.

Barriers to attendance.  Things that have worked and things that haven’t:
Forcing – doesn’t work and causes more trauma.
Thinking about treatment/responding to school can’t:
Kindness and patience and an adult with time to provide unhurried support – helps (even if it’s the
receptionist).

Flexibility to respond to changing needs and to truly listen to the child, parents an external support
team – if it’s missing nothing will work.

Psychological support and anti anxiety medication also help in my daughter’s case.

Page 4

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 124


 Giving the child a sense of choice and agency throughout the day.

The school has often tried to use other children as supports eg walkling in to school woth friends.
This has helped when she is well but when she is very anxious she needs the support of a warm
trusted adult and children are unequipped to deal with her needs.

Thinking about proactive strategies to prevent school can’t:

In my daughter’s case it was originally triggered by the trauma of being left lying on the
floor in pain for two hours before receiving any medical attention for her/calling us
(abdominal pain).  The second phase of school can’t this year was due to the school not
meeting the needs for adult support and consistent implementation of support plans
Givng the child regular trusted adults to connect with and a sense of agency and choices is key. And
required by an autistic child with trauma.
lots of encouragement as the system is telling them they are failing whereas in fact the ‘one size fits
all’ system is failing them.

How has your relationship / conceptualisation of education changed or been challenged
Kindness, warmth, empathy and flexibility are everything. You can’t trust private schools as kids with
as a result of your parental lived experience of school can’t?
disabilities and challenges aren’t as protected eg the school can deny your request to have an
advocate attend meetings.  It doesn’t matter how amazing their program is on paper if your child
can’t access any of it and there are unwilling to help her try.  In our case we are moving to a smaller
more supportive school with a less fancy program and facilities but more adults available and a focus
on warmth and community inclusion.

Families dealing with school can’t need support, not threats.
Summary and recommendations for the committee:
Private schools should be required to support students with trauma and disabilities (especially neuro
diverse students) and families of these students as much as those in the government sector.

Covid was already a particularly tough times for neuro divergent children – this is compounded by
schools not meeting their needs – especially the need for flexibility and a sense of secure connection
with adults.

Although financially  and emotionally strained and work impacted, our family has the education and
skills to try to navigate the threats, needs and supports needed. It has still be brutal, devastating and
ultimately we can’t manage the David and Goliath flight to get the school to meet our daughter’s
needs.  Advocacy services are vital but not funded – they should be.  As should independent
mediation services to help schools and families work together to meet students needs.

We are considering moving our child to a small alternative independent school – we are fortunately
that we can afford to do so but many children with similar needs may not have these met in the
public sector.

 Independent schools may be more open to welcoming and retaining neuro divergent children if they
had access to funding for aide support on a par with the government sector. This aide support is
make or break for my daughter – with it she can attend and without it she can’t – but the school is
unwilling to provide more than 30 minutes per day.
