Grade 6, who has experienced School Can’t from the beginning of school and is the child
referred to throughout this document; and a neurotypical child going into Grade 4, who has
never experienced School Can’t.

. We have two school-aged children: an Autistic child going into

 with more than 20 years’ experience

Our story of School Can’t predates the Covid-19 pandemic; I would say it even predates
school. It is the story of a girl who is kind and creative, intelligent and conscientious, the sort
of child you might expect to enjoy and do well at school - and she does both of those things.
And yet, she has always had difficulty getting there. Nearly every morning she freezes at
some point while getting ready, as her nervous system detects that she is headed towards
danger - towards an intense and exhausting environment where she has little access to her
safe people, spaces, objects and activities.

Not being familiar with the term ‘school refusal’ or understanding how our nervous systems
perceive threat and safety, I previously framed this difficulty as separation anxiety. From
when she was a tiny baby, my child always seemed to feel most secure in my presence and
had trouble separating from me. Preschool drop-off was regularly difficult. She had trouble
getting ready to go, would resist going, and would cling to me when we got there. School
was the same. By grade 2 (when she had no close friends in her class) there were many
mornings when I left her crying in her teacher’s arms.

It was probably around that time that I heard of school refusal, along with its reframing as
School Can’t. I had never viewed my child’s behaviour as any sort of deliberate
disobedience – she was clearly having a hard time. It was also that year that I started
looking more deeply into the reasons for her difficulty going to school (and other places). It
wasn’t only that she had difficulty separating from me, she had difficulty entering the school
environment. She was diagnosed with autism as we were putting together the picture of why
school was hard. As I listened to Autistic adults online I began to see why the near-constant
sensory onslaught, social interactions, demands and expectations in the school environment
were overwhelming for her. As I was piecing this together, the pandemic arrived.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 125



 The lockdowns were very positive times for our family. The stress of school was gone and I
saw my child’s anxiety reduce greatly. We were not under any financial pressure and we all
enjoyed the extra time we could spend together. It was like a mental health reset.

It also allowed me to see how things could be different. Since having children and learning
about child development, I’ve been interested in alternative forms of education, as traditional
schooling seems quite out-of-sync with biological needs. My husband initially did not share
these views and our children are in a mainstream school. But he too could see the difference
learning at home was making, and we decided to look into homeschooling for our Autistic
child. However, she wanted to continue on at her school, because she has friends there.

When school reopened later in 2020, our principal asked me to put together a return to
school plan for my child (Appendix 2). I also made a list of various ‘stressors’ that tax her
energy and ideas for reducing them, in the hope that we could reduce her exhaustion from
school and help her feel safer there. With a letter of recommendation from our child’s
paediatrician, we requested keeping school hours at a ‘sustainable’ level for our child - that
is, whatever she could manage, and still have energy for life outside of school. The school
has continued to accommodate these requests.

School Can’t still affects our family. Reduced hours and other accommodations make it
easier for my child to get to school, knowing she won’t be pushed past her limits. The school
no longer sees her difficulty, as she can usually leave me at the front gate without too much
trouble and walk to her classroom with her sister or a friend. Yet she still gets ‘stuck’ most
mornings at some stage while getting ready to go, even if there’s something she’s looking
forward to. I’m just glad I found the information and resources to help me understand my
child’s experience and advocate for her needs.

Impact of School Can’t on our family

Impact of School Can’t experience on my child:

School Can’t (or the reasons behind it) has caused my child to miss many days or parts of
days of school, although never a lot of consecutive days, so there has been no sustained
disruption to her learning. She’s a quick learner with an excellent memory, which has made it
an easy decision to prioritise her wellbeing over her academic learning, but she has missed
a lot of curriculum. Last year’s reports show her missing an equivalent of 79.5 days; this
includes things like sickness and appointments, but is largely due to the reduced hours
which allow her to get to school at all.

I have been very careful to be supportive of my child throughout her experience, and have
never shamed or punished her for her emotions or struggles (this is not to say I’ve never
been frustrated or upset, but I don’t place blame on my child and I always repair ruptures in
our relationship). I hope this has been somewhat protective for her mental health, but I have
no doubt that being forced regularly into an intense and exhausting environment has caused
trauma. The reduction in her anxiety during lockdown showed just how much of it was being
caused by the school environment.

Impact of School Can’t experience on our family and myself as a parent:
My other daughter is often slightly late to school because of my child’s anxiety in the
mornings, but the biggest impact on our family is the effect on my mental health. Co-
regulating with a distressed child, and knowing I’ve sent her to a place that is not well suited
to her needs, is a huge drain on my emotional energy. It’s often hard to bounce back and get
any type of work done in the mornings, and sometimes leads to short periods of mild

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 125 depression. The reduced hours that enable her to attend school also require flexibility on my
part. It’s not practical for me to work outside of my home, and when I attempted to set up a
freelance writing business last year, I found the mental energy hard to come by.

Addressing barriers to attendance

Responding to School Can’t - what’s working:
The key to helping my child get to school more easily has been for her to know that she
won’t be pushed past her limits when she’s there. She needs to know and trust that her
teachers will give her breaks whenever needed, and that she can come home when she has
spent her energy for the day. I consult with her each morning about when I will pick her up,
with the decision based on a number of factors. Unless other commitments of mine make it
impractical, she knows that she can ask her teacher or office staff to call me to pick her up
earlier or later than planned.

Other accommodations that make it easier for her to be at school include using ear
defenders whenever needed, always being able to sit with a friend (as friends are her brain’s
main cue for safety at school) and not participating in activities that are overly stressful (eg.
timed quizzes, using paint, reading books with worrying themes).

Contrary to common advice, I’ve also found that giving my daughter breaks from school
when she is very anxious or nearing burnout has always made it easier, not harder, for her
to go back. I remember my husband was reluctant to let her have a day off preschool
because he felt that it would be harder for her to return, and he could see it leading to days
off school in the future. I gave her some days off - a break from the preschool environment
and the stress of being forced to go there - and she was much happier going back. This has
been my ongoing experience. Yes, she is missing time at school, but forcing her to go all
day, everyday would no doubt lead quickly to burnout or crippling anxiety and a necessary
extended absence for recovery. We shouldn’t be afraid of letting our children listen to what
their bodies are saying.

Responding to School Can’t - what’s not working:

When attendance tips in the school newsletter include lines such as ‘There is no safe
number of days for missing school’ and ‘Talk positively about school and the importance of
attending every day’, I don’t get the impression that the school understands my child’s
experience. It’s not their fault; there are many common narratives around children and
school that are accepted in our society. However, narratives are not facts, and this sort of
messaging causes anxiety rather than provides support.

The school leadership and my child’s teachers have all been caring and supportive, but I
don’t believe they are well-informed about the causes of School Can’t. We’re living in a time
when we know more than ever about the brain and body, and are beginning to recognise the
importance of listening to people’s lived experience. Our children need us to ditch the
narratives and delve into their human needs and experiences. Everyone who works with and
makes decisions about students - including education ministers, department of education
heads and staff, school leaders, teachers, aides, allied and mental health professionals -
would be much better able to support students’ needs with an understanding of:

•

the neurophysiological underpinnings of human needs and behaviour (including
concepts such as stress response, the autonomic nervous system,
neuroception, interoception, co-regulation and the vital importance of warm,
connected relationships for wellbeing)

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 125

 •

trauma-informed and trauma-responsive care (recognising that traumatic
experiences are not always obvious to the observer, school itself can cause trauma,
and that these strategies benefit ALL students)

•  neurodiversity and neurodiversity-affirming practices, with a focus on listening to

people with lived experience

•  disability and inclusion (including an understanding of ableism and the social model

of disability) with a focus on lived experience
•  cultural safety with a focus on lived experience.

I would love to see all schools take a proactive, collaborative approach to School Can’t
(along with everything else that is currently framed as a behaviour problem). Dr Ross
Greene’s Collaborative and Proactive Solutions (CPS) model of care, based on the premise
that ‘kids do well when they can’, is an ideal approach with a focus on problem-solving.

The benefits of using this model to support students experiencing School Can’t (and other
‘behavioural’ issues) include:

•  getting to the root of the problem for a more sustainable solution
•  more effectively understanding and supporting neurodivergent students and others

who may have more difficulty meeting expectations

•  strengthening the adult-child relationship, which is foundational to wellbeing, along

with the school-family relationship

•  working in sync with the latest scientific understandings of bodies, brains and

behaviours, rather than taking for granted outdated societal ideas.

CPS, and other respectful and curious approaches such as those I’ve listed in Appendix 1,
would be far more effective in discovering and addressing barriers to school attendance,
than occasional notices in the newsletter, compliance-based strategies that employ rewards
and punishments, or placing the problem solely with the child’s mental health.

Proactive strategies to prevent School Can’t:

While I’m extremely grateful for the school’s accommodations, I would love the school
environment to be such that it didn’t take every ounce of my child’s energy. True inclusion
happens when we collaboratively create an environment where everyone can thrive, and
where it’s normal to flexibly cater to diverse needs without accommodations singling
students out as being different. Truly inclusive schools will look quite different to the
framework we’re familiar with and we need to actively pursue the change.

When we think about the fact that human brains have changed very little for thousands of
years, yet human societies like ours have changed dramatically, it is little wonder that mental
health problems are increasing and School Can’t along with them. The stress of the
pandemic may have added fuel to the fire, but it’s long been burning. Schools were not even
originally designed with children’s biological needs in mind, and they certainly weren’t
designed with neurodivergent students’ needs in mind.

Imagine if we conceived of schools as communities of people who genuinely know, love and
support one another; communities that are flexible in meeting humans’ diverse needs, with a
holistic view of human flourishing, rather than a narrow view of education. Imagine how that
might change the lives of children experiencing School Can’t. Children spend upwards of six
hours of their day at school. They live there for that time. They need school to be that place.

I realise that reconsidering the function and structure of school is a huge undertaking, but I
believe it is a necessary one if we want all students to thrive and remove barriers to
attendance. Just because we’ve been doing something for a long time doesn’t mean it's a
good fit. Some of the topics which should be up for reimagining include:

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 125 •  Attendance. The requirement for ‘full attendance’ seems to be based on the fact that
the curriculum is designed for it. It’s not based on any biological need for children to
participate in adult-led learning for a particular amount of time. There are many
reasons why full attendance is problematic; for example, neurodivergent children like
mine may not thrive in the environment, it may be impossible for children with chronic
illness, and pandemics are also known to cause difficulties! Re-thinking both
attendance requirements and the curriculum structure is overdue.

•  Autonomy. Control and compliance are like pillars in our education system, and yet

research strongly suggests that autonomy is necessary for psychological flourishing.
Students are micro-managed all day long, which not only forces them to override
their interoceptive sense of their own bodies’ needs, but robs them of the autonomy
they need to develop optimally.

•  Play. We understand the importance of play for young children, but it is rarely given

any priority in the school setting and is generally seen as less important than
‘learning’. Yet children continue to learn most effectively through play long past the
preschool years.

•  Self-directed learning. Humans learn effectively when they are interested and

motivated. While there are obviously some important skills for students to learn, the
education system’s complete top-down control of what and how students learn
effectively squashes students’ natural curiosity, creativity and motivation to pursue
what interests them.

•  Nature. Research is showing the importance of nature for wellbeing. Our culture’s

tendency to see humans as separate from the rest of the natural world has led us to
exploit and damage our habitat. For the wellbeing of our children and their home,
living among and reconnecting with nature is vital (and First Nations peoples can
teach us a lot about this).

•  Music. Like play, music seems to fall out of favour in the school setting. Music is
thought to be a fundamental part of human evolution, and is linked to things like
learning and social connectedness. Containing it to specialist classes greatly limits its
benefits.

Summary and recommendations for the committee:

My child experiences School Can’t because of a mismatch between her way of being in the
world and the school environment. She does not have a behaviour problem, nor can we
solve the problem merely by ‘fixing’ her mental health. Other children’s experiences will be
different. Only an individual, collaborative and curious approach can solve the problem.

The knowledge and tools for solving School Can’t are readily available; the hard part is
getting them into the education system, especially as they involve a shift in thinking from
behaviour management to problem solving, and within a context where change is difficult
because of the ever-turning cogs of the system we’ve created.

These are my recommendations:

1.  Create two key competencies for all education staff: an understanding of the

importance that children have warm, connected relationships with caregivers, and the
ability to provide that relationship in a school setting; and the ability to approach
‘behavioural’ issues, including School Can’t, with respect, curiosity, collaboration and
a problem-solving mindset - as ‘lifelong learners’, you could say.

2.  Have education departments reframe ‘school refusal’ as School Can’t, or similar

terminology that recognises students are experiencing barriers to attendance, and
start educating schools about the barriers. Please look into the work of and get in

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 125 touch with Dr Naomi Fisher in the UK. She is a psychologist who works with young
people experiencing School Can’t, and she has written extensively on this topic. (see
Appendix 1)

3.  Work towards training all school staff (and pre-service teachers) in Collaborative and
Proactive Solutions (or other similar frameworks that use respect, curiosity and
scientific knowledge to understand behaviour and provide support). Dr Ross Greene
met with the NSW Minister for Education last year and is keen to work with Australian
departments and schools. I understand that he will be training the new behaviour
specialists in NSW.

4.  Work towards training all education staff (and pre-service teachers) in: the

neurophysiology of behaviour; trauma; neurodiversity; disability; inclusion; and
cultural safety. These can’t be one-and-done, tick-the-box type trainings.
Understandings in these areas are dynamic so training must be ongoing, with a
commitment to changing mindsets and practices, and it must include trainers with
lived experience.

5.  Work towards reimagining the function and structure of schooling.

6.  Ensure that any working groups have participation and representation from all

appropriate parties - including students.

Thank you again for this opportunity. I dream of a day when every school is an inclusive,
flexible and nurturing community where every child can flourish. It will require curiosity,
creativity and courage to step out of the comfortable narratives that have been shielding us
from understanding the complexity of human experience. Our children are counting on you
to take strong, brave steps towards making this happen.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 125

 Appendix 1 – Resources

The following are excellent resources for helping educators move towards a
neurophysiological understanding of behaviours:

Dr Naomi Fisher – Barriers to education
https://www.naomifisher.co.uk/

She has also written extensively about School Can’t and related topics on her new Facebook
page: https://www.facebook.com/drnaomifisher

Dr Ross Greene – Collaborative and Proactive Solutions model for identifying and solving
problems that cause concerning behaviours

https://livesinthebalance.org/

Dr Stuart Shanker – Self-Reg framework for understanding and dealing with stress
https://self-reg.ca/

Dr Mona Delahooke – Neuroscience-based tools to transform childhood behaviours
https://monadelahooke.com/

Dr Lori Desautels – Educational neuroscience
https://revelationsineducation.com/

Kelly Mahler, Occupational Therapist – Interoception resources
https://www.kelly-mahler.com/

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 125




 Appendix 2 – Back to School Plan (returning from
lockdown)

Overall aim: That *student* may participate to her full potential in school activities and life
outside of school, including being supported to develop understanding and strategies around
her particular needs and self-regulation.

Immediate – Week 1, during remote learning

·  Continue with remote learning, including flexibility to modify tasks if needed.

·

If teachers are at school, offer *student* the opportunity to meet and visit the
classroom.

·  Meet to discuss stressors in the school environment and ways to reduce them.*

 Short-medium term – Return to onsite learning

·

Limited hours – gradual increase (assess weekly).

·  Allow *student* to chew gum on walk to classroom.

·  Teachers begin implementing strategies to reduce stressors.

·  Find calm activities that can give *student* a rest from stress while at school.

·  Teachers to check in on *student* as a precursor to self-advocacy (find mutually

suitable ways of communicating).

·  Keep hours at a sustainable level (*student* able to participate in life outside of

school).

·  At home, *student* to practise strategies for understanding her own needs and self-

regulation.

 Longer term

·  Continued ‘accommodations’ to reduce stressors in order to keep them at a

manageable level, including keeping hours at a sustainable level, whatever that may
be.

·

·

*Student* able to understand and articulate her needs and use strategies for self-
regulation.

*Student* able to participate to her full potential in school activities and life outside of
school.

*All stress – including good stress – uses energy, and as an autistic person, *student*
experiences many stressors in the school environment. Keeping stress at a manageable
level will enable *student* to learn freely, self-regulate effectively and participate fully in life.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 125

Committee Secretary

I only learned about this Senate Inquiry today when I listened to ABC Radio
you are still receiving submissions, but I hope that someone may read this and note my
comments. In the past years I  have been writing to numerous people in government and have
recently made a submission to the Disability Royal Commission in an effort to gain more support
for my 8 year old neurodivergent granddaughter who is autistic with a Pathological Demand
Avoidance (PDA) profile.

. I am not sure if

I am a retired pre primary teacher with 40 years teaching experience so I feel qualified to express
my observations about the positive and negative experiences of neurodivergent children in our
school system from the perspectives of a teacher and a grandparent.

BELONGING, BEING & BECOMING -The Early Years Learning Framework outlines these outcomes
for ALL our children. Sadly, many children like my granddaughter are not able to attend school so
their sense of belonging, being and becoming is compromised.

My granddaughter is home schooled. This is NOT a fuzzy lifestyle option or for religious or any
other philosophical reasons. She simply cannot tolerate the sensory, academic, social, emotional
and mental demands required of her in our school systems. Her paediatrician has confirmed this.
My granddaughter’s mental health is our priority.  She coped with kindergarten because the
program was part time, play based and child led. She was not coerced to participate in classroom
activities; instead encouraged to participate when she was interested or felt comfortable to do
so.

Terms of Reference

a. The increasing number since COVID-19 pandemic, of young people and their families who

are experiencing school refusal;

I am not in a position to know about the increasing number of “school refusal/ school
can’t”  since the COVID-19 pandemic. My granddaughter had already experienced
separation anxiety and reluctance to attend pre kindy and kindergarten prior to the
pandemic so there is no link in her case.

b. How school refusal is affecting young people and their families and the impacts on

employment and financial security of parents and carers;

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 126 My daughter, my granddaughter’s mother, needed to resign from her permanent
position in the
teacher. I look after my granddaughter 2 full days per week so that my daughter can
work part time and have a little respite time. I do not grudge this, but I feel like I’ve never
retired except that now I am not paid and don’t get holidays. LOL!

 to stay home with her daughter. I am a

 year old  retired

Children like my granddaughter tend to avoid direct demands, challenging tasks and
explicit teaching. They often learn by observing others so my granddaughter’s inability to
attend school limits these opportunities for incidental learning.

c.  The impacts and demands of the increasing case loads on service providers and schools to

support these children and their families;

In my granddaughter’s case there are few demands or increasing case loads on service
providers and schools because she currently receives very limited support. My
granddaughter receives some NDIS funding which is used for psychology support. My
granddaughter is too anxious/demand avoidant to actually attend in person so her
support is through sessions between her mother and the psychologist.

Her opportunities to connect and have a feeling of BELONGING are not optimal. She
attends a weekly home co-op group with her mother. This is held in someone’s garden
or at a public play area. These facilities are not ideal in hot or wet weather and have
limited resources.

I have suggested that the
hubs for these children and their families. I made a detailed submission to the

 government investigate setting up meeting

 Education Department, outlining how hubs could operate and the benefits
they could bring regarding opportunities for families to connect and feel less isolated.
Meeting hubs could also help anxious children to gain confidence and be a bridge
between home and school. This was rejected by the
 Education
Department who restated that home education was a parental responsibility and that
the Department already funded home education moderators. This is true. My
granddaughter gets one visit each year!

Neurodivergent/anxious children have additional needs so they need additional staff
support and flexible school attendance. This will obviously require increased and
appropriate government funding. Anxious children have elevated fight, flee or freeze
responses. Schools need to be more generously staffed to ensure the safety and
wellbeing of all children and to allow anxious children to choose activities that are of
interest to them and to work at their own pace. Mental wellbeing is the priority, not just
academic achievement.  Money invested in the school years will reap benefits in the
future and hopefully prevent dysfunctional behaviours that impact individuals, their
families and the wider community.

d.  How relevant state, territory and federal departments are working to monitor and address

this growing school refusal challenge;

I do not know how relevant state, territory and federal departments are working to

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 126







 monitor and address this challenge except that Lisa Rodgers, Director General of
Western Australian Education Department, has stated that she is setting up an Advisory
Panel to investigate how to improve educational opportunities for neurodivergent
children in the system.

e.  Any other related matters. Meeting Hub Plan below.

Copy of my Proposal for

 State Government funded “Meeting Hubs”

 recently I learned that
After listening to Director General for Education,
the Education Department is currently setting up a special committee to examine Best Practice options for
neurodivergent children in our state.

, on ABC Radio

I would like to propose that more resources and support are offered to neurodivergent children who are
home schooled because they cannot cope in the school system .

I have attached background information for your information to explain my professional and personal
experiences with autistic children and the school system in
Andrew Whitehouse.

. This was sent to Professor

I would like the committee to give serious consideration to the possibility of setting up drop in centres in
various locations to operate as “Meeting Hubs” to provide social opportunities for children who are not able
to attend school due to their high levels of anxiety or other conditions. These children would continue their
home education pathway, but would have a safe space to visit with their parent/carer to experience
opportunities to socialise and have access to a variety of different resources outside of their homes.

Presently parents are left to source their own resources and opportunities for children to engage with peers.
This is an additional workload and expense for parents and does not always meet the needs of the
children. Some groups meet in outdoor spaces where weather extremes can be disruptive and/or
uncomfortable.

The “Meeting Hubs” could be set up in/on various locations and be funded by the State Government. At
present home educated children do not receive much funding from the Education Department, apart from
an annual visit by the Home Education Moderator.

The cost of staffing each “Meeting Hub” would be minimal as only one teacher or teacher assistant would
be employed and they could be operated on a part time basis. If these children could attend school they
would likely be eligible for 1:1 education assistant allocation. Home schooling is thus saving the
government money!

The “Meeting Hubs” would be a community support space for home educated children and their
parents/carers. There would be no assessments or compulsory attendance required or documented, except
by the child’s parents/carers as part of their home learning journey.

Many parents of home educated children do not need or want interference and control by the Education
System because they have tried various education systems, both public and private, which have led them
to home education as the only path to cater for their child’s education and mental well-being. Parents can
provide an environment that is tailored to meet the needs that are unique to their neurodivergent child. This
is essential for autistic children with a PDA (Pathological Demand Avoidance) profile. More details about
the challenges for children who have a PDA profile are outlined in my letter to Professor Andrew
Whitehouse at the Telethon Kids Institute.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 126












 The “Meeting Hubs” could be set up in/on available government owned buildings or land. They would
require facilities including toilets, kitchen and outdoor play space.

The main objective would be to provide a safe space for children (who can’t attend school) to have
opportunities to interact with other children without any pressure to join in or complete tasks. Also, to
provide access to a range of resources which can be changed as required depending on the needs and
interests of the children.

Age ranges (Primary and Secondary) would be catered for by allowing different groups to drop in at
different times on a part time
basis.

Each “Meeting Hub” (room) could be called a Drop In Club, Meeting Space, Activity Centre or whatever is
deemed an appropriate name to encourage children to drop in and feel at ease.

A parent or carer would be required to attend with their child in order to supervise and provide support. The
presence of a parent or carer would help alleviate the child’s anxiety. It would also ensure that the child’s
needs could be met individually (e.g. being able to go home when he/she wants to).

A teacher or education assistant would be employed to set up learning resources. It would be a space
where children could choose activities such as art; craft; games, puzzles, construction, books, etc. The
teacher/education assistant would be a constant person at the centre so that the children and parents feel
secure and supported.

Supervision and duty of care at the “Meeting Hub” would be a parental/carer responsibility.

Accountability for their own child’s home education would continue to be the responsibility of parents.

The teacher/education assistant would be a facilitator to encourage and guide the children. Group story
times, singing, etc. could be incorporated for children who want to participate.

Children would be enrolled on a needs basis to ensure that eligible children do not miss out if they want to
drop in.

There would be a cap (maybe 10?) on the number of children enrolled at each “Meeting Hub” so that in the
unlikely event that all
children dropped in at the same time the room could accommodate all the students and their
parents/carers.

To optimise the use of the buildings and to cater for older and younger cohorts perhaps children could be
grouped and organised to drop in on different days, as happens in our kindergartens at present and/or for
morning or afternoon sessions

Maybe a pilot centre could be established to assess the viability of “Meeting Hubs” for home educated
children who cannot cope in the school system.

I would be happy to help and collaborate.

To fund a centre where these children could feel comfortable “dropping in” so as to engage with resources
and activities not
available at home and to have the opportunity to interact with a familiar peer group, or even just to observe,
seems a very small request?

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 126 Thank you for taking the time to read this.

I am sure other people on the Committee will have innovative ideas to help support and engage children,
particularly autistic children with a Pathological Demand Avoidance profile.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 126

When he was seven, I had him tested for intellectual potential and academic performance. His potential was

potential. Other tests showed he had ADHD, mainly “inattentive type” with a tendency to “over focus”. This
meant he had great difficulty “splitting and switching” his attention between two activities or moving from

physical pain and over-sensitivity to crowds, bright lights and loud noises. I suspected he had Autism
Spectrum Disorder (ASD), but he refused to do any more testing so he still does not a formal diagnosis.

My son responded strongly to Ritalin; both his social skills and academic performance improved markedly.
But because stimulant-type medications suppress appetite and interfere with sleep, he was unable to take
them after school. This meant he was unable to concentrate enough to do any homework at all. When he

Dear Senator

Senate Inquiry into School Refusal

I am writing regarding the senate inquiry into school refusal.  I am the foundation Principal of Queensland
Pathways State College (QPSC), which was formally established in 2018. We are a specific purpose State
High  School  supporting  vulnerable  students,  aged  15  to  18,  at  risk  of  disengaging  from  mainstream
schooling in their senior years.  Many of our students would fall into the category of ‘school refusal’ prior
to enrolment at QPSC.

We  are  a small school with 6 campuses  across  Queensland, namely Brisbane,  Ipswich and Townsville.
QPSC has been built on the foundations of BELIEF, RESPECT, UNITY and STUDENT SUCCESS which are our
college  values.    Each  campus  enrols  approximately  30-40  students,  with  a  total  enrolment  across  the
college of 200 students.  We offer a 12-month, senior transitions program and further develop student’s
literacy,  numeracy  and  workplace  skills.    We  are  also  a  registered  training  organisation  (RTO)  with  7
qualifications of scope.

Our curriculum is complemented with external qualifications in areas of student interest, utilising school-
based apprenticeships, work experience, Vet in Schools (VETiS) and TAFE courses.  Our program includes
transition support at the completion to ensure all students can exit to further learning or employment
and link them to support services (e.g., health, employment, disability) if required.

We  have  developed  our  own,  evidence-based  wellbeing  program,  to  address  student’s  barriers  to
attending school.  Our topics include (but not limited to): locus of control, peer connection, cooperation,
empathy and self-worth.  Our curriculum has First Nations content throughout activities and our teaching
practice  acknowledges  their  ways  of  learning.    We  partner  with  organisations  such  as  The  Healing
Foundation, to ensure all staff are confident in their teaching capabilities and understanding of our First
Nations students and barriers they have faced.

Enrolment at QPSC is by referral only and students must demonstrate they face multiple and complex
barriers  to  education.    Referrals  come  from  other  state  high  schools,  however,  various  government

1

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 129











































 organisations (Child Safety, Youth Justice, Queensland Health) and other non-government organisations
(resi-care, private clinicians, private schools, special assistance schools) do make referrals.

Students attending QPSC are able to work towards achieving their Queensland Certificate of Education
(QCE) but not ATAR.  For students wishing to pursue university entrance post school, they enrol in various
tertiary preparation programs delivered by universities on exit from QPSC.

Our student self-disclosed data at enrolment, suggests disengaged students are challenged by multiple
complex barriers to education, which include mental health presentations (65%), trauma (34%), transient
families (23%), unstable housing (9%), gender identity (14%), bullying experiences (16%) and low school
attendance  (42%).    Our  Nationally  Consistent  Collection of  Data  (NCCD)  for  students  with  a  disability,
classified 80% of our students in 2022 with a disability.  The breakdown was 70% social/emotional, 10%
cognitive, with required adjustment levels of 43% at supplementary and 24% substantial.

We have a capped enrolment, limited by the number of campuses.  We are state funded, not federally
like other Special Assistance Schools.  Our enrolment process ensures that students can be referred to
QPSC at any time throughout the year and our curriculum delivery is student centred.  This allows students
to  progress  at  their  individual  pace,  and they  are  not  disadvantaged  if  they  need  to take  time  off  for
various reasons due to their complex challenges.

Our partnerships contribute to the success of the college.  We have formal agreements with Youth Justice,
Queensland Health and Queensland Police, where we all agree we have a shared responsibility to ensure
student success.  For example, when students require ongoing educational support while accessing health
facilities or youth detention, we work alongside these organisations so our teachers can still make contact
and deliver our curriculum.

Supporting  a  cohort  of  vulnerable  students  requires  a  different  staffing  allocation  compared  to
mainstream schools.  For each campus we have a fulltime Head of Department, 0.5 Guidance Officer, 2
teaching staff and 0.5 teacher aide.  We also have a student support officer across campuses to assist
students when they need help  with housing, transport  or gaining independence.  In addition,  we  have
additional executive team members that specialise in teaching and learning and health and wellbeing.
We also ensure our staff have time to manage their student case management workload and timetable
afternoon debrief to support staff wellbeing.

The curriculum at QPSC is delivered through a positive  teaching approach, which reflects a philosophy
that  is  respectful,  trusting  and  calm.    All  staff  at  QPSC  are  trained  in  Trauma  Informed  Practices,
Restorative Justice, Youth Mental Health First Aid and hold a Certificate 4 in Training and Assessing.  We
have  primary,  secondary  and  special  education  trained  teachers  to  support  the  various  needs  of  our
students.    This  minimum  skillset  allows  our  experienced  staff  to  support  students  and  collaboratively
develop a student’s individual learning plan, ensuring student voice is heard and supported.

Parent/carer  connection  is  established  when  students  enrol  at  QPSC.    Many  parents  share  feelings of
hopelessness, distress or disconnect from their child.  Rebuilding and supporting parents to engage in
their young persons educational journey is part of the outreach support we give to students and their
families.  We’ve established strength-based approaches to communication and connection.  Celebrating
success  with  parents  and  inviting  them  to  come  in  see,  connect  and  be  part  of  their  child’s  learning
journey.

By  utilising  a  highly  effective,  individual  case  management  approach,  that  supports  a  young  person’s
wellbeing and education, we are able to achieve high quality outcomes for our students which is evident
in our data.

PARENTS FOR TRANSGENDER YOUTH EQUITY
P.TYE.NSW@gmail.com

PGDC
PARENTS OF GENDER DIVERSE CHILDREN
info@pdgc.org.au

Transgender and gender diverse children –

Submission to the Federal Senate Inquiry into

The national trend of school refusal and related matters

March 2023

Submitted by: Parents of Trans Youth Equity NSW (P-TYE); Parents of Gender Diverse Children
(PGDC)

Authors:  Dr Cris Townley (P-TYE) and Meagan Moss (Founder PGDC)

This submission advocates for children and young people who are transgender and gender diverse
(TGD), and are living with School Can’t.

P-TYE is an advocacy group based in NSW, made up of parents and carers of transgender and gender
diverse children. PDGC is a peer support network of parents and carers of gender diverse children.
The online PGDC network has over 1,250 members. PGDC is based in Victoria, but has a national
membership. This submission is based on our own lived experience as carers and parents of TGD
children and young people, and our involvement in online peer support. If you would like to invite us
to appear as witnesses at a public hearing, we would be happy to do so.

Summary:

•  For some children, attending school is severely detrimental to their wellbeing.
•  The underlying reasons for an inability to attend school are not the same for all children.
•  Schools are hostile environments for transgender and gender diverse children, despite the

best efforts of some teachers and some schools.

•  Forcing a TGD child or young person to attend school is detrimental to their wellbeing.
•  Transgender and gender diverse children and young people want to go to school and want
to have friends at school. However, a significant number of them reach a point where they
can’t.

•  The child needs to be seen at the centre of an ecological system that includes family,

communities such as sports clubs, education environments, and their medical and (in some
cases) legal support team (Grace, Townley & Woodrow 2023; Robinson & Townley, 2023).

•  The mental health of transgender and gender diverse School Can’t children and young

people is poor, many TGD children self harm or attempt suicide. However, addressing the
problem as one of an individual child’s mental health is not the answer.

•  We must listen to TGD children and respect their knowledge of themselves and how they

want to be in the world.

•  Parents and carers are, in most cases, the best advocate for the child.

The impact on the child and family

We estimate that around half of TGD children and young people have an extended period of School
Can’t. Often, the child or young person is unable to leave their house, or bedroom, for months. This
places great stress on the family, who fear for their child’s wellbeing and education, and often have
to take time off work to take care of their child, with resulting financial loss. We reiterate, this

               1

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 130









 P - TYE
PARENTS FOR TRANSGENDER YOUTH EQUITY
P.TYE.NSW@gmail.com

PGDC
PARENTS OF GENDER DIVERSE CHILDREN
info@pdgc.org.au

problem can only be addressed in an ecological way, it is not only school environments and systems
that need to change.

Some TGD children who are disrespected by education environments disengage from learning, and
learn to distrust authority figures such as teachers, isolating them further. Sometimes this results in
behaviour that is self-protective for the child or young person, but results in suspension from
schools.

Research is needed into the prevalence of School Can’t for TGD children and young people, and to
document the impact on TGD children, siblings and families.

Parent/carer strategies

Parents and carers try a number of strategies over time to respond to deterioration in their child’s
wellbeing. Parents and carers usually start from a position of knowing very little about how to
support a TGD child or young person. Parents learn from peer support networks like Parents of
Gender Diverse Children. TGD children face discrimination in the school system (Ferfolja and Ullman,
2021). Parents act as advocates for their children in the face of sometimes ignorant and often hostile
schools and medical practitioners. Parents and carers:

1.  Engage with the school to advocate for change on matters such as:

Uniform – many TGD children have body dysphoria, and uniform requirements make attending
school difficult. For example, uniforms are often binary gendered, which is hard for non-binary
young people, or students who are forced to wear uniform of the wrong gender. Boys have to
wear white shirts, which can be difficult for trans boys who have breasts. The cut of trousers is
gendered. Body dysphoria can be reduced through simple changes like allowing different brands
of clothing in the right school colour, but this is read by schools as an infringement of rules which
is often punished. It helps some students to wear an item of clothing that reflects their identity,
such as colourful socks, which can also get them into trouble. If you haven’t had this lived
experience, these things sound minor, but they add to the ongoing stress of functioning in an
environment that feels hostile, and make a major difference in whether a child is able to go to
school.

Recognition of their child’s preferred name and pronouns - too often, school systems, processes
and attitudes refuse to enact this basic acknowledgment of a child’s identity and agency.
Without basic respect, people do not learn curriculum content. Instead, they learn not to trust
school as a place of safety.

Toilet access – Children and young people should be able to access toilets aligned with their
gender, if school toilets are gendered.

School climate - culture change is needed within schools. School should be places where there
are conversations about gender diversity, sexuality, and positive relationships. Teachers need
support and encouragement to challenge transphobia in schools. Children need teachers that
are able to challenge transphobia, and most do not have this (Ullman 2017).

2.  Seek out a different learning environment:

Change schools - This sometimes results in finding a more supportive environment for the child,
but more often does not. Some parents move house in order to try this strategy, leading to
disruption of family networks and a financial penalty.

               2

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 130








 P - TYE
PARENTS FOR TRANSGENDER YOUTH EQUITY
P.TYE.NSW@gmail.com

PGDC
PARENTS OF GENDER DIVERSE CHILDREN
info@pdgc.org.au

Alternative schools – these can be a smaller, more supportive environment for young people.
However, these are most accessible in years 10 and 11.

Distance Education – this can work for some children and young people. Distance education
schools are generally more supportive of gender diversity.

Homeschooling – this requires an extraordinary amount of work by the family, financial
capacity, and other resources.

TAFE – TAFE can be a better environment where students are respected, and there are fewer
unnecessary rules and a less punitive attitude. However, for most young people TAFE can only
be accessed many years after the onset of School Can’t.

3.  Attempt to access health care:

Accessing gender affirming health care such as puberty blockers at the onset of puberty, then
hormones that allow the child to develop physically in line with their peer group, improve the
body dysphoria, identity and self esteem of TGD children and young people. This results in safer
social interactions and improved engagement with community and school activities.

Accessing healthcare is difficult. Because of this, many TGD children and young people access
healthcare years after they should, which severely exacerbates School Can’t.

Parents struggle to find knowledgeable GPs, affordable medication, and knowledgeable
supportive practitioners. Accessing healthcare in the public system takes too long and is in many
cases limited. Accessing health care in the private system is expensive, and still hard to find
practitioners. Some practitioners would like to follow best practice guidelines but are
constrained by their insurance arrangements. Many parents need to seek legal advice or go
through the court system to access healthcare.

The impact of the COVID pandemic

For many children and young people, learning from home during COVID was beneficial as they did
not have to enter the school and classroom. In addition, their peers were also learning from home,
so they were safely able to be part of a collective experience.

Systemic solutions

There are many resources available that could be used to address this problem across the child’s
ecological environment. A lack of political will and a hostile media prevent change, and our children
are the casualties.

Listen to children and young people. They are awesome.
Improve school cultures (Stapleton & Morris, 2021).

•
•
•  Have conversations in schools about gender diversity.  Over 80% of Australian parents

•

want schools to discuss gender and sexuality with children (Ullman, Ferfolja and Hobby,
2022).
Improve access to gender affirming healthcare for TGD children and young people. See
the Australian Standards of Care endorsed by the Australian Professional Association for
Trans Health (Telfer et al. 2020)

•  Change in education policy to embrace an affirmative approach using a trans-inclusion

model (Horton & Carlile 2022)

•  Develop and use resources for teachers and schools (Horton, 2020)
•  Empower young people to change their school cultures and create connection and

learning  through LGBTQ and Ally networks

Less punishment, more affirmation

•  Relax uniform requirements
•
•  Create flexible pathways across schools and distance learning options
•  Support community sports clubs to be more inclusive of TGD people (Australian Human

Rights Commission, 2019)

Thank you for this opportunity to present our experiences.

Mansfield Autism Statewide Services
Submission to Inquiry into The National Trend of School Refusal & Related Matters

Key Recommendations

1.  Increase the availability of early intervention and transition to school programs for autistic children –
families can wait for years for diagnosis, and even with a funded plan often struggle to find service
providers with vacancies.

2.  Incorporate Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) training as a requirement into

a.  relevant undergraduate degrees and certificates including for Education Support Officers and
b.  professional development opportunities for teachers and allied health professionals.
3.  ‘Inclusion’ is not a panacea for all; we need more satellite classes and special schools including for

those with an IQ over 70 as with our highly successful Dookie Campus.

4.  Low attendance rates must become a responsibility for school to follow up and report with a flag or
trigger for intervention.  High attendance rates but low enrolment hours eg 2 hours per week, masks
the problem & the lack of compliance with the requirement to produce a formal plan to increase
enrolment hours must be addressed.

5.  Resolve the disconnect between the NDIS & Education Departments/schools for improved whole of

child wrap around learnings & outcomes.  NDIS funding does not cover 9-3, making it very difficult for
whole of child handover and learnings.

6.  Provide additional public infrastructure funding for the expansion of the Mansfield Autism Statewide
Services model, as per ‘Operation Gamechanger’, to provide increased capacity and services for
families living with autism and training opportunities for teachers and allied health professionals, in
the context of a world’s best practice Therapeutic Care Farm.

7.  Replicate the Mansfield Autism Statewide Services model of wrap around care across Australia, that
includes the in-home practitioners, who can also work with the child’s family, community, support
workers, teachers, ESOs and school.

8.  Review proposed changes to NDIS for unintended negative consequences.  Example: Proposed

changes to the NDIS to abolish the Appeals Tribunal, will be vastly detrimental to autistic children,
many of them school refusers.  The bulk of students referred for Term Therapeutic Placement only
occur after successful appeals.  The program is not well understood by NDIS planners, but the well-
established benefits for the child and family are transformative.

Diagnosis: Inattentive ADHD, Sensory Processing Disorder, OCD

The immense family stress and confusion dealing with school can’t has prompted me to write this
personal account to submit.

Our emotions are still in turmoil after dealing with a “school can’t” NOT a school refuser.

Welcome to the world of a family with a neurodivergent. The child that is slipping through the safety net
of education. The quiet child sitting in a corner trying to act normal, hoping the teacher doesn’t ask
them a question that will expose that they AREN’T.

Already from an early age knowing that they are different. Wondering why they don’t understand the
work and where to start. Triggered by too much noise and the seams in their socks and underwear.
Confusion daily as this happens and not able to communicate to anyone their dilemma. Exhausted from
masking their true selves. Maybe they have friends but maybe they struggle as the kids around them
sense they are different. Maybe they can be annoying and don’t read social queues. Imagine being that
kid that once finally diagnosed is made to feel broken and unsupported. The schools only focusing on
trying to fix them and making them conform into this outdated conventional system of neuro-typicals.

My son’s school can’t journey started a couple of years ago. He had often told us he couldn’t focus at
school. We brushed this off as he was meeting the school’s standards. His behavior was exemplary and,
on the outside appeared engaged and happy. The teacher was shocked when we told them how
unhappy he was and that he was struggling. It seemed that as the workload increased,
couldn’t keep up and didn’t know how to articulate this.
 had only a brief period of lockdown
and as an essential worker my son was still sent to school when possible. School refusing was probably
triggered after Covid as perhaps
 enjoyed staying at home as it was his safe haven and the world
had become an uncertain and scary place.

felt he

Still feeling unsupported at his primary school, we moved him to a smaller school which helped in the
short term. This year, 2022 was the first time it was compulsory for year 7’s in South Australia to move
into the secondary setting. This was a disaster for our son. He was overwhelmed and wasn’t coping with
his transition at a busy new catholic school. The solution after several meetings, was to give him a card
to leave the class when required, but he didn’t use it once. He didn’t want the other kids to notice.
Didn’t want to be asked where he was going? An advertisement that he was different. When he finally
got the courage to ask for help in the class, he got told its high school now so you have to lift your game.
Learning is self-directed. A bad nightmare to someone with faulty executive function and virtually no
working memory. He wasn’t offered the struts required to survive in this environment even after we
finally got the diagnosis from his psycho-educational assessment mid-year. The school counsellor
suggested we look at another school. Obvious to me, that they didn’t know how to deal with his
challenges.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 133




 Schools are forced to protect attendance records and not look at the reason why a child may feel
threatened and not attend. “Use tough love’ I was told by the professed experts. Make the home
environment boring so school will look more appealing. I did this and my son’s empty response was, “I
would rather look at the walls than go to school”. We did tough love and took away his only happy
place, his technology. Where did that leave him but no safe space to de stress and he fell into a deep
depression. I wish I could rewind and start over again. Give him unconditional love and salvage his self-
esteem. The sink or swim analogy sent him to the depths of the ocean. He was often challenged when
picked up early by an educator who was supposed to be supporting him. Why are you leaving so early he
would ask???

The truth was my child didn’t feel safe in your hostile environment. Bottom line.

He was in fight or flight mode.

“Why don’t you get it? “I wanted to scream.  I felt they went through the motions of offering help,
without offering help.

 was made to feel like a failure and his self esteem plummeted. He felt awful when we got the

diagnosis as he felt that something was wrong with him and he had let us down. As parents we didn’t
know how to support him, and felt sad at the life ahead for him and the challenges he faced.

I have taken on the personal responsibility to home school my son. This was not my choice. It was the
ONLY option. This has caused a change in family dynamics that has improved all our mental health in
some ways but had taken a financial and emotional toll. I have reduced my working hours to support
homeschooling. I never thought I would be in this position.   My son loves to socialize and be around his
peers so given the choice he would go to school, he just CAN’T. We are still getting used to the rhythm
of homeschooling. I feel sad every time I pass the school he should be attending knowing he won’t get
to enjoy the experience with his peers and is at times lonely and isolated.

I know that my son has been let down, but I’m hoping no other family has to go through this process
which is why I am lobbying for change.

I love this great observation from an author unknown, that schools are trees and if you are a monkey,
you can climb them easily but if you are a fish, you can’t. The solution is to put them in an ocean and
they will swim. I am still looking for that ocean.

A child will always learn if given the choice. Our son is clever but learns in a different way. Once the laser
beam of his hyper focus locks onto something worthwhile, he will succeed. Of that I am confident. Not
through the efforts of the education department, but through our own blood, sweat and tears. To find
his tribe and to find life’s purpose despite all his challenges and despite an education system that just
doesn’t understand. He isn’t damaged or abnormal but just has different wiring in his brain. Like a phone
running on a different platform, Apple vs Samsung.

The world is a better place because of people with neuro diversity. It is believed, a person with ADHD
was essential for the survival of the clan in cave man times. Their heightened senses and hyperactivity
could help catch prey and look out for imminent danger. In today’s society they are the doctors,

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 133
 scientists, sports people and innovators. The lateral thinkers and the problem solvers. Why don’t we
celebrate these humans as a society rather than stifle their creativity. Their very essence.

The confusion and distress I’ve felt has turned to anger.

I’m mad that my child has been made to feel broken. I’m mad that I’ve been made to feel like a failure. I
will not accept this anymore. Unless you walk a mile in someone else’s shoes you can’t understand. I feel
that the school can’t parents have been judged unfairly. It is easier for the educators to blame the
parents for not getting their kids to school. I cannot convey to you enough the lengths that have been
gone to behind the scenes that are not visible to the outside world. We tried everything from
punishment to rewards and everything in between. Just imagine going through this stress as an adult let
alone a child. You wouldn’t want to go to a place where you are made to feel unsafe and undervalued.

The time has come to stop killing these kids’ self-esteem and work together to solve this dilemma.

I am a member of an online support group of neuro-divergent, school cants and I feel the pain of every
single member that posts. The helplessness and misunderstanding of a system that is broken. Why not
look at why the children are refusing. It’s the current education pedagogy that is the problem. Not these
beautiful, confused, trusting children.

Recommendations:

I implore you as an educational institution don’t let these kids and families down. Make a school where
learning is fun. Flexible learning styles with a focus on mental health and well-being. Support their
strengths and not punish them for their inherent weaknesses. Disciplining them by keeping them in at
lunch or recess is not helpful. Often, they haven’t got the skills to finish their work and they are missing
out on valuable social time. Throw out this draconian school system which doesn’t suit our evolving
future. I know this Utopia of schooling has many barriers such as funding, trained teachers and neuro-
divergent children being the minority. There needs to be more funding on many different levels. In the
ideal world we would have teachers who are not too stressed and adequately trained to pick out these
kids. They could be given extra support not just in Maths and English but part of a mentoring and life
skill program. Flexible school attendance and maybe some home learning and part involvement at
school to help with socializing. A focus on building their individual strengths and promoting their mental
health and esteem. We were looking at a school called
here in
these in the future. More services for homeschooling communities such as funded programs through
the daytime. The other major hurdle at the moment is access to health care professionals for diagnosis
and treatment. The waiting time is incredibly long and the financial strain placed on families is
unrelenting. There is currently no NDIS funding in our son’s case as ADHD is not covered. It would be
great to have an umbrella organization for children with ADHD which helps in the numerous challenges
they face such is afforded kids with autism.  Please educate the educators that their policies and
practices are no longer valid and are actually detrimental to our special kids. The square pegs being
forced into round holes.

but the school is at capacity. Maybe we should look at more options like

 for

Please start the conversation. I am happy to advocate and answer any other questions your may have.

Brief history of school can’t for my child
Red flags began when my daughter started 4 yo kinder. She was very hard to get there, often
wanted me to stay for lengths of time until she settled, but generally after she’d settled I could
leave. Then she was happy to be there. Over time (around 2 terms) as she became comfortable with
her environment getting her to kinder wasn’t an issue. There were some red flags there that I can
look back on now and realise this is where it all began. Eg. Refusing to wear a hat to go outside so
she would stand in the doorway watching for the whole of outside play and refusing to put her hat
on even though she loved outdoor play. But putting on a hat was not an option.

Her journey to prep was a whole different story. The refusal to go was more severe and constant.
Everyday was a battle. I was often the parent carrying a kicking and screaming child, trying to get her
out of the car. This started at home. I often carried her kicking and screaming in her underwear to
the car at home. Then try and get her school clothes on in the car out front of the school. Then she’d
latch onto the car, then I’d free her from holding the car door and she’d latch onto the school
entrance gate. By the time we made it to the classroom we were both crying and the teacher would
have to pry her off me. This happened for 3 terms. The teacher told me once she was there she was
fine, but over time I couldn’t even get her out of the house. She had big absences for terms 2 and 3.
Weeks on end. She’d wake and straight away be crying, complaining of pains in her tummy,
screaming and begging not to go. I couldn’t even get her out of the house. Over the years Ive been
kicked and scratched as I forced my traumatised child to school. I felt so alone. Parents would stare
(no one ever tried to help). I often called the admin staff to help but they were always too busy. We
had countless meetings with the school teachers, wellbeing officer, principle and they just said you
just have to get her here. But they couldn’t understand that this was easier said than done. Her prep
teacher ended up putting her hands in the air saying “I don’t know what to do with her”. We were
gobsmacked. She was only 5!! Even though our daughter never misbehaved she was often placed on
the “naughty kids” table because she was so far behind in her learning. She was still on golden words
in term 3. She had big red crosses all over her school books and I feel was given the message “you
are naughty and wrong”. The school told us she was so behind they had no support in place for her
in years 1 and going forward. At this point we felt we had no choice but find a more supportive
school soi we shifted her into the Steiner system. This started off well because prep and year 1 in
Steiner are very play based so initially she adjusted well into the system. But as the learning
intensified – end of yr 1 and 2 the same school refusal signs amped up. Sometimes both her dad and
I would drive to school with both of us prying her out of the car. In her trauma of being taken to
school she even once tried to open the car door in the freeway. That was scary. I turned around and
went straight back home. On many occasions I turned around and wen straight back home. We were
so lucky her Steiner teacher had a daughter with ASD and with her gentle encouragement out=r
daughter was officially diagnosed with ASD at seven and also severe school refusal. It was just too
tragic to hear her screaming and begging. Her school attendance has wavered over the last 4 years
but never been higher than about 60/50%. She’s now at the end of grade 4, and her current
attendance in around 30% but probably lower. Her school can’t was greatly affected by Covid and I
often wonder if it would be different now if she hadn’t spent 2 years at home

 Her anxiety was so high in covid we often couldn’t even get her

out of the bedroom. We were so grateful to have horse therapy (further details below) that still

Impact of School Can’t experience on my child:
The impact of school can’t on my child and our family is enormous! She is ashamed. When she does
go to school she is embarrassed, doesn’t want to be pulled aside to do separate learning because
she doesn’t want to look different. She tries to mask how much she struggles with learning and the
school environment because she has high sensory needs so if easily overstimulated. She misses out
on the social side of school and even though we feel lucky she has one or two close friends she often

missing out on the day to day building of friendships. She says to me: “School is just so hard
mummy”. Even when she just goes for the morning she is so exhausted when she comes home. The
whole experience takes so much out of her. We have had her principle say to us: “well she obviously

with other kids her own age. These comments make me feel so frustrated at the total lack of

Impact of School Can’t experience on our family and myself as a parent:
It’s always been hard on our older daughter because often she was late for school due to the
difficulties we had. Although she is a beautiful, supportive sister. It created further tension between
her dad and I, and we are now separated. And has also greatly affected my ability to work more (I’m

I am currently renting but am worried about my ability to increase my income because my daughter
is home all the time. I would like to buy a house (since separating we did sell a home so I have some
money put aside for a house) but am worried at my financial ability to even borrow money as a
single mum on a low income to buy another house.

I’ve received so much judgement over the years from family, the school, initially her dad (although
he’s on board now). Every day I have to notify school admin of her absence – I constantly receive a
barrage of texts and emails asking where she is. This constantly makes me feel shame and
judgement. I’ve felt a complete failure as a parent. The Steiner school has been more understanding

daughter. It took three years to get her properly diagnosed because we never really knew where to

The Stephanie Alexander Kitchen Garden Foundation was established in 2004 with the sole
charitable purpose of improving the health and wellbeing of Australian children and young
people. As such, the Foundation welcomes the opportunity to make a submission to the
Senate Education and Employment References Committee Inquiry into school refusal.

Although the challenge of school refusal is not new, in the wake of natural disasters and the
COVID-19 health crisis, supporting the wellbeing of children, their educators, families and
communities has never been more important.

Enhancing a sense of belonging to support student attendance

Experts agree that a sense of belonging is a supportive condition for student attendance at
school.

“While student disengagement is complex and varies from student

to student, there is sufficient evidence now to support the view that
relationships and school belonging are key factors” 1

Evidence suggests that providing hands-on, contextual learning opportunities, delivered
through kitchen and garden settings, improves educational outcomes across diverse
curriculum areas, while also supporting student retention, school enjoyment and parent
engagement.

“School belonging is defined as feeling accepted, safe, and respected
within the social, cultural, and physical surroundings of a school” 2

An important predictor of mental health is social connectedness. An evaluation of the
Stephanie Alexander Kitchen Garden Program by the University of Melbourne 3 found strong
evidence of positive social outcomes for children, schools and communities involved in the
Kitchen Garden Program.

Working in the kitchen and garden in groups creates opportunities for children to work with
others beyond their usual friendship groups. This teaches children a valuable skill in
teamwork and offers a means for widening social networks.

Further connections are built through an inclusive and immersive program which links in
family and community engagement for social cohesion and community pride.

Not only did participation in the program lead to more positive attitudes towards school, it
also led to an increase in children’s self-esteem, with some of the most significant outcomes
seen in children at the lower end of the academic achievement scale who were considered at
risk of long term disengagement from education.

Beyond the kitchen and garden sessions, newfound confidence was observed both at home
and in the classroom, positively impacting children’s lives more broadly. Feeling more
engaged and enthusiastic about school, a previously discouraged student demonstrated how
the experience of success in the program was able to be transferred into a new growth
mindset, saying ‘I’m really good at this and I can do other things as well.’

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 139
















 To quote the Victorian Department of Education’s own learning materials for the delivery of
Health and Physical Education:

“A sense of connectedness or belonging to school and to family is the
single most important protective factor for young people. Several
longitudinal studies have documented the way in which initiatives
provided in the primary years can have a lasting effect, promoting
resilience and school connectedness well into the high school years.” 4

The Kitchen Garden Program has been described by parents and educators as an
environment that facilitates the creation of a ‘learning community’. Without the competitive
structure of academic or sporting activities, the program creates a level playing field allowing
all children the opportunity to experience success.

Being outdoors enhances feelings of calm and positivity

“…it’s really, really, relaxing and it helps take your mind off things and it
de-stresses you. It’s really good and helpful because school can be really
stressful.” 5

As well as fostering a sense of belonging, Kitchen Garden Programs increase access to the
sensory and therapeutic benefits of green spaces for children, young people and their
communities, improving health and wellbeing with more time spent being physically active
outdoors.

“Sometimes it’s the simple tasks that bring the most happiness and calm
within the space.” 6

The Kitchen Garden Program for impact

The Kitchen Garden Program is a holistic program with significant cross-portfolio impacts in
the areas of education, environment and climate change, food systems and agriculture, and
health and wellbeing.

Our evidence-based program supports children and communities to proactively strengthen
community resilience, improve education outcomes, strengthen social and community
inclusion and address health inequities. 7

Over the past 20 years, the Program has impacted over a million children and young people.
Our national community of practice supports educators in over a thousand schools to deliver
the Program in all states and territories across Australia.

With Federal Government funding, the Stephanie Alexander Kitchen Garden Foundation
would be in a position to amplify its impact, supporting more children, young people their
families and communities to develop positive health, wellbeing, educational and
sustainability habits for life.

Dr Cathy Wilkinson Chief Executive Officer

TRIPLE P–POSITIVE PARENTING
PROGRAM

SUBMISSION

INQUIRY INTO THE NATIONAL TREND OF SCHOOL REFUSAL AND
RELATED MATTERS

SENATE EDUCATION AND EMPLOYMENT REFERENCES
COMMITTEE

Triple P International Pty Ltd
ABN: 17 079 825 817

www.triplep-parenting.net.au
contact@triplep.net | Tel: +61 7 3236 1212
11 Market Street North
Indooroopilly, Qld, 4068
