The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 145 The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 145 Introduction
Based at the Melbourne Children’s Campus, the Centre for Community Child Health (CCCH) is one of
Australia's leading research and policy centres focused on understanding and redressing childhood
inequities. Our submission draws on nearly 30 years of providing paediatric clinical care, undertaking
translational research and implementing workforce training and education to promote child health,
development and mental wellbeing. Our submission focuses on solutions that enhance school
engagement starting from birth to 12 years – recognising that prevention and early intervention
during these years lays the foundation for future wellbeing and educational enagement.

The impact of mental health and wellbeing on school engagement and school refusal
Poor mental health and wellbeing is a significant driver of school refusal and disengagement.
Children who experience mental health difficulties such as anxiety (including social phobia and
separation anxiety) and depression may feel overwhelmed by the demands of school and develop a
pattern of avoidance. Similarly, children with low wellbeing may experience a lack of motivation,
interest, or enjoyment in school activities, leading to disengagement and ultimately school refusal.
These factors can have a profound impact on the child's academic progress as well as the ongoing
mental health, wellbeing and development. Even before the COVID-19 pandemic, many Australian
children experienced poor mental health and wellbeing:

•  Almost 14 per cent of children aged 4-17 years in Australia had a mental health diagnosis

pre-pandemic,i

•  nearly half of all adult mental health conditions begin before the age of 14 years,ii  with clear

problems emerging from age fiveiii and

•  more than one in five children are developmentally vulnerable by the time they begin

school.iv

Findings from the Young Minds Matterv survey demonstrate the impact of mental health and
wellbeing on learning and school engagement:

•  Students with metal health disorders have poorer NAPLAN results than students with no

mental health disorder in every test domain and Year level.

•  On average students with a mental health disorder in Year 3 were 7 to 11 months behind

students with no mental health disorder. By Year 9, students with a mental health disorder
were on average 1.5 - 2.8 years behind students with no mental disorder.

•  Students in Years 1-6 with a mental health disorder missed an average 11.8 days of school
per year compared with 8.2 days per year for students without a mental health disorder. In
Years 7-12 this increased, with students with a mental health disorder missing an average
23.8 days per year compared with 11.0 days per year for students without a mental health
disorder.

•  Students with mental health disorders have lower levels of connectedness to school and

engagement with schoolwork.

•  Students living in socio-economic disadvantage unfairly experience burden of mental ill-

health, with students experiencing socio-economic disadvantage more likely to experience
mental health disorders, further impacting learning and school engagement.

We also know that children who experience diverse learning needs, such as autism spectrum
disorder (ASD) or learning difficulties, as well as children living with chronic conditions, are at
increased risk of school refusal for a range of reasons including challenges experienced in connecting

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 145

 with peers, communicating with teachers and engagement with school curriculum and meeting
curriculum expectations.vi This leads to increased anxiety, stress and hopelessness that result in
school avoidance and refusal.

Innovative solutions are necessary and available to improve mental health and wellbeing of children,
increase children’s engagement with school and realise the immediate and long-term benefits on
health, development, wellbeing, education and engagement outcomes. We propose that one, single
intervention will not result in change, but recommend a combination or stacking of approaches to
ensure children have what they need to engage in learning, starting from birth through to primary
school, sustained throughout secondary school and beyond.

Recommendations to increase school engagement and reduce the risk of school
refusal
Supporting children and families before they start school

Despite the Inquiry’s focus on the impact of school refusal in primary and secondary school students,
we argue there is a need to intervene even earlier – before a child starts school. With more than one
in five children developmentally vulnerable before they start school with these vulnerabilities
persisting throughout primary schoolvii and mental health symptoms emerging from age five –
interventions before students starts school are imperative.

‘Stacking’ evidence-based strategies across the early years

The rapid development in a child’s earliest years (0-8) provides the foundation for lifelong health,
development and wellbeing. Improving children’s health, development and wellbeing requires
combining or ‘stacking’ multiple effective evidence-based strategies across these early years and
implementing them concurrently and continuously.viii

CCCH is working in collaboration with Social Ventures Australia (SVA) and Bain & Company on the
Restacking the Odds (RSTO) program. RSTO aims to drive more equitable outcomes in the early years
by ensuring that children and families can and do access a combination of high-quality, evidence-
informed services where and when they need them. It focuses on five evidence-based platforms and
programs to boost children's health development and wellbeing: antenatal care; sustained nurse
home visiting; early childhood education and care; parenting programs; and the early years of school
(defined as reception through to Year 3). These five strategies are notably longitudinal (across early
childhood), ecological (targeting child and parent), evidence-based, already available in almost all
communities (i.e. better use of existing service infrastructure), and able to be targeted to those with
the greatest needs. RSTO provides a foundation for prioritising locally-responsive services –
ensuring children have access to the supports that enable them to thrive and engage with learning
across early education and care and into primary school.

Evidence-based sustained nurse-home-visiting

Setting children up to thrive from birth is vital to breaking the trajectory of developmental
vulnerability and poor mental health outcomes for children. Sustained nurse home visiting (SNHV)
programs using the universal maternal and child health (MCH) serviceix, have shown to benefit child
development outcomes, parenting practice, and maternal mental health for vulnerable families.x
With benefits for both child and mother sustained until a child starts school,xi SNHV programs enable
children and families experiencing adversity to receive timely, non-stigmatising early intervention

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 145

 from birth.  SNHV interventions in Australia have been shown to be successful however, without
dedicated investment for evidence-based SNHV integration as part of a proportionate offering,
children and families are missing out on the early support required to enhance child development
outcomes and ensure children are ready to engage in learning when they start primary school.

Accessible and skilled universal preventative health care workforce

Preventative health care provided by universal health care practitioners including GPs and maternal
and child health nurses, is important in the prevention and early intervention of child mental health
problems. GPs provide the most mental health care to childreni and play a central coordination role
in the multidisciplinary care for children requiring additional support. Families are missing out on the
benefits preventative health care provides due to cost and access barriers, low levels of workforce
confidence and capacity to respond early and lack of implementation of successful workforce
practices that have been shown to enhance childhood behavioural and developmental outcomes by
the preventative health care workforce. New models of care and workforce capability
improvements are needed to ensure children can access quality preventative care in a timely and
accessible way.

Promising models of care are currently being trialled that enable GPs and the primary care
workforce to better respond to emerging child mental health difficulties. This includes the
Strengthening Care for Children (SC4C) initiative, a novel, integrated GP-paediatrician model of care
that aims to build quality of care provided by GPs, increase access to specialist paediatric care via co-
consultation with children, families and GPs, and reduce referrals to hospitals.xii Trials have shown
this model is feasible and acceptable, with families reporting increased confidence in GP care.
Further scaling of the SC4C model of care will collect data on school refusal and monitor impact of
the SC4C approach on school engagement.

Innovative workforce capacity building models, using Communities of Practice (CoP) approaches,
have also been shown to be successful. One example is the COMPASS initiative that brings together
GPs, mental health nurses, allied health, paediatricians and child psychiatrists in online case
conferencing and skill development. COMPASS has been shown to reduce referrals to tertiary child
mental health services as well as increase GP confidence in providing first line behavioural and
prescribing treatments to children – meaning children are getting support they need in their
community and in a timely manner.xiii COMPASS was successfully rolled out via Primary Health
Network (PHNs) platform, demonstrating successful use of existing primary care platforms to deliver
quality practice improvement initiatives for children and their families.

Improving access to paediatricians as part of an integrated community-based response

Most families are referred to paediatricians for their child’s mental health.xiv Mental health and
neurodevelopmental problems are the most common presentations managed by paediatricians.i
Access to paediatric mental health support for children is difficult, and families face unacceptably
long wait times (12 -18 months in the public systemxv) or substantial costs. Children and families are
languishing on wait lists, meaning delays in assessment, diagnosis and treatment. In many states and
territories, access to paediatricians is highly restricted and inequitable because paediatricians
overwhelmingly work in the private sector. The limited access to community based publicly funded
paediatric services disproportionately impacts lower income children as well those living in rural,
regional and remote areas. Increasing access to community-based, publicly funded paediatricians is

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 145






















 central as part of integrated community-based response to providing mental health care and
support for children.

There is opportunity to build on existing models which have successfully demonstrated integration
of paediatricians in community-based responses to child and family mental health such as the Infant,
Child and Family Mental Health and Wellbeing Hubs. Paediatricians in these services would also have
a capacity building role in supporting the local primary care workforce to respond and care to
emerging child mental health problems as demonstrated by SC4C and COMPASS.

Increasing access to quality early childhood education and care (ECEC)

The benefits of children attending high-quality early childhood education are well established.xvi xvii
xviii Significant cognitive and emotional benefits have been shown for children who receive high-
quality preschool education in their early years.xix xx These benefits are strongest for children from
lower socio-economic backgrounds and for children whose parents have lower levels of education.xxi
Unfortunately many children are missing out on these benefits, particularly children experiencing
socio-economic disadvantage, from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds and Aboriginal
and Torres Strait Island backgrounds.xxii Governments have made early childhood education and care
more financially accessible to families, but barriers still exist that prevent children from receiving
quality early childhood education. These include high cost, lack of parent/carer understanding of the
benefits of early childhood education and how to access these services,xxiii and a lack of access to
local services.xxiv Ongoing investment to improve access to high quality early education and care
sets the foundation for ongoing engagement in learning and education.

Enhancing parent mental health and child development literacy

Only 35% of parents feel confident they could recognise signs of a mental health problem in their
child, 44% feel confident in knowing where to seek help if their child is experiencing mental health
issues (this drops to 35 % for parents with infants and toddlers) and one in three parents think
mental health problems in children might be best left alone.xxv Enabling parents to respond to their
child’s needs, reduces the risk of unaddressed issues that are more complex to address.

By building on existing universal platforms (i.e., accessible to all) and using multimodal
communication approaches, we can increase parent mental health literacy. This includes:

•  enhancing digital platforms – such as Raising Children Network (RCN) - to promote, develop
and disseminate tools and resources for families. RCN has existing resources on supporting
students experiencing school refusal that can be scaled.

•  developing a shared language of child mental health and wellbeing that engages children,

•

families, education, health and support sectors in conversations early
continuing to build the capacity of the health, education and social care workforces to
provide tailored, consistent information and support to families about child mental health
and wellbeing.

Supporting service providers to collect and use lead indicators for continued improvement

Using evidence-based lead indicators can reveal otherwise hidden gaps in services and allow those
gaps to be acted on.xxvi While outcome data is the ultimate arbiter of success, lead indicators are
direct measures of quality and are easier to interpret yet are rarely used. Our research and

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 145


 The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 145 The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 145 Tailored support - Developing co-design response for students experiencing school
refusal

Supporting children experiencing school refusal requires a collaborative approach that involves
students, school staff, parents/carers and health professionals, including mental health
professionals. There is opportunity to undertake a comprehensive, national approach to
addressing school refusal that facilitates and enables localised responses that meet the needs of
students. We propose the development of this approach occur in four phases:

1.  Literature review of current international and national evidence for responding to school
refusal including understanding of the core components of successful models that would
form the basis of a national approach.

2.  Mapping of current school refusal initiatives across Australia and internationally and where

possible any evaluation results of those initiatives.

3.  Establishment of a national coalition of partners with students and parents/carers at its core

to co-design evidence-informed framework that addresses school refusal.

4.  Dissemination and support strategy to enable schools, services and families to implement

the framework in response to their local needs.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 145

















































































































































































































































































































































 Trialling multi-disciplinary teams working across schools, health and families

One of the challenges experienced by students experiencing school refusal is the disconnect
between their teacher/school supports and the care and support provided by health care
professionals such as GPs, paediatricians and mental health professionals. The establishment of
multi-disciplinary teams that bring together the expertise of educators and health care professionals
with families and students is needed to ensure a shared understanding of a student’s objectives and
strategies to return to school and their role in supporting the student achieve returning to school.
Currently, there is no mechanism that enables educators, health and social care providers to meet
regularly and shared understanding of supports and care provided both at school, at home and
health care. The trialling of multi-disciplinary team models of care is recommended to best
respond to students currently disengaged from school.

CCCH is currently trialling this approach as part of our Learning Difficulties Clinic which aims to
support students to engage in their learning. As part of the clinic, we have identified the need for an
Education Specialist role. This Education Specialist acts as the conduit between students, families,
paediatric health and education professionals to support children to engage in learning in the
classroom.  Initial feasibility assessment of this roles is promising but further investment is required
to trial and evaluate this approach.

Co-designing resources and tools for parents and carers

Parents and carers play a critical role in promoting their children's engagement with school.
Supporting parents with resources on how to support their children's academic and social-emotional
needs can reduce the risk of school refusal (Martin & Marchant, 2019). Engaging parents and carers
in co-designing resources and tools that they can use when supporting a child to re-engage with
school ensures that tools best reflect and respond to the needs of parents and carers. Existing
digital platforms such Raising Children Network provide school refusal resources for parents/carers
and are good starting points to initiative co-design collaboration with parents/carers and other
support agencies.

Scaling successful interventions

There are many evidence-based initiatives that have demonstrated success in supporting students to
return to school; however, these initiatives experience challenges in scaling. We suggest there is a
role in governments at both national and state/territory levels to provide the enabling
environment that enables the translation and scale of success initiatives to ensure equitable access
to interventions that are shown to work.

Monitoring student wellbeing and evaluating impact
Supporting schools to monitor and respond to student wellbeing

Measuring student wellbeing is an important mechanism that enables students, families, educators
and clinicians to obtain an accurate understanding of student wellbeing and informs appropriate
responses at both the student, year-level and school level to increasing student wellbeing. Yet
schools are often left on their own to decide how to monitor student wellbeing and which of the
numerous student wellbeing survey tools to use. We recommend that schools are supported to
regularly monitor student wellbeing including support to identify a survey tool that meets their
needs but is also informed by the evidence-based and then supported in how to best interpret and
respond according to identified need.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 145

 Using lead indicators to track strategies in schools

As noted above, using evidence-based lead indicators can reveal otherwise hidden gaps in services.
RSTO has identified evidence-based quality indicators for the early years of school. These indicators
are tied to school processes (i.e. process indicators at the classroom, student or lesson level that
contribute to the achievement of high-quality outcomes) and teaching staff competencies (i.e.
provider indicators).xxx  The indicators include measures of social and emotional wellbeing. Support
for schools to use evidence-based lead indicators to monitor these aspects of school quality can
assist schools and teachers to understand and how strategies have been implemented, what
progress is being made, and what can be done to further improve practice.

Schools as multi-opportunity communities
To conclude, in realising a true systemic change for how schools achieve healthy childhood
development and deeper learning and engagement for all, we propose a new vision for Australian
schools – schools as multi-opportunity communities. This vision requires a shift from narrow view
of learning for academic intelligence only, to equally focusing on learning, wellbeing, and health for
whole child development and wellbeing. Some schools are already making great changes to equally
prioritise whole child learning, health, and wellbeing (e.g. Our Place: https://ourplace.org.au). Still,
the radical transformation needed for all will require changes at the system level. Nordic countries,
Canadian provinces, Wales, Scotland, and New Zealand are prioritising health and wellbeing more in
education and moving beyond words into real action. We propose four principles to underpin this
change to school as multi-opportunity platforms (see Figure 1). For more detail please read our
paper – Building it back better: Schools as multi-opportunity communities.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 145
















 About the Centre for Community Child Health

The Centre for Community Child Health (CCCH) is part of the world-class Melbourne Children’s
Campus, which unites community and clinical care, research, and education. CCCH a research group
of the Murdoch Children’s Research Institute, a department of The Royal Children’s Hospital, and an
affiliate of the University of Melbourne’s Department of Paediatrics.  Our purpose is to see every
child thrive. To achieve this, we have established a multidisciplinary team of researchers,
paediatricians, managers, evaluators and educators with expertise in children’s health, development
and wellbeing. For over 25 years, the CCCH has worked collaboratively with families, communities,
practitioners, organisations and decision makers to drive sustainable improvements in children’s
health, development and wellbeing.

Raise Foundation submission to the Senate Education and
Employment References Committee’s Inquiry into

‘The national trend of school refusal and related matters’

About Raise Foundation

Raise Foundation is a national charity building resilience, hope and engagement for young people in
early high schools across Australia. Since our inception in 2008, we have supported close to 11,000
young people, trained more than 7,200 mentors and delivered 868 mentoring programs.

We currently deliver programs in every Australian state as well as the Australian Capital Territory,
prioritising public and low fee-paying non-government schools with secondary enrolments.

Our 23-week evidence-based Raise Youth Mentoring program is delivered in schools during school
hours. Our program is delivered in collaborative partnership with the school wellbeing team. Schools
identify up to 15 students who are at risk of disengagement or poor wellbeing to be invited to
participate in our program. Students are then matched by our degree qualified Program Counsellor to
a volunteer mentor, who is fully trained and screened prior to their commencing in a Raise mentoring
program.

Our second offering, Youth Introduction to Mentoring, is a ten-week workshop style program,
facilitated by a Raise Program Counsellor with the support of 2-4 Raise volunteer mentors. We deliver
this program in areas where we have been unable to recruit the required number of mentors for one-
to-one matching, and the school has chosen not to deliver our online version of the 23-week Raise
Youth Mentoring program.

Profile of the Students in the Raise Program

In 2022, we supported 2,088 students in 180 programs. Of these students:










Their average age was 14 and the majority were in grades 8 or 9
49% identified as female, 39% as male and 8% identified as outside the gender binary
32% had caring responsibilities for family or friends due to mental illness, disability or health
condition
31% speak another language at home
12% identified as having a disability
13% were born outside of Australia
6% identified as Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander

At the beginning of the program 84% of students identified having faced at least one mental health or
environmental (such as bullying, drug and alcohol use, financial stress and insecure housing) issue. For
students who identified outside the gender binary this rose to 95%.

In relation to how students felt about school, at the beginning of the program:

The power of showing up

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 147

 

1 in 3 rated their attendance as only ‘Okay’, ‘Not so good’ or ‘Terrible’ (note we do not
distinguish between non-attendance due to illness or non-attendance due to school refusal)
Close to half (47%) did not agree with the statement ‘I feel safe at my school’


 More than half did not agree with these statements:

o
o
o

‘Teachers treat students fairly at my school’ (54%)
‘I feel happy at my school’ (54%)
‘I belong at my school’ (56%)

The Raise Foundation Curriculum – building a toolkit to navigate life’s challenges

The Raise Youth Mentoring Program Curriculum has been designed and developed in order to
improve outcomes in:

 Mental health literacy – key outcome area of help seeking



Social and emotional wellbeing – key outcome areas of resilience and hope for the future
School engagement – key outcome area of belonging at school

We employ a scaffolded learning approach. Each session has been designed to focus on one of these
key outcome areas through group activities and prompted discussion for 1:1 mentoring time.

The Impact of Raise Mentoring

Each year we comprehensively evaluate our program’s impact, through measuring outcomes for
students at the beginning and the end of the program and validating these outcomes through
capturing observations from mentors, school contacts and Raise Program Counsellors.

In 2022, with a return to in-school learning in every jurisdiction, we saw improved outcomes across
our programs. For the majority of outcomes we saw significant improvements at the whole of cohort
level as well as for those who started the program with a low score in the given outcome. For example,
for Resilience, Hope and Help seeking and associated secondary outcomes we saw statistically
significant improvements for our whole cohort of students and stronger improvement for those who
started the program with a low score in the given outcome.

The exception to this was in School Belonging and self-reported attendance where we saw
improvement for those who started the program with low scores in these areas, but not at the whole
of cohort level.

We did however see improvements at the whole cohort level for intention to finish school and make a
positive post school transition, as well as relationships with teachers and friends at school.

Our conclusion from this was that currently outcomes relating to the whole school environment are
harder to shift, whereas outcomes relating to how the young person feels about themselves, their
capabilities and their future are able to be improved. We do however feel confident that students
attend more on mentoring days:

We see these themes confirmed in our qualitative evaluation, in the feedback provided from students,
mentors and parents/carers:

‘[The biggest impact of Raise mentoring has been my] confidence and probably looking forward to
coming to school more because of the program.’ (Student)

The power of showing up

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 147

 ‘[The biggest impact of Raise mentoring has been that] I have been less anxious coming to school. I
have also been better at talking to new people and adults.’ (Student)

‘I've been feeling more grateful to be here and I've attended school every day this term and brought
my attendance up 40% since term 2’ (Student)

‘I had less to deal with myself as I had someone to talk to, it also helped me come to school on days
where I felt I couldn't.’ (Student)

‘The Raise program has helped me in many ways I got a job because of it and I am starting to come to
school more often’ (Student)

‘He seemed to be well engaged and making positive steps in his life. He only attended two classes in
the first term, but then attended all in the second term’ (Mentor about impact on student)

‘Definitely school attendance has improved. Seems more confident.’ (Parent/carer about impact on
student)

‘Improved relationship with parents and improved attendance at school’ (Parent/carer about impact
on student)

The connected, safe and inclusive environment we create at Raise

From feedback and data we collect directly from students as part of our formal program evaluation we
know that we create a safe and engaging space for the young people in our program.

o 94% of mentees rated their connection with their mentor as ‘Excellent’ or ‘Very good’
o 98% of mentees felt safe talking to their mentor
o 95% felt safe talking to their Raise Program Counsellor
o 85% felt safe talking in their mentoring group
o 96% of mentees felt supported by their Program Counsellor

We see the environment we create as integral to the impact of the program. Education research
consistently finds that students are more engaged and ready to learn in environments that are
psychologically safe and respectful (Clapper, 2010).

Australian Research Alliance for Children and Young People’s Nest six wellbeing domains (ARACY,
2018) also underpin the importance of connectedness and belonging. We know that connectedness
and belonging is closely linked to social and emotional wellbeing outcomes and to learning outcomes
(Baumeister & Leary, 1995),

“An environment that is spiritually, socially, and emotionally safe as well as physically safe for students;
where there is no assault challenge or denial of their identity, of who they are, and what they need. It
is about shared respect, shared meaning, shared knowledge, and experience of learning together”
(Williams, 1999)

The power of showing up

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 147

 From delivering our program in schools and hearing directly from schools about the challenges they
are facing, we understand that this is impacting their ability to provide the environment in which every
student feels connected, feels psychologically safe and can thrive.

How we co-design with young people

We co-design the solutions we create and the programs we deliver with young people. Our dedicated
youth engagement function reviews and improves our program curricula and resources provided to
support students in the Raise programs using feedback from and the experience of:




Students in the Raise program through evaluation focus groups and surveys
Raise Youth Advisory Committee

In 2022, we ran our inaugural Raise Youth Summit, in partnership with six diverse schools based in
Sydney and will do the same this year, looking to expand into other states.

We recognise that young people are experts in their own lives and have valuable insights into what
they need to thrive. We also know from research that co-design in service delivery improves idea
generation, service and most importantly outcomes (Steen, Manschot & DeKoning, 2011).

Our Recommendations for consideration by the Inquiry

Based on our 14 years of experience delivering programs in the school environment as well as our
more recent experience of delivery in the disruption of the pandemic, we recommend the Inquiry
consider the following:







Engaging directly with young people and co-designing solutions to ensure they are youth
centred, appropriate, inclusive and accessible.
The value of mentoring relationships, both formal and informal, in the school environment
and engaging with mentoring organisations to help design solutions.
The importance of the school environment and ensuring it is student centred, safe and
inclusive. The myriad of challenges schools face is impacting the environment schools are
able to create for students.

 Measuring and providing access to attendance data to support programs to monitor and
evaluate their own outcomes and ensure a wholistic approach to attendance, school refusal
and associated impacts.
The particular challenges around safety and environmental and mental health issues that
students who identify outside the gender binary face.



References

young Australians, Canberra, <https://www.aracy.org.au/the-nest-in-action>.

Baumeister, RF & Leary, MR (1995), ‘The need to belong: Desire for interpersonal attachments as a
fundamental human motivation’, Psychological Bulletin, vol. 117, no. 3, pp. 497–529,
<https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.117.3.497>.

Clapper (2010), Creating the safe learning environment. PAILAL, vol 3, no. 2, pp. 1-6.

submissions.text:
The Senate Education and Employment Committees
Inquiry into The National Trend Of School Refusal And Related Matters

Submission by Community School Startup Support Australia (unincorporated)
Written by Deborah Schiel Zaini and Nicole Gorring

Recommendations highlighting the need for alternative schools and programs

The Home Education Network’s submission to the Senate Inquiry states in their conclusion:
“There is inadequate provision and availability of alternative schools/settings to provide for
young people who have detached from mainstream education.”

The School Refusal Clinic’s submission to the Senate Inquiry states in their Recommendation
#7: “Consideration be given to alternative education-based programs that cater for the complex
presentations of school refusal clients that don’t fit into existing mainstream settings.”

Office of the Education Registrar’s submission to the Senate Inquiry states in their
Recommendation #1: “Consideration of clear alternatives to standard classroom delivery of the
key learning areas in the Australian Curriculum and capacity for students to opt out of some
areas in order to focus on re-engaging with school.”

Interrelate’s submission to the Senate Inquiry states in their Recommendation #2:
“New models are required to support child-centric education. Schools need to be seen as
communities and a safer place for more children to re-engage.”

The Yellow Ladybugs’ submission to the Senate Inquiry states in their Recommendation #8:
“Fund and further investigate alternative schooling models as they are valid and often preferred
educational settings for school can’t students. This includes community and alternative
schools…”

About Community School Startup Support Australia

Community School Startup Support Australia (“CSSSA”) is a private Facebook group established
in 2017 by Deborah Schiel Zaini, currently with 450 members.

“This is an Australian support group for people interested in starting their own small independent
school. Founded in March 2017, this group was originally a support group for parents in the
Cassowary Coast Region (Queensland, Australia) interested in starting a school inspired by
Montessori, Steiner, Forest Learning and Nature Play philosophies. After a year of hard work, The
Rainforest School received official accreditation in March 2018. Much of the process, logistics and
research collected along the way has been recorded in this group and will hopefully be a useful
resource for other community groups wanting to start their own school.”
https://www.facebook.com/groups/communityschoolstartupsupport

Members of CSSSA currently span eight established small community schools, six groups in the
process of founding schools, and a number of members who have been involved with attempts to
start new schools. The average length of time it takes our members to successfully open new
schools is 3-5 years and the attrition rate is high, primarily due to three factors: finance, town
planning, and state departments of education.

Page 1 of 3

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 148 Terms of Reference Item (e): Any other related matters

The SPSR’s submission to the Senate Inquiry states in their Recommendation #35:
“That State and Territory DOEs acknowledge and provide for the needs of students whose
nervous systems require: smaller schools, smaller classrooms, buildings that are designed and
outfitted to account for sensory needs, pedagogy that accommodates interest based or
self-directed learning, no uniforms, shorter days, later start times in secondary schools, low
demand and low arousal environments in order to maintain student wellbeing and capacity for
learning.”

The above statement describes the small community schools founded by the members of CSSSA,
including the primary school founded by Ms Schiel Zaini in 2021: Darlingia Forest School.

These schools are very small “alternative” schools that teach the Australian Curriculum, in an
accessible way, to all children, including those who have detached from mainstream education.
School Refusal or “School Can’t” affects children in Prep/Foundation when they start school as
well as young people in high schools. Darlingia has children who were affected by school refusal
before they came to our school. They are now happily attending our school and are re-engaging
with learning.

Darlingia is a school that provides, “smaller classrooms, [accounts] for sensory needs, pedagogy
that accommodates interest based or self-directed learning, no uniforms, shorter days, later start
times… low demand and low arousal environments in order to maintain student wellbeing and
capacity for learning.”

Many other Democratic or small community schools provide similar environments for their
students. Many of the parents/teachers in CSSSA join our group as they start their journey
towards establishing an independent school. Their reasons for wanting to start their own school
are to provide their children and others the accommodations described in SPSR’s
Recommendation #35.

Hurdles facing the founders of small community schools

Starting a non-state school is a complicated and difficult venture. As a parent-teacher who has
founded two small non-state schools, and from my experience with supporting other start-up
schools/groups, the main hurdles facing the founders of small community schools are the
requirements of state/council town planning departments (“Town Planners”) and the non-state
schools authorities (“NSSAs”).

Town Planners require a school of 30 students to meet the same codes as a school of 300
students. NSSAs audit a school of 12 students the same way they audit a school of 1,200
students. There are no exemptions or concessions based on size or age.

The Building Code of Australia is an example of a system that has exemptions or concessions
based on size and/or age. For example, D2.20 Swinging doors
“A swinging door in a required exit or forming part of a required exit-
(b) must swing in the direction of egress unless-
(i) it serves a building or part with a floor area not more than 200m2…”

Page 2 of 3

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 148 Exemptions or concessions based on size and/or age

Our recommendation is for Town Planners and NSSAs to provide exemptions or concessions to
new and fledgling small schools based on size and/or age. This would make it significantly more
feasible to establish and run the kinds of educational provisions that SPSR, in their
Recommendation #35, have identified are so very needed

Recommendation #1 for state planning departments

A small school of 12 or 30 students would not have the same impact on a neighbourhood as a
school of 300 or 1,200 students. We ask state planning departments to amend their planning
policies and schemes to encourage/require local councils to permit very small schools in existing
buildings or established settings without a planning approval, but subject to compliance with a
range of matters, for example, parking, access, location, size, sanitary considerations etc. This
would assist with the establishment of very small schools with enrolments under 30 students.

Recommendation #2 for non-state schools authorities

There is much to learn and do when it comes to governing and operating a new small independent
school. In a school of 12-30 students, a small team of 2-5 teachers, staff and volunteers are
responsible for all operational and governance matters. We ask NSSAs to provide legal
concessions to new and fledgling small schools based on age and size while continuing to ensure
that new and fledgling small schools are meeting legal child safety & WHS requirements.

In summary, the establishment of the kinds of schools that re-engage disengaged students,
provide the learning environment that neurodiverse students need, and therefore reduce school
refusal, is dependent upon parent/teacher community-led groups working together to establish the
kinds of schools their children need. But they are continually roadblocked by legislation and
planning codes that are designed for large government and church schools with the funding and
political networking options that small community developed schools simply do not have.

In order for there to be more of the type of schools that other submissions have identified as
necessary to combat school refusal, changes must be made to legislation to make the
establishment of such schools realistic.

Submission supported by

Deborah Schiel Zaini of Darlingia Forest School, member of CSSSA since 27/03/2017

Cheniel Norris of Darlingia Ltd 2019-2021, member of CSSSA since 02/05/2017

Nicole Gorring of Arcadia Agile Learning Center, member of CSSSA since 14/08/2017

Amy Cox and Meg Foley of Reimagining Education And Learning (REAL) Schools Inc,

members of CSSSA since 13/04/2018

Suzanne Lanzon of Corymbia Community School, member of CSSSA since 05/04/2019

Nicole Punt, member of CSSSA since 08/05/2019

Angie Kelly of My Independent School 2019 - 2021, member of CSSSA since 23/09/2019

Sarah Richards of Evergreen Steiner School, member of CSSSA since 18/07/2021

Submission to the
 Senate Inquiry into

 Meg McIntosh & Tara Broughan
 hello@megandtara.com
 www.megandtara.com

 Yallambie Victoria 3088

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 149
  Introduction

 We welcome the opportunity to provide a submission to this inquiry. Meg &

 Tara client cohort include a signiﬁcant number of families with

 neurodivergent children (for example autistic, adhd, anxiety, learning

 di�erences) and/or those who have experienced trauma, and are often

 experiencing signiﬁcant challenges to attending school or participating

 meaningfully in the school environment. We acknowledge there are many

 barriers in children’s lives that may inhibit their ability to attend, or

 meaningfully participate in school.  We recognise t  he way intersecting

 barriers to a safe environment include social exclusion, bullying,   racism,

 poverty, mental health, gender identity discrimination, sexuality and other

 marginalised identities and experiences for families. In this submission we

 narrow our focus to the signiﬁcant portion of our client cohort who are

 neurodivergent ( for example autistic, adhd, anxiety, learning di�erences )

 and experience signiﬁcant challenges at di�erent times attending and

 participating in the mainstream school environment.

 Our intention is to highlight how critical it is to examine the feedback this

 behaviour is providing to the current mainstream educational environment

 and relationships for children.  School avoidance or “school can’t” and the

 signiﬁcant challenging behaviours that are often seen when these children

 are forced to attend school, is communicating that school environments

 are not feeling safe or supportive.  In addition to sca�olding skill

 development for children we need to support parents/carers and teachers

 to respond to the causal reasons for not attending school.

 We believe strongly that it is important to refrain from pathologizing or

 problematising individual children and families, who, in our experience, are

 incredibly dedicated, committed, and willing to support their children to

 participate in meaningful relationships and learning.

 2

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 149  About Meg & Tara

 Meg & Tara is a business partnership with Meg McIntosh, a Pediatric

 Occupational Therapist and Tara Broughan, a Human Rights & Community

 Consultant. Together we facilitate parent group sessions, private family

 consultations, and professional development drawing from our

 professional and personal experience.

 In the last 3 years Meg & Tara have facilitated over thirty 6 week parent

 groups grounded in the Tuning into Kids/Teens (REF) methodology of

 facilitating social and emotional competence in children and teens. We

 have adapted this content for our specialist cohort of families with

 neurodivergent children (including autism, adhd, anxiety, depression)

 and/or signiﬁcant complex behaviours including the inability to attend

 school. Additionally we have provided professional development to allied

 health professionals, teachers and principals and early childhood learning

 environments.

 Our focus is to support the development of safe, respectful, authentic and

 connected relationships between adults and children that identify and

 proactively respond to the cause of signiﬁcant behaviours.

 Meg McIntosh has been working with neurodivergent, and wonderfully

 complex families in public and private settings for over 12 years.

 Tara Broughan is an autistic/adhd adult who has spent over 12 years

 working in human rights, community consultation specialising in childrens

 experiences with UNICEF, government and community organisations.

 We are committed to creating change within relationships, environments,

 systems and processes that support equity for all children, families, and

 professionals in our communities.

 3

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 149  Background

 Firstly we would like to challenge the framing of children “refusing” to

 attend school which suggests a lack of willingness on the behalf of

 children to attend school and/or the willingness of parents to enforce

 reasonable boundaries. Rather, our experience with families when a child

 can’t attend school is that the child does not have the current capacity, or

 ability to attend school.  Returning requires a relational, child paced

 graded response, that supports their reengagement, where this is the

 family goal.

 “I  don’t choose not to go to school! I just

 struggle, and it's really hard.”  ~  8yo child

 Secondly, school attendance is a limiting goal.  A more inclusive goal is the

 meaningful participation in social and educational experiences that

 support the health and learning of the child and the needs of the family.

 Forced attendance at school, in cases where this is even possible, in our

 experience often reduces meaningful engagement in learning and

 friendships for the children and erodes parent/teacher to child

 relationships.

 Families and schools have often attempted many strategies before coming

 to us for support. This includes rewards and punishments, discipline,

 enforced attendance, with increasing distress experienced by the children.

 We often ﬁnd that regardless of physical attendance at the school, where

 this is possible, a lack of engagement in learning or social relationships is

 observed. Often the families we work with describe that these interventions

 4

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 149  result in children and young people who’s nervous systems are

 overwhelmed and enter a freeze, ﬂight, ﬁght or fawn response. For example;

 ●

 Children in ﬂight sobbing, begging not to be forced to leave

 parents/carers or go to school. Running from school grounds, hiding

 at home.

 ●

 Physically unable to move in a freeze state, unable to speak,

 shutdown.

 ●

 Children in a ﬁght state behaving in an aggressive and violent ways

 with their families and in the school environment.

 ●

 Children in fawn while at school being very agreeable and

 cooperative, not requesting any adaptations, and then having

 meltdowns at home when back in a safe space.

 ●

 Children feeling so ashamed at they engage in self-harm and

 suicidal ideation.

 Children and young people are reliant on the adults around them to

 co-regulate with them and keep them safe, they do well when they can.

 Children and young people are not served by being in challenging

 relationships with the adults around them,  if they can easily conform to

 the school environment they will.  Those who can’t are often punished

 through the behavioural systems.  Positive reward based behavioural

 systems include the punishment of not receiving rewards that their peers

 easily achieve. This erodes the capacity for safe relationships and can

 escalate signiﬁcant behaviours.

 Impact on children and their families

    “I have given up my career, my potential superannuation. I have taken on tasks like having

 to teach my child to read because the school hasn’t even covered the basics. I have had to

 support healing for the damage mainstream school has done to my child's mental health.

 5

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 149  The decision to homeschool was a last resort and we were forced into it for lack of options.”

 ~  Parent to Grade 5 child now homeschooling

 “He is now only attending school for half days as he is in recovery after burnout. His

 nervous system cannot as yet manage any longer at school. He requires one to one

 support to manage school. He has funding for Support Sta�. He has Tier 5 level support

 however, I am told this equates to 15 hours a week of support sta� for my son. Which goes

 nowhere near to what he needs to extend his days. I can not return to the o�ce for my

 work. Despite the fact that I had to go into work during covid lockdowns ( I am an essential

 worker), I now have to work from home to manage his schooling.”

 “In our case, I work in an industry that allows for some ﬂexibility for working mothers. My

 partner has the potential to earn more than me and his industry is not so ﬂexible, so to

 date, the burden falls on me to sacriﬁce my career. My child has experienced a high level of

 mental distress and in my opinion, everyone has/ and will continue to have to work harder

 to undo the loss of education that he has experienced.

 RECOMMENDATIONS

 1.   Fund professional development for teachers / support sta�

 and support the prioritisation of connected and relational

 responses to children.

 “The school’s strategy for drop o� was for the receptionist to hold him while he screamed

 and assured me he was ﬁne when I left. I was not impressed, it was traumatic. We then had

 my child start early and it was agreed he would be doing some things with the acting

 principal to help him transition, this didn’t happen as my child would be asking when are

 we….? So I knew what we discussed wasn’t carried through. We were not supported, we were

 told we would be.” ~  Parent to Grade 5 child now homeschooling

 “The factors that allowed return to school were   that the teacher was willing to make

 accommodations that encouraged our son to feel safe and understood. So that he was

 able to begin to understand his learning needs and not feel criticised or ‘a di�cult pupil’.” ~

 have a felt sense of safety through co-regulation. Children are particularly

 critical that the people responsible for children in school have excellent

 emotional intelligence and skills in co-regulating.  A regulated state is

 critical for a brain to be able to attend, concentrate and learn.

 Evidence based programs that develop self-reﬂection and emotion

 coaching strategies for adults to respond and empathise with children’s

 emotional experience while upholding boundaries are recommended. This

 includes programs that educate adults on the development of emotional

 intelligence in children and adolescents such as Tuning in to Kids and

 Tuning in to Teens and collaborative problem solving with children such as

 Lives in the Balance Collaborative and Proactive Solutions.

 Children need to feel that they are held in positive regard by their

 educators,  that their experiences and feelings are considered and

 acknowledged.

 For neurodivergent or trauma a�ected children the school environment

 skilled at proactively responding when the child is communicating this

 7

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 149  through their words, body or behaviour. This requires adequate resourcing

 and valuing of these skills equally to academic outcomes.

 Emotion coaching and collaborative problem solving are skill sets that are

 evidence based and support the development of emotional intelligence

 skills in children.  Identify the lagging skills that mean a child cannot meet

 expectations, deeply consider the childs perspective and collaborate with

 them to create adaptations that improve participation and wellbeing, and

 support their long term skill development.

 2.   Implement a developmentally appropriate environment and

 curriculum.

March , 2023

Submission to:  Inquiry into the national trend of school refusal and related matters

I write to you as a parent of three children on the autism spectrum with additional learning needs.  Both
prior to, throughout 2022 and continuing this new year, the issue of “school refusal” is having a huge
  I have more than 20 years
impact on my oldest child and our family life.  (Also, I am a
experience working in varied positions in the areas of disability support, community health, education,
early intervention, family case management and support).

Children and young people who have “fallen off” with schooling need as much help as can be possibly
given to “get back ”, so they are not left way behind.  We need to stick with them and not be too quick
trying to move them on to the next option, whether this be another support service or school trying to
assist them.  They need the best possible and right support  from the start, so there is not wasted time
trying to navigate the service system to find it.  There needs to be understanding of the complex and
multiple factors that can contribute to difficulties.  The students and their families should not have to
carry blame and shame on top of all they are already dealing with in day to day life.

My friends/ carer contacts (having similar experiences with school refusal) and I have frequent
conversations about our experiences and the immense challenge of school refusal.  We are emotionally
and practically supportive of one another.   We have talked about and been aware of this inquiry, but I
know from these conversations  it is unfortunately  the very people who need to have their voice heard
that are coping with so much hardship and stress every day that are not in a position always to write in.
I would see that my individual case, and views for action needed  is representative of so many other
carers I know and don’t know, particularly parents of autistic children and young people.  Within my
own extended family, family members are continually connecting with others in their “circles” who are
going through similar problems in their families.  The problem seems to be so widespread.

In talking generally with other adults I have found there are many who describe the difficulties they are
experiencing  getting back to normal work, socialising and activities post Covid.  I feel we have not given
enough to the children who have needed more support.  I am very concerned about the impact of the
last three years on my child’s future.

 attended school almost every day in primary school.  He started year 7 in 2020 and
My son
over the two main “Covid years” his attendance reduced to poor, then non-attendance.  Last year he
missed half a year of schooling.  The “stretch” to make his way back becomes so much harder given now
much school has been missed.  The most disadvantaged students who could not manage remote
learning due to disability and learning difficulties have now had this compounded by a further year (and
more)  of disadvantage, as they have not had the capacity to just “bounce back” into learning.  It is hard
to feel things are or will be okay when a child is so far behind. My child identified he would probably still
be at school if Covid did not come.   It made a difference for my son to know that it was not just him
having difficulty getting back to school post-Covid.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 151
  (Separate to my son, I have seen  too in my primary aged daughter
refusal and have had to intervene with a higher level of support to get through this).

 the red flags of school

 son has not been attending school there has been an escalation in his anxiety,

When my
problematic and violent behaviour.   Police have needed to come on occasions and I have needed to  get
extra mental health support.  The impact has been significant on all family members, and a lot of time
we have been or are just in “survival mode” .  (I was already at capacity dealing with the needs and
challenges in my family pre-Covid).  The impact on other siblings can be extreme. for example, there is a
behaviour episode which goes into the night, we leave the home for safety reasons or the police come.
This causes great disruption to our night routine and impacts on siblings schooling (being late the next
morning) and their wellbeing, causing on-going anxiety.  We all may not be able to get sleep til the early
hours of the morning.  The police response was always helpful, but if my child was able to be in school
and we were able to access the services to better meet our needs we would likely not have the only
option, to be using emergency services.

We have been through many services to try and find the right ones.   I have found it difficult to get a
good support system in place for us, despite my education and extensive work background in the sector.
How must it be for other families who are facing so many more barriers to access support?  Most
services rely on the young person engaging, but it is high anxiety related to their disability that is the
very problem that makes connecting with services overwhelming and difficult.  My experience with
support services has been mixed, of which I can give some examples.

With Child and Adolescent Mental Health at Intake the “gatekeeping  bar “ is very high, so last year it
took a number of attempts over more than 6 months to get through.  My initial concerns even though
high level to me were not seen as at the level  to be eligible for this service.  Even once a referral is
finally accepted, the way the service operates was not accessible for my child at that time.  He would
not attend at the office and an extra effort was made with one home visit, but as he did not engage the
case was closed and referred out to Family Support Services.  The blame is put onto the child when we
say “we can’t work with your son because he has not engaged with our service”.  Actually, the focus
more needs to be: how accessible is the service to young people with very high anxiety in need of help?
Also, when a child is non-attending, schools request a Mental Health Plan to ” justify non-attendance
and to outline a plan for re-engagement”.  If the local mental health service is not accessible to my child,
I can’t get the needed plan.  (Following another recent  escalation in level of mental health concerns, my
child has now been able to access this service.  This time there has been a different approach to
engagement which has worked so far.  It does require so much of parents to get through to this point).

We were referred to a number of different  Family Support Services (Family Support X2, Adolescent
Violence, Family Violence)  who were involved for varied lengths of time.   Workers need to listen, be
able to work with the complexity in families and work with where the family is at.  Family Support
Services  I thought do have scope to work flexibly but I found them to be varied in their level of help.
For us, it has been the skill and experience (or not) of workers that has made both a positive and
negative impact.  Family Support Services however do not replace needed mental health support.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 151  I have had good experience with the Navigator Program as they considered the individual situation and
asked for my input about engagement.  They had the scope to respond to this and my child was able to
meet staff and hear about the service.  Though to access Navigator your attendance has to be 30% or
below in the previous term.  So, the situation needs to get to bad level before eligibility for help.

I have also had good experience with the NDIS.  Through the review process additional funding was
allocated to enable getting some different specialist help (Psychology- complex behaviour support, OT-
assessment).  Having access to a Support Co-Ordinator through the NDIS has assisted me greatly in

We blame the child when we to quickly try to force them into other education options.   Due to his
disability and time lost through Covid my son’s social and emotional development is delayed.  He still
needs the social development school can provide and the support structure of a school environment.
Virtual  School/Distance Ed as has been suggested does not provide this, and this means of education
does not work for him.  He is also not ready to move on to further education or a job as have been other
suggestions.   Also, when more time had passed and we started to explore other options just in case
needed, I have found  the waiting lists are so long ie.for a local community school with a different model
for learning.

When you are a parent outside of a school (particularly secondary), it can be difficult to find your way
within it and know who the best staff to talk to are and when.  It takes time to learn this, particularly
when your child starts in year 7 and Covid comes along.  Upon reflection, once you know the school
better you can look back and see how you could have done things differently from the start of problems
or along the way.  This is not going to make a difference now and may not have meant a different
outcome anyway.  Within school what I have seen that work well is the things that happen and personal
relationships that make my child feel connected with school.  I am appreciative of the staff who have

try and re-engage  with school.  Where schools and families can work well together, it makes a

for these young people:

-  Work hard to maintain young people in the school system and keep their connections.  The

benefit of this  is supported by research, that strong connections in secondary school can be a
preventative factor for anxiety and depression. (theconversation.com  28/11/22  Research
suggests one way to prevent depression and anxiety is a strong sense of connection at high

-  Maybe we need to look at how the law is used towards families trying their absolute best (and

are not meeting the needs???

-

-

-

It is difficult when a young person is not open to support, due to anxiety or other issues.

In services and schools, what helps most, is the personal/individual approach where if the time,

It  is needed  to have more programs in the community or resourcing in schools to enable more

Senate Inquiry - National Trend of School Refusal and Related Matters – March 2023

SUMMARY RESPONSE

This response is submitted by an early childhood teacher and mother to a neuro-divergent teen residing

through  prose,  offering  an  insight  into  the  lived  experience  of  an  education  system  that  is  unable  to

respond to ‘difference’ flexibly, particularly when and complexified by catastrophic global, local, familial

  It  addresses  the  Terms  of  Reference

and individual grief.

SUBMISSION

"Twenty-twenty”  resonates  within  us  still.  2020  when  a  bell  tolled  to  call  us  attention  and  take  us  on  a

journey  of  learning  that  we  couldn’t  refuse.  For  many,  it  was  learning  to  live  with  varying  levels  of

disruption, discomfort and dis-ease but for some; the nature and volume of learning was, and continues to

be,  utterly  overwhelming.  For  some,  the  overwhelm  surged  at  a  time  in  their  lives  deemed  potent  with

potential  for  learning  -  the  school  years.  For  some,  the  overwhelm  has  become  disabling,  unable  to

continue to function in a system that appears to suit the many and suggests the some are the problem. As

an educator and mother, I refuse the implication that the some are the problem. It is the system that is dis-

eased, the discomfort of the some, is in fact, an alarm bell, a call to disrupt the system for the some, and for

the many.

We are the some. This is our song.

‘Canary in the coalmine’ idiom 1. An early indicator of potential failure

or danger.

I want to speak to you about our little bird. Our bright little bird who sang before many and the story of the

silence that quieted him.

Our bird wasn’t always quiet. He sang of love, songs rich with clarity and confusion. Our beautiful bird

sang  out  to  others  and  made  connections.  Songs  echoed,  lines  were  repeated,  words  understood  and

misunderstood – clarity and confusion, shared; until the song of the many took on a regulated form: too

loud, too unified, with words that our birds did not understand. Clarity was quieted by confusion. As our

bird  failed  to  understand,  and  be  understood,  he  began  to  sing  wordlessly.  A  song  sung  in  sick  bays  as

aches  and  pains.  A  malaise,  descending.  Too  much.  Too  loud.  Silence  within  grew  to  equal  the  silence

without; the silence of a system that that tells you are alone in the shadows.

Love drew me to sing in his stead. My voice, replacing his, for so long and so loudly that my soul ached.

Our songs of distress fell on loving ears but grew quieter as we strained under the burden of words that

made  us  the  problem.  We  hung  the  labels  around  our  necks.  ADHD  –  yes.  Bereavement  -  yes.  Neuro-

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 153
 Senate Inquiry - National Trend of School Refusal and Related Matters – March 2023

divergent  -  yes.  ASD  –  yes.  Anxiety  –  of  course.  Depression  –  no  wonder.  PTSD  –  God,  really?  School

refusal  /rɪˈfjuːzl/ noun1. an act of refusing to do something.

refusal – what?.

Refusal? – wait!

Then just quietly it appeared on the electronic attendance system - where once we had notified school of

our bird’s absence under the definition of ‘Compassion’ - a new selection under ‘Reason for Absence’ -

School refusal.

No. Not refusal. Too far. I do refuse. I refuse that song.

Our bird’s song rang through me. “I’d go if I could but I can’t. I can’t tell you why, I don’t know.”

No. Not refusing. Not defiant. Not unwilling.

Not able.

I told our bird of the update to the system. We laughed “It’s like I’m in AA.”

We  laughed  because  we  love  and  it’s  our  way  but  that’s  not  the  way  for  some.  Some  shouldn’t  have  to

laugh at pain. Some shouldn’t have to be anonymous or ashamed. The shadows are silent but the silence is

not empty. Silence has volume. Silence, when it is systemic, is violence. Our canaries are singing songs of

danger and the system is silencing them. Our birds are not the problem, they are alerting the system to a

fault line, to its failure and I will sing of it.

Here in shadows, we tend to our silent birds, giving voice to what they can no longer express. An email

acknowledging my request to refer to ‘attendance anxiety’ rather than ‘school refusal’ felt life changing.

There is love in systems and we will seep into the cracks.

The day that our family accepted that attendance anxiety would necessitate a period of ‘unschooling’ and

unenrolling from our much-loved school, I asked our bird “Do I need to worry about suicide?”

“Of course you do,” our bird whispered, “I’ve failed.”

That day we flew towards the light to escape with his life.

An  enrolment  application  to  virtual  schooling  came  with  an  acknowledgement  that  they  are  receiving  ‘a

high volume of emails’.

This is a love song into the silence, for our bird, and for all the others. We may not be the many, but we are

the some. We are loved and we do not sing unheard.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 153 Senate Inquiry - National Trend of School Refusal and Related Matters – March 2023

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 153 Senate Inquiry - National Trend of School Refusal and Related Matters – March 2023

RECOMMENDATIONS

1. TERMINOLOGY

a.

‘School  refusal’  should  be  deemed  a  potentially  damaging  term  that  fails  to  convey  the

lived experience of families and youth.

b. The term ‘school can’ting’ though well-intentioned, does not land well for families who

may  already  feel  stigmatised  by  ‘labelling’.  Though  ‘can’t’  as  opposed  to  ‘won’t’  is

closer to the truth for many families the term sounds psychobabblish.  Additionally, in our

case  school  ‘can’ting’  was  inadequate  for  a  child  who  wants  to  learn  but  is  unable  to

attend.

c. Propose  ‘attendance  anxiety’  as  an  umbrella  term  for  a  range  of  factors  that  result  in  a

child  being  unable  to  attend  school.  It  is  my  experience  and  observation  that  anxiety

(whatever the cause) is at the root of being unable to attend onsite learning.

CLOSING

The vast majority of our experience is lived within the confines of our home; it can be incredibly isolating,

utterly exhausting and absolutely life-affirming. Along the way we have encountered heart-full individuals

trying  to  operate  within  the  constraints  of  an  outdated  educational  model  that  does  not  satisfy  the

contemporary  learning  styles  or  needs  of  the  majority  of  divergents  (and  ‘typicals’).   The  pandemic

exposed  an  aged  curriculum  that  is  failing  to  engage  hyper-technological  individuals  who  want  to  deep

dive, change course quickly and go at light-speed. Disengaged as we are from fulltime onsite learning, we

are wary of return; disempowered by an outdated system of assessment that fails to unbundle the person

from the curriculum. We long for assessments that are equitable: genuinely capable of accepting responses

that evidence diverse capacities and able to respond with meaningful pathways for interest-based learning.

V

The canaries are singing a song for change. We can’t keep singing the same old song in response.

Thank you for considering this submission.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 153

My son is now almost

I  write  first  as a  mother of  a  child  who  experiences  school can’t.  I  write secondly  as  a

Due to our school can’t, medical and emotional challenges and ongoing effort to find the

Our son
 is a blessing. Not only does he challenge me to be a better parent, a more
informed human and a critical thinker, he also led to me know why I am how I am. See I
was diagnosed with innatentative Adhd 6 months after he was diagnosed with combined
Adhd, in my 42nd year on earth. I already had the social and post-natal anxiety labels but
they never quite explained my way of being in the world. We had a quite risky, traumatic
birth and as a result I put a lot of effort into his life succeeding and I will always back him,
teach him and encourage his development and seek to understand how he interprets the
world.

It is this connection and passion that has led to the open, honest, oversharing information
below. I tried to keep it to 5 pages. I need to have this story told to help all the other
families going through it. I hope you can follow my line of thought.

Summary

I am writing to question the big picture; I want the enquiry to wonder …

“what is school for”?
My son wants to know what is school for. When he had his really hard school can’t days,
we could both see that school environment was not a safe place for him and he most
certainly could  not  learn in  the  traumatised state he  was  in, so  why was  I, his  Mother
trying so hard to get him to attend his school? Because “he has to”, that is what kids do,
go  to  school,  right?  Now  we  want  to  know  why  he  has  to  attend  school  when  it’s  so
painfully rejecting of who he is.

Add that I had a full-time paid job at the hardest times of this journey that simply was not
sustainable  under  the  pressure  of  daily  school  can’t  battles  and  early  calls  to  pick  up
“your” son
. If you picked up the blame and implied

1

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 154 shame in that statement, then thankyou because that is what happened whenever I had
to leave work to collect my often uncontrollable, physically violent and utterly distraught
son, in front of the school community again. I was always torn between being his mum,
comforting him in his clearly distressed state and making sure the community knew I was
going to make him accountable for his “behaviour”. The balance of those views almost
ripped our family apart.

After all my professional youth focused years and my personal battle to “just get my child
to go to school” I now wonder if School is about education at all. I know that many children
come  out  of  the  education  system  well  educated.  I  know  that  many  teachers’  deliver
fantastic classes daily and work way too many hours to teach their students, this question
is not about them. Nor the wonderful Principles, LSA’s, P and C’s and other students and
their families, it’s about the entire system over the 13 years they attend and what we
expect them to find out about themselves by the end of that time.

Is it really a pecking order game? A social status via compliance to the rules game to find
the winners and losers, to show everyone their place in society and expect them to stay
in that pigeon hole for life? Because that what is feels like. And it feels like neurodiverse
kids are being pegged for the outsider, the reject, the delinquent and the loser because
their brains work differently.

So, if we want a society that segregates and defines the status and value of children based
on their resources and mind wiring, maybe we could keep the current compliancy based
control model of a system we seem to have. But if we are brave leaders, if we want less
people rejected and marginalized in the first place, we can implement a trauma informed
and ACTION led, person centred education system.

HOW could the system work differently to support more children and therefore make
the environment safer for staff, children and families to engage with?

We can implement a trauma informed and ACTION led, person centred education system.
This could include;

•
•

•
•

•

all the human diversity, physical, mental and developmental
seek  strengths  in  every  student  and  develop  them  at  the  child’s  pace  over  13
years (E2 kids would move faster and many kids would move slower -that’s OK)
allow the autonomy of body placement (see whole body listening example above)
include  all  the  styles  of  learning  that  adults  are  supported  to  use,  making
engagement points at each stage, not JUST the Planning stage of Kolb’s learning
circle. (Adhd kids start at impulsive Action, then review, thinking planning comes
later).  We  can’t  plan  without  doing  something  first  and  we  can’t  do  without
interest being engaged).
support children going through traumatic reactions to school and home events
without blaming them for their biological survival reactions by giving all staff and
community the skills to do better within the real time situations of stress

2

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 154


 This  approach  would  create  a  diverse  ecology,  the  right  environment  to  help  children
thrive in all the diversity in which they are born. The key is understanding how Trauma
affects developmental capacity, how to coregulate with children, how to support teachers
with extra staff training in occupational therapy and trauma 1st aid responses in real time,
as  they  happen.  Look  into  Dr  Ross  Greens  work  on  CPS  training,  Mona  Delhooke’s
“Beyond  Behaviours”  book  and  podcasts  as  great  informants  of  how  to  make  the
changes.

Can we design a system that allows kids to exist in their own skin, without fear of being
different, without fear of being punished for impulses they have no control over? If we
could, surely teachers would also feel safer, more equipped to handle student meltdowns,
more in control of their own responsibilities to not add to the presenting trauma, but seek
to regulate the student in a safer manner before continuing with learning.

I’m not suggesting for one second teachers take on this role with all their over stretched
teaching roles. I for one have experienced the most effective roles in this regard are LSA’s.
I also know they are the least trained, lower paid staff in the school systems. If they are
best placed to add this trauma informed element to the system as a whole, we need to
quadruple  their  numbers  and  add  OT  specialists  to  the  support  them  with  students
sensory needs in the first year of school. Why wait until a child is diagnosed, suspended
and rejected socially already? That is TOO late.

Across  the  student  population  in  Kindy  we  could  implement  OT  led  sensory  profiles
