My name is

 I’m a parent, a neurodivergent woman, an advocate for my autistic child and an avid

consumer of research. I have been embroiled in our own journey to school can’t for the last 15 months. Our

school system is so toxic that if we applied workplace health and safety definitions of psychosocial hazards,

the level of risk our children are exposed to would be deemed unacceptable.

Let me begin with my child, who is autistic. My child attended daycare from 2 years old; in 2021 they attended

kinder 4.5 days a week. During that time, they had no separation anxiety, no anxiety behaviours and only

minor behavioural difficulties. My child started prep last year and began to experience minor disruptions and

isolated incidences of physical behaviours at school. This year, it quickly escalated to separation refusal and

repeated physical behaviours at school and pervasive mood and regulation changes at home.

Our communication with the school has been lengthy, frequent and explicit. A private psychologist has been

making fortnightly visits to support staff. IEPs are in place; regular

 occur; 4 different education supports

have been delegated to work 1:1 with my child for the majority of the day. The last fortnight we had at school

this term consisted of 2 hour days outside of the classroom completing modified activities. And yet, the

separation and behavioural issues persist; issues which have occurred in no other context.

The school is unable to apply:

•
•

•

The expert advice of our educational psychologist and specialty pediatrician

The advice from government supported resources including Raising Children’s Network or the

Even their own department guidelines around behaviour management and de-escalation.

I have boiled those resources down to the simplest terms for the school on multiple occasions:

Listen to what my child says and ask more

Curiously and kindly ask my child what’s up

•
•
•  When my child verbalises a concrete problem, talk through solutions
•  Get down to my child’s level to talk to them
•  Remain calm, warm and kind
•
•  Move a short distance away if that's what my child’s behaviour is communicating
•

"Sportscast" my child’s feelings and reactions

Let my child’s have an 'escape' when they’re feeling unable to regulate in the current space

This has been dismissed in favour of:

Continuing to make demands despite obvious, extended and increasing escalation

Speaking sternly
Ignoring my child’s concerns when they are still calm enough to speak

•
•
•
•  Reprimanding my child when non-preferred behaviours occur
•  Reprimanding my child for seeking their safe retreat at a non-preferred time
•

Standing over my child or sitting right next to my child when they are demonstrating indirect physical

behaviours

•  Remaining in close physical proximity when my child finally escalates to hitting or kicking
•
•

Loudly and sternly saying “Stop!” or “use your words!”

Trying to elicit demonstrations of contrition, shame or empathy from my child immediately after they

have stopped hitting/kicking

This is the question I keep coming back to: how is behaviour I would never tolerate from a workplace manager

the norm for how a primary school aged child is treated? I ask, would you feel safe and ready to work in a

workplace where:

•

•

Your boss sternly reprimanded you for not completing work tasks beyond your training or ability

Your boss reduced your lunch break because you weren’t able to complete a work task within their

If you raised clear concerns about unrealistic job expectations, but were ignored and then told to

In fact, there’s only one institution I can think of that as adults where we have no personal agency over:

•  Whether or not we attend that institution

… and you only end up in that institution if you’ve run afoul of the law first.

The following is a list of psychosocial hazards children experience at school, either in direct quote or slightly
reworded from Safe Work Australia’s information on psychosocial hazards and bullying behaviours1:

•
•

Too high or too low demands on children

Little control or say over their breaks, meeting their bodily needs or work tasks, including how or

regard in educational relationships to learn

•

even angry tone, standing over, leaning forward and pointing fingers, threats to withhold

•  Reprimands in front of peers that would feel belittling or humiliating to a child
•  Unjustified criticism or complaints

On top of this, for kids have been exposed to trauma or who have a socioemotional and/or learning disability,

the school environment can also feature:

Setting timelines that are unreasonable

Speaking from my child’s experience, autistic kids are the canary in the coal mine. Autistic kids are more likely
to have difficulty verbalising thoughts and feelings as well as comparatively lower emotional regulation2 to
their neurotypical peers. Yet they are put in environments focused on seeing group compliance through
personal control. Autistic kids are also more likely to be ‘rule-based’ thinkers3, but then aren’t supported with
rules that are concrete, explicit, fair and achievable. Then when an autistic child is struggling, their verbal

and/or behavioural communication is ignored to the point of meltdown. Strategies are then aimed at fixing the

behaviour by attempting to force empathy despite research debunking autistic empathy deficits, or by

reiterating rules the child cannot follow, or by relying solely on sensory regulation esactivities, or by teaching

emotional regulation strategies designed to push down their natural reactions to systemic barriers. These

approaches are used in place of the adults stopping to identify and solve the barriers that caused the child’s

difficulty in the first place.

So why is it coming to a head now and not just with neurodivergent kids?

Modern parenting norms have shifted so that the average Australian parent prefers support over control. Even

as far back as 1998, the majority of Australian parents aligned with “authoritative (loving, supportive,
consistent, firm)” parenting over “authoritarian (strict, power-based, and punitive)” parenting4. The increasing
availability of research regarding attachment, brain development and neurodivergence mean that parents are

increasingly understanding how to best support their children as complete human beings.

Remote learning during the pandemic meant that for a large period of time, most children were learning in a

familiar, comfortable and safe space with regular individualised support from a caring and supportive adult,

even accounting for high levels of accompanying mental distress. If you take a frog out of the boiling water,
good luck trying to make it jump back in.

The pandemic-related increase in mental health difficulties also plays into why so many kids are now struggling

to meet unrealistic and demanding school expectations. Along with the increase in mental distress, the

pandemic also reduced access to assessment, diagnosis and treatment of mental health and

neurodevelopmental conditions, which has in turn created downstream shortages. The end result is higher

2 What is autism? (no date) Autism Spectrum Australia (Aspect). Available at: https://www.autismspectrum.org.au/about-autism/what-is-

autism (Accessed: March 22, 2023).

communities (Research Report No. 5). Melbourne: Australian Institute of Family Studies.

 rates of struggling kids with less available support. Previously, that support that may have been enough to help

kids to keep it together in a hostile environment, masking the underlying problems with the system or passing

it on to exhausted and isolated families who managed the fall out at home.

Finally, consider in school we are now seeing:

•  A higher proportion of struggling under-supported students
•

Teachers who are beyond exhausted from implementing distance learning during lockdown, then

covering the sporadic staff shortages caused by post-lockdown covid clusters, then covering

permanent shortages caused by an industry wide exodus

•

Schools that are concerned about how far behind kids are both socially and academically

Add all of these factors together and you have a group of burnt out professionals with little dedicated training

in behaviour management who are worried about their students. None of this supports those adults in charge

to act calmly, be flexible or utilise creative problem solving, especially when it goes against the status quo.

So what needs to change?

Funding has been stripped from out of schools for so long, why is anyone surprised that  they’re so
dysfunctional that neither students nor teachers want to be there? At this stage, what is needed is a

transformation across the education system to create a culture that is:

•
•
•
•
•

Transparent

Collaborative

Evidence based

Focused on continuous improvement

Trauma

Inclusive, informed by:
•  Neurological development
•
•  Neurodivergence
•  Disability

However, culture change is only as good as it’s practical applications. For my family, the following would make

a significant difference:

•
•

Fund one generalist education support person for every primary school classroom, over and above

the current funding for students with additional needs

Train all staff in collaborative problem solving and inclusive, evidence-based behaviour management
Institute a department wide policy and procedure around managing incidents of escalated student

behaviour that requires the school to:

o
Identify in collaboration with the student underlying barriers that lead to the incident
o  Collaborate with the student to identify and agree on some potential strategies to address

those barriers

o  Notify the family of the incident, identified barriers and proposed solutions
o  Consult family for any additional input
o  Recommend referral for additional skill/medical support for student if needed
Create a family support role in education departments to advise, advocate, support and refer

•
•  Use a collaborative approach to identify and solve the biggest stressors for teachers; there is no way

that happier, better resourced teachers won’t have a positive down-stream effect

 Collaborative and Proactive Problem Solving, the

our education culture and to support our teachers with the training and resources they need to be able to apply

 What is needed is a policy level push to embed these approaches into

them.

A final note.

My child has now been home for about 3 weeks. He is belly laughing again. He is resolving big disappointments

and frustrations with minimal support. He attended a drop off

 this week: he said goodbye after a

short transition period and completed the 3 hours with no behavioral issues. He is chatty and engaged – it’s a

relief to see him happy again after so long.

There needs to be a much greater understanding of the relationship between school refusal/
school can’t/ school avoidance and suicidal thoughts and acts. This is urgent.
There needs to be greater understanding of when school avoidance becomes Complex-Post-
traumatic stress disorder (C-PTSD).
The focus on attendance being the first measure to success, and the narrative that not
attending 100% will mean less successful individuals is causing harm, significant harm.
School is not a one-size fits all option, and schools have become much more stressful and
pressured places for everyone in them.
Awareness of ableism and discrimination in the classroom.
Removing the narrative of ATAR as the biggest measure of success and celebration, and
removing NAPLAN and scores/ranks is a matter of urgency. Schools that have recognised the

Senate Standing Committee on Education and Employment

Inquiry into the National Trend of School Refusal and Related Matters

Personal Submission

***

I am writing this submission as a parent of a child who does not attend traditional school, and as an
adult who refused school as a child myself. I wish to share my experiences and insights, specifically in
relation to the second term of reference regarding the affect of school refusal on young people.

My daughter is a very intelligent and sensitive child. At the beginning of her Foundation year at school,
we sent her off to commence her education. However, it became quickly clear to us that our child was
not thriving in the school context where she had to substitute her creativity, agency, initiative,
independence and insatiable interest in learning about everything, with sitting quietly, shallow
investigation, and reliance on a teacher to tell her what to learn and how to learn it.

Our daughter quickly lost her spark and began to show signs of generalised anxiety and depression, all at
the tender age of 5 years old. When she started refusing to attend school, we agreed to try
homeschooling. As she found her educational autonomy, so she found her love for life and learning
again. She has happily been homeschooling ever since. We have a thriving homeschool community in
our local region and regularly connect with other families for free play as well as organised activities and
workshops. My child is truly the happiest child I know.

I would like to take a moment to point out here that while the effect of school was certainly negative for
my child’s well-being, the effect of school refusal was not. This is because my partner and I were willing
and able to identify and respond to her needs and pivot our educational approach to homeschooling.
We did not force her to attend school, which would certainly have had significant negative
consequences for her. I believe that it is erroneous to automatically identify school refusal as the
problem. Refusal to attend school is perhaps better understood as the child communicating their dis-
content with school. Rather, it is the forced attendance of a child who refuses to attend school that is
problematic.

My partner and I have experienced personal challenges as a result of our situation – emotionally,
mentally, financially and in relation to our careers. However, we do not see this to be as a result of our
daughter’s school refusal, but rather as a result of the lack of support available to parents who choose
not to force their children into an educational context that is unhealthy for them. There is very little
practical or financial support for parents choosing to homeschool their children, despite homeschooling
being a legitimate and important educational option.

Our decision to homeschool was also informed by my own experience as a school-refusing child. I hasten
to add that when my daughter was in her pre-school year, I sought professional support from a therapist
to work through my own school trauma, so that I could continue to consciously make the best decisions
for my child uncoloured by my own experiences. My experiences are relevant here to illustrate the
impact of forced school attendance.

As a school-refusing child, I was sent to a child psychologist with the goal of getting me to attend school
without having to be physically restrained while I screamed.  My memories are of terror as I watched my

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 157 mother leave me in the physical grip of a school teacher. The psychologist used behavioural therapies
(still commonly used today), which essentially taught me to internalise my emotions and attend without
complaint. This has resulted in a lifetime of impact on my emotional and mental well-being resulting in
perfectionism, anxiety, externalised self-esteem and bouts of depression.

I implore you to consider a goal beyond just getting kids to attend school. Beyond “fixing” the problem
kids. Indeed, I would like to finish by commenting that I believe an additional important question is why
- -
there is an increasing number of children refusing to attend school. The answer to this is complex and
varied in its nature. Notably, I would like to emphasise that school refusal is not exclusively the domain
of neurodivergent children (as may sometimes be assumed). Though there is no doubt that the
institution of school, generally, does not support neurodivergent children to flourish well. I encourage
you to consider more deeply that the current paradigm of school, based on principles of coercion,
hierarchy and competitiveness, is failing all children and resulting in an epidemic of poor mental and
emotional health.

I would be happy to provide more information as to any of these matters if the Committee so requires.

Thank you for reading my submission.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 157

submissions.text:
Regarding the increase in school refusal, I would like to submit my perspectives, both as a qualified

 and as a homeschooling parent

I believe that the increase in school refusal is not the problem, but a symptom of a broken schooling
system, and reflective of deep faults with how we have come to view education and learning. I believe
these faults have been brought to bare to a greater degree to people as a result of removal from this
broken system during Covid 19 lockdowns. Through parents and students being able to mitre easily
contrast mental health and education outcomes during phases outside the normal school environment
(i.e. during lockdowns), they have been able to at least see the effects of these faults, and then also to
identify factors that may have contributed to poorer mental health prior to phases of lockdown.

While I believe this applies to all students, I feel neuro-diverse students are particularly poorly
accommodated in the mainstream school system, as class sizes are so big that they do not allow true
differentiation, or inclusion of individual student’s needs and interests.

I believe that these faults are numerous, and while my time is limited in the preparation of this
response, I will try and touch on where I see some of them:

Class sizes are way too big – research by Hattie showed that class sizes needed to be reduced to around
8 students per class to see change – these smaller class sizes should be rolled out.

More training of teachers on understanding how to better identify their students needs – models such
as non violent communication should be considered, as well as the work of Gabor Maté in considering
how a child’s context and history of life experiences and trauma influences their current feelings,
behavior, needs and ability to learn, as well as teachers’ own trauma is informing their reactions to
students, values, etc.

Curriculum is far too rigid – flexibility to not only allow, but encourage students’ passions to be pursued
in meaningful, authentic ways, not just in scant electives, but as major, valued parts of their learning.
Above mentioned reductions in class sizes will allow for such flexibility. This will not only improve
educational outcomes, as students are given autonomy to learn more effectively and deeply, but also
improve mental health outcomes, as student self efficacy and self esteem will drastically improve, as
their interests are tangibly valued, rather than paid lip service to – I have witnessed this transformation
time and again within home schooled children. I have no doubt that reshaping how we think about
curriculum and learning will drastically reduce school refusal.

Home school parents need more support – home schooling families sacrifice significant income and
career development, among other things, to provide their children with better education that places
more value on the acknowledgment of the child as a person, not a vacant vessel to be filled. Home
schooling should be acknowledged for the amazing education our us providing and reducing burden on
the school system.

Positively, there are models to turn to to help improve the system (like Village High School in Gippsland,
Victoria, and Woodline Primary in Geelong, as well as other examples here and abroad – I’m looking at
you, Finland – as well as innumerable case studies in waiting from successfully home schooled children),
though I believe it will take boldness and bravery to create the substantial structural change that I
believe is required to achieve a system that is equitable, engaging and enriching, and will result in
reducing school refusal.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 158

CatholicCare Diocese of Broken Bay -Northern

The National Trend of School Refusal and Related Matters

Catholic Care Diocese of Broken Bay (CCDBB) appreciates the opportunity to respond to this
inquiry.  CCDBB  was  formed  in  1987,  as  a  Social  Care  agency  operating  in  communities  in
Northern Sydney, Northern Beaches, and the Central Coast NSW.  CCDBB is the official not-
for-profit, professional social justice and care agency of the Catholic Church in the Diocese
of Broken Bay.

As  a  family  service,  CatholicCare  Diocese  of  Broken  Bay  (CCDBB)  works  extensively  with
families. Our organisation has recorded an increase in parents struggling with school refusal.
In the month of November 2022, at least 50% of referrals made to the Child, Youth and Family
Support team identified school refusal as being one of the reasons for referral. Additionally,
through our casework, school refusal is reported to be increasing in prevalence, despite this
not always being identified as a reason for referral.

CatholicCare  has  engaged  through  Northern  Sydney  networks  to  address  locally  the
challenges  parents  and  schools  are  currently  facing  concerning  school  refusal.  Our
Communities of Practice, and our partnerships have formed the basis of the below submission
and recommendations.

1.  The  increasing  number  since  the  COVID-19  pandemic,  of  young  people  and  their

families who are experiencing school refusal.

➢  CCDBB have worked with young people whose development has been impacted during
the  COVID-19  pandemic.  It  has  been  identified  remote  learning  has  significantly
impacted  child  and  youth  learning  routines  resulting  in  difficulty  for  children  to  return
directly to the school premises.

➢  During COVID 19 the focus rightly shifted to Mental Health, and therefore reducing focus
on key learning curriculum outcomes impacting all year groups, and in particular, those
approaching HSC or completing HSC.

➢  Students with existing learning challenges are now facing increased learning gaps, which
can  prevent them  being  able  to  do the  work  at  the  required  level.  For  some  of  these
children, the thought of returning to school with these conditions is too overwhelming.

➢  School avoidance has been normalised in peer groups and schools through months of

remote learning, uncertainty, and isolation from friends.

 ➢  Many  children  are  avoiding  school  for  legitimate  reasons  such  as  anxiety  and  social

situations that make the child feel unpleasant or general distress.

2.  How school refusal is affecting young people and  their families and the impacts it is

having on the employment and financial security of parents and carers.

➢  Families’  financial  resources  are  heavily  impacted  by  the  current  cost  of  living  crisis  in
NSW.  Therefore,  parents  who  have children  school  refusing  are  often  caught  between
having  to  stay  home  and  supervise/attempt  to  engage  in  learning  vs  maintaining
employment.

➢  Families who are employed often have to take further disrupted time off work to attend
educational and other support meetings in an attempt to re-engage children back into
the education system.

➢  Families are often struggling with maintaining new boundaries between navigating a new
work from home/back to school culture which creates additional relationship pressures
where  school  refusal  is  concerned.  Parents  report  it  can  be  an  ongoing  battle  to  get
children to school in the morning.

➢  Some  reports  identify  the  precedence  has  been  set  of  children  being  out  of  school,

making it difficult for some families to set new routines.

➢  The  education  system  has  not  adapted  any of  it’s  newer  learning  forms  and therefore

may have missed an opportunity to transform learning styles for all children.

➢  Caring responsibilities due to school refusal may impact or jeopardise employment in the

longer term.

➢  Parents  report  the  impact  school  refusal  has  on  their  own  mental  health  including
increased  anxiety  and  depression  and  the  stress  of  maintaining  employment  while
addressing the emotional needs of their child.

➢  Children’s  2-year  learning  gaps  has  consequently  disrupted  the  early  intervention  and
identifications  systems  schools  would  previously  have  had  in  place,  therefore  children
requiring assessments are now identified later.

➢  As a result, children’s learning would have fallen further behind than expected had lock

downs not occurred.

➢  Families do not always have the resources available to meet the various needs including
waiting for psychosocial assessments, psychiatrist appointment through the public system,
and within the private sector waitlists are just as high.

➢  Sibling groups observing behaviours can be challenging for families to manage.

➢  Parents often feel overwhelmed and a sense of hopelessness when their children avoid

school.

➢  Parents often feel a current stress and uncertainty for their child’s future in the present, as
well as an uncertainty about what the future may hold, causing heightened distress and
worry.

 3.  The impacts and demands of the increasing case load on service providers and schools

to support these students and their families.

➢  Detailed  assessment  is  required  as  each  family’s  circumstances  are  different  and  this
requires  detailed,  time  consuming  assessment  using  evidence-based  assessment  and
measurement tools.

➢

Interventions are now requiring more intensive case coordination efforts which is reducing
the capacity of an already stretched family support sector model.

➢

Interventions are also remaining within family services caseworker for longer than usual
which compounds the already difficult capacity issues.

➢  Families are unable to move towards their goals in a timely manner due to the extensive
waitlists of key Allied Health professionals when requiring an assessment or diagnoses.

➢  Assessments are not always holistic and may not always capture the voice of the child,

which can be lost in the goal setting process.

➢  Services are reaching out for further resources and further training on the issue.  In June
2022, the Northern Sydney Local Health District in conjunction with School-Links provided
a detailed webinar on School Refusal aimed at helping services understand school refusal
and what they can do due to address the increase in school refusal numbers. Whilst these
strategies  are  helpful,  they  do  not  negate  providers  existing  capacity  issues  within  the
family support sector.

➢  When managing school refusal, parents are often left to deal with and manage the strain
of school refusal themselves initially.  Parents in our family support program report feeling
ill-equipped and shamed when managing school refusal.  Parents struggle around their
own expectations, school expectations and managing the wellbeing of the child/young
person.

➢

It is also known the longer the problem exists the more difficult if can be for the child or
young person to get back into the routine of going to school. Therefore, responding earlier
to assist parents in this journey is pivotal. However, the current rate of increased matters
suggests that a current response-based solution will need to be actioned as well as an
early intervention approach to ensure we respond to current issues and further prevent
others.

4.  How  relevant  state,  territory  and  federal  departments  are  working  to  monitor  and

address this growing school refusal challenge.

➢  School refusal is a complex and growing issue in the community and anecdotal evidence
suggest parents feel overwhelmed and unskilled in managing the issue. Furthermore, co-
morbidity presentations involve a cross section of state and federally funded programs
and  services,  and  relies  on  all  of  these  services  working  succinctly  and  effectively  to
address this matter.

➢  As an example, it has also been proven children with mental health issues and disabilities
are a higher risk of school refusal therefore requiring a cross effort between NDIS, Health,
and Education and the coordination of their efforts to support a young person and family.
Currently those coordination efforts are usually managed by external services such as Not
for Profits, or parents fighting to have better coordination across.

 5.  Other related matters

➢  Additional  resources  should  be  allocated  to  school,  Health  and  NGOs  to  ensure  that

children experiencing school refusal receive a systemic and holistic support.

➢  By providing education and knowledge to parents around the complexities with school
refusal  we  hope  to  improve  the  child  and  young  person’s  wellbeing,  as  well  as  at  the
whole family and work towards the child or young person becoming independent and
engaged with the community and school.

➢  CCDBB  recommend that  Education,  NSW  Health  and  Community  work  with  families to
provide  education  and  knowledge  to  parents  dealing  with  school  refusal  to  build
confidence and capacity to deal with issues as they arise. The support would need to be
targeted at two separate cohorts; parents of primary school children with school refusal
and parents of high school children with school refusal.

Recommendations

CatholicCare  would  recommend  State  and  Federal  Government  work  together  to
understand the prevalence of the issue and to target resources systemically to address the
need. Including;

➢  Recognising that response based, targeted programs and supports are different to Early

Intervention, noting both of these areas need attention.

➢  Consider  implementing  School  refusal  Specialist/Family  Support  credentialled  workers
within  schools  to  provide  advice,  support  and  outreach  to  the  child,  families  and
coordinating  internal  education  services  such  as  wellbeing  team  and  student  support
officers.

➢  CatholicCare recognises responses and resources may lack the required evidence base

given the issue has largely been increased through COVID 19.

➢  Children  must  be  involved  in  their  own  story  about  school  refusal,  and  they  must  be
allowed to set their own goals and pace to ensure improved success with outcome.

Learn i ngC rea tes

AUSTRALIA

Learning Creates Australia thanks the Senate Standing Education and Employment

References Committee for undertaking this important inquiry.

As an independent, non-proﬁt organisation, Learning Creates Australia convenes a diverse alliance of

people and organisations to create innovative, evidence-based and practical solutions for a more fair, deep

and wide learning system. Over the past 3 years, this has included more than 2,000 young people,

educators, parents, policy makers, First Nations communities, employers, academics and tertiary providers

across the Australian learning landscape.

The many stories and the expert advice we’ve collected over the past few years echo many of the

sentiments of the submissions and expert witness accounts the Committee has received - our schooling

system is outdated, stagnating at best and underperforming at worst.

We recommend the prioritising of two interconnected activities to ensure all young people can learn and

beneﬁt from an Australian learning system that meets their needs.

Listening to young people

As many witness accounts have already recommended, Learning Creates echoes calls for the collection of

new and better data on the young people missing school is an important ﬁrst step to better understand and

shine a light on the seriousness of the challenge and build appetite for more serious reform.

Most importantly we strongly urge that a formal process to listen deeply to the experience of young people

who are disengaged with school is central to understanding what’s not working. This crucial engagement

can contribute to the valuable evidence base needed to support longer term, systemic interventions. Within

this focus of listening with young people, Learning Creates Australia would also recommend a process to

listen closely to the perspectives of First Nations young people and educators.

Learning Creates has worked directly with thousands of young people across Australia to listen to their

perspectives and ensure young people’s voice and agency is embedded at all levels of our work particularly

those from disadvantaged backgrounds. In the ﬁrst 2 years of work, over 1200 young people have been

involved in The Learner’s Journey project to provide their expertise and lived experience within the system.

Overwhelmingly, young people said they felt inappropriately deﬁned by success or failure in school and

through examinations and assessments associated with senior secondary certiﬁcates. They rejected the idea

that the breadth and depth of who they are, what they know and can do is represented in those credentials

or reﬂected in their learning environments.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 161 Re-thinking how we recognise learning

How we recognise learning and the focus on ATAR is impacting the wellbeing, in school experiences of

young people and limiting their life trajectories.

Learning Creates also undertook an analysis of 22 policy papers and reviews from the past 4 years,

including federal and state policy and curriculum reviews and reports from The Business Council of

Australia and other leading academics. It revealed that there is:

-

Universal agreement that there is an over-reliance on the ATAR, which is increasingly irrelevant to

post-school pathways and is often unfair especially to those who are already starting from a

position of educational disadvantage.

- Maintaining the status quo isn’t good for Australia’s economic strength and resilience and isn’t good

for society as disconnection and disengagement in learning entrenches disadvantage.

The common themes emerging in these ofﬁcial reports and expert opinions and in the views of young

people, is that schooling in Australia does not reliably deliver or recognise what young people need if they

are to thrive and contribute to a healthy economy and society. This situation is counter-productive for

learners and for the economy, for society, for communities and for families.

Learning Creates research has illuminated an appetite amongst Australian educators and education

stakeholders for serious reform to educational recognition systems and the subsequent beneﬁts to school

connectedness. This reﬂects change across developing nations around the world. UN member states have

been rallying to create and share visions and plans for transforming education between now and 2030.

Redeﬁning the purpose of education is one of the most powerful levers for transforming the system and

inclusive and intentional dialogues are needed to surface values and beliefs about education and to develop

a broadly shared vision of the purpose of education.

Australia needs to redesign our education system to prepare young people for their future rather than for

our past. Without a ﬁt-for-purpose learning system for young people, we are putting limits on their

engagement and the outcomes of their learning. This has a ﬂow on effects that impact individuals,

communities and our economy.

The ﬁrst step, and our recommendation, is a community engaged public dialogue, with young people,

parents, employers, educators, designed to ensure participants feel secure enough to think beyond the

current reality of their experience of an education system. There are global models this could be based on

such as The Big Education Conversation and Big Change in the UK. These models could inform us in

developing an appropriate form of engagement in Australia which would need to take into account the

unique needs of our young people, community and First Nations people.

We would value the opportunity to provide further information or suggestions to the Committee.

Bronwyn Lee, CEO, Learning Creates Australia

Learning Creates would like to acknowledge the traditional custodians of the land throughout Australia who

have been learning and educating on Country for over a thousand generations.

21st of March 2023

Committee Secretary
Senate Education and Employment Committees
PO Box 6100
Parliament House
Canberra ACT 2600

RE: The national trend of school refusal and related matters inquiry

To whom it may concern,

 and I am a final year Social Work student at

My name is
currently on my final placement within a youth support service, where I work with at-risk youth
and young people who are referred to us for case management and support. School refusal and
disengagement is something many of the young people we work with are experiencing. With
my own experiences of school refusal, I felt that it was necessary for me to put in my own
submission to the committee for your consideration.

 I am

What is school refusal?

School refusal is a multifaceted issue that can significantly impact a young person’s academic
performance, mental health, and overall wellbeing. It is not merely a matter of truancy or
skipping school, but rather a term that encompasses a wide range of behaviours and emotions
that lead students to avoid or refuse to attend school (Garfi, 2018).

Various forms of school refusal can affect young people, including anxiety-based refusal,
avoidance-based refusal, and school attendance problems (Garfi, 2018). Anxiety-based refusal
is one type that is quite prevalent, and it involves students feeling intense fear and worry about
going to school. Avoidance-based refusal is where students avoid attending school due to social
or academic pressures. This type may arise from bullying, low self-esteem, or academic
struggles that leave students feeling overwhelmed or hopeless about their ability to thrive in
school. Additionally, some students may have school attendance problems, which make it
difficult for them to attend school regularly due to a range of factors such as health issues,
family problems, or transportation challenges.

Truancy, which is the act of skipping school without permission, is often associated with
delinquent behaviour. However, it is important to acknowledge that truancy can also be a
component of school refusal (Garfi, 2018). Sometimes, students may skip school because they
feel overwhelmed or anxious about attending, or because they lack the necessary resources
and support to manage their attendance. Truancy can be othering to young people because it
reinforces negative stereotypes about individuals who struggle with school attendance and may
result in them being punished or excluded from educational opportunities. Additionally, truancy

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 165 can worsen pre-existing mental health concerns and lead to negative outcomes such as low
academic achievement or involvement in the justice system. Therefore, it is crucial to address
truancy as a part of school refusal and to provide support and empathy to young people who
may be grappling with school attendance issues (Garfi, 2018).

Regardless of the specific manifestation of school refusal, it is essential to acknowledge that it
can be a severe and distressing problem for young people, their families, and their
communities.

My Story

When looking at my own experience, it is clear that school refusal has been on ongoing issue
for many years. I was in high school in the early to mid-2000s, a time when there was little
support available for student wellbeing nor was there the understanding of ADHD and ASD that
there is today. The stigma around mental health issues was real, and it still wasn’t okay to talk
about them.

From grade 8 onwards I had severe depression and anxiety because I felt broken, like there was
something wrong with me. That I was unlovable and unwanted. I had suicide ideations, self-
harming behaviours, and maladaptive coping mechanisms of isolation and trying to escape into
my own fantasy world. I didn’t want to live in the real world, and for me at that time, the real
world was high school.

I wasn’t diagnosed or treated for ADHD or any mental health conditions until my mid-20s. For
almost 15 years, I hated myself because I had no other option, no knowledge about self-care,
self-compassion, mental health, or what a healthy wellbeing looked like.

At the end of term 3 of grade 8, I had two weeks off due to the flu. Once term 4 started, my
school refusal began. I can’t remember exactly why, but I do remember the fear and terror
responses I had whenever my mum drove me to school. I wouldn’t get out of the car, I wouldn’t
get in the car, I wouldn’t get ready, or I would get there late. I drove my mum to a breakdown.

I was terrified of school.

Of my peers.

Of Myself.

Looking back at it now, I can see that it was probably a combination of puberty and hormones,
undiagnosed ADHD and ASD, traumatic experiences with my peer group and their forced
alienation of myself at the end of grade 7, and trying to cope with a multi-week absence from
school, which I hadn’t had before, and the consequences of being behind on school work, trying
to catch up with that, and not being able to.

I didn’t have support from the school – my school refusal was just allowed to happen. I fell
through the cracks because I was the good kid, I wasn’t a student that made problems for the

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 165 school. They did what they thought was best for me; by leaving me alone. My parents didn’t
know what to do, where they could go for help, what I needed.

So, I suffered. I loathed myself. I wanted to end it all, but I was too afraid to. No one listened to
me, or cared about me, so I disengaged from the people around me and self-isolated. My
experience of school refusal continued throughout the rest of high school. I didn’t participate, I
didn’t engage, I was often late – I didn’t want to be there.

I escaped reality.

The problem, though, was by doing that I only made things worse for myself. I needed
connection, therapy, medication, understanding, assistance, and solutions. If I could have
reached out, or someone recognised what was happening and offered help, I would be a lot
more adjusted and happier today without all the suffering that I experienced.

Unfortunately, that did not happen. Instead, I’ve spent the past ten years – from my late 20s to
mid-30s – regretting the life that I have missed out on, and it is only through intensive therapy
that I am only now able to start moving past that.

I don’t want other young people to go through what I did.

Why school refusal, and what can we do?

School refusal can have a significant impact on young people and their families. Research has
identified several risk factors that may increase the likelihood of school refusal (Heyne et al.,
2019). Students with a history of anxiety or depression, academic problems, poor social skills,
and family conflict may be at higher risk. Additionally, school-related factors such as a lack of
support from teachers or peers, high academic pressure, and negative school experiences can
also contribute.

Trauma and bullying can also have a considerable impact (Ingul et al., 2019). Traumatic
experiences can lead to feelings of fear, shame, and low self-esteem, making it difficult for
students to attend school. Bullying can cause students to feel anxious and afraid and can result
in them avoiding school altogether. These experiences can be extremely damaging to a young
person's mental health, and their effects can persist for a long time (Ingul et al., 2019).

Family issues can also contribute to school refusal (Ingul et al., 2019). Students dealing with
family conflict, divorce, or other family-related stressors may struggle to attend school
regularly. These issues can cause distraction, anxiety, or depression, making it difficult for
students to focus on schoolwork (Ingul et al., 2019).

It is crucial to recognise that school refusal is not a choice but a symptom of underlying issues
that require understanding and support (Finning et al., 2022; Garfi, 2018). By identifying the
reasons a young person may be struggling with school attendance, we can develop appropriate
interventions that address the root causes of school refusal and support young people in
returning to regular school attendance.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 165 Identifying school refusal can be challenging. However, there are several signs that can be
looked for, including (Finning et al., 2022; Garfi, 2018):

1. Frequent absences or tardiness: If a student is frequently absent or arrives

late to school, it may be a sign of school refusal.

2. Physical complaints: Students may complain of physical symptoms such as

headaches, stomach-aches, or nausea as a way to avoid school.

3. Emotional distress: Students may exhibit emotional distress such as crying,
tantrums, or meltdowns when faced with the prospect of going to school.

4. Academic decline: School refusal can lead to a decline in academic
performance, as students may struggle to keep up with schoolwork.

5. Avoidance behaviours: Students may exhibit avoidance behaviours such as

hiding, running away, or refusing to leave the house.

It is important for everyone to work together to identify school refusal early on to prevent it
from becoming a long-term problem. Collaboration between all involved can help to identify
the underlying causes of school refusal and develop appropriate interventions to address them.

One effective intervention is cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT), which focuses on challenging
negative thoughts and beliefs that contribute to school refusal while teaching coping strategies
to manage anxiety and other symptoms (Elliott & Place, 2019). Family therapy is another
effective intervention that involves working with the family to address any family dynamics or
issues that may be contributing to the school refusal (Elliott & Place, 2019).

It is also important to consider making necessary accommodations in the school environment
to support the student. This may include a modified school schedule or gradual return to
school, and support in the classroom such as providing additional resources or assigning a
buddy for social support (Elliott & Place, 2019).

Lastly, a whole-school approach is crucial for addressing school refusal. This involves promoting
positive mental health and wellbeing throughout the school community, providing education
and resources, and implementing policies and procedures to address school refusal when it
arises (Elliott & Place, 2019).

Overall, taking a holistic and collaborative approach that incorporates evidence-based
interventions and best practices is key to supporting students struggling with school refusal and
ensuring they can succeed academically and emotionally.

Impact of COVID

The COVID-19 pandemic has presented students with various challenges that have affected
their mental health and school attendance. The disruption of daily routines, isolation from
peers and teachers, and the uncertainty caused by the pandemic have all contributed to an
increase in school refusal cases (Finning et al., 2022).

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 165 For some students who were already struggling with anxiety or depression, the pandemic has
made their symptoms worse and may have led to school refusal (Finning et al., 2022). The
transition to online learning has also brought new challenges, including difficulties with
accessing technology and a lack of structure and supervision at home. For some students, their
home environments may not be suitable for learning due to issues like domestic violence or
poverty (Finning et al., 2022).

It is important to acknowledge that the pandemic's impact on students' mental health will not
simply disappear, and schools must be ready to provide continuous support to address the
resulting rise in school refusal cases (Finning et al., 2022).

Schools can begin by building strong relationships with students and families to create a
welcoming and supportive environment. Regular check-ins with students and families, involving
them in decision-making processes, and creating opportunities for students to connect with
each other and with school staff can foster a sense of belonging and encourage students to
engage in learning (Finning et al., 2022).

Providing targeted interventions and support for students who struggle with attendance and
school refusal is also essential. This may involve working with mental health professionals,
providing individualised academic support, and creating flexible learning environments that
accommodate different learning styles and needs (Finning et al., 2022). Addressing any
underlying issues that contribute to school refusal, such as anxiety, trauma, or bullying, is
equally important.

Schools should also work with families and community organisations to provide wraparound
support for students. Connecting families with resources for mental health support, housing,
and food security, as well as providing transportation and other logistical support for students
who face barriers to attending school, can make a significant difference (Finning et al., 2022).

Finally, schools can take a proactive approach to address the root causes of school refusal, such
as systemic inequities and barriers to access. Creating a more inclusive and supportive learning
environment for all students is essential (Finning et al., 2022).

The COVID-19 pandemic has highlighted the importance of schools being flexible and
responsive to the unique challenges faced by students and families.

Concluding Remarks

As the issue of school refusal continues to affect many students, it is crucial for us to recognise
the importance of addressing this problem. The impact of school refusal can have far-reaching
consequences, such as decreased academic achievement, social isolation, and mental health
difficulties. Therefore, it is essential that we prioritise interventions and support for students
struggling with school refusal.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 165 As someone who struggled with school refusal and lacked the support needed to overcome it, I
know firsthand the detrimental effects it can have on a student's wellbeing and academic
success.

By focusing on evidence-based interventions and best practices, we can ensure that students
have the best possible chance of success. Whether it is through individualised plans,
counselling, or other forms of support, it is imperative that we take action to address school
refusal and provide students with the tools they need to succeed.

In conclusion, I urge the committee to recognise the importance of addressing school refusal
and to prioritise interventions and support for students struggling with this issue. Thank you for
taking the time to consider the critical issue of school refusal and its impact on the wellbeing
and academic success of young people. It is my hope that the information presented has shed
light on the challenges that students with school refusal face and the importance of
implementing evidence-based interventions and support systems to address these challenges.

With the right resources and support, we can help students overcome school refusal and
achieve their full potential.

Submission to the Senate Inquiry

into ‘The National Trend of School Refusal and Related Matters’

Terms of Reference

The national trend of school refusal or ‘School Can’t’ – as distinct from truancy – that
is  affecting  primary  and  secondary  school  aged  children,  who  are  unable  to  attend
school regularly or on a consistent basis, with specific reference to:

a.  the increasing number since the COVID-19 pandemic, of young people and

their families who are experiencing school refusal;

b.  how school refusal is affecting young people and their families and the

impacts it is having on the employment and financial security of parents and
carers;

c.  the impacts and demands of the increasing case load on service providers and

schools to support these students and their families;

d.  how relevant state, territory and federal departments are working to monitor

and address this growing school refusal challenge; and

e.  any other related matters.

1. Introductory Comments

Although the topic of ‘school refusal’ has attracted particular attention in the past year

and in the wake of recognised effects of the lockdowns on children’s school attendance,
studies,  and  mental  health 1  resulting  in  the  apparent  significant  increase  in  the

incidence of it, and this context has led to the present Senate inquiry,2 this problem was

recognised overseas at least half a decade prior to the pandemic, and in some countries

measures to minimise the risk (such as founding alternative schools) were implemented

1 Cf. e.g. https://www.abc.net.au/news/2022-07-22/abs-first-comprehensive-mental-health-
survey/101260384?utm campaign=abc news web&utm content=mail&utm medium=content shared&
utm source=abc news web
https://www.abc.net.au/news/health/2018-11-03/anxiety-more-common-in-
women/10454582?utm campaign=abc news web&utm content=mail&utm medium=content shared&
utm source=abc news web
2 E.g. "School attendance rates are dropping. We need to ask students why" —
https://theconversation.com/school-attendance-rates-are-dropping-we-need-to-ask-students-why-
200537
"Back-to-school blues are normal, so how can you tell if it's something more serious?" —
https://theconversation.com/back-to-school-blues-are-normal-so-how-can-you-tell-if-its-something-more-
serious-198671
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2023/feb/25/no-one-really-knows-senate-inquiry-into-
school-refusal-told-first-step-is-to-track-invisible-students?CMP=share btn link
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2022/oct/27/senate-to-investigate-growing-trend-of-school-
refusal-after-covid-pandemic-classroom-disruptions?CMP=share btn link

1

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 166






 reportedly even decades ago. Like other problems that have been exposed due to the

pandemic but have not been caused by it, so also ‘school can’t’ must be seen within a

much broader and more complex combination of causal factors that have evolved in

our  societies  over  the  past  20  years  or  more;  those  factors  do  not  only  affect  our

children. Such problems do not tend to emerge suddenly or as mono-causal phenomena.

Multiple factors that arguably contribute to this issue have been known in Australia for

close to two decades, but have unfortunately attracted no government recognition or

policy response, while such policy responses as have been formulated have been far

from sufficient to resolve any of the constitutive problems.3

This submission does not pretend to explain all of the probable causes of ‘school

can’t’ or the  circumstances of individuals; it falls primarily under  (d)  and (e) of  the

terms of reference. The author has no school-age children and is not directly involved

in  schools  or  childhood  education.  It  would  be  presumptuous  to  assume  that  every

individual case of ‘school can’t’ can be explained by any single factor or combination

of  factors.  As  testimony  presented  to  this  Inquiry  has  made  clear,  the  full  extent,

demographics and causes of this challenge are not known, and relevant data have not

yet been collected and analysed. Any suggested explanation can only be tested against

such  data  when  they  have  been  collected  and  evaluated.  This  submission  does,

nonetheless,  seek  to  draw  attention  to  the  fact  that  a  range  of  socio-economic  and

psychological stressors that do have significant influence upon both children and their

parents or guardians are already known, or  should be, and  that unless or until  these

stressors are reduced, more convincingly addressed, or eliminated, it is unlikely that the

challenge of ‘school can’t’ will be resolved.

In the study of sociology and of mental health, it is conventional to identify all

possible factors that may in varying combinations and degrees of intensity and duration

adversely  affect  the  individual,  and/or  particular  demographics,  thereby  creating  a

problem.  These  are  designated  as  ambient  or  environmental  [health]  determinants.

These are factors that exercise a sufficient influence upon the individual, which are not

necessarily caused or compounded by the individual, over which the individual may

have no control and therefore cannot escape the effects of, but for which others in their

environment, whether parents, or governments, or others, are responsible; until those

3 It is not immediately germane to this Inquiry, but the American phenomenon of school shootings does
suggest an analogous pattern of behaviour that could perhaps usefully inform this Inquiry.

2

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 166

 environmental  circumstances are  actually  changed, the  individual can reasonably  be

expected to continue to be adversely affected, may remain so even if those factors are

removed,  and  may  persist  in  behaviour  deemed  undesirable.  It  is  argued  here  that  a

number  of  recognisable  determinants  are  adversely  affecting  our  children,  that  the

severity of these problems has worsened both because of compounding circumstances

such as the pandemic and because of government failure to sufficiently address them

over many years, and that as with other mental health and socio-economic problems,

so also in this case, there is not one single problem but an interaction and compounding

effect of multiple problems that are affecting individual children in various ways and

to varying degrees.

No  two  individuals  respond  in  identical  ways  to  any  given  stimulus.  The

significant variable here is our unique personality, which is shaped by both genetic and

environmental  factors,  and  which  is  not  adequately  understood  or  captured  in

discussions of issues affecting groups. At the same time, larger groups within a society

can and do behave in similar ways under the same stimuli, and the so-called copy-cat

effect is neither a sufficient explanation nor of significant importance here. Anybody

behaving  in  a  ‘copy-cat’  manner  still  has  problems  that  need  to  be  recognised  and

addressed, and which predispose them to such behaviour. Simply describing behaviour

as  ‘copy-cat’  therefore  explains  nothing,  any  more  than  simply  suggesting  ‘mental

health’  problems  account  for  ‘school  can’t’:  what  is  actually  causing  those  mental

health problems, which are not genetic or biological but environmental, preventable,

and psychological?

There is an historically recognisable phenomenon of collective anxiety, collective

suicide, collective trauma. We have described historical epochs such as the Fin de siècle

period through to the inter-war years as ‘an Age of Anxiety’. Cases of collective suicide
have  been  described. 4 Survivors  of  the  Holocaust,  of  the  Yugoslavian  Wars  in  the

1990s, the German civilian war and post-war generations, and the phenomenon of ‘shell

shock’  following  World  War  I  have  all  been  studied  as  examples  of  collective

4 Florian Huber, Promise Me You’ll Shoot Yourself: The Mass Suicide of Ordinary Germans in 1945
(Melbourne:  Text,  2019).  Cf.  also  e.g.  Thomas  Garrigue  Masaryk,  Der  Selbstmord  als  sociale
Massenerscheinung der modernen Civilisation (Vienna: Carl Konegen, 1881); Anne Case and Angus
Deaton, Deaths of Despair and the Future of Capitalism (Princeton: Princeton University Press, 2020).

3

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 166

 traumata. 5  Other  historical  periods  (including  in  the  20th  century)  have  also  been

characterised  by  evidence  of  collective  anxiety.  These  phenomena  can  be

intergenerational (as that of the Australian Indigenous population also is), and involve

population groups or entire societies displaying recognisable signs of mental distress

and  compensatory  behaviours.  Excepting  some  types  of  complex  trauma, 6  these

patterns are most commonly caused by major social change. Sudden, major, perceptible

change invariably causes stress, insecurity, and anxiety, and requires time to adjust to

it, which we do not usually have. How we then respond to it, whether we are able to

effectively resolve the problems it causes, whether we are able to creatively adapt to it,

or  whether  we  allow  it  to  because  a  self-perpetuating,  ever  worsening  nexus  of

unresolved  problems,  depends  upon the  collective mentality  of any  given society or

individual and the available capacity it is otherwise possessed of. Different societies

and individuals react differently.  It seems reasonable to suggest that  we now live in

exactly such a period of collectively traumatising and anxiety-inducing change, which

is increasingly causing a range of phenomena including symptoms of that stress such

as ‘school can’t’. Alvin Toffler’s 1970 Future Shock, for example, accurately describes

our present. The nature of this change and the causes of that anxiety are multiple, as

discussed further through this submission. In these terms, ‘school can’t’ is a symptom

of far larger problems, which we have also still not fully recognised or appreciated the

consequences of.

If ‘school can’t’ has become a tangible problem only within approximately the

past  20  years,  but  was  not  evident  beforehand,  and  is  distinct  from  garden-variety

truancy, from small numbers of parents withdrawing their children for home schooling

for  religious  or  other  reasons,  and  from  chronic  poor  attendance  amongst  the

Indigenous  population,  then  this  suggests  sufficiently  profound  socio-economic

changes having occurred in Australia and affecting the entire population to have created

5 Cf. e.g. Traumatic Pasts: History, Psychiatry and Trauma in the Modern Age, 1870-1930, ed. Mark S.
Micale  and  Paul  Lerner  (Cambridge:  Cambridge  University  Press,  2001);  other  references  can  be
provided.
6 The term ‘trauma’ has come increasingly to be used in very diverse ways that no longer sufficiently
accurately define or differentiate between experiences and levels of severity or causes of mental health
conditions, while the term is also now applied to completely normal, universal human experiences that
cannot be viewed in the same terms as other conditions of severe, enduring and complex trauma, which
result from abuse or other exceptional adversity. Even ‘complex trauma’ is now being used in differing
ways. This term of ‘trauma’ therefore needs to be understood in relation to the specific experiences and
contexts in which it is used. It is encouraging that we are becoming more conscious of the impact of life
experiences upon our psychological well-being, but we are not yet drawing the implications and acting
where preventative action is possible.

4

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 166

 this problem, among  others. Certainly, when  this author attended high school in  the

1970s, ‘school can’t’ was not on anybody’s horizon and there was no suggestion that

school attendance was particularly stressful or anxiety-inducing. So what has changed?

An attempt has been made to distinguish truancy and ‘school can’t’, including in

the  terms  of  reference  of  this  inquiry. 7 Insofar  as  truancy  may  be  occasional  and

random, that it may have no specific rationale or explanation, and might be accounted

for  in  terms  of  predictable  adolescent  behaviour,  this  is  admittedly  not  the  same  as

‘school  can’t’.  The  latter  is  understood  as  being  somewhat  more  sustained  and

enduring, as well as having more specific and possibly articulated justifications, and is

in some cases being supported by parents. However, causal factors contributing to both

truancy and school refusal may be identical.

At the same time, it should be acknowledged that children are not always able to

explain or even to articulate their feelings, or circumstances that are making them feel

and act in particular ways, and that if they do so they may not mention all of the relevant

problems they are experiencing. Their perceptions will not always be those of adults,

and are at risk of being trivialised. They will not understand their circumstances in the

same way that we may expect an adult to do so. This remains true for children through

adolescence. For both children and adults, psychological and behavioural reactions may

also  be  sub-conscious  and

instinctive,  and

therefore  easily  overlooked  or

misinterpreted. We also react in particular ways that can be triggered by circumstances

separate from the contexts within which those reactions are manifest.

In the case of some domestic violence, for example, this is behaviour learned in

childhood that persists unquestioned in adults and which is triggered unconsciously and

directed against people and situations which have no relationship to the actual causes

of that behaviour. Coercive  behaviour is a sub-consciously learned survival strategy

intended to prevent the individual from ever feeling vulnerable and powerless again as

they did as children subjected to abuse and trauma, and there are obvious reasons why

it is most obvious in intimate relationships – it is precisely in such relationships that

trust was betrayed in childhood and in which the adult feels most vulnerable. As such,

it has nothing to do with misogyny, toxic masculinities or male privilege. Children’s

7 E.g. "School refusal is not the same as wagging" — https://theconversation.com/school-refusal-is-not-
the-same-as-wagging-40238 All links included in this submission have been accessed or re-accessed
between 24th-28th March 2023.

5

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 166

 anxiety about school will often be caused by things specific to their school, but they

can  just  as  easily  be  triggered  by  circumstances  unrelated  to  school.  Yet  surely,  the

fundamental question is, why is any child feeling anxious at all, and what do we need

to do in order to remove the cause of that anxiety?

These  observations  ought  to  be  obvious.  They  place  the  primary  burden  of

responsibility  upon  all  of  us  to  recognise  how  and  why  our  children  are  being  so

affected,  and to look beyond the immediate factors that may be  easily  recognisable.

This author attaches no particular importance to assumed influences such social media

or any other online or video leisure activities, at least in the first instance.

It is assumed that parents typically desire the best for their children and would

not  knowingly  or  willingly  subject  their  children  to  harmful  circumstances  or

influences,  and  that  many  parents  and  extended  family  members  are  struggling

themselves to understand and respond to these problems. Media reports suggest that

‘school  can’t’  affecting  their  children  is  having  ripple  effects  upon  the  relationships
within  and  economic  circumstances  of  entire  families. 8  At  the  same  time,  some

environmental factors affecting children do also affect their parents and guardians, and

their  teachers,  these  are  likewise  beyond  the  control  of  those  adults,  and  in  some

specific contexts that have also been the subject of public debate, the ways in which

problems may affect children or adults have not always been seen to adversely affect

the other with equal or worse severity, although they do. For example, concern in recent

years  with  domestic  violence  has  tended  to  focus  overwhelmingly  upon  the  women

affected,  but  has  not  recognised  that  every  child  who  is  exposed  or  subjected  to

domestic violence is equally traumatised, may continue to be adversely affected for life

(and the younger the age at which that began for them, the more lasting and complex

the  effects),  and  in  some  cases  that  childhood  trauma  causes  adult  perpetration  of

domestic violence. This has still not been sufficiently understood, and it is disturbing

for  our  limited  ability  to  understand  such  problems  that  this  has  not  been  properly

recognised  from  the  outset  of  our  concern  with  domestic  violence;  the  effects  of

domestic violence upon all children as children must be taken more seriously, including

8 E.g. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2022/oct/10/readers-share-stories-of-school-refusal-
in-australia-it-scarred-us-and-changed-us-forever?CMP=share btn link
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2022/dec/19/school-refusal-parents-forced-to-quit-jobs-to-
care-for-children-who-wont-go-to-class-inquiry-told?CMP=share btn link
https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2022/sep/26/families-can-fall-apart-over-this-stuff-the-
children-refusing-to-go-to-school?CMP=share btn link

6

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 166

 in relation to ‘school can’t’: children living with domestic violence cannot simply block

out that trauma and anxiety and continue to learn as if nothing has happened, but they

are not getting the support and protection they need. Conversely, figures for children

living  in  poverty  in  Australia  have  become  common  in  some  contexts,  but  it  is  not

always  recognised  that  children  are  living  in  poverty  because  their  parents  and

guardians  are  also  living  in  poverty,  and  that  if  poverty  is  ever  to  be  ended  in  this

country, then all of the causes of poverty – which typically have little or nothing in the

first  instance  to  do  with  those  suffering  it  –  must  be  more  decisively  addressed  by

government. Poverty, and its multiple consequences including psycho-social, are also

a factor relevant to ‘school can’t’.

This submission suggests a number of factors that should be considered as causes

of ‘school can’t’. None  of  these factors  should be unfamiliar,  and  yet sadly, despite

being  familiar  in  Australia  now  over  many  years,  none  of  them  have  yet  been

convincingly  addressed  and  resolved,  as  far  as  possible,  by  government.  From  this

perspective,  ‘school  can’t’  is  then  yet  another  consequence  of  larger,  long-standing,

unresolved problems.

2. The School System

The Australian primary and secondary school system has no parallel or model in any

other country in the world. It is an extreme hybrid of public and private institutions,

which has been permitted to evolve in recent decades from an essentially public system

with reasonable funding, resources, and staffing in most regions with a private element

comparable  with  the  US  and  the  UK,  into  an  increasingly  inadequately  funded,

resourced and staffed public system and gross inequality in some groups of the private

schools, with dramatically increased attendance at various categories of private schools.

It  would  not  be  unreasonable  to  expect  that  every  public  school  in  the  country

potentially  enjoyed  the  same  funding  and  capacity  as  our  leading  private  schools,

properly funded by government, and educated every Australian without exception to

the same level of Year 12. No other national school system in the world has an estimated

35% of children attending some form of private school, and this should be seen in itself

as a serious failure.

7

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 166


 Education, like health, has always been a political football and viewed as a major

cost  to  government  that  tends  to  be  subject  to  cuts  and  attempts  to  find  ever  more

‘efficiency  dividends’,  not  regular  commitments  to  meet  rising  need  and  costs  as

necessary.  It  has  been  a  consistent  victim  of  the  inability  of  this  country  to  resolve

differences  between  State  &  Territory  and  Commonwealth  spheres  of  responsibility

and  funding;  and  they  have  also  become  a  battlefield  of  other  vested  interests,

particularly  with  the  private  schools  and  religious  lobbies.  This  continuing  religious

influence within what ought to be a clearly secular democracy is, possibly, also one

contributing  factor  in  ‘school  can’t’,  insofar  as  it  represents  discrimination  against

LGBTIQ+-identifying students and teachers, and hence remains a focus of prejudice

within the community. This situation should be a cause for national embarrassment and

shame, considering that it is, ultimately, our children and future generations who are

most immediately affected by it; the majority of our children do not benefit from any

of these anomalies.

In addition, and particularly in the past year, we have seen growing burnout and

attrition amongst our school teachers, to the point that we are now confronted with an

entirely  preventable  national  shortage  of  teachers.  We  do  not  have  a  shortage  of

teaching graduates or Australians interested in being teachers: we have a shortage of

teachers  willing  and  able  to  continue  working  under  conditions  comparable  with

modern slavery imposed by governments.9 The list of their unresolved grievances is

very  long,  governments  should  have  prevented  those  grievances  from  having  ever

arisen at all, or convincingly resolved them as soon as they became apparent. Instead,

many of those grievances are consequences of the failure to properly and equitably fund

a  national  public  school  system  fit  for  purpose  over  decades,  and  the  compounding

effects of those failures. They have, like so many other problems, been exacerbated by

the  additional  pressures  of  the  pandemic,  but  they  have  not  been  caused  by  the

pandemic: they are all legacies of long-standing attitudes held by government.

Australia  has  never  since  white  settlement  fully  funded  a  national  public

education system fit for purpose, and it has always viewed education as essentially only

for the purposes of employment but not as also providing other social benefits. Given

these attitudes, it is not surprising that Gonski has never been properly implemented,

9 E.g. "No wonder no one wants to be a teacher: world-first study looks at 65,000 news articles about
Australian teachers" — https://theconversation.com/no-wonder-no-one-wants-to-be-a-teacher-world-
first-study-looks-at-65-000-news-articles-about-australian-teachers-186210

8

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 166


 and  that  governments  have  considered  it  preferable  to  continue  subsidising  private
schools rather than investing adequately in public schools.10 Constant cost-cutting is

also driven by a refusal to spend what is necessary in order to achieve results we claim

we  want,  which  we  will  never  achieve  without  greater  spending,  and  the  refusal  to

implement  a  tax  regime  that  accrues  sufficient  revenue  to  properly  fund  all  public

service delivery, despite the fact that low taxes, massive tax evasion and multiple tax

concessions  have  not  resulted  in  a  more  developed  and  robust  national  economy,

contrary  to  the  repeated  pretensions  of  the  business  community.  In  addition  to  this

attitude, particularly since the 1980s, public education has also become a victim of our
extreme  national  form  of  ‘neoliberalism’  as  embraced  by  government, 11  and  the

underlying  ideology  of  management  consultancy,  which  has  now  fully  infected

government  at  all  levels,  and  which  has  had  a  wide  range  of  catastrophic

consequences.12 Among these consequences is the over-working and casualization of

our teaching workforce, which has viewed teachers, like everybody else, as disposable

and  replaceable,  rather  than  properly  investing  in  them  and  securing  their  lifelong

career employment, ensuring that they can adequately support themselves from their

earnings, that they have a sustainable work-life balance, and recognising that they all

have expertise and skills that are not instantly replaceable. Exactly the same problems

now  also  characterise  our  entire  national  public  health  system,  our  tertiary  and

TAFE/VET  education  and  training  sectors,  and  the  APS,  for  identical  reasons.

‘Neoliberalism’ and management consultancy thinking have created all of the problems

that we are now beginning to recognise, but as long as we continue to think within the

parameters of, and to uncritically accept these ideologies, as well as our other national

aberrations, we will not solve any of our problems. It is unlikely that even the most

appropriate and determined responses could undo the damage to our school system in

10 Counting the cost of the education revolution
https://www.abc.net.au/news/2018-11-22/counting-the-cost-of-the-education-revolution/10495756
11 Cf.  e.g.  David  Harvey,  A Brief  History  of  Neoliberalism  (Oxford:  Oxford  University  Press,  2005);

8. Conclusions

I lived in a family situation of domestic violence for more than a decade, which has

affected  my  entire  life,  and  for  which  neither  I  nor  my  brother  nor  my  mother  ever

received the mental health care that we each needed. I also experienced at least four

years of bullying at two schools, which was not stopped or addressed by teachers. I was

effects  of  climate  change,  while  providing  adequate  and  immediate  responses  to  all

affected by any effects of climate change; (3) ending all poverty in this country and its

causes, ending the housing crisis, ensuring uniform quality service delivery and welfare

assistance  without  prejudice  and  discrimination; (4)  convincing  measures  to  address

domestic  violence,  ‘closing  the  gap’,  and  ending  both  juvenile  detention  and  its

negative effects and the socio-economic and racism problems affecting the Indigenous

 population;  (5)  investing  in  adequate,  immediately  accessible  and  affordable  mental

health  services,  and  ensuring  better  education  and  training  of  all  mental  health

professionals; (6) properly funding and managing a national public school system fit

for  purpose,  and  resolving  all  of  the  grievances  of  our  teachers;  and  (7)  achieving

national bipartisan enforceable recognition and protection of all human rights, without
