About Us

We are a family with two children.  Both our children have experienced School Can’t to the extent that
home-schooling became our only viable option, temporarily for one child, and temporarily then later
permanently for the other.

For us, School Can’t was just the point at which the triggers experienced at school overwhelmed our
kids’ ability to cope.  Once that happened, we had to decide as a family how to respond.  Our
interactions with teachers and administrators indicated to us that the schools did not have the
knowledge, capability or will to reduce the triggers or reverse the resultant trauma.  Therefore the only
responsible option left to us as parents was to withdraw our children and seek help to address our
children’s needs from alternate sources.

The Definition of School Refusal

Refusing to go to school is the highly logical reaction of a person who has a good reason not to be there.
As adults, when we find ourselves in discomfort in our workplace, we resign.  When we find ourselves in
an awkward social situation, we leave.  Just want to do something more fulfilling, we seek it.  And yet as a
society we do not extend our children the same courtesy even when they are on the verge of self-harm.
We label it “School Refusal” and it is a negative label placed on the child and their family.

Why is this inquiry about “School Refusal”?  This implies that the problem is with the child.  Why is the
inquiry not about the fact that education departments and schools do not place the child’s welfare as the
most fundamental building block of their philosophy?  Should “School Refusal” be re-defined as “the
refusal of schools and school systems to create a safe and fulfilling learning environment for all children”?

Our Experience: Both my two children have been School Can’t at various stages.  We have experienced
lack of catering for their learning needs including lack of recognition / accommodations for giftedness,
poor teaching and pastoral care practice, onerous behaviour management plans, shaming and
discrimination by teachers, bullying, boredom and lack of accommodation and inclusion.  I fully support
my children when they identify that these factors are impacting their ability to attend school and we
work together to identify the next steps.

Does Discrimination Exist in Schools?

Indirect discrimination exists in workplaces where a job requirement or policy is the same for everyone
but has an unfair impact on a particular group.  A disproportionately high number of children with a
diagnosed disability and indigenous children are represented in the limited data that does come out of
education departments in Australia for suspension and home-schooling (noting that children with an
undiagnosed disability are likely to be a good proportion of the balance).  This is clear evidence of
systemic discrimination and a lack of inclusiveness in our schools.  It could be strongly argued that school
environments currently hold mechanisms of indirect discrimination against children with a disability, with
the outcome being disproportionate representation in school exclusion.

Our Experience: Both my children have been identified as neurodivergent with specific needs, one with
a formal diagnosis and the other with a written psychologist’s recommendation.  Neither has ever been
provided with a suitable Individual Education Plan that meets their needs to allow equitable access and
education at school.  One was home-schooled
and chose to return to a particular high school which
was carefully selected to meet their needs so accommodations were not so vital.  The other has spent
two years at home in burn-out after threats of self-harm, and we have embarked on an unschooling
approach.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 167 How are Schools Dealing With Students?

Those of us who have been called to schools after our child has a meltdown are rarely informed of the
events that led up to the meltdown.  Yet if we track back and find out, we can see that the needs of our
children are not being met and eventually it has come to a predictable outcome.  There is a reason that
families are supposed to be engaged and consulted in the development of a child’s IEP.  Families, schools
and treating professionals need to work together to provide a plan that allows the child access to the
same education as their peers.  Schools might see a quiet, compliant child.  Families might see a child who
is struggling to hold that mask in place all day and then explodes when they get home.  Therapists might
see a child who needs particular accommodations in order to drop the mask and be able to focus on their
learning.

Our Experience: The reality for our family was that the schools our kids went to only saw a compliant
child and no reason to work with anyone.  It was our problem if they exploded at home (clearly the
home environment was the problem, despite the extensive contemporary acceptance of the
phenomenon of masking) or refused to go to school (there was never any self-reflection by the school
that the school environment might be at issue).  They didn’t need to consult, they were experts at this,
we could stop worrying and leave it to them.  They didn’t need to talk to professionals who had
expertise that they do not.  Our family was thanked for being courteous and professional in our
communications but still considered as trouble-makers and it was clear we were being “managed”
which was unproductive, insulting and unhelpful.  When I expressed that my child was having difficulty,
it was suggested by the Principal that we home-school.  The schools just did not have the mechanisms
or the mind-set to work with our family.  The schools’ solution was to be so unresponsive and make it so
uncomfortable for our family that we had no option but to withdraw our child.

Individual Education Plans

The purpose of an IEP is for the school to make appropriate accommodations to enable equitable access
to an education for a child with a disability.  This should be done in consultation with the family and any
specialists available whether there is a formal diagnosis or not.  Funding for children with a disability is a
can of worms and the response of schools in spending this funding is highly variable.  It is left to the
school’s discretion on how to spend the funds provided, and this is not a transparent process.

Our Experience: IEPs were used in some cases to set goals for our child rather than for the school to
identify and make appropriate accommodations or provide suitable professional development for staff
who dealt directly with our child.  In some cases our child’s teachers were not even informed of the
diagnosis and this led to misunderstanding and poor management of the situation.  We have been
pressured to gain formal diagnosis in order for the school to obtain funding, but then we were not
consulted with nor informed how that funding would be used.  An IEP has never been volunteered by a
school and has only ever superficially included parent consultation.  Most parent-school meetings
minuted by the school have placed most action on the parents to seek help outside the school rather
than looking at aspects of the child’s interaction with the school.

Behaviour Management System or Student Welfare System?

The Education Department in our State has heavily pushed the requirement for a Behaviour Management
System in all schools (public and private).  These typically follow a similar pattern of looking at student
response through a behaviourist lens and a reward/punishment regime.  It is outside the scope of this
inquiry to look at why this is an issue, but it is relevant to School Can’t to note that this contributes
significantly to the issue of School Can’t.  This is not because students are misbehaving, but because the
definition of ‘good’ behaviour sits outside the normal expectations of neurodiverse and culturally diverse

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 167 students and creates a situation where they are labelled ‘bad’ because they respond differently to
different cues.  Whole body listening is one example, where sitting quietly, not moving, maintaining eye
contact can be very difficult for a neurodiverse student.  The number of negative responses to these kids,
even if individually very small, adds up to them feeling picked on and unwelcome.

In contrast, student welfare appears to take a back seat to student behaviour.  For example, a procedure
to identify and appropriately address student self-harm and suicidal behaviours has been downplayed
and not promoted by successive State Education Ministers.  Teachers have identified they are not even
aware this document exists, whereas every teacher has been required to implement the behaviour
management system in their class.

Our Experience: Our children’s particular neurodivergence is a pervasive drive for autonomy (official
designation Pathological Demand Avoidance) which means they respond very poorly to rewards and
punishments as methods of behaviour management.  When a star chart was introduced to an early
class for our older child, we were blown away by their behaviour after school.  We went in the next
morning and asked whether something had changed at school and the only thing the teacher could
think of was the star chart, and we started our long road in trying to communicate to teachers that this
kind of control was counterproductive for our kids, and at the same time trying to help our children
develop strategies to manage their response.  It has been a long road through school as advocates for
our kids on this and other issues they have encountered.  When our younger child expressed distress to
the point of self-harm, we had no confidence in the school’s ability to address the issues and have
promised her she will never have to return to school.

We are lost in how to help our child, but just try to fly under the radar because the Education
Department is unhelpful to the point of belligerence.  Our Education Minister recently attacked
alternate pathways to tertiary education as encouraging slackness in children.  We rely on reading,
networking and educating ourselves on alternate theories of education to fill the void left after the
school system ceases to be an option.

Dear Committee

Re: Senate inquiry into the national trend of school refusal and related matters

We are grateful for the opportunity to make our submission to this important inquiry into school refusal.
As  part  of  this  submission,  we  share  our  then
  year  old  daughter’s  horrific  experience  with  school
refusal, and identify a number of areas we think the Committee should consider in order to address this
insidious problem.  Specifically, these areas relate to the terms of reference outlined in b. and c. with
the following used to summarise our experience:

1.  Background & Overview
2.  Role of the School
3.  Access to Support Services
Impact on our Family
4.

In our case we are extraordinarily lucky that we managed to turn our daughter’s trajectory around.  We
feel passionately that every child in Australia should have access to an education that supports their
social, emotional and psychological well-being.

Thank you again for the opportunity to make a submission in this essential inquiry. We welcome the
opportunity to discuss our experience with the committee further.

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 168










 1.  Background & Overview

We  are  a  family  of  5  with  three  children
  My  husband  is  the
 currently
primary carer
working in two roles which include an urgent care centre and virtual health service. We relocated from
  in  December  2021  for  lifestyle  reasons.  We  specifically  timed  our
move  so  that  our  children  started  at  their  new  school  at  the  beginning  of  the  school  year  in  2022  –
advice we had received to help ensure a smooth transition.

  I am a

  to

Our two eldest children commenced at a school within the
 district in January 2022.
Both appeared to settle in smoothly in the first few weeks, until week 4 when our eldest child developed
severe anxiety and subsequent school refusal. Up until the move, our children had thrived at school
with nil attendance issues, and without any requirement for extra input or services from their school.
This was in spite of an extremely disrupted start to school for each of them, as both had commenced
school in the midst of the pandemic in 2020 and 2021 respectively.

With extreme effort and distress for our daughter and our family, we were able to contain the number
of missed school days to 1 - 3 days per week.  Every single school day was emotionally draining and
damaging for our daughter and the household on multiple levels.  In our daughter’s experience, school
refusal ranged from not being able to get out of bed, to resisting getting dressed and ready for school,
to lashing out at siblings, and to arriving at school and refusing to go into class  – clinging to us and
sometimes even running away from the school in extreme distress and anguish. We had never seen
our daughter behave like this in any shape or form.

The  exact  form  which  school  refusal  takes  may  differ  slightly  for  every  child,  but  the  patterns  and
resultant impacts are likely similar. Understanding that school refusal is not just what is observed at the
school  gate  is  critical  to  supporting  children  and  their  families  in  developing  solutions  to  what  we
understand is an increasing problem.  Identifying pattens of attendance and behaviour is imperative in
order to address the underlying problem before it becomes entrenched. In our daughter’s circumstance
we identified the problem quickly and proactively engaged the school.  Unfortunately the school seemed
ill-equipped on many levels to adequately manage this issue.  We felt like we were continually driving
the process, requesting a referral to the school counsellor and attempting to establish a regular pattern
of  communication  with  our  daughter’s  teacher  and  the  school  leadership.  Despite  Department  of
Education  documentation  stipulating  regular  communication  as  being  essential,  our  request  was
overlooked.

The school counsellor conducted a Connors_3 assessment with results indicating generalised anxiety,
separation anxiety and depression. Unfortunately it took more than one school  term to receive these
results when time was of the essence.  At her previous school our daughter had been identified as a
high  potential  learner  and  regularly  talked  enthusiastically  about  learning.  At  this  time,  it  became
apparent that our daughter had become disengaged and was no longer interested in sharing what was
she  was  studying.  With  this  in  mind,  we  decided  to  arrange  for  private  psychometric  testing  to  be
completed. Our daughter’s result for the WISC-V was FSIQ of 140 (99.6th percentile).

Despite every effort to advocate for our daughter, engagement with the school was problematic – they
seemed unwilling or unable to understand the issues or provide the necessary expertise, resources or
appropriate  support.  At  the  end  of  Term  2  in  2022,  we  made  the  difficult  decision  to  withdraw  our
daughter from the public school system and enrol her at a small catholic-independent school in the local
area.  Her younger sibling remains at the school.

Since starting at her new school, our daughter has missed just 1 day across the remainder of the school
year – this occurred in her first week due to some anxiety. She is happy and thriving again and our
family life has been restored. Our daughter’s current school has demonstrated that when schools have
the appropriate expertise, adequate resourcing and willingness to work together with families, school
refusal can be avoided or if it occurs it can be reversed before a long-term pattern develops.

2.  The Role of the School | Refer to Terms of Reference (item b.)

Engaging with the school executive and learning support team was a new experience for us, having no
need to do so for either of our children at their previous school. From the outset, the school appeared
inexperienced and/or unwilling to engage in addressing the issue of our daughter’s school refusal. There
did not appear to be any defined process, protocol or overarching framework to address what we now
understand  to  be  a  common  challenge.  We  have  tried  to  document  below  those  areas  we  felt
significantly impacted the situation:

Page | 1

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 168









 Identification
The school appeared to miss and fail to communicate some of the early warning signs of the evolving
problem. In a meeting with our daughter’s teacher, the staff member described signs of a panic attack
which had occurred the previous day – nil episodes prior.  There seemed to be a failure to recognise
that  some  unusual  behaviours  our  daughter  was  exhibiting  in  class  (frequent  crying  and  verbally
repeating the teacher’s instructions) were likely due to anxiety and  distress. On another occasion we
were required to collect our daughter from school after she was complaining of a stomach ache.  It was
not  until  later  that  the  teacher  suggested  this  was  likely  due  to  anxiety.  By  failing  to  identify  and
proactively communicate these significant health and well-being concerns regarding our daughter, we
lost an opportunity to intervene earlier.

Attitudes
As  mentioned  above,  it  took  close  to  one  and  half  terms  to  receive  the  results  of  our  daughter’s
assessment  undertaken  by  the  school.  When  we  expressed  our  concern  about  this  timeframe,  the
school executive advised us that that this is a “good turn-around time for the public system”. In a highly
acute  scenario  like  our  daughter’s  this  is  obviously  unacceptable  –  we  had  previously  informed  the
school that our daughter demonstrated signs of depression and even mentioned wanting to kill herself.

Despite  our  assertions  that  our  daughter’s  behaviour  at  home  and  at  school  was  entirely  out  of
character,  episodes  of  crying  and  distress  were  attributed  simply  to  separation  anxiety.   The  school
leadership stated that they were not interested in what was taking place in the home environment and
likened  our  daughter’s  unprecedented  meltdowns  at  home  to  an  adult  relaxing  after  a  workday.  On
another occasion it was intimated to us that because we had come from the catholic-independent school
system

, we should not expect the same level of pastoral care in the public system.

When  we  expressed  concerns  about  our  daughter’s  engagement  with  her  teacher  and  school
environment,  the  situation  was  again  attributed  to  separation  anxiety.  There  appeared  to  be  an
unwillingness to recognise any role that the school may have been played in the school refusal despite
it developing since our daughter had started at the school.

Ownership & Accountability
It felt as though we had to drive and manage the situation.  We initiated meetings with the teacher and
school  executive.   We  contacted  the  Department  of  Education
  and  asked  for
additional  support.   We  requested  an  individual  education/learning  support  plan  (ILP)  and  how
accommodations would be integrated into the plan. We requested the referral to the school counsellor
– which was promptly actioned.  We had to ask for learning resources for those days our daughter did
not attend school – provided on one occasion only.  We also located department resources and shared
these  with  the  staff  members.  This  was  only  exacerbated  by  having  to  liaise  with  four  separate
individuals who fulfilled the role of principal over a 6-month period.

Communication
Despite  department  documentation  highlighting  the  importance  of  open  channels  of  regular  and
ongoing  communication,  communication  was  problematic.   We  were  unable  to  establish  a  regular
weekly check-in with our daughter’s teacher – we were advised that as they were in the classroom there
was no opportunity to make calls. We had to regularly request follow-up meetings with both the teacher
and school principal when the situation did not improve. One of the few means of communication we
did receive was a literal 'tick-a-box’ letter indicting that the
 had discussed our
daughter  in  their  meeting.  The  purpose  of  this  letter  was  unclear  which  only  added  to  the  existing
ambiguity and frustration.

Resourcing & Continuity
During this time our daughter had to contend with significant teacher and leadership upheaval.  Most
weeks our daughter had three different teachers taking her class at various times  – occasionally she
had three teachers in one day. In an attempt to address this uncertainty, the school counsellor and our
daughter identified a
 safe people she could go to on any given school
day. Not infrequently our daughter would find that not one of these   people were at school. There was
never a back-up plan in place, and it often fell to the office staff to try and assist our daughter and family.
The pattern of our daughter’s school refusal often followed ad-hoc changes in her class teacher.

We requested notification of changes to the teaching schedule as this served as a source of anxiety for
our daughter. This was inconsistently communicated. The frequent changes and failure to communicate
these  with  our  daughter  was  a  significant  contributor  to  her  school  refusal  with  a  clear  pattern
established. There seemed to be no appreciation from the school executive about the impact of these

Page | 2

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 168









 changes,  nor  acknowledgement  that  some  degree  of  consistency  needed  to  be  prioritised  for  our
daughter. The inconsistency was above and beyond the effects of the pandemic. We were simply told
these changes were normal and that schools are dynamic places.

Our  daughter  was  lucky  to  develop  a  strong  relationship  with  the  school  counsellor  –  providing
strategies she was able to implement. Unfortunately the counsellor’s caseload appeared extraordinarily
high.  This was made more challenging given the counsellor was providing services to several schools
in the district across the week.  This had obviously implications for the availability of student counselling
sessions and timeframes for providing feedback reports.

Process & Approach
, one tool used to try and address the situation
At the suggestion of the department
was a Part Day Exemption
 whereby our daughter’s school hours were slowly
scaled up over 5 weeks. This seemed like an unusual approach given she was still attending between
3 – 4 days per week and what was suggested was to drastically reduce hours. There was no attempt
to understand the core issues driving our daughter’s school refusal despite us being very instructive in
this regard. Against our better judgment we agreed to the plan which as predicted had the reverse effect
–  our  daughter  now  recognised  that  school  hours  were  negotiable.    The  school  executive  were  so
focussed on following process and signing off documentation, the approach appeared to be driven by
preserving attendance records rather than our daughter’s well-being and learning.

Throughout  the  experience  we  felt  continually  judged,  at  fault  and  that  somehow  our  daughter  and
family were to blame for the events that had unfolded. We felt they we had become an inconvenience
or  burden  to  the  school.  There  appeared  to  be  no  real  consideration  for  the  traumatic  effect  of  this
experience on our daughter and our family.

New School
When our daughter moved to her new school, she and our family were immediately supported. The new
school  invested  resources  proactively,  providing  a  dynamic  and  reliable  team  of  principal,  assistant
principal and classroom teacher. After 10 days in this environment, she was attending school without
issue. We would highly recommend that the inquiry seek to consult this outstanding team on how they
turned the trajectory around for our daughter and family. The factors we identified as having a significant
positive impact were:

•  Leadership – authentic, empathetic and proactive
•  Communication – consistent, timely and responsive
•  Student-centred  –  engaging  students  as  individuals  with  unique  social,  psychological  and

intellectual needs

The single largest difference between the two schools was attitudinal. In our daughter’s new school we
worked in partnership with the school executive and staff. Our experience of the public system seemed
more distant, punitive and operating from a place of judgement rather than compassion.

We  were  also  extremely  lucky  that  our  daughter  found  herself  in  the  classroom  of  an  extremely
intelligent, inspired and enthusiastic newly graduated teacher. This wonderful teacher is an example of
what all of our children and the education system needs more of. She introduced novelty and delight
into the learning environment. She used evidence-based strategies which cater  for neurodivergence
(including gifted learners), transition away from ineffective behaviourally based classroom management
strategies that still seem to be encouraged (e.g. the 6 Ls and extrinsic reward systems).

Our daughter’s new school is proactively seeking opportunities to meet her unique learning needs. It is
well recognised that gifted and high potential students at our daughter’s level require specific strategies
to ensure they remain engaged and reach their potential. Appropriate engagement is essential to not
just protect against future deterioration in mental health, but ultimately allow our daughter to flourish.

3.  Access to Support Services | Refer to Terms of Reference (item b.)

Psychological Support
One  of  the  more  challenging  aspects  was  the  difficulty  in  finding  and  accessing  qualified  and
experienced child psychologists.  Many psychologists had either closed their books or had significantly
long wait times which was not an option given the urgency of our daughter’s situation.

Page | 3

The national trend of school refusal and related mattersSubmission 168












 Our daughter ended up attending a limited number of sessions with a provisional psychologist  – the
only  option  that  we  could  access  quickly.  She  was  fortunate  to  develop  good  rapport  with  the
psychologist with some marginal benefits, but there were a number of other factors that we feel hindered
progress:

•  Approach: There was little consideration for the broader ecological systems perspective, including
interactions between our daughter, the family, and school in the context of school refusal. This is
integral in identifying underlying factors and informing strategies. This intervention was hindered
and fragmented by little opportunity for parents to participate in sessions. Our understanding is that
parental involvement in counselling interventions in this age group is critical to their success. Setting
up separate consultations with the psychologist to discuss our daughter was both financially and
logistically challenging.

•  Accessibility:  Due  to  significant  demand  for  psychological  services,  we  were  unable  to  secure
regular appointments and those that were available were usually  during school hours. This only
exacerbated  the  school  refusal  challenge.  The  evidence  is  for  intensive  focussed  therapy,  and
unfortunately the best we were able to obtain was sporadic and inconsistent.

One significant positive was the Cool Kids Program – a group-based therapy program offered through
the University of Wollongong. We were extremely lucky to be offered a position on the program at a
critical time which proved to be life changing for our daughter and family. If there were an opportunity
to  develop  a  program  specifically  targeting  school  refusal,  we  would  highly  recommend  adopting  a
similar  model.  The  program  was  affordable,  supportive,  and  evidence-based,  providing  tools  and
strategies that provide children with skills for all aspects of life.

Paediatrician Access
Accessing a paediatrician was also problematic, with significant wait times and closed books. In our
daughter’s scenario it would have been ideal to access a developmental paediatrician however many
are  already  over-subscribed  and  not  taking  new  patients.  We  had  to  opt  for  the  first  available
paediatrician,  rather  than  someone  with  specific  experience  dealing  with  school  refusal  and  the
particular  concerns  we  had  regarding  our  daughter.  Our  experience  was  counter-productive  and
highlighted the glaring lack of available services for families in our position.

4.  The Impact on Family | Refer to Terms of Reference (item c.)

During the period of our daughter’s school refusal, the impact on our family was profound.  This included
the following:

•  Well-Being Impact: There was a huge burden on our entire household psychologically, emotionally
and physically.  This unprecedented level of stress tested our own relationship and our relationship
with our daughter and our two younger children. We were extremely lucky that our then 6 year old
and  3  year  old  were  extremely  resilient  throughout  this  uncharted  territory.   At  times  we  felt
completely isolated and overwhelmed, with so few people able to relate to our daughter and family’s
struggle.  We  subsequently  sought  our  own  counselling  to  help  manage  what  became  a  fairly
desperate and dysfunctional situation.

•  Career  Impact:   Our  daughter’s  refusal  to  attend  school  and  all  the  problems  surrounding  that
increasingly  impacted  our  respective  careers  with  reduced  work  hours,  increased  absenteeism
(carers  and  sick  leave),  and  reduced  productivity  due  to  logistical  and  emotional  impacts.   My
husband who had recently been on a leave of absence and was transitioning careers, had to place
this on hold and extend his period of leave for what another ~10 months.  The impacts of this on
his career progression are not yet known.

•  Financial Impact: Aside from the obvious increase in financial costs associated with medical and
specialist  appointments,  we  also  had  to  survive  on  one  income.  We  consider  ourselves  very
fortunate to have a degree of flexibility and financial wherewithal. For many families the reduced
working capacity and increased costs would have led to financial ruin and family breakdown.

work at all. Initially I thought this was probably partly because of his autism but also partly

In
 my son commenced secondary school at a local public school. This was particularly
difficult for him and he hated going to school. On some of the days when he would try to go

This year,
a solution, I enrolled my son in a school that is especially set up for children who are
disengaged from the education system. This school takes a very flexible approach to
education, employs social workers and other staff who can assist the children and accepts
that not all children will agree to attend school for full days, five days a week. The school
provides breakfast and lunch to its students and has a curriculum which includes basic
academic subjects as well as sports, social activities and various excursions. However, once
again, a key issue for me has been that it can be very difficult to get my son out of bed and

his current and previous schools have all been very supportive and, on one occasion over

son to get out of the car and go into the school without success.

Conclusions

Based on my experiences as outlined above, I would like the committee to note that as a
single parent
, I have found having a child who refuses to go to school very
stressful. When I go to bed at night I never rest easily because I am always worrying about

 what the next morning will bring. I also worry about the short and long term effects not
going to school will have on my child in the short term and in the long term. In the short
term, I particularly worry about the possibility of self-harm and in the long term, I
particularly worry that he may never have a meaningful career or the associated security
that comes with that.

I would like the committee to note that my son’s various teachers have tried to help
wherever possible, but I am not convinced teaching staff have the necessary training or
experience to handle complex cases such as this. In addition, in the absence of being able to
access the medication that has been recommended for my son, I am not sure that his
current issues in attending school will ever be able to be completely resolved. As depressing
as this is for me, I do not have the means to continue to pursue these issues through legal
channels so I am at a loss as to what to do next. Going forward, I urge the Australian
Government to act on its undertaking to review the operation of the Family Court as, based
on my experiences, it is not currently providing the resolutions families need and in some
situations, such as mine, it is actually working against the interests of children.

I would like to thank the committee for taking the time to read my submission.

When children are faced with uncertainty, particularly beyond their coping abilities they need
routine, structure and a choice in their environment to feel safe.
Children and families are being told that they can “choose” to mitigate Covid risks themselves, take
personal responsibility. Public health is not a child’s personal responsibility. That’s the government’s,

It’s every child’s right to feel protected and safe at school. To be healthy.

I also strongly believe systematic changes need to be made across the countries educational
departments. Specifically teaching methods. 1 in 5 students in each classroom across our nation, has
a learning disability. These children are trying their hardest and falling behind regardless. The toll it
takes on a child’s self worth is enormous.
Quite often learning difficulties and specific learning disabilities aren’t realised until end of primary
school, where parents are faced with going on lengthy waitlists for cognitive assessments that cost
thousands of dollars. Sometimes after these assessments schools are “recommended” to make
adjustments to that particular child, evidence based systematic sythonic phonics programs over seen
by a specialist particular speech pathologist for a period of 6 months to see if the child has a specific

There’s no evidence that the 4/5 children in each classroom in Australia, who don’t have specific
